abstract: Weighted rectangular matrices record relations between two types of objects, such as occupations and industries, documents and terms, origins and destinations, or annotated classes and computed clusters. Their heatmaps become difficult to read when arbitrary row and column orders scatter related objects, while equal size cells hide large differences in row and column totals. We present MHeatmap (Mosaic Heatmap), which addresses these problems in two stages. Two-Walk spectral seriation first represents the matrix as a weighted bipartite graph. Ordinary bipartite ordering uses only observed row to column links. Two-Walk also uses length-two walks, so rows that share columns and columns that share rows receive explicit similarity links. Sorting a Fiedler vector of the resulting graph Laplacian gives coordinated row and column orders. The Mosaic layout then partitions a unit square so that row height is proportional to the row total and column width is proportional to the column total, while color represents the observed entry. We prove how the Two-Walk energy combines direct alignment with shared-neighbor smoothness, derive an exact matrix vector product that permits sparse computation, and formalize the tiling and area semantics of Mosaic. Across 300 synthetic matrices and seven real data sets, Two-Walk obtains the lowest normalized 2-SUM in all 15 synthetic regimes and the highest Band@10% in 14. The largest gains occur when shared neighborhoods express the latent relational structure.

title: Normal approximation, moderate and large deviations for the elephant random walk with stops and random step sizes
abstract: We study the elephant random walk with stops and independent positive random step sizes. Building on fixed-movement estimates, we obtain quantitative normal approximations for an empirically normalized statistic by controlling its random denominator and the independent movement clock. A permutation comparison preserves the diffusive Kolmogorov rate, while variance matching permits third-order Zolotarev estimates. We also derive self-normalized Cramér-type moderate deviations. For regularly varying step-size tails, we obtain uniform precise large deviations and establish the necessity of the diffusive and critical threshold orders. Further applications of the clock representation yield large deviation principles for Weibull-type and light-tailed step sizes, and a precise light-tailed expansion in the balanced case.

title: Conditional Reflected Backward Stochastic Differential Equations
abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new type of reflected backward stochastic differential equations (reflected BSDEs), referred to as conditional reflected BSDEs, in which the conditional expectation of the Y-component of the solution with respect to a given sub-σ-algebra appears in both the generator and the obstacle. Under a Lipschitz condition on the loss function with sufficiently small Lipschitz constants, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the solution for both the case of Lipschitz generator and the case of quadratic generator, bounded terminal value and bounded loss function. When the generator has quadratic growth and the terminal value and loss function are unbounded, we establish the uniqueness with the help of θ-method. Finally, a penalization approximation scheme holds under an additional monotonicity structure imposed on the generator and the loss function, without any restriction on the Lipschitz constants of the loss function.

title: Algebraic criteria for complete relaxation in autonomous and periodically driven open quantum systems
abstract: We derive sufficient criteria that guarantee convergence of open quantum system dynamics to a unique long-time state independent of the initial conditions. We refer to this behavior as complete relaxation. Focusing on systems described by Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equations on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, our approach uses only elementary mathematical arguments. For autonomous systems, we recover three previously derived relaxation criteria, which can be expressed as algebraic conditions on the Lindblad operators and the Hamiltonian entering the GKSL equation. For periodically driven systems, we obtain a new criterion involving a similar algebraic condition and a local continuity requirement on the time-dependent GKSL generator. This result implies an earlier criterion for complete relaxation formulated in Ref. [J. Phys. A 52, 43LT01 (2019)]. We also discuss implications of our approach for periodically modulated classical master equations, as well as extensions to driven systems without a periodicity constraint.

title: Pappus configurations in the Hall plane
abstract: In this paper, we investigate Pappus configurations in the finite affine Hall plane. In particular, we show that for any two lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$ and for any triple of points on $\ell_1$ there is a triple of points on $\ell_2$ that are contained in a Pappus configuration, thus improving on the results of [F. Lazebnik and L. Leshock. On Pappus configurations in Hall planes. Des. Codes Cryptogr. 90 (2022), 1203--1219.].

title: Refined Cramér-type moderate deviations by Stein's method under dependence
abstract: In this paper, we establish refined Cramér-type moderate deviations for dependent random variables at any fixed order $m\geq3$. Combining higher-order Stein identities with exponential tilting, we obtain cumulant-corrected tail approximations with explicit error bounds for boundedly supported kernels. Our main application gives a fourth-order expansion under bounded local dependence, reaching an $O(n^{3/10})$ deviation range under standard normalization with fixed dependence parameters. It improves on previous work in both deviation range and applicability, and also covers bounded $m$-dependent sequences without an independent-base representation. Further applications to the generalized combinatorial central limit theorem and the Curie-Weiss model also extend some earlier results under permutation and mean-field dependence.

title: General Criterion for a Poset to Admit a Partition Into $ω$-Chains
abstract: Given a poset $P$ with no maximal element the question naturally arises of when $P$ can be partitioned into $ω$-chains. In this paper we give general criterion for when this can be done. We show that in the case when a poset with no maximal element is countable or a well-founded forest, then it can always be partitioned into $ω$-chains. We then introduce the lifting property for posets with no maximal element and show that a poset can be partitioned into $ω$-chains if and only if it has the lifting property.

title: Free energy and fluctuations of generalized bipartite Sherrington-Kirkpatrick models and generalized Hopfield models
abstract: We consider the free energy of generalized bipartite Sherrington-Kirkpatrick models in the high temperature regime, with one spin normalized and the other either normalized or i.i.d. We derive a unified formula for the limiting free energy in both settings. We also prove that the fluctuations of the free energy converge to a Gaussian distribution under mild assumptions. The proof is based on a bipartite multigraph expansion, which also gives free energy results for generalized Hopfield models and log likelihood ratio of spiked rectangular models.

title: Proofs of Li, Wang and Guo's conjectures on (signless) Laplacian spectral radius
abstract: Let $μ(G)$ and $q(G)$ be the Laplacian and signless Laplacian spectral radii of a graph $G$. Li, Wang and Guo (2026) conjectured that, if $H$ with $|V(H)|\geq 1$ is an induced subgraph of a graph $G$, then $μ(G)\le\max\limits_{v\in V(H)}μ(H_v^t)$ and $q(G)\le\max\limits_{v\in V(H)}q(H_v^t)$, where $t=e(G)-e(H)$ and $H_v^t$ is the graph obtained from $H$ by adding $t$ pendant edges to $v\in V(H)$. We prove this conjecture by establishing a spectral comparison theorem for a broader family of positive semidefinite graph matrices which includes the Laplacian and signless Laplacian matrices. We also characterize all equality cases for the prescribed subgraph $H$ with $e(H)\geq 1$ and $t\geq 1$.

title: HumanCentric-Scenes-AI: A Human-Curated Multimodal Dataset of AI-Generated Human-Centric Scenes Across Surveillance, Occupational Portraits, AI-Edited Images, and Short-Form Video
abstract: We introduce HumanCentric-Scenes-AI, a human-curated dataset of 296 AI-generated stimuli that depict people across four contexts in which people encounter AI-generated media. The Surveillance subset contains 85 AI-generated CCTV-style images. The Occupations subset contains 128 AI-generated occupational portraits in a balanced paired design covering 64 occupations with one female and one male version of each. The AI-edited subset contains 27 real photographs in which a region was altered or replaced by a generative model. The Video subset contains 56 AI-generated short videos. We curated the images and videos manually over multiple rounds to make them as photorealistic as possible. For each stimulus we release the file, the generation prompt where recorded, and per-stimulus metadata. We report depicted-gender distributions from an initial set of 134 generations without a specified gender and compare them with U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational gender shares. We report edit-region size and its association with zero-shot detection difficulty for the AI-edited subset. We report image-quality distributions for the Surveillance subset and subject-category coverage for the Video subset. HumanCentric-Scenes-AI is intended first for human-perception research, and also for calibration of AI-detection classifiers and bias analysis of generative models.

title: Non-trivial intersecting families for direct products
abstract: A family of sets is intersecting if any two of its sets intersect, and non-trivial intersecting if there is not any element which appears in every set of the family. The study of intersection problems (or Erdős-Ko-Rado problems) on families of sets is one of the most important topics in extremal combinatorics. A natural extension of the Erdős-Ko-Rado problem in direct products setting was introduced by Frankl, and developed by Alon and Katona et al. In 2018, Kwan, Sudakov and Vieira [J. Combin. Theory, Ser. A 156 (2018), 44--60] determine the maximum size of a non-trivial intersecting direct product family under the assumption that the sizes of all parts are sufficiently large relative to the set sizes in all parts. Meanwhile, they raised the question of whether this result holds for the size of each part which depends only on its corresponding set size, and the question of characterizing the extremal families. In the present paper, we answere these two questions. Furthermore, the bounds on the size of each part in our result are best possible.1

title: Every tournament of dichromatic number $10 k^2$ has a vertex whose out-neighborhood has dichromatic number more than $k$
abstract: The dichromatic number of a tournament is the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices so that no directed cycle is monochromatic. Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour (2025) asked whether every tournament with dichromatic number $2k$ has a vertex whose out-neighborhood induces a subtournament of dichromatic number at least $k$. We answer their question negatively by finding an example with dichromatic number $Ω(k^2)$. Furthermore, this quadratic bound is tight up to a constant factor; we show that for every integer $k \geq 1$, every tournament of dichromatic number $Ω(k^2)$ contains a vertex whose out-neighborhood induces a subtournament of dichromatic number more than $k$. This improves the previous best bound $\mathcal{O}(k^2\log k)$ due to Colinot and Newman (2026). To show this, we prove that every tournament of fractional dichromatic number $c$ has a dominating set of size at most $5c-1$. The proof uses Brouwer's fixed point theorem.

title: Beyond Tokens: NumAnchor for Address-Grounded Numeric Operand Representation in Assembly Language Models
abstract: Assembly language models (ALMs) are becoming important for automated binary analysis, yet their token-level interfaces often obscure numeric-like operands. In two corpora, such operands account for 45.7% and 40.9% of operand occurrences and may denote branch targets, global data, stack slots, constants, or unresolved pointer-derived values. Existing normalization strategies often lose their identities and structural relationships. We present NumAnchor, an input-boundary adapter that represents recoverable numeric-like operands as typed, canonicalized program entities. NumAnchor encodes code, data, and stack context in compact structural side descriptors, preserving entity identity and locality without increasing the host sequence length. These descriptors are fused into input embeddings before the first Transformer layer, while the host architecture, pretraining objectives, and downstream protocols remain unchanged. Probing frozen instruction-level embeddings yields 98.7% hierarchical-location accuracy and AUROC scores of 0.932 and 0.907 for jump and call target alignment, respectively, showing that the encoded structural information remains recoverable. Across multiple ALM families, NumAnchor achieves relative improvements of up to 35.0% in Recall@1 and 31.7% in MRR on 10k-candidate function retrieval, and improves execution-aware type recovery by up to 5.2 F1 points. Ablations show complementary gains from code, data, and stack descriptors with modest overhead.

title: Influence of embedding depth on the pullout of a plate from a confined granular medium
abstract: Understanding the behaviour of moving objects within confined granular media is important in many technical applications. In this work we study the vertical pullout of a plate-like intruder buried at different depths within a dense granular aggregate from the onset of motion to flow around the intruder in the steady state by means of a two-dimensional polygonal Discrete Element Method. We find that the peak and steady-state drag forces depend differently on their embedding depth for different friction coefficients. Depending on the strength of friction the plate may interact with the domain walls, which enhances the drag force until failure of the aggregate, but not in the steady-state as dilation around intruder directs the force chains emanating from the plate upwards and away from the walls. If the inter-particle friction is weak, it is possible for the overhead pressure to overcome frictional resistance beyond a certain embedding depth. This prevents the formation of dilated failure zones above the intruder and changes the failure mode of the aggregate, leading to a slower decay of the steady-state drag forces with pullout distance.

title: On the Number of Iterations in a Kruskal-Type Process
abstract: Motivated by the Kruskal counting procedure, this paper investigates a combinatorial elimination process defined on a deck consisting of $m$ copies of each value $1,2,\ldots,n$. Starting from an arbitrary arrangement of the $mn$ cards, the process repeatedly removes a number of consecutive cards equal to the value of the first remaining card. This generates a sequence of elimination steps whose length determines $T$, representing the total number of iterations required to exhaust the deck. The main objective of this paper is to analyze an upper bound $σ(m,n)$ for $T$, valid for every initial configuration of the deck, and to show that this bound is attained by a specific configuration.

title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
abstract: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.

title: Affine $G$-multibiquandle modules for colored links I: representability of coloring functors and color-profile polynomials
abstract: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity, let $G$ be an abelian group, and fix $u\in R[G]^\times$. For each component-labeled oriented link diagram $(D,σ)$, we construct a finitely presented $R[G]$-module $M_u(D,σ;R[G])$ with a universal affine coloring $U_{D,σ}$. Every affine coloring with values in an $R[G]$-module factors uniquely through $U_{D,σ}$ by a module homomorphism. Thus the module represents the affine coloring functor. Each specified colored Reidemeister move induces a unique module isomorphism compatible with coloring transport, and the module isomorphism class is a colored-link invariant. The representing modules and universal colorings commute with arbitrary scalar extension, without a flatness assumption. For classical links, simultaneous rescaling of the component labels removes the common deformation unit. For any multibiquandle, associated-biquandle colorings decompose into fibers indexed by component labelings. For finite targets and palettes, we define a color-profile polynomial recording the joint distribution of fiber sizes and numbers of palette labels used, and prove its invariance under oriented link isotopy. In the affine case, the representing modules determine these fibers, and their specialized dimensions determine the coloring counts over finite fields. The color-profile polynomial is not determined, in general, by the full unweighted distribution of coloring-fiber sizes. It therefore retains information beyond the associated-biquandle coloring count.

title: A Jump-Modified Wasserstein Gradient Flow for Maximum Mean Discrepancy with Energy Kernels
abstract: We study a jump-modified Wasserstein gradient flow of the squared maximum mean discrepancy generated by the energy kernels $K(z)=-|z|^q$, $0<q<2$, in every dimension $d\ge2$ as well as the one-dimensional range $1\le q<2$. Under subcritical density and finite-moment assumptions, we prove global well-posedness. The added jumps transfer mass toward smaller values of the first variation and dissipate the same MMD energy as the transport term. Under our hypotheses on the target and jump rates, every Borel probability measure with finite MMD energy and zero jump dissipation is equal to the target. Combining this rigidity with compactness and a second-moment identity yields convergence to the target from finite-second-moment data, without additional uniform-in-time density or moment assumptions. We also construct a global collision-free particle process whose energy is nonincreasing along each path. A quantitative mean-field estimate applies to general initial empirical approximations, including deterministic configurations; propagation of chaos for exchangeable data and long-time target approximation follow as consequences.

title: Nonexistence of Constant Congruences for the Cumulative Partition Function
abstract: Let $p(n)$ be the ordinary partition function and let $c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}p(k)$, with $c(0)=0$. We prove that, for every $a\geq1$, $b\geq0$, and $m\geq2$, the sequence $c(an+b)$ is not eventually constant modulo $m$, thereby answering a question posed by Chen. The proof combines the algebraicity over $\mathbb C(j)$ of modular functions for finite-index subgroups of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ with Voloch's theorem on the transcendence of elliptic modular functions in positive characteristic.

title: Two refined Wilf-equivalences for patterns of length 4 and a conjecture on Dumont permutations of the first kind
abstract: We construct a bijection between $2143$-avoiding and $3421$-avoiding permutations that preserves the descent top set and the ascent top set and reverses the left-to-right order of the peaks. This bijection allows us to establish a bijection between $1243$-avoiding and $3412$-avoiding permutations with the same properties. These results refine two cases of a conjecture posed by Burstein and prove a conjecture posed by Burstein and Jones.

title: Path-dependent rough differential equations in the full step-two range
abstract: We establish the existence of solutions to path-dependent rough differential equations with non-anticipative coefficients whose regularity is formulated in terms of horizontal and vertical Dupire derivatives. Under the same regularity assumptions as in Ananova~\cite{An23}, we develop a new causal Taylor argument and establish a second-order remainder estimate. This removes the regularity loss responsible for the restriction $2\leq p<1+\sqrt{2}$ in~\cite{An23} and extends the existence result to the full range $2\le p<3$.

title: On the generation of the symmetric group by index relations of three prefix reversals
abstract: The cubic pancake graphs are Cayley graphs over the symmetric group Sn generated by three prefix reversals. There is the folllowing open problem: characterize all the sets of three prefix reversals that generate Sn. Blanco and Golubyatnikov give a complete solution of the problem when any of the two smallest or the two largest lengths but n are included in a triple of prefix reversals. According to their conjectures, we give some conditions implying a triple of prefix reversals does not generate Sn. Moreover, Using the symmetric groups that can already be generated by three prefix reversals, we can derive some recurrence conditions.

title: Strong uniqueness for fractional stochastic differential equations with sign drift
abstract: Establishing pathwise uniqueness for stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H>1/2$ remains challenging, particularly for discontinuous drifts beyond the regularity regimes of existing theories. A canonical example is the sign drift, for which uniqueness fails in the corresponding deterministic equation. In this paper, we complement recent strong existence results by establishing pathwise uniqueness for the equation with sign drift perturbed by fractional Brownian motion for every $H\in(1/2,1)$, thus obtaining strong well-posedness. Our proof develops a new approach based on the infinite iteration of an inequality arising from a fixed-point relation, combined with tail probability estimates exploiting the Gaussian structure of the noise. The methods and results cover a broader class of Gaussian Volterra processes satisfying suitable local nondeterminism and positivity conditions.

title: Spectral and edge conditions for negative Hamiltonian cycles in unbalanced signed graphs
abstract: Spectral conditions for Hamiltonian cycles are a fundamental subject in extremal spectral graph theory. For simple unsigned graphs, Fiedler and Nikiforov [Linear Algebra Appl., 432 (2010), 2170-2173] pioneered this direction, and Li and Ning [Linear Multilinear Algebra, 64 (2016), 2252-2269] later extended these results by introducing minimum degree parameters. In this paper, we study the spectral conditions for the existence of a negative Hamiltonian cycle in unbalanced signed graphs of order n > 8. We first determine the maximum index among all n-vertex unbalanced signed graphs containing no negative Hamiltonian cycle, and characterize the corresponding extremal graphs up to switching isomorphism. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound on the number of edges in unbalanced signed graphs of order n >= 7 with frustration index one, and classify all extremal graphs achieving this bound.

title: On the maximal index of $C_4^-$-free unbalanced signed graphs of prescribed size
abstract: The extremal problem of determining the graphs with maximum spectral radius among all graphs with a prescribed number of edges was resolved by Rowlinson [Linear Algebra Appl. 110 (1988) 43--53]. A signed graph $Γ=(G,σ)$ is called $C_k^-$-free if it contains no negative $k$-cycle as a signed subgraph. The index of a signed graph is defined as the largest eigenvalue of its adjacency matrix. This paper addresses the maximization of the index of unbalanced signed graphs. For signed graphs of a prescribed order, Wang and Lin [Discrete Appl. Math. 372 (2025) 164--172] determined the maximum index of $C_4^{-}$-free unbalanced signed graphs. Subsequently, Wang, Peng and Hou [Discrete Math. 349 (2026) 114871] characterized the unbalanced signed graphs of prescribed size with maximum index. This paper treats the edge spectral Turán-type problem for $C_4^-$-free unbalanced signed graphs. The all-positive signed graph with underlying graph $G$ is denoted by $(G,+)$. Evidently, $A((G,+))=A(G)$. In particular, $(H_{d,t},+)$ is the all-positive signed graph whose underlying graph is $H_{d,t}$, where $H_{d,0}=K_d$ and for $t>0$, $H_{d,t}$ is obtained from $K_d$ by adding a single vertex adjacent to exactly $t$ vertices of $K_d$. Let $m-3=\binom{d}{2}+t$ with $0\le t\le d-1$. Up to switching isomorphism and the addition of isolated vertices, the unique extremal unbalanced signed graph is obtained by attaching a negative triangle to a specified vertex of the all-positive signed graph $(H_{d,t},+)$.

title: Dual medial axes in finite-dimensional normed spaces
abstract: We study medial axes of nonempty closed sets in finite-dimensional real normed spaces whose norms are $C^1$ away from the origin. Using the differential of the norm, we define the dual $k$-medial axis by requiring the contact covectors associated with nearest points to have affine dimension at least $k-1$. In dimension $n$, we prove that this set is $(n-k+1)$-rectifiable for every $1\le k\le n+1$, and hence has Hausdorff dimension at most $n-k+1$. We give a direct geometric proof and characterize the dual medial axes through the superdifferential of the squared distance function, obtaining an alternative proof from a theorem of Alberti, Ambrosio, and Cannarsa on singularities of semiconvex functions. Under the additional assumption of strict convexity, the ordinary and dual medial axes coincide for $k=2,3$, yielding the corresponding rectifiability results for ordinary medial axes. For $k=4$, however, the ordinary rectifiability conclusion can fail even for norms arbitrarily close to Euclidean: we construct norms on $\mathbb R^3$ with smooth positively curved unit spheres arbitrarily $C^\infty$-close to the Euclidean sphere, together with four-point sets whose ordinary $4$-medial axes contain nondegenerate line segments.

title: The signless Laplacian spectral Turán problems for disjoint triangles
abstract: The classical Turán-type problem for graphs forbidding $k$ disjoint triangles has been resolved firstly by Erdős [Arch. Math. 13 (1962) 222-227] for graphs of sufficiently large order and improved by Moon [Canad. J. Math. 20 (1968) 95-102], who established that the unique edge extremal graph is $K_{k-1}\vee T_2(n-k+1)$ for $n> \frac{19k-11}{2}$. In this paper, we determine the maximum signless Laplacian spectral radius among all $kK_3$-free graphs of order $n$ and characterize the unique signless Laplacian spectral extremal graph $K_{k-1}\vee T_{2}(n-k+1)$ for all $k\ge 2$ and sufficiently large $n$.

title: Bipartite solutions of the set-theoretic Yang--Baxer equation
abstract: We introduce a new class of unitary set-theoretic Yang--Baxter solutions, called \emph{bipartite} solutions. This class, which is purely combinatorial in nature, forms a full subcategory of $\mathcal{LYB}$, the category of Lyubashenko type solutions of Agore, Chirvasitu and the author, and is particularly amenable to explicit classification results. We give an intrinsic necessary and sufficient condition for a solution of the Yang--Baxter equation to be isomorphic to a bipartite solution, we settle the isomorphism problem within this class and, as an application, we determine their automorphism groups. If $X$ is a finite set with $|X| = n$, the number of isomorphism classes of bipartite solutions on $X$ is $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1 + \sum_{m=2}^{n} \bigl( o(m, n-m) - 1 \bigr)$, where $o(m, k)$ denotes the number of orbits of the symmetric group $S_m$ acting by conjugation on the $k$-element multisets of elements of $S_m$. The paper also offers a comparative study: for small $|X| = n$ we count, up to isomorphism, all set-theoretic Yang--Baxter solutions on $X$, together with five distinguished families of solutions. Throughout the range we were able to compute, the class $\mathcal{LYB}$ accounts for a large share of all bijective and of all non-degenerate solutions, strikingly close to the total.

title: Central limit theorem for the Smoluchowski--Kramers approximation
abstract: We establish the central limit theorem (CLT) for Smoluchowski--Kramers approximation of Langevin equations with state-dependent, possibly non-symmetric friction and multiplicative noise. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first such result, even in the case of constant friction and additive noise. The result differs in an essential way from classical averaging CLTs and reveals a new two-scale fluctuation phenomenon. The normalized difference process retains a persistent fast component and is generally not tight in $C([0,T];\mathbb{R}^d)$, thus the usual continuous-path CLT cannot hold. We derive an exact decomposition of the normalized difference into an accumulated slow fluctuation and a rapidly relaxing velocity correction. The auxiliary slow fluctuation converges to a linear diffusion driven by both the original Brownian motion and an additional independent Brownian noise whose effective covariance is characterized explicitly through a quadratic Poisson corrector. For every fixed $t>0$, the fast correction converges conditionally to its local Gaussian equilibrium. Consequently, the fixed-time fluctuation limit is identified as a Gaussian mixture: $$ \frac{\bar X_t-X_t^\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}} \Longrightarrow \bar Y_t+N^{1/2}(\bar X_t)ξ, $$ where $\bar X_t$ is the overdamped limit, $\bar Y_t$ is the limiting slow fluctuation, $N$ is the covariance of the terminal velocity correction and solves a Lyapunov equation, and $ξ$ is a standard Gaussian random variable independent of $(\bar X_t,\bar Y_t)$. A quantitative convergence rate is also provided. The result fills the remaining gap in the asymptotic theory of the overdamped approximation at the central limit scale, complementing the existing law of large numbers, moderate deviation and large deviation results.

title: Arithmetic Conditions for the Invertibility of Circulant Matrices over Finite Fields
abstract: This paper investigates arithmetic conditions, over finite fields, for the invertibility of circulant matrices whose first row is $(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})$, in terms of linear constraints on the entries $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$. The coefficients of such linear constraints are determined by field traces arising from Frobenius orbits of roots of unity, and under additional assumptions they are given by Ramanujan sums reduced modulo the characteristic of the given field. These results provide finite-field analogues of the corresponding criteria over $\mathbb{Q}$, where the relevant Ramanujan-sum linear constraints can be formulated without such additional assumptions, while also showing some differences caused by reduction modulo the characteristic. The constraints can often determine invertibility using aggregate information about the entries of a row, rather than the particular pattern of the entries. We also discuss the polynomial gcd criterion, which gives necessary and sufficient conditions for invertibility and yields further consequences for special families of circulant matrices.

title: Stationary Half-space Geometric Last Passage Percolation without Random Shift
abstract: We derive exact formulas for the diagonal distribution of half-space geometric last-passage percolation with a two-parameter family of stationary initial conditions throughout the phase diagram. Unlike previous results, our formulas remove the random shift at the origin. Under critical scaling, we obtain new formulas for the half-space stationary KPZ fixed-point distribution at $x=0$ in the high-density and maximal-current phases. In the low-density phase, we derive a new representation and show that it matches the corresponding formula from the stationary log-gamma polymer.

title: Probabilistic and game thresholds
abstract: Let $X$ be a finite set and $\mathcal{F} \subseteq 2^X$ a non-trivial increasing property. We show that the bias-threshold $b(\mathcal{F})$ for the Picker-Chooser $\mathcal{F}$-game satisfies $b(\mathcal{F}) \ge α/ p_c(\mathcal{F})$, where $p_c(\mathcal{F})$ is the threshold for the property $\mathcal{F}$ and $α> 0$ is an absolute constant. This proves that Picker-Chooser games satisfy one-sided ``probabilistic intuition''. The proof is based on the notion of influence from the theory of boolean functions.

title: Weighted odd-cycle transversals and fractional colorings of planar graphs
abstract: We bound fractional chromatic numbers by establishing a connection with low-weight odd-cycle transversals. Let $\ell\geq 3$ be an integer and let $G$ be a graph of odd girth at least $\ell$ whose odd-cycle covering polyhedron is integral. For every nonnegative weight vector $w=(w_v)_{v\in V(G)}\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{V(G)}$, we obtain a set $Z\subseteq V(G)$ such that $G-Z$ is bipartite and $w(Z)\leq\frac{mad(G)}{2\ell}w(V(G))$. Here, $w(S)=\sum_{v\in S}w_v$ for any $S\subseteq V(G)$, and $mad(G)$ denotes the maximum average degree of $G$. Consequently, if $mad(G)<2\ell$, then $G$ has fractional chromatic number at most $\frac{4\ell}{2\ell-mad(G)}$. As applications, we prove that, for every positive integer $k$, every $n$-vertex planar graph of girth at least $2k+3$ has fractional chromatic number at most $\frac{2k+1}{k}(1-\frac{1}{kn+1})$, establishing the girth version of Naserasr's fractional coloring conjecture with a strict inequality. For $k=1$, we furthermore prove that the upper bound $\frac{3n}{n+1}$ holds for every $n$-vertex triangle-free planar graph and this is attained for infinitely many values of $n$.

title: Fuglede's conjecture holds in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d}$ for $p=2,\,d=8$ and $p=11,\,d=3$
abstract: Fuglede's conjecture in $\mathbb{F}_p^d$ says that a nonempty set tiles by translation if and only if it is spectral. We prove the conjecture in $\mathbb{F}_2^8$ and $\mathbb{F}_{11}^3$. Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ we show more generally that the Fourier support of a nonconstant indicator of density different from one half contains a plane. Consequently every spectral set of density one quarter has a subspace tiling complement. This supplies one of the dimension-eight reductions left by Kadowaki; the others are completed using classified Hadamard matrices and perfect binary codes. In $\mathbb{F}_2^9$ we prove that every tile is spectral and that every spectral set has power-of-two cardinality. All spectral cardinalities except $64$ are shown to tile, and we give further reductions of the remaining case. We also construct a spectral set of density one eighth whose Fourier support contains no three-dimensional subspace. For $\mathbb{F}_{11}^3$ we extend the geometric method of Fallon, Mayeli, and Villano by using moment identities, polynomial plane profiles, weighted incidence counts, and exact finite computations. The computations and their verification programs are described in the appendices.

title: Complete Determination of the Gallai--van der Waerden Number \(\mathrm{GW}(r;3,3)\)
abstract: This paper completely determines the Gallai--van der Waerden number \(\mathrm{GW}(r;3,3)\) for all integers \(r\ge 3\): \[ \mathrm{GW}(3;3,3)=\mathrm{GW}(4;3,3)=9,\qquad \mathrm{GW}(r;3,3)=r\quad (r\ge 5). \]

title: On Arithmetic-Progression Biases in Random Partitions: Limiting Laws and the Li-Zhao Conjecture
abstract: Let $\cR=\{r+jm:j\geq0\}$ and $\cS=\{s+jm:j\geq0\}$ be disjoint arithmetic progressions of positive integers, and choose a partition of $n$ uniformly at random. We determine the limiting probability that the number of parts in $\cR$ is larger than the number of parts in $\cS$. More precisely, if $a=r/m$ and $b=s/m$, then this probability converges to $I_{1/2}(a,b)$, the regularized incomplete beta function. We prove the stronger distributional statement that, after multiplication by the partition saddle-point parameter, the difference of the two numbers of parts converges to $m^{-1}(\log G_b-\log G_a)$, where $G_a$ and $G_b$ are independent gamma variables. The proof uses the Boltzmann conditioning device for random partitions, a $q$-gamma evaluation of the unconditioned characteristic function, and a uniform Fourier estimate showing that conditioning on the total size does not change the limit. We also evaluate the finite-truncation limit studied by Li and Zhao. The two evaluations coincide, proving their conjecture on the commutation of the truncation and large-size limits.

title: The Laplace transform of the stationary measure of the open KPZ equation in the shock region
abstract: The stationary increment measure of the open Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation on a bounded interval can be represented as the independent sum of a Brownian motion and another process defined via an explicit Radon-Nikodym derivative with respect to the measure induced by a Brownian motion. In the fan region, its finite-dimensional Laplace transform was previously expressed in terms of the continuous dual Hahn process. The main contribution here consists of computing the finite-dimensional Laplace transform for a range of parameters in the shock region by an analytic continuation argument. As an application, we provide a direct proof of the convergence of the finite-dimensional distributions of the increment height function of open WASEP under the stationary measure in the shock region, by computing the convergence of finite-dimensional Laplace transform without relating to the open KPZ equation.

title: Affine fractional Orlicz--Sobolev inequalities and optimal star bodies
abstract: In this paper, we establish an affine fractional Orlicz--Sobolev inequality by replacing the Euclidean fractional Orlicz seminorm with an energy obtained by minimizing over origin-symmetric star bodies of prescribed volume. Under finite lower and upper power growth assumptions, a subcritical upper growth bound, and a monotonicity condition on $t^{n/s+2}Φ''(t)$, the resulting inequality has the same best constant as its Euclidean counterpart. The power case recovers the affine fractional Sobolev inequality of Haddad and Ludwig with the corresponding Luxemburg normalization. To establish this inequality, we investigate the underlying geometric extremal problem. For every nonzero smooth function of compact support, the existence and uniqueness of an optimal star body are proved under the growth assumptions alone, and its radial function is characterized by an equation involving $Φ(t)+(s/n)tΦ'(t)$. We also establish an anisotropic rearrangement inequality, together with its equality conditions under additional strictness assumptions. Moreover, the normalized local limit is investigated. The optimized energies converge to the local energy, and the radial functions of the minimizing bodies converge uniformly on the sphere. The limiting modular is determined by $\overlineΦ(t)=\int_0^tΦ(τ)\,dτ/τ$. Finally, we compare optimization over star bodies with optimization in the affine orbit.

title: Scaling Laws for Safety Probes
abstract: Safety probes trained on a model's activations are a standard tool for monitoring language models in real time. Each time a new model is released or a new harm area needs to be monitored, the probe must be retrained, which requires new labels and a choice of probe architecture. Yet neither the model nor the labels tell us in advance how well the resulting probe will perform. Finding out requires training and comparing many probe configurations. In this paper, we ask whether probe performance can instead be predicted in advance from model size and the number of labels. Existing safety datasets are insufficient for this, as they are either limited in scale or already saturated. We therefore construct six new safety datasets of sufficient size and difficulty. On these datasets, we train two probe architectures on 20 base models from five model families, with 32 to $10^{6}$ labels for each model. We measure performance using probe error, defined as 1 - AUROC, where lower values are better. We find that probe error follows two simple scaling laws. First, the lowest probe error a model can reach falls as a power law in its size. Second, probe error decreases towards its floor as the number of examples increases; the slope increases as the target model size increases. Both laws hold across tasks, model families and probe architectures, and only their fitted constants differ. When fitted on the smallest models of a family, the laws predict the error of the next larger model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases. They also identify whether more labels or a larger model is the cheaper way to reach a target error in 73% of cases. Finally, they choose the probe architecture with an extra error of only 0.006 on average when they pick the worse one. These laws allow safety researchers to determine how to create the best probe for any given model and label budget.

title: Your Token Is Gone: A Token-Consumption Countermeasure for Disrupting LLM-Based Scam Systems
abstract: LLM-based scam systems increasingly combine adaptive dialogue, persistent context, external tools, and multi-agent coordination to automate personalized fraud. These capabilities also create a resource dependency: every reasoning step, model call, and coordination round incurs inference cost. We present TokenTrap, a resource-oriented defense that redirects suspected scam systems toward benign, low-value computation while withholding credentials, payments, and other exploitable information. TokenTrap combines three components: an architecture-specific token-task library, a router that selects among single-agent, hierarchical, and flat multi-agent workflows, and a bounded anti-guardrail strategy that varies task presentation while enforcing token, round, time, and safety limits. Across 50-round traces, TokenTrap amplifies token consumption by $2{,}487.0\times$, $1{,}616.0\times$, and $567.8\times$ relative to a no-token-task baseline for the three workflows. Its router achieves 85.67% accuracy on 300 architecture-labeled prompts. These results demonstrate that short, non-sensitive requests can impose substantial context-processing and coordination costs, motivating resource-aware defense as a complement to scam detection.

title: Aleshin graphs are expanders
abstract: We prove that the Aleshin level graphs are two-sided expanders. We establish linear diameter bounds for Belaterra and Aleshin graph families. At level $n$, the diameters of the Bellaterra and undirected Aleshin graphs are a $|V_n|=2^n$. This improves the quadratic diameter bounds of Malyshev and Pak to the correct order of growth. For the Aleshin graphs we obtain a normalized spectral gap of at least $1-2\sqrt2/3$ and an edge-expansion constant of at least $3-2\sqrt2$, thereby establishing a Malyshev--Pak's Conjecture with explicit constants. An exact calculation at level ten also proves that the undirected Aleshin graphs are not Ramanujan for any $n\geq10$.

title: NP-Hardness of Generalized-Turán Graph Modification Problems
abstract: For graphs $G, T$ and a graph-family $\mathcal{H}$, let $ex(G,T,\mathcal{H})$ denote the maximum possible number of copies of $T$ in an $\mathcal{H}$-free subgraph of $G$. Alon and Shikhelman conjectured that for every family of graphs $\mathcal{H}$ with $χ(H) > s$ for every $H \in \mathcal{H}$, it is NP-hard to compute $ex(G,K_s,\mathcal{H})$, and even to approximate it up to additive error $n^{s-δ}$ on $n$-vertex graphs, for any fixed $δ> 0$. The case $s=2$ was established in a breakthrough result of Alon, Shapira and Sudakov. We prove the Alon-Shikhelman conjecture for finite families $\mathcal{H}$. In particular, we obtain an elementary proof of the Alon-Shapira-Sudakov result when $\mathcal{H}$ is finite.

title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.

title: Couplings with prescribed maxima: A short proof of the quasi-copula characterization
abstract: We provide a short probabilistic proof of the classical characterization of multivariate quasi-copulas, addressing the call for a simpler and more transparent proof expressed by Sempi (2017). Our approach is based on a coupling construction for random variables with fixed marginal distributions and a prescribed distribution of their maximum. In our main result, we show that such a coupling exists if and only if the maximum is stochastically no smaller than each component and the distribution of the maximum is dominated by the sum of the marginal measures. The construction applies to arbitrary distributions and relies only on a decomposition of the maximum law and monotone quantile couplings. A direct consequence of our main result is the existence of copulas with prescribed values along an increasing track.

title: Multiple Stopping and Exercise Boundaries for American Put Options
abstract: This article studies a finite-horizon American put option with up to $m$ exercise rights under the risk-neutral Black--Scholes model, where consecutive exercises must be separated by a prescribed refractory period $δ>0$ and unused rights may expire. For each number of remaining rights, we show that optimal exercise is characterized by a single exercise boundary and that these boundaries are ordered by the number of remaining rights. We prove optimality of the first boundary-hitting time and establish local Lipschitz continuity of the exercise boundaries within each open deadline strip. Away from the deadlines, we derive smooth fit, the associated quasi-variational inequality and free-boundary formulation, an early-exercise-premium representation, recursive Volterra-type boundary equations, and a verification theorem. We also extend the recursive formulation to an independent random termination time, thereby allowing for exogenous termination of the option contract.

title: Model-intrinsic, Weight-level, and Training-free Spectral Fingerprinting for Large Language Models
abstract: The increasing release and reuse of Large Language Models (LLMs) as open-weight checkpoints make model fingerprinting important for ownership protection and offline auditing. Existing fingerprinting methods typically construct evidence from query responses, generated outputs, or input-induced activations. Although effective in representation-based settings, they can be affected by prompt selection, decoding configuration, inference environment, and forward-pass implementation, which may limit their applicability. Here we introduce a model-intrinsic weight-level framework that derives compact fingerprints from spectral structures encoded in LLM parameters. Specifically, the framework constructs GATE spectral scalar features from the singular-value distributions of GATE projection weights in gated feed-forward networks (FFNs), and aggregates the resulting layer-wise features through depth-wise segmented pooling to form a model-level fingerprint. Such representation preserves coarse layer-depth organization while reducing dependence on strict layer-to-layer alignment, enabling comparison across LLMs with different depths. The similarity between fingerprints is computed by linear centered kernel alignment. The entire pipeline is training-free and does not require input samples, generated outputs, forward activations, or an auxiliary verifier. Experiments on representative LLM families and post-training variants have demonstrated a clear separation between source-related models and unrelated ones, and stable similarity under instruction tuning, quantization, pruning, and distillation-related modifications, which verify that spectral features are robust evidence for LLM fingerprinting.

title: Optimal Mixing for Local Edge-Coloring Dynamics on Trees
abstract: We study the mixing time of two local Markov chains for uniformly sampling proper edge colorings of trees. For a tree with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $Δ$, we establish optimal mixing-time bounds for the single-edge Glauber dynamics when $q\geΔ+2$ and for the neighboring-edge heat-bath dynamics when $q\geΔ+1$. Both chains mix in $O_Δ(n(\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)))$ steps, uniformly over the number of colors $q$. These bounds are tight in their dependence on $n$ for fixed $Δ$. Our proof establishes log-Sobolev inequalities through local color release, reusable recoloring buffers, and component entropy mixing. The two dynamics require different local constructions: a two-spare-color buffer for single-edge updates and a second-layer controller for neighboring-edge updates. The resulting entropy analysis applies to general bounded-degree trees, including regimes where worst-case spatial mixing fails.

title: The Ternary and Quaternary Cases of the $\{2,4\}$-Distance Code Conjecture
abstract: For an integer $q\ge2$, let $A_q(n,\{2,4\})$ be the largest cardinality of an unrestricted $q$-ary code of length $n$ in which any two distinct words have Hamming distance $2$ or $4$. We prove that \[ A_q(n,\{2,4\})=1+\binom n2 \qquad(q\in\{3,4\},\ n\ge6), \] thereby settling the two remaining alphabet sizes in the conjecture of Boyvalenkov, Delchev, Zinoviev, and Zinoviev; the binary case was settled previously. The quaternary result implies the ternary result by alphabet inclusion. For $n\ge16$, the quaternary upper bound is proved combinatorially. After normalizing one word to zero, the weight-four supports form a $2$-intersecting family; exact support intersections force symbol synchronization and restrict support multiplicities. We combine the nontrivial intersection theorem with matching arguments and a three-coordinate projection lemma. The finite lengths $6\le n\le13$ are handled by a complete Hamming-isometry reduction to exact clique decisions, and $n=14,15$ by a smaller exact weighted-clique relaxation. All finite decisions are reproduced by two standalone integer-only C++17 verifiers provided as supplementary source files.

title: Asymptotically Sharp Length Thresholds for \texorpdfstring{$q$}{q}-ary Codes with Distances \texorpdfstring{$2$}{2} and \texorpdfstring{$4$}{4}
abstract: For an integer $q\ge5$, let $A_q(n,\{2,4\})$ be the largest cardinality of a subset of a $q$-ary Hamming space of length $n$ in which every two distinct words have distance $2$ or $4$. Set \[ N(q)=\left\lceil\max\left\{2q+1, \frac{17+\sqrt{8q^2+96q-95}}2\right\}\right\rceil. \] We prove that $A_q(n,\{2,4\})=1+\binom n2$ for every $n\ge N(q)$. In particular, $N(q)=2q+1$ for $q\ge26$. An explicit code of size $q(n-2)$ shows that the least eventual threshold $N_*(q)$ satisfies $N_*(q)\ge2q-1$; consequently $2q-1\le N_*(q)\le2q+1$ for every $q\ge26$. The argument applies to arbitrary integer alphabet sizes, without a linearity assumption. Its main ingredients are synchronization of symbols on intersecting supports, weighted bounds for $2$-intersecting families of four-sets, and a joint estimate for the weight-two and weight-four layers in a common-three-core configuration. No computational verification is required.

title: PATH: Preference-Aware Traversability Estimation for Robotic Teleoperation in Off-Road Navigation
abstract: Traversability estimation is critical for ground vehicle teleoperation, yet existing methods often neglect the human operator's preferences for speed and risk tolerance. To address this gap, we propose PATH-Net, a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network that adaptively generates preference-conditioned traversability cost maps and speed profiles for off-road teleoperation. Our framework integrates visual and geometric bird's-eye-view features with short-term historical vehicle states through a multi-head shared-backbone architecture. Our PATH-Net infers traversability cost maps while optimizing speed recommendations by using maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning and sparse speed supervision. Our method incorporates operator preference via an asymmetric feature aggregation mechanism, splitting inference into a cost branch that prioritizes high-risk traversability regions and a speed branch that outputs preference-adjusted recommended speeds. Experiments with 15 operators across 225 teleoperated trajectories show alignment with user-specific navigation strategies, achieving modified Hausdorff distance of 0.17 m (aggressive) and 0.15 m (conservative). In the questionnaire assessment, participants reported lower NASA-TLX workload scores with PATH-Net recommendations than without recommendations, decreasing from 34.7 to 22.2. These results support preference-conditioned trajectory and speed recommendation for off-road teleoperation.

title: HiMark: Hierarchical and Controllable Multi-bit Watermarking for Large Language Models
abstract: With the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in text generation applications, it has become increasingly difficult to trace generated content and assign responsibility for its use, raising concerns about provenance, copyright protection, and accountability. Multi-bit watermarking addresses these issues by embedding multi-bit provenance information into generated text, but reliable extraction remains difficult due to sparse per-bit evidence and the trade-off between watermark-extraction accuracy and text quality. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiMark, a hierarchical and controllable multi-bit watermarking framework for LLM-generated text. During watermark embedding, HiMark uses a hierarchical candidate-control mechanism, including initial candidate sampling, layer-wise tournament elimination, support-based refinement, and support-threshold filtering. During watermark detection, a model-agnostic evidence aggregation mechanism computes multi-layer support evidence for each observed token, and then accumulates these token-level votes into the corresponding information for robust watermark extraction. Experiments show that HiMark improves watermark extraction accuracy while maintaining text quality, e.g., the watermark extraction accuracy is 90.01% under the paraphrasing attack when 32 bits were embedded within a text containing 300 tokens, demonstrating its effectiveness for provenance tracking.

title: Impacts of generative AI skill development on academic adaptation and learning outcomes among university students
abstract: Understanding how university students perceive the development of their generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) skills over time can clarify how GenAI use relates to learning and academic outcomes. This study examined perceived skill-development trajectories, changes in learning practices, and associated academic gains using a retrospective questionnaire with 313 analyzed responses and interviews with 18 students across subject areas. Descriptive and comparative analyses and exploratory structural equation modeling (SEM) were integrated with thematic analysis. Perceived developmental trajectories were heterogeneous: 34.2% of students reported rapid early improvement followed by a plateau, 28.4% steady improvement, and 21.1% delayed acceleration. Development was also uneven across skills, with improvement in evaluating GenAI outputs perceived as more challenging; assignments were the most frequently selected driver of skill growth. Interviews further indicated increasingly specific prompting, tailored verification, and selective delegation, although some students reported stable routines, dependence, skipped reasoning, or improvements attributable partly to better GenAI tools. Academic gains were reported more often for assignments than for examinations. The SEM indicated a positive indirect association between perceived skill growth and academic gains through adaptation of assignment processes, whereas academic gains did not clearly differ across developmental trajectory groups after multiplicity correction. The findings suggest that perceived GenAI skill development varies in both trajectory and skill domain and is associated with changes in learning practices and differentiated academic benefits.

title: DLT Terms 100: a learner's glossary based on ISO 22739:2024
abstract: We propose ``DLT Terms 100'' aimed at improving literacy regarding blockchain (distributed ledger technology: DLT). The pace of DLT's social implementation has been slower than initially expected, partly due to a shortage of engineers and literate individuals. In particular, the discrepancy between business and technical terminology, and the confusion caused by the repurposing of existing financial terms, are barriers to understanding the concepts and technologies. Our proposed glossary is based on ISO 22739:2024, and categorizes and labels terms based on their frequency of appearance in representative domestic and international literature and their difficulty level.

title: Bridging the Closed-World Gap: Interpretable Anomaly Detection via a Hybrid TSK-FCM Ensemble on the BETH Dataset
abstract: A fundamental paradox plagues the deployment of Machine Learning in cybersecurity: supervised models generalize poorly to novel, Out-of-Distribution (OoD) attacks, whereas unsupervised models often suffer from poor separability, leading to unmanageable false-alarm rates. This challenge is exemplified by the BETH dataset, a kernel-level benchmark in which the training data consists solely of benign and suspicious insider behaviors, whereas the test set consists almost entirely of novel botnet activation attacks. To bridge this detection gap, we propose a Hybrid Fuzzy Ensemble that synergizes the precision of supervised learning with the adaptability of unsupervised clustering. Our architecture integrates a gradient-optimized Takagi-Sugeno-Kang (TSK) fuzzy classifier to act as an expert on known insider threats, with a parallel Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) module to detect geometric anomalies. A critical finding of our research is that traditional fuzzy membership scores degrade in high-dimensional feature spaces due to the curse of dimensionality. We overcome this by introducing a robust Min Distance metric that exploits the raw geometric isolation of botnet activation attacks. This approach yields a state-of-the-art AUROC of 0.9951 on the BETH test set, outperforming the original Isolation Forest baseline by 17.1%. By combining near-perfect OoD detection with the intrinsic interpretability of fuzzy logic, our framework offers a viable path toward robust, transparent, and autonomous network defense.

title: Beyond Better Ideas: How Human-AI Collaboration Shapes Scientific Ideas and Human Perceptions
abstract: As AI increasingly becomes a collaborator in scientific research, its impact may extend beyond improving ideas to reshaping how they are evaluated, attributed, and perceived by humans. Yet existing research has largely examined these dimensions in isolation. We present a unified empirical study of Human-AI scientific ideation, investigating two complementary perspectives: i) how AI collaboration shapes scientific ideas and their evaluation, and ii) how firsthand collaboration reshapes human perceptions of AI. Through a shared experimental setting involving Human-AI and Human-Human research teams, human and LLM evaluators, collaboration-provenance analysis, and participant surveys, we uncover several counterintuitive findings. First, AI collaboration shows no significant advantage in human-evaluated idea quality, while iterative revision consistently improves quality. Second, AI judges can approximate human scores yet disagree on idea rankings; notably, an AI judge favors AI-assisted proposals without a corresponding advantage in human evaluations. Third, collaboration provenance remains only partially detectable, revealing substantial overlap between Human-AI and Human-Human scientific outputs. Finally, firsthand AI collaboration is associated with greater perceived usefulness but smaller efficiency gains than expected, suggesting a nuanced recalibration of human expectations. Overall, our findings challenge the notion that AI's value in scientific ideation lies primarily in producing better ideas, revealing instead its broader influence on scientific creation, evaluation, attribution, and human perceptions.

title: Atlas: Making Sense of Long Horizon Agent Trajectories
abstract: AI agents can now search literature, generate hypotheses, analyze datasets, and run experiments at a scale difficult for researchers to match. Yet scaling scientific execution does not automatically scale researchers' ability to make sense of what agents produce. When researchers return to a long-horizon run, they must evaluate work they did not monitor: what the agent produced, which decisions shaped those outputs, and whether those decisions served the research goal. We frame this post-run sensemaking as a representation problem across three linked levels: goal, decision, and artifact. From this framework we developed Atlas, an agentic workspace with a trajectory tree, which renders the run as a branching structure showing what the agent chose and set aside, and artifact projections over six representations. In a within-subjects study (N=14), participants reported higher decision transparency, artifact sensemaking, and goal connection with Atlas than with a standard baseline, together with substantially lower subjective workload.

title: Quantum dynamics on the sparse Erdős-Rényi graph
abstract: We analyse the large-time asymptotics of the Schrödinger time evolution of a free quantum particle on the Erdős-Rényi graph $\mathbb{G}(N,d/N)$, where the quantum Hamiltonian is given by the adjacency matrix of $\mathbb{G}$. Starting from a state localized at a vertex, the wave function is approximately radial, and we characterize precisely its asymptotic form. Our results in particular cover vertices whose degree is close to $2d$, hence probing the emergence of bound states from a dynamical perspective. This provides a dynamical counterpart of the coexistence of localized and delocalized states established in [arXiv:1905.03243,arXiv:2005.14180,arXiv:2106.12519,arXiv:2109.03227,arXiv:2305.16294], with the former giving rise to a localized mode and the latter to a dispersive wave. Our results hold in the regime $\sqrt{\log N} \ll d \ll N^{o(1)}$, which is the full region in which such dynamical phenomena may exist, and for times $1 \ll t \ll T_N$ for some explicit $T_N \gg 1$.

title: On the stability of learning
abstract: Learning algorithms are usually analyzed under the assumption that informative gradients are continuously available. But this is not always true---learning signals in biological neural networks, for example, may be sparse, local, and only intermittently available at any given synapse. In this work, we show that if gradient information is noisy and only intermittently available, learning may be unstable. In particular, even if average learning dynamics converge to the correct optimum, variance in learning may be asymptotically infinite. We explore this point in a number of analytically tractable settings, including single-layer and multi-layer linear networks, and derive explicit conditions under which learning is stable. These conditions complement, but are conceptually distinct from, existing conditions related to the stability of stochastic gradient descent. Our work demonstrates that unbiased credit assignment is not enough for reliable learning; sufficiently frequent and informative feedback is also required, which yields an additional constraint on models of biologically plausible learning.

title: Exploring the Tractability Frontier of Hylland-Zeckhauser Models
abstract: The Hylland-Zeckhauser (HZ) mechanism provides a market-based approach to one-sided matching, making efficient equilibrium computation central to its implementation. Bi-valued utilities admit a strongly polynomial-time algorithm [VY], whereas with four values per buyer, the problem is PPAD-hard under inverse polynomial approximation [CCPY]. To understand the tractability boundary, we study two extensions of the bi-valued case: a third linear utility value and separable concave utilities with two common marginal slopes. For every fixed rational $a\in(0,1)$, we prove that computing a normalized additive $\varepsilon_{*}(a)/N$-equilibrium in an $N$-buyer HZ market is PPAD-hard for some constant $\varepsilon_{*}(a)>0$, even when all utilities belong to the same prescribed set $\{0,a,1\}$. This resolves the main question left open by [VY, CCPY]: whether three utility values already suffice for PPAD-hardness. Using the same market gadgets, we show that hardness at a specified constant accuracy on the recognizable family generated by our construction is equivalent to the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture. Consequently, assuming that conjecture, general markets over $\{0,a,1\}$ admit no PTAS unless $\mathrm{PPAD}\subseteq\mathrm{P}$. For the concave extension, we compute an exact equilibrium in polynomial time with two marginal slopes common across goods for each buyer and arbitrary rational buyer--good breakpoints. The algorithm selects a cheapest utility-maximizing bundle for each buyer. With three common marginal slopes, suitable breakpoints encode the three valued linear case, yielding PPAD-hardness. Thus, our paper identifies two thresholds separating tractable and intractable cases of HZ models with utility functions specified by utility values or marginal slopes. In both cases, the tractability threshold lies between two and three.

title: Dynamic heart rate variability for classification of arrhythmia burden
abstract: Purpose: Heart rate variability (HRV) may provide information beyond heart rate (HR) for identifying arrhythmia burden, but the value of temporal HRV variation remains unclear. This study developed a dynamic HRV measure quantifying the interquartile range of window-level root mean square of successive RR-interval differences (IQRRMSSD) and evaluated its utility in classifying total abnormal-beat and premature ventricular contraction (PVC) burden compared with the conventional RR-based HRV measure, RMSSD. Methods: Manually annotated 30-minute ECG recordings from 43 individuals were analyzed using overlapping windows. A linear support vector classifier was used to classify individuals as having high or low arrhythmia burden, defined using 1% and 10% burden thresholds. Four feature sets were evaluated: HR alone, HR with RMSSD, HR with IQRRMSSD, and all three measures. Performance was assessed using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Results: HRV-containing feature sets generally outperformed HR alone, depending on outcome and threshold. At the 1% threshold, IQRRMSSD showed particularly high sensitivity for total abnormal-beat and PVC burden ($0.970 \pm 0.064$ and $0.882 \pm 0.193$, respectively). At the 10% threshold, conventional RMSSD showed the strongest overall discrimination, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.947 for PVC burden. Combined features sometimes improved the sensitivity-specificity balance but not overall discrimination. Conclusion: These findings suggest that a conventional RR-based HRV measure is informative for elevated ectopic burden, while a dynamic HRV measure may provide complementary information for lower-burden abnormalities.

title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
abstract: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly. We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent. To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities. We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.

title: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
abstract: In federated learning (FL), secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of local model updates of $N$ clients, without revealing any information on the individual model updates to the server, beyond their sum. Different clients may be subject to heterogeneous bandwidth constraints, and consequently may choose different numbers of quantization levels to represent the information they send. Most secure aggregation works require the clients to project the values of their update parameters to a common finite group (or field), which does not directly accommodate heterogeneous precision constraints on their transmitted masked updates. Existing approaches of secure aggregation with heterogeneous quantization levels reveal partial aggregates of model-updates, and can reveal segments of individual model updates, under certain dropout and client-server collusion patterns. To prevent this privacy breach, we propose an information-theoretic secure aggregation scheme that tolerates client drop-outs, and up to $T$ semi-honest clients that collude with each other and with the server, under heterogeneous quantization at clients. Our protocol utilizes the $(T+1, N)$ threshold black-box secret sharing construction, where secret shares of the client updates, despite belonging to distinct algebraic groups owing to different quantization, are generated from identical linear integer systems.

title: Improved lattice-packing bounds in small dimensions
abstract: We strengthen the upper bound on the density of a lattice packing in small dimensions. A lattice cannot have too many short vectors; we modify the Cohn--Elkies linear program accordingly by allowing the auxiliary function to be positive on a short interval beyond the minimum distance. For $11 \leq n \leq 16$, our bound is tighter than the three-point bound of Cohn, de Laat and Salmon. For $n \in [17, 23] \cup [25, 40] \cup [43, 57] \cup [62, 75]\cup [83, 91]$, our bound lies below the published numerical values of the Cohn--Elkies bound.

title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
abstract: A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered. As coding agents generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a first line of defense screening each new function in real time. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long for real-time screening. Faster detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM's generated verdict is unreliable even when given some of it. We present REVA (REal-time Vulnerability Analysis), an AI vulnerability detector that brings the security context and code understanding components behind agentic detectors into a single forward pass of an LLM. For each new function, REVA gives the LLM a pre-computed threat model of its module, lightweight static analysis findings and call-graph information. REVA leverages a trained probe to read the LLM's internal representations of the new function in this context. On PrimeVul's held-out test set, REVA on GLM-5.3-Flash reaches 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function. This matches VulTriage (59.2%), the state-of-the-art agentic detector, run on the same LLM, while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. On the same prompt, the probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict. Across three open LLMs, REVA is at least as accurate as VulTriage, and about 10% more accurate on two of them. An LLM's internal representations thus encode much of what agentic detectors obtain through reasoning.

title: Seeing Through Distractions: Context-Stable Attribution via the Least Core
abstract: Shapley-value-based explanations are widely used for feature attribution in machine learning. However, in computer vision, a feature may reduce the target-class score when added to the complete genuine image, even when the predicted label remains unchanged. We formalize such features as contextual distractors and investigate their attributions under semivalues and the least core. Under a weak average marginal monotonicity assumption, we derive quantitative semivalue--least-core gap bounds and sufficient conditions based on the probability of sampling smaller contexts. We further show that shifting semivalue weights toward larger contexts decreases the signed gap. Finally, controlled image-classification experiments and evaluations on Salient ImageNet provide strong empirical support for our theoretical findings.

title: Spectroscopic Survey of Small Solar System Bodies with Ariel
abstract: The small Solar System bodies (SSSBs) preserve records of the formation and evolution of the Solar System. In particular, the near-infrared wavelength region around 3 $μ$m provides crucial insights into the origin and transport of hydrated materials and organics, although it is difficult to observe from the ground because of strong telluric absorption. We assess the observability of SSSBs as complementary science to the ESA Ariel space mission, operating in the visible to mid-infrared wavelength range (0.5--7.8 $μ$m). Using the NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris system, we evaluate the visibility of known SSSBs from 2032 to 2035. Our analysis shows that Ariel can spectroscopically characterize up to 402 unique SSSBs under a conservative limiting visual magnitude of $V=13.6$. If observations can be extended to somewhat fainter targets ($V=16$), the number of observable SSSBs could increase to 2144. Assuming operational scenarios in which one SSSB is observed every 3, 7, or 30 days over a four-year mission, the total numbers of observable targets would be 357, 209, and 49, respectively. We further model the spectral energy distributions of candidate targets to evaluate their observational performance. We demonstrate that Ariel can resolve critical absorption features, such as those at 2.7 $μ$m and 3.4 $μ$m, with a higher spectral resolution than the previous infrared survey with AKARI. Observations of SSSBs with Ariel can provide insights into the distribution and evolution of life-forming materials in the Solar System and constitute a scientifically compelling component of Ariel's complementary science program.

title: Properties C and D fail for $C_n^r$ whenever $n \equiv 2 \bmod 4, n\geq 6$ and $r\geq 4$
abstract: Let $s(C_n^r)$ be the Erdős--Ginzburg--Ziv constant (zero-sums of length exactly $n$) and $η(C_n^r)$ the short zero-sum constant. Properties C and D of Gao et al.\ assert that every sequence of the extremal length without the relevant zero-sums has the form $T^{n-1}$. For even $n$ they imply $s(C_n^r)=2^r(n-1)+1$ and $η(C_n^r)=(2^r-1)(n-1)+1$. G.~Wang recently disproved both for $C_6^r$, $r\ge4$. We prove that both fail for $C_n^r$ for every $n\equiv2\pmod4$ with $n\ge6$ and every $r\ge4$. More precisely, for these $n$ we have: $s(C_n^r)\ge2^r(n-1)+2^{r-2}+1$.

title: Operator limits of random matrices: Edge universality and sharp approximations
abstract: We establish operator universality at the spectral edge of general Wigner matrices by showing that their suitably rescaled Lanczos tridiagonalizations, constructed from deterministic initial vectors, converge to the stochastic Airy operator with Dirichlet boundary condition. The result requires control of the entire tridiagonal structure on the scale relevant to the limiting differential operator. The Lanczos coefficients for non-Gaussian Wigner matrices are strongly dependent.
