By studying signed binomial sums, Stirling numbers of both kinds, and factorial moments, we obtain certain cancellations in the computation of centred moments $\mathbb{E}[(X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_n])^k]$. This allows us to conclude that $\frac{X_n - \mathbb{E}[X_n]}{\sqrt{Var \ X_n}} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)$ when the factorial moments $\mathbb{E}[(X_n)_k]$ are rational functions satisfying some simple conditions on the coefficients. A particular class of such random variables are those whose factorial moments are products and quotients of falling factorials in $n$; we apply our result in this situation and we discuss specific examples arising from block statistics of $k$-divisible non-crossing partitions and from outdegree statistics of rooted plane trees with $k$-divisible outdegrees.

title: Performance Guarantees for Permissionless Lending
abstract: We propose a lending protocol with far fewer risks than existing pool-based lending protocols (e.g., Aave, Compound). In our protocol, lenders and borrowers embody the spirit of decentralization by making competing interest-rate offers, resulting in the discovery of the prevailing interest rate through tâtonnement-like dynamics as opposed to taking rates partly determined by a central authority (e.g., Aave, Federal Reserve). We eliminate the risk of manipulation by creating loans with a fixed interest rate throughout the loan---like US Treasury bills. In particular, we further derive performance guarantees probabilities of repayment shortfall and liquidation by modeling the value of the collateral as a random walk, thus allowing participants to more efficiently manage their risk. To do so, we use characteristic functions and Fourier inversion to derive exact integral representations of the liquidation and repayment shortfall probabilities under the most general assumptions. We illustrate empirically this method by using Bitcoin as collateral and fitting its historical prices to Gaussian, Student-$t$, and symmetric stable Paretian distributions.

title: From AI-assisted to AI-native Industrial Control: Architecture, Agent Design, and Challenges
abstract: The integration of AI and industrial control is rapidly transforming industrial automation. However, current approaches remain predominantly AI-assisted, where AI functions are incorporated as auxiliary components without fundamentally altering the underlying architecture of industrial control systems. Consequently, the potential of AI to enable higher levels of autonomy, adaptability, and continuous evolution remains underutilized. This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control paradigm, which reconceptualizes industrial control systems by positioning AI as the intrinsic core rather than an external enhancement. The proposed paradigm is built upon an AI-native infrastructure and a collection of collaborative agentic AIs, each encapsulating a set of advanced skills. Among them, the industrial control agent plays a central role in orchestrating the system lifecycle. Through this paradigm, industrial control shifts from a closed, capability-oriented, human-driven, and passive engineering process to an open, task-oriented, intent-driven, and autonomous solution delivery mechanism. The paper further analyzes the key challenges of the AI-native paradigm from both AI and industrial control perspectives, including issues related to AI model reliability, formal verification, real-time assurance, and heterogeneous resource orchestration. Overall, this work outlines a forward-looking vision for industrial control in the AI era and identifies critical research directions toward autonomous, evolvable, and adaptive control systems in complex and dynamic industrial environments.

title: The Impact of Personalized AI Response Suggestions on Content Creators' Direct Messaging
abstract: Direct messaging is often employed by social media content creators to directly interact with followers. Those creators attempt to engage with followers in private communication, but they often encounter a large volume of messages. Through formative interviews with 15 creators, we found that creators frequently experience fatigue from writing suitable content, as they moderate audience expectations while concurrently integrating their media personas into responses. To explore how AI can address these challenges, we designed a system providing personalized, AI-generated response suggestions tailored to creators' writing styles to maintain their media personas. In a comparison study with 13 creators that examines how the system affects response behaviors, creators valued the system's ability to soften potential impoliteness and anticipated higher response rates, helping them maintain a professional image. However, creators reported additional labor in verifying the authenticity of AI outputs to mitigate risks caused by AI misalignment. Our results indicate that while AI suggestions enhance efficiency, they can undermine a creator's engagement in communication by shifting their attention toward monitoring AI.

title: Learning by Confusion Locates a Parametrization-Dependent Fisher Information Maximum
abstract: Learning by confusion (LBC) is a machine-learning method for locating phase transitions without assuming a known order parameter. Its characteristic accuracy curve contains a central maximum that is interpreted as the transition point, but what determines the location and finite-size scaling of this maximum has remained unclear. We derive an exact balance condition for the Bayes-optimal confusion peak and show that, for equilibrium systems with a single swept parameter, the peak closely follows the maximum of the corresponding Fisher information. This immediately gives its finite-size scaling and reveals an unexpected dependence on how the data are sampled: the same configurations arranged on grids uniform in $T$, $\ln T$, or $β=1/T$ can yield different finite-size pseudocritical trajectories. Tests on the Ising, Blume-Capel, Potts, and Baxter-Wu models confirm the prediction across continuous, tricritical, and first-order transitions. Our results identify the statistical quantity measured by LBC and show that finite-size machine-learning estimates can depend on the parametrization of the training data as well as on the underlying physics.

title: Experimental Validation of Double-Blind Fourier Holography in an HWO-Like Segmented Aperture
abstract: Double-Blind Fourier Holography (DBFH) is a phase-retrieval method that has been shown numerically to address wavefront-sensing challenges for future segmented-aperture space telescopes, including the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). DBFH uses a set of carefully selected pupil-plane amplitude masks and their corresponding focal-plane intensity measurements to construct an algebraically linear inverse problem, enabling computationally efficient and stable reconstruction of the complex pupil field. Here, we present the first experimental demonstration of DBFH using a spatial light modulator and an HWO EAC5-like segmented-aperture geometry. We reconstruct challenging pseudo-random wavefronts and compare DBFH with the established Focus-Diverse Phase Retrieval (FDPR) method. The two methods achieve comparable reconstruction precision, while exhibiting distinct strengths and limitations. We further demonstrate DBFH wavefront sensing in the presence of a binary source, a scenario that is not naturally accommodated by conventional FDPR. These results provide experimental proof of concept and establish technology readiness level 3 for DBFH as a wavefront-sensing method for space telescopes with segmented primary mirrors.

title: Exceptional times of compact support for $α$-stable superprocesses
abstract: We consider symmetric $α$-stable Dawson--Watanabe superprocesses on $\mathbb R^d$ for every $d\geq1$ and $0<α<2$, started from an arbitrary nonzero finite measure. We prove that, almost surely, the times at which the spatial support is compact and nonempty have Hausdorff dimension one in every nontrivial interval before extinction. We also prove that, almost surely, the times at which the support is contained in any prescribed neighborhood of the extinction point have Hausdorff dimension one in every nontrivial interval ending at extinction. These results extend the corresponding conclusions for $0<α<2/3$ to the full stable range. The key new ingredient is a uniform zero-set theorem of independent interest for Feller branching diffusions started from zero with deterministic continuous cumulative immigration. It shows that sufficiently small total immigration ensures that the zero set on a prescribed open interval has Hausdorff dimension arbitrarily close to one, with arbitrarily high probability. The estimate is uniform over the immigration profile and allows singular continuous immigration measures.

title: Linear Hashing Is Poissonesque
abstract: The Poisson approximation theorem states that when $m$ balls are tossed uniformly and randomly into $n$ bins, the distribution of the bin loads can sometimes be approximated by $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. We show that when the balls are tossed via a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map, the load distribution is still governed by this Poisson distribution, albeit in a (necessarily) weaker manner. This allows us to show that a random linear map behaves like a fully random map in the following ways: 1. $\textbf{Expected loads.}$ We show that the expected value of the $r$th largest bin is governed by the $r$th largest value among $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. Specializing to the canonical setting of $m=n$ and $r=1$, our bounds show that the expected maximum load when $n$ balls are hashed into $n$ bins by a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map is no more than the corresponding expectation for a fully random map $\textit{plus}$ $\frac{3}2 + o(1)$. Specializing to $m\gg n\log n$, we show that the expected max load is $(1+o(1))m/n$ in this regime. 2. $\textbf{Concentration.}$ When $m\gg n\log (1/ρ)$ balls are tossed into $n$ bins randomly, we expect with $0.99$ probability that $\textit{every}$ density-$ρ$ subset of bins will contain a $(1\pm o(1) )ρ$-fraction of the balls. We show that this remains the case if the $m$ balls are tossed using a random linear map, and our bound matches the $o(1)$-factor produced by the fully random case. This gives a stronger version of the Leftover Hash Lemma for linear maps. An implication of this is that all bins have load $m/n \pm O(\sqrt{(m/n)\log n})$ with probability $0.99$. We obtain these results by showing that the average of a log-potential on the bin loads is upper bounded by the cumulant generating function of a Poisson random variable of mean $m/n$.

title: Multivariate Augmented Prediction-Powered Survival Inference for EHR Association Studies With Limited Chart Review
abstract: Objective: To reduce bias and improve precision in survival association studies using electronic health record (EHR) data when computational phenotypes (CPs) for outcomes and covariates are error-prone and chart review is limited. Materials and Methods: We developed Multivariate Augmented Prediction-Powered Survival (MAPS) regression, which combines chart-reviewed and CP-derived labels across different validation patterns. MAPS uses a discrete-time survival model with a complementary log-log link to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). It incorporates data-adaptive augmentation weights, inverse-probability sampling weights, and patient-level cluster-robust variance estimation. We compared MAPS with chart-reviewed data (CRD) and CP-only analyses in simulation studies and a masked-validation study of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) among 1,026 patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Results: In the main simulations, MAPS produced approximately unbiased estimates and generally near-nominal 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, with narrower intervals than CRD. CP-only estimates became increasingly biased as CP errors increased. In the EHR analysis, MAPS estimates closely agreed with fully validated estimates and improved precision over CRD, particularly at lower validation rates. CP-only analysis suggested increased irAE risk associated with pre-existing autoimmune disease (AID; HR=1.53; 95% CI, 1.12-2.09), whereas the fully validated analysis did not (HR=0.93; 95% CI, 0.67-1.29). Discussion: Precision gains depended on CP quality and validation rates, while small validation samples may affect confidence interval coverage. Conclusion: MAPS provides a flexible and efficient approach to EHR-based survival inference by combining limited chart-reviewed data with error-prone CPs across different validation patterns.

title: Babysitting AI Agents: A User-Centered Taxonomy and Study of Agentic Delegation Failures
abstract: Users are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, allowing agents to perform long-running, multi-step workflows on their behalf. However, agents may perform these tasks in ways that depart from users' expectations for how they should be carried out, leading to what we call agentic delegation failures. We leverage a large corpus of 163,487 Reddit posts, describing AI agent use, to develop MANDATE: a taxonomy of 23 failure categories organized into seven groups. A follow-up study with 73 AI agent users examined the relationship between prevalence and perceptions of severity and noticeability, finding that failures rated as more severe are considered harder to notice, and that prior experience with a failure is associated with greater noticeability. Finally, we assess the maturity of research on each failure and identify commonly encountered failures that have received little attention (e.g., agents running without making progress). Our findings inform opportunities to make delegation easier for users to oversee and better studied by the research community.

title: Affective and Functional Needs in AI Use: User Patterns and Their Relation to Real-Life Support and Well-Being
abstract: Conversational AI systems are increasingly used to fulfill both functional and affective needs, yet how users perceive the AI-adoption effects varies. Existing research tends to treat these two needs as binary categories and to classify users by a single dominant need. However, this approach fails to capture users who engage with AI for both affective and functional purposes simultaneously, leaving it unclear how these needs combine in real-world AI use. To capture the multifaceted nature of users' AI engagement, we developed the AI-Support measurement with 1,090 participants, grounded in social support theory, which evaluates four dimensions of perceived AI support: emotional/esteem, social companionship, informational, and instrumental support. This study provided (1) an AI-Support Scale developed to measure the perceived support types from human-AI interaction, (2) evidence that users might adopt AI with a high level of both functional and affective use, and (3) exploratory indicators of users' real-life social support and well-being, enabling descriptive results aligning with theoretical expectations. Overall, this study highlights the importance of understanding individual differences in AI affordance use, enabling AI systems to be designed in alignment with different user adoption profiles rather than assuming uniform benefits across all users.

title: An isometric embedding of the space of non-increasing sequences with non-negative terms into the Gromov-Hausdorff space
abstract: The Gromov-Hausdorff space is a certain metric space induced by the Gromov-Hausdorff convergence, and we study an isometric embedding into this space. While the subspace of non-negative real numbers in the Euclidean space admits an isometric embedding, we prove that the subspace of $\ell^\infty$ consisting of non-increasing sequences with non-negative terms can be isometrically embedded into the Gromov-Hausdorff space.

title: Data-driven acquisition offset correction for telescope networks using machine learning and sensitivity analysis
abstract: Reliable target acquisition is essential for maximizing observing efficiency, particularly for robotic telescope networks that operate across many sites, instruments, and environmental conditions. Although these facilities generate large volumes of operational and observational data, acquisition procedures often continue to rely on static pointing models and manual adjustments by observatory staff. These approaches can be effective, but they may not fully capture changing behavior associated with telescope configuration, observing conditions, instrument state, or other time-dependent effects. We present a data-driven machine-learning pipeline for automatically predicting and correcting telescope acquisition offsets, demonstrated using archival operational logs from the Las Cumbres Observatory network. Our approach applies both traditional machine-learning methods and deep-learning regression models to learn relationships between measured acquisition offsets and a range of observing, telescope, and instrumentation conditions. By using historical performance data, the pipeline is designed to complement existing pointing models and reduce the need for repeated manual correction. We also present an open-source, Dockerized software service that makes the trained models accessible through a browser-based graphical interface. The service is intended to support straightforward, real-time use by observatory staff while remaining portable across computing environments. Together, the prediction pipeline and deployment framework provide a practical path toward more adaptive, automated, and data-informed telescope acquisition.

title: Simplified Parisi Ansatz III: Constructive Cavity Method and Ultrametricity
abstract: We present a physical explaination of the Constructive Cavity Method (CCM) for the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model, which identifies the decomposition of the cavity variables into layers with the random overlap structure of Aizenman--Sims--Starr. We describe the low-temperature excitations through a dilute gas of defects relative to the ground state. The sharing of these defects among the descendants and the renewal of the fluctuations along new branches produce the GREM structure and the ultrametricity of the overlaps. This mechanism is developed first with a finite number of defects and then extended to exponential populations of states. At fixed kernel, the Gaussian covariances of the fresh fields connect the complete cavity variables, including their common components, to the same hierarchy that determines the Gibbs masses. We also correct some ambiguities of earlier formulations.

title: From Speech Tokens to Stolen Voices: Attacker-Chosen-Text Speaker Impersonation via Representation Inversion
abstract: Speech interaction systems have gradually evolved from traditional cascaded systems that use text as intermediate information to end-to-end speech language models that directly process speech representations. In some applications, the speech frontend runs on the user's device and sends speech representations to a remote server for inference, while the original audio remains local. However, these representations may still contain speaker identity information. If an attacker obtains them, it may use this information to imitate the user's voice, threatening their voice privacy. To investigate this risk, we propose \stia, a Speech Token Inversion Attack that generates speech with attacker-specified text in a victim's voice using a single short leaked representation, without access to the original audio or its transcript. Specifically, \stia converts discrete, continuous, or mixed speech representations into conditioning sequences and trains a conditional flow-matching speech generation model using pairs of different utterances from the same speaker in public speech datasets. The model combines speaker characteristics contained in the leaked representation with the specified text to generate speech in the victim's voice. Experiments show that, with a Moshi representation leak corresponding to 3 seconds of speech, \stia achieves an average CAM++ speaker cosine similarity of 0.78 and a target-text word error rate of 3.80\%. These results show that speech frontend representations reveal reusable speaker identity information and highlight the need to consider privacy risks when designing speech frontend representation methods.

title: Machine Learning Applications in the Solar Interior and Atmosphere
abstract: The solar interior and atmosphere constitute a strongly coupled, multiscale dynamical system defined by continuous temporal evolution. Predicting the state of this system requires modeling physical interactions that span disparate spatial and temporal scales, constrained by heterogeneous and sparse data. This chapter formalizes the Sun within the mathematical framework of dynamical systems theory, defining a global state vector ($\vec{S}$) governed by thermodynamical, kinetic, and magnetic properties. Because solar observations represent projected, multi-modal, and partially observable measurements ($\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$) of this hidden state, pure physics-based deduction is fundamentally constrained. We present a unifying thesis: the primary role of machine learning in heliophysics is to act as a structured family of mathematical operators---specifically Inference ($\mathcal{I}$), Emulation ($\mathcal{E}$), Propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and Control ($\mathcal{C}$)---that reconstruct, simulate, and couple this global state vector across disparate physical layers. By framing the vast, multi-disciplinary literature within this unified state-space taxonomy, we demonstrate how data-driven techniques bridge observational gaps to resolve hidden multiscale couplings and dramatically accelerate the simulation of non-linear processes, establishing a rigorous pathway to predict the global evolution of the Sun.

title: Beyond Deduplication: Sharp Retrieval Limits for Attention with Correlated Distractors
abstract: Redundant context affects attention through two distinct mechanisms: repeated items add normalization mass, while score variation within correlated groups can produce extreme individual scores. We separate these effects in a planted retrieval model with exponentially many Gaussian distractors arranged in known, exponentially large clusters. The model is a two-level generalized random energy model, whose classical free energy yields exact retrieval thresholds. Gaussian interpolation further shows that increasing positive correlation at fixed token count lowers the distractor free energy, unlike adding duplicates. Our main result identifies a sharp limitation of subtracting log cluster size from pre-softmax scores: this correction removes multiplicity but retains within-cluster extremes. Even a temperature chosen after observing all scores cannot lower the required signal below $\sqrt{2α_1}$, where $α_1$ is the exponential rate of the number of clusters. Averaging scores before exponentiation instead suppresses these fluctuations and achieves $\sqrt{2ρα_1}$, where $ρ$ is the within-cluster correlation. The gap persists after adding exponentially many singleton distractors, so group size alone does not identify the target, and extends to fixed finite hierarchies of light-tailed independent-increment scores. Finite-sample, stability, and participation results complement the asymptotic analysis. A controlled retrieval experiment with frozen sentence embeddings supports this distinction while delineating its scope: averaging helps when the relevant item is a singleton, but can discard useful evidence when a relevant group contains multiple matching items.

title: From Representations to Computational Trajectories: Intrinsic Fingerprinting for Large Language Model Provenance Verification
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are valuable digital assets, yet their weights can be easily modified after unauthorized acquisition, making model provenance difficult to verify. Model fingerprinting provides a promising solution for model ownership protection without modifying the model or embedding ownership information. However, parameter-based fingerprints can be sensitive to model transformations, limiting their robustness, while representation-based fingerprints may assign high similarity to unrelated models, limiting their uniqueness. To address these limitations, we propose TrFP, an intrinsic fingerprinting method based on computational trajectories. Instead of comparing model parameters or representations, TrFP captures how representations evolve across network depth and constructs compact fingerprints using permutation-invariant trajectory descriptors. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that TrFP reliably distinguishes related and unrelated models. It also remains robust under fine-tuning, pruning, quantization, model merging, parameter permutation, and adaptive attacks, while requiring less than 0.3 MiB of fingerprint storage. Overall, TrFP provides stronger provenance discrimination than several existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of computational trajectories for reliable LLM provenance verification.

title: Compound Environmental Operating Stress and Cyber-Induced Pump Disruption in Water Distribution Networks: Matched Hydraulic Impacts, Service Continuity, and Sustained Recovery
abstract: Digitally controlled water distribution systems must maintain service during disruptions, yet restoring water delivery does not necessarily ensure hydraulic recovery. This study evaluates cyber-induced pump outages under hypothetical environmental operating stress using two EPANET benchmark networks (Net1 and Net3) simulated with the Water Network Tool for Resilience. The experimental design comprises 288 simulation records (240 distinct configurations), including 192 verified attack scenarios, with four- and twelve-hour outages, six hydraulic configurations, and four mitigation strategies. All attack scenarios satisfied pump-shutdown verification and pre-attack hydraulic-equivalence criteria. Twelve-hour outages produced an average of 404.96 m$^3$ of unmet demand in Net1, while Net3 maintained full modeled demand delivery despite pressure deviations. Sustained pressure recovery occurred in 103 of 192 scenarios, with 65 exhibiting subsequent relapse, whereas all scenarios satisfied the post-outage water-service recovery criterion. Combined mitigation eliminated unmet demand in evaluated Net1 scenarios, while outage shortening achieved the highest sustained-pressure-recovery count. These findings highlight network-dependent resilience and the distinction between service restoration and hydraulic recovery. Environmental stress scenarios represent sensitivity assumptions rather than empirically calibrated climate impacts.

title: Reference-state dependence and interface scaling of superfluid response in a two-dimensional crystal
abstract: Grain boundaries modify both transport paths and the surrounding crystal, making their contribution to superfluid stiffness difficult to isolate. We quantify these contributions in stationary two-dimensional soft-core Gross--Pitaevskii (GP) crystals using tensor response, independently prepared bicrystals, and measured interface lengths. A one-percent change of lattice spacing alters the bulk stiffness by approximately 5--9\%, comparable to the boundary contribution. For the same defective state, two bulk references give relative excesses of 0.027\% and 4.15\%. Matching the comparator to grain strain and chemical potential yields positive diagonal excesses in paired preparations at three interaction strengths. Within a twelve-state family with comparable grain interiors, the excess is robust to 288 bulk substitutions and follows an approximate length-per-area relation. Independent fixed-area pairs yield a line-response coefficient 3.1\% higher than the three-size estimate. Size and directional dependence restrict this relation to the specified crystal conditions. Reduced link networks relate the directional response to the organization of boundary connections but do not accurately resolve every small bulk-subtracted excess. The results distinguish boundary enhancement from changes in the surrounding crystal and establish a quantitative comparison protocol for superfluid transport in defective crystals.

title: The CAPED Framework: Characterizing User Skills in Chart Authoring through the Lens of Tasks and Tools
abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new framework for characterizing the user skills required for chart authoring. Despite growing attention to authoring systems, we lack a conceptual framework that characterizes the diverse and multifaceted skills involved and helps identify opportunities for system design and development. Our initial investigation revealed that skill is a complex and elusive concept, and that existing theories on skills from other disciplines are too high-level to capture the importance of tasks and tools in data visualizations. To address this gap, we formulate the CAPED framework that characterizes skill as the ability to create a chart involving five dimensions pertinent to tasks and tools: input data, output chart, paradigm, abstraction, and expression. We demonstrate the framework's descriptive power by highlighting different skills involved in similar authoring situations and identifying the types of knowledge associated with chart authoring. We further present examples illustrating how the framework can be used to identify new research opportunities in supporting users with varying skills.

title: Approximating the Euclidean Ball by Polytopes: Surprising Rates in High Dimensions
abstract: We determine the sharp dimensional dependence of the asymptotic approximation error for the Euclidean unit ball $B_2^d\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ by polytopes with a prescribed number of vertices in the relative symmetric difference metric. Specifically, we prove that $$\lim_{N\to\infty}N^{2/(d-1)}\inf_{P\in P_d(N)}\frac{\operatorname{vol}_d(P\triangle B_2^d)}{\operatorname{vol}_d(B_2^d)}=Θ(d^{-1/2}),$$ where $P_d(N)$ consists of polytopes with at most $N$ vertices and no containment restriction. Equivalently, the classical Laguerre-Delone triangulation numbers satisfy $\operatorname{ldel}_{d-1}=Θ(d^{-1/2})$. This improves the lower bound $Ω(d^{-1})$ of Böröczky (2000) and the upper bound $O(1)$ of Ludwig, Schütt and Werner (2006). In contrast, the corresponding asymptotic coefficient for approximation with a prescribed number of facets has order one, as shown by Kur (2020). We also establish non-asymptotic bounds showing that, for every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, the ball admits an $\varepsilon$-approximation with at most $\exp(C(\varepsilon)\sqrt d)$ vertices, whereas approximating the hypercube to the same accuracy requires at least $\exp(c(\varepsilon)d)$ vertices. Consequently, the ball does not maximize the optimal relative approximation error among convex bodies, even up to an absolute multiplicative constant at the same vertex budget. Thus Macbeath's theorem (1951) on the extremality of the ball for inscribed approximation does not extend to polytopes in arbitrary position.

title: Dream to Assist: Intent-Conditioned World Models for Shared Vehicle Control
abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.

title: Rewriting the Self: User Perceptions of AI-Mediated Cognitive Reframing
abstract: Individuals are increasingly using AI for psychological support. One specific paradigm, AI-mediated cognitive reframing (AIM-CR), uses AI to automatically reframe users' negative thoughts ("I failed...") into more adaptive perspectives ("I am learning..."). While prior work suggests that AIM-CR tools reduce users' negative emotions, the complexities of AI automatically modifying users' personal narratives remain underexplored. In this work, we investigated these complexities through a mixed-methods study in which 28 participants engaged with an AIM-CR tool that reframed narratives about their stressors. Our findings suggest that participants had mixed perceptions of AIM-CR: although reframing reduced negative emotions for most participants, participants felt less ownership of, and less authenticity in, the reframed narratives. Participants perceived AIM-CR as a validating "mirror," as "another self" that could motivate or alienate them, or as an external social actor. These perceptions shaped therapeutic dynamics. We conclude by discussing design implications for future AIM-CR tools to better preserve user agency in narrative co-construction and more effectively support mental health and well-being.

title: Regional prediction of hematoma expansion from non-contrast computed tomography in spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage patients
abstract: Background The combination of hematoma location, expansion and final volume influence neurological outcome. The aim of this study was to derive and validate a quantitative and interpretable region-based NCCT image feature model for predicting hematoma expansion. Methods The Ethnic/Racial Variations of Intracerebral Hemorrhage(ERICH) study was used for derivation and the Virtual International Trials in Stroke Archive(VISTA) was used for validation. NCCT images at presentation and 24+/-6hours were pre-processed, segmented and categorized into lobar, basal ganglia or thalamic regions. Hematoma expansion was defined by region and according to its effect on clinical outcome. Transport-based morphometry (TBM) produced a unique transport-based representation from each NCCT hematoma image. Linear classifiers applied to transport representations were used to derive a predictive model. The regional TBM model's performance was compared to alternate methods using AUROC analyses. Results The derivation dataset included 574 patients, comprising 162 lobar, 257 basal ganglia and 155 thalamic hematomas. The validation dataset included 196 patients, comprising 31 lobar, 119 basal ganglia and 46 thalamic hematomas. A combined regional model predicted hematoma expansion in the validation dataset with an AUROC of 0.787. The principal image features which varied by location were size, heterogeneity, eccentricity and density distribution towards the hematoma periphery. The regional TBM model outperformed alternative clinician based and machine-learning methods. Conclusions TBM discriminated and visualized regional features of hematoma expansion from presentation NCCT scans. This provides preliminary evidence for regional radiographic features of hematoma expansion. It has the potential to improve hematoma expansion prediction and understanding of hematoma expansion pathophysiology.

title: SlowLab: Benchmarking Autonomous AI Agents on a Year of Experiments They Cannot Undo
abstract: AI agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous experimenters, yet the benchmarks that test them mostly offer cheap experiments that answer at once. Experiments in physical facilities are different: they take months, occupy scarce equipment and cannot be undone. We present SlowLab, a benchmark in which an agent runs a one-year campaign in four simulated greenhouse compartments on a site whose crop, facility and prices are hidden. The agent decides when to plant which climate policy, whether to stop a crop and which measurements to read while crops grow, and at the end recommends one policy, which a private evaluator scores in weather the agent never saw. In a preregistered study on 48 unseen sites, three low-cost language-model agents ended near a standard grower setting and clearly below a Bayesian-optimisation baseline that starts from that setting. They ran the facility as two synchronous batches, so measurements taken during the season never changed what they planted, and these measurements improved no method's result. Letting other methods re-read the evidence a campaign had collected did not yield significantly better recommendations, which points to where the models start and which experiments they try. Code is released under the MIT license.

title: Competitive exploration in structured environments
abstract: Organisms must constantly weigh exploiting the resources they know against exploring for better ones. When foragers compete, the best behavior for each forager also depends on what its competitors do. How does competition change the strategic balance between exploration and exploitation? Here we address this question in a minimal model: two $ε$-greedy temporal-difference learners on a one-dimensional lattice, who start at a small reward at one end and are unaware of a larger reward at the other. For a lone forager, the optimal exploration rate increases monotonically with the value of the distant reward, and with its distance up to a critical distance. When two foragers share the lattice and split rewards, the choice of exploration rate becomes a game whose Nash equilibria have both foragers exploring, both staying, or one exploring while the other stays (anti-coordination). Under local best-response dynamics, pairs of foragers often converge on both exploring or both staying, even when anti-coordination would be socially optimal. This social dilemma arises for a wide range of parameters, and it persists even in a simplified model without explicit spatial structure. A minimal, naturalistic signal, in which one forager informs the other that it has found the distant reward, can remove many of the dilemmas in which both foragers explore, and can produce a Nash equilibrium whose collective payoff exceeds that of every outcome available without signaling.

title: Sharp Stability of Brenier Potentials and its Link to Poincaré Inequalities
abstract: We prove a new functional inequality for uniformly log-concave measures, stronger than the Poincaré inequality. This new inequality bounds the variance of differences of convex functions and is motivated by the stability theory of optimal transport: for a fixed uniformly log-concave source measure, it provides a sharp stability bound for Brenier potentials with respect to variations of the target measure. Applying this inequality to Gaussian measures, we recover the fact that the Bures-Wasserstein distance between two positive semidefinite matrices is equivalent to the Frobenius distance between their square roots. Our proofs hinge upon linearization arguments for the Monge-Ampère equation governing the quadratic optimal transport problem.

title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
abstract: We introduce Heads of Security (HoS), a prompt injection defense that enforces instruction-data separation via a small set of learned per-head attention gates. HoS learns how each head should redistribute attention between trusted and untrusted tokens, enabling models to reason over untrusted content without following injected instructions. We evaluate HoS on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B. We compare it against SecAlign++, a state-of-the-art finetuning-based defense, and ASIDE, a defense that, like ours, builds instruction-data separation into the model architecture. We show that HoS offers greater robustness to adaptive attacks, better performance on standard utility benchmarks, and matches top performance on standard agentic prompt injection benchmarks. More specifically, the black-box RL-Hammer attack reaches 97% ASR against GPT-OSS-20B and 85% against SecAlign, but only 10% against HoS. Claudini, a state-of-the-art white-box attack, strengthened against HoS through autoresearch, requires 3 times more FLOPs to reach the same ASR on HoS as it does on GPT-OSS-20B or SecAlign. HoS preserves base-model utility across standard multiple-choice benchmarks and prompting setups, whereas SecAlign and ASIDE degrade in few-shot settings. On agentic benchmarks with static attacks, HoS and SecAlign perform similarly and substantially improve the security-utility trade-off over the base model. ASIDE struggles with tool use, achieving only 10% utility. These results show that prompt injection robustness can be achieved and improved through targeted attention interventions.

title: Hodge--Riemann relations for nef bundles
abstract: We introduce the $(m,p,q)$-Lefschetz property for $(1,1)$-type endomorphisms of Hodge--Lefschetz modules, providing a framework for studying nef $(1,1)$-classes and characteristic classes of nef vector bundles on compact Kähler manifolds. Under a Hall--Rado type condition on nef twisted vector bundles, we prove Hodge--Riemann relations for products of top Chern classes and, in suitable bidegrees, for products of derived Schur classes. For products of nef $(1,1)$-classes, we show furthermore that the Hall--Rado type condition is equivalent to simultaneous Hodge--Riemann relations. Our proofs build on the purity theorem and descent lemma of Cattani, Kaplan, and Schmid. We extend the descent lemma to Schur classes of nef vector bundles. We also establish formal analogs for projective bundle modules over Hodge--Lefschetz modules, with applications to tautological classes and descent on matroid Chow rings.

title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

title: Sharp approximations for the stationary measures of the open ASEP I: The shock region
abstract: We investigate the role of asymmetry in the stationary measures of integrable probabilistic models with boundary interactions. This paper is the first in a series of three focusing on the open asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP). The stationary measure of open ASEP admits a two-layer Gibbs representation in which a correction term, which we call the Bryc polynomial, encodes the dependence on the asymmetry parameter. We give a probabilistic interpretation of the Bryc polynomial in terms of a birth-death-type Markov chain. As an application, we obtain sharp total variation approximations of the stationary measure by Bernoulli product measures in the high- and low-density phases of the shock region. These approximations yield further applications, including moderate deviation estimates for the stationary measure of open ASEP, as well as asymptotic results for the related model of open ASEP with light particles.

title: Sharp approximations for the stationary measures of the open ASEP II: The coexistence line
abstract: We study the stationary measure of the open asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) on the coexistence line. Our starting point is Bryc's two-layer Gibbs representation, together with the probabilistic interpretation, established in the first paper in this series, of the associated Bryc polynomial in terms of an inhomogeneous birth--death chain. Our main result gives a sharp approximation of the stationary measure. Specifically, we identify the shock location as an explicit observable of the particle configuration and obtain optimal bounds on the total variation distance between its law and the uniform measure on the lattice. Conditional on the shock location, we approximate, in total variation distance, the joint law of the occupation variables away from the shock by Bernoulli product measures with different densities to its left and right. These approximations lead to further applications, including fluctuation limits, moderate deviation bounds for the particle density, and limits for correlation functions under the stationary measure.

title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
abstract: It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier. The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries. The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so Håstad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.

title: Approximate Counting for Mixed $p$-Spin Glasses in Weak External Fields via Cluster Expansion
abstract: We give algorithms for approximating the partition function $Z_N$ of the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) model and finite mixed Ising $p$-spin models with $p\ge 3$. The algorithms apply at a fixed margin below the second-moment threshold $β_{\mathrm f}$ with homogeneous weak external fields $|h|\leqρ_0N^{-1/4}$, for fixed $ρ_0>0$. For any accuracy $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and failure parameter $δ\in(0,1)$, they approximate $\log Z_N$ to additive error $\varepsilon$. The number of exact operations is polynomial jointly in $N$, $\varepsilon^{-1}$, and $δ^{-1}$. The disorder variables have i.i.d symmetric distribution with unit variance. The failure probability is at most $δ$ plus an explicit disorder tail bound. This tail bound tends to zero under a finite fourth moment condition. Our approach builds on the cluster expansions of Aizenman--Lebowitz--Ruelle~\cite{ALR87} and Dey--Wu~\cites{DW23,DW26}. For higher-order mixtures, we retain hypergraphs using few vertices and evaluate their total weight deterministically through local spin averages and inclusion--exclusion. For SK, we impose cutoffs on the number of vertices of degree at least three and on the total number of edges. We estimate the retained sum using randomized color coding~\cite{AYZ95}. A lower tail control based on reverse hypercontractivity~\cite{MOS13} converts the mean-square approximation of the normalized partition function into logarithmic accuracy.

title: Shape exclusion for diffusion-limited aggregation
abstract: For diffusion-limited aggregation on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $d \geq 2$, we rule out convergence in volume to bounded regions with boundary measure zero. Moreover, the number of boundary edges grows linearly. For Euclidean DLA in dimensions $2$, $3$, $8$, and $24$, we prove an analogous shape exclusion.

title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

title: Linear-quadratic mean field games with Volterra dynamics
abstract: We study a class of linear-quadratic mean field games in which the state of each agent follows a stochastic Volterra equation of convolution type. The resulting dynamics are non-Markovian and account for memory effects through a completely monotone kernel, while the mean field interaction enters both the drift and diffusion coefficients. Exploiting a Markovian lifting of the Volterra dynamics, which restores the Markov property at the price of moving to an infinite-dimensional state space, we characterize the optimal response of a representative agent for a given population mean through a system of Riccati equations in Banach spaces, thereby obtaining a feedback representation of the optimal control. We then study the consistency condition defining the mean field equilibrium, which reduces to a forward-backward fixed point equation for the equilibrium mean: we prove existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium on short horizons and, when the control does not act on the diffusion coefficient, on arbitrary horizons under a monotonicity condition on the interaction. Finally, we consider the corresponding finite-player game and establish a quantitative propagation of chaos result. As a consequence, the feedback control of any mean field equilibrium, when implemented by each agent on its own state, yields an $\varepsilon_N$-Nash equilibrium for the $N$-player game, with an explicit rate as the number of agents tends to infinity.

title: Sharp approximations for the stationary measures of the open ASEP III: The fan region
abstract: We study the stationary measure of the open asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) in the fan region with general boundary rates. The stationary height fluctuations in the maximal current phase and on its boundaries within the fan region are known to have limits involving Brownian excursions or meanders. We establish discrete counterparts of these limits: on intervals away from the boundaries, the joint law of the occupation variables is approximated in total variation distance by particle configurations constructed from lazy simple random walk excursions and meanders. In the high- and low-density phases of the fan region, we establish Bernoulli product approximations with errors that decay exponentially in the distance from the relevant boundary. Our methods combine refined combinatorial estimates for Motzkin paths and the matrix product ansatz in the totally asymmetric case with a Fourier-type decomposition (based on Askey--Wilson polynomials) of the change of measure for general asymmetry. In addition, in the maximal current phase and on its boundaries within the fan region, we prove moderate deviation estimates for particle counts on arbitrary sets of sites. These estimates rely on a covariance identity for an auxiliary path measure, through which total nonnegativity (of order two) of the matrices yields negative correlations.

title: Stationary measures of the open KPZ equation: A short proof
abstract: In this note, we give a short probabilistic proof of the two-layer Brownian representation of the stationary measure of the open Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) equation on a finite interval with arbitrary Neumann boundary parameters, conjectured by Barraquand and Le Doussal and recently established in full generality by Dunlap, Gu and Rosati. Our starting point is Bryc's two-layer Gibbs representation of the stationary measure of the open asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) under Liggett's condition, together with our previously established probabilistic interpretation of the associated Bryc polynomials in terms of inhomogeneous birth--death Markov chains. Martingale estimates yield uniform asymptotics for these polynomials under weakly asymmetric scaling. Combined with known convergence results from open ASEP to open KPZ, these estimates recover the stationary height profile of the open KPZ equation as the first marginal of a reweighted pair of Brownian motions.

title: Generic tensor products are not maximal
abstract: We construct tensor products of uniform matroids which are strictly freer than their generic linear tensor products. In particular, the generic tensor product of two copies of $U_{7,9}$ is not maximal. More generally, for every $a,b\ge2$, this holds for $U_{7,a+7}$ and $U_{7,b+7}$. The construction disproves the uniform tensor-product formulation of Mason's conjecture. Its dual is a relaxation of an explicit circuit-hyperplane of a generic birigidity matroid. By the author's representability theorem, the resulting matroids are non-representable over every field. We also obtain full-rank counterexamples to the Jackson--Tanigawa hyperconnectivity conjecture in every dimension $d\ge2$.

title: A unified coarse-grained neural network potential for the dynamics of biomolecular complexes
abstract: The behavior of biomolecular complexes is governed by chemically specific interactions and often involves rare events that atomistic molecular dynamics struggle to capture within accessible timescales. Here we introduce AMARO v2.0, a coarse-grained neural network potential that retains all heavy atoms and treats solvent implicitly. Hydrogen-aware bead types and total-charge conditioning provide a shared representation for proteins, drug-like molecules, and their complexes, including ternary protein-protein-ligand systems. The model preserves folded proteins and captures key features of protein conformational free-energy landscapes. Across 262 complexes spanning 11 targets, the learned potential retains most ligand poses, although quaternary structure reorientation is observed for the HIF2A ternary complex. In targeted case studies, AMARO v2.0 distinguishes the two protonation states of trypsin-benzamidine and reaches the crystal binding pose in 3.3-fold more trajectories than all-atom molecular mechanics at a fixed estimated GPU-time budget. The same framework also recovers a reference binding pose in TYK2 and supports binding free-energy estimation for both trypsin-benzamidine and TYK2-EJM31, although the resulting values are more energetically favorable than the experimental references. SHP2 and CDK8 systems expose remaining limitations in binding-pose recovery and site specificity, respectively. Together, these results support AMARO v2.0 as a shared heavy-atom potential for biomolecular complex dynamics.

title: SLICE-CiM: Selective Layer-wise Inference Control Engine with Confidence-Based Early Exit for SRAM based Digital Compute-in-Memory
abstract: Digital SRAM compute-in-memory (CIM) macros enable energy-efficient CNN inference by eliminating off-chip weight transfers; however, peripheral control logic introduces three inefficiencies: bit- slice over-activation at reduced precision (L1), unnecessary accumula- tion depth (L2), and idle precision-transition stalls (L3). To address these, we present four synthesizable peripheral blocks: a Flush-Merge Enable (FME) controller, a Confidence-Based Early-Exit (EE) module, a Precision Register with Decoder (PR/PD), and a Bit-Serial Cycle Controller (CC), co-designed to minimize switching activity, wordline overhead, and leakage. Implemented in TSMC 65-nm CMOS at 335 MHz, the peripheral framework occupies 1769.760 μm2 post-synthesis and 1982.131 μm2 post-PnR. Gate-level VCD analysis reports 6.0706 μW leakage and 288.2902 μW (post-synthesis) / 322.8850 μW (post-PnR) dynamic power, totaling 328.9556 μW (0.2402% of system power). The EE module dominates dynamic power (58.2%), while WLG dominates area (58.1%). System evaluation on MobileNetV2 (CIFAR-100) shows efficiency scaling from 31.35 TOPS/W (8b/8b, 1.2 V) to 454.91 TOPS/W (2b/8b, 0.8 V), achieving 13.33x improvement without bitcell modification or retraining. The framework targets CNN workloads exploiting sparsity, with Transformer extension as future work.

title: GAS-PFN: Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Zero-Shot Traffic Forecasting
abstract: Traffic forecasting requires modeling complex temporal dynamics and the spatial dependencies imposed by road topology. Supervised graph-based models achieve strong performance, but are often trained for a particular dataset and sensor graph, making deployment to new or evolving networks costly. Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) offer a zero-shot alternative by learning in-context inference from synthetic task priors, which provide an explicit mechanism for encoding domain-specific assumptions. Existing forecasting PFNs, however, do not explicitly represent the graph-structured dependencies governing traffic dynamics. To combine graph-aware traffic modeling with zero-shot adaptation, we introduce the Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Network (GAS-PFN). GAS-PFN incorporates sampled road topology into its synthetic task prior through random-walk diffusion, teaching the model to learn graph-coupled dynamics during pretraining. Its co-designed inference architecture uses two mask-conditioned passes through a shared Transformer backbone to separately model sensor-specific temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal interactions among neighboring sensors before integrating their representations for prediction. This design enables GAS-PFN to use target-network structure and context without parameter updates. Across six benchmarks at the 90-minute horizon, GAS-PFN reduces MSE by 34.0% on average relative to TimePFN, its closest PFN-based predecessor. It also reduces MSE by 27.7% on average relative to four recent industry-developed general-purpose zero-shot forecasters. In this comparison, all models receive 90 minutes of contiguous recent history, and any additional context is drawn from each dataset's chronological training split. These results indicate that aligning PFN priors and inference architectures with graph structure improves in-context learning for zero-shot traffic forecasting.

title: A Fast and Memory-Efficient Algorithm for Searching Faint Moving Objects using Synthetic Tracking
abstract: Detecting unknown faint moving objects using optical imaging is challenging. Long exposure times are infeasible for such targets, as the resulting image streaking causes a loss of signal-to-noise ratio due to energy dispersal across multiple pixels. To address this, synthetic tracking, a track-before-detect method, replaces long exposures with many short exposures, integrating them in post-processing to recover the moving signal. Enabled by modern CMOS detectors with fast readout and low read noise, this technique synthesizes telescope tracking by searching over a grid of velocities. However, the conventional brute-force implementation imposes a significant computational burden: integrating N_f frames of size (N_x,N_y) requires O(N_x N_y N_f^3) operations. This cost becomes prohibitive for megapixel-scale frames with N_f~100. Although dynamic programming can reduce the computational complexity by a factor of N_f, it requires a prohibitive memory of O(N_x N_y N_f^2), unsuitable for large-format detectors. This article presents a novel algorithm to achieve the computational efficiency of dynamic programming while maintaining a memory footprint of just O(N_x N_y N_f) by slightly approximating the computation of frame shifts for alignment. By expressing the shift as a sum of terms proportional to the digits frame index in binary and rounding up each of these terms, frames can be integrated efficiently by hierarchically adding intermediate sums that are shared across different velocities with the same higher bits in binary. The approximation only introduces a small tracking error that increases logarithmically with the number of frames. This advancement enables synthetic tracking to be executed with high energy efficiency, making it practical for deployment on standard workstations rather than requiring high-performance computing infrastructure such as GPU servers or CPU clusters.

title: TANDEM: Balancing Centralized and Decentralized Critics to Address the Information Gap in Complex Multi-Agent Environments
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) shapes decentralized policies with a centralized critic that observes the global state, then removes the critic at execution. The policies are optimized to rely on information they will not have when they act, an information gap between training and execution. It widens under partial observability, observation noise, and openness, where the set of agents and tasks present changes during an episode. Existing methods transfer centralized guidance in one direction only, removing or distilling the critic once, so the policies never rehearse acting without the critic while they can still be corrected. We propose TANDEM, which keeps one centralized critic and reads it two ways at each training step: a centralized read from the global state, and a decentralized read restricted to the information each agent will have at execution. A parameter-free gate compares the two reads for each agent and trains the policy on the decentralized read where they agree, reinstating the centralized read only where the local view is misleading. A shared target pulls the decentralized read toward the centralized one. We formalize the setting as a task- and agent-open decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (TAO-Dec-POMDP) and evaluate TANDEM on three cooperative domains, each isolating one form of the information gap: discovery for partial observability, sampling for observation noise, and openness in wildfire suppression. We compare against six CTDE baselines and ablate the gate and the shared target; the supplementary material holds the full variant sweep, diagnostics, and learning curves. We measure return at execution, once the centralized critic is removed. TANDEM is the best method on eight of the nine setups and never significantly worse than any baseline.

title: GNBG-C: A Unified and Configurable Benchmark Generator for Constrained Continuous Optimization
abstract: Many real-world optimization tasks are governed not only by what should be optimized, but also by what is allowed: a solution must first satisfy physical, operational, safety, budgetary, or structural requirements before its objective value becomes meaningful. Yet benchmark design for constrained continuous optimization often treats these restrictions as fixed properties of predefined test instances. Existing generators and benchmark suites provide essential foundations for reproducible comparison, but they either focus primarily on configurable objective landscapes or expose constraint properties within limited, predefined regimes, making it difficult to ask targeted questions about constraint-induced difficulty: whether an optimizer struggles because feasible regions are small, boundaries are restrictive, variables are tightly coupled, or constraint information is poorly scaled. We introduce GNBG-C, a Generalized Numerical Benchmark Generator for Constrained Continuous Optimization. The central idea is to treat the feasible region itself as a configurable object rather than as an inseparable attachment to a fixed test function. By generating controlled constraint regimes around the known GNBG global minimizer, the generator enables systematic studies in which feasibility pressure can be varied while preserving that point as a global minimizer of the constrained problem. This allows researchers to examine how optimizers discover feasibility, handle constraint pressure, and improve objective quality under diverse and controllable feasibility conditions. GNBG-C therefore provides a flexible and auditable framework for probing the strengths and weaknesses of constrained continuous optimizers under targeted forms of feasibility-side difficulty.

title: Every route counts, but some count more: a max-plus view of the C. elegans brain
abstract: Brains do not simply add up every signal they receive: they select which routes dominate. Yet connectomes are usually analyzed with tools that sum over all paths and place neural states in Euclidean spaces, blurring the feedback circuits that may sustain internal states. Here we treat neural signaling as routing instead of diffusion and describe it with max-plus algebra, in which signals accumulate along a path and the strongest route prevails. We propose a model in which the functional connectome of Caenorhabditis elegans emerges from the time-varying combination of electrical, synaptic, monoaminergic, neuropeptidergic and hormonal layers, and analyze five networks within this framework. Each collapses onto a handful of dominant feedback loops, which recover well-characterized circuits and point to new candidates for experimental study. Unlike linear spectra, these structures keep the biological meaning of the data, and their order-based description suggests that brain states live in lattices rather than Euclidean spaces.

title: On-the-fly Estimation of Quantum-Corrected Thermodynamics in LAMMPS
abstract: We present a native implementation of the Two/Three-Phase Thermodynamics (xPT, $x \in \{2,3\}$) method within the LAMMPS molecular dynamics framework, termed FixXPT. xPT is an approach for obtaining absolute, quantum-corrected thermodynamics (entropy, enthalpy, free energy, heat capacity, diffusivity) from the density of states function, obtained from the velocity autocorrelation function of an equilibrium trajectory. FixXPT addresses non-trivial integration challenges, including atom reordering, compute scheduling, FFT backends, unit systems, and partitioning of atomic velocities into molecular modes. Two autocorrelators are provided: a Wiener-Khinchin FFT correlator with one cumulative window-end operation, and an in-line multi-tau correlator whose memory footprint grows only logarithmically with the window length, removing the principal scaling bottleneck for long analysis windows. The velocity history of each window is distributed across the MPI ranks, so the memory the fix adds to a node stays nearly constant as ranks are added and its cost falls with the number of GPUs. Replaying identical velocity frames through FixXPT and the stand-alone pyxPT post-processor reproduces every thermodynamic observable of well-sampled groups to within 0.1 to 0.5% across the full analysis-mode matrix; sparsely populated ionic species agree within their statistical uncertainty, and the multi-tau VACF converges monotonically to the FFT result as its buffer grows, from 0.8% to 0.1% drift across a 16-fold buffer sweep. The code is distributed as a drop-in LAMMPS package.

title: Water at the molecular frontier
abstract: Much of the water that matters most - flowing through biological cells and membranes, percolating through soils and rocks, or processed by filtration and desalination technologies - is not bulk water. It is water in nano- and molecular-scale confinement or at interfaces. Nanoscale water is therefore central to many challenges of our time, from the global water crisis and the water-energy nexus to catalysis, electrochemistry, and health. Beyond its applications, nanoscale water has emerged as a rich scientific field in its own right: discoveries are accumulating rapidly, revealing that confinement and interfacial forces produce a range of behaviours absent in the bulk. Sometimes this amounts to a renormalization of bulk properties; in other cases, new and non-intuitive phenomena emerge - exotic phases, anomalous transport, and dielectric responses that defy continuum expectations. A convergence of atomically precise nanofluidic devices, novel spectroscopies and microscopy approaches, and machine-learning-accelerated simulations is now exposing the molecular mechanisms behind these behaviours. This Perspective argues that the recent findings should not be viewed as isolated nanoscale anomalies, but as evidence for a molecular regime of water in which continuum descriptions must be rethought and molecular-level understanding becomes essential. Recognising and exploring this regime should have consequences ranging from fundamental physics to the rational design of future technologies that rely on water and dissolved ions.

title: Spectral Braids: A Topological Descriptor for Dynamic Directed Networks
abstract: Eigenvalues are a workhorse of graph machine learning: spectral clustering, spectral graph neural networks, and graph kernels all summarize a network by the eigenvalues of a matrix. These eigenvalues are almost always treated as a static list of numbers. When a graph changes, however, its eigenvalues move, and when the matrix is not symmetric, they move in the complex plane, where they can wind around each other. The pattern of this winding is a braid, a classical object from topology. We propose spectral braids, a methodology for dynamic directed networks: each snapshot is aggregated into a community-level transition matrix, its complex eigenvalues are tracked over time, and the braid they trace is read off as a word. The word is then mapped to a matrix by the Burau representation, which gives a fixed-size feature vector for any classifier. The braid has a concrete meaning: each eigenvalue describes how a group of communities behaves, and each crossing records one group overtaking another. We evaluate the method on dynamic network classification, using synthetic networks of online communities whose labels describe how the network evolved between the same starting and ending states. Our experimental results show that the proposed features reach 97.1% accuracy on four classes, against 44.5% for the best feature set that does not track eigenvalues, and that the Burau features also separate networks containing the same events in a different order, which simple counts of crossings cannot do. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that defines braids and braid monodromy on graph data and uses them as features for learning on dynamic networks.

title: A cubic chromatic bound for capped graphs
abstract: An ordered graph is capped if, for any four vertices $a<b<c<d$, the edges $ac$ and $bd$ imply the edge $ad$. We prove that every nonempty capped graph $G$ satisfies $χ(G)\leq\min\{3^{ω(G)-1},18ω(G)^3\}$, where $χ(G)$ and $ω(G)$ are its chromatic number and clique number. This proves a conjecture of Davies, Krawczyk, McCarty and Walczak.

title: Quantum critical scaling in convective active matter
abstract: We construct a minimal field theory for critical quantum active matter, describing a nonconserved scalar order parameter with Landau-Ginzburg ordering and self-advection. When diffusive noise dominates, higher-order quantum vertices and non-Gaussian noise fluctuations remain relevant alongside the deterministic nonlinearities, with an upper critical dimension $d_c=2$. A one-loop renormalization-group analysis in $d=2-ε$ reveals a purely dissipative fixed point, where nonlinear noise suppresses convection, and a quantum convective saddle, where interactions, convection, and non-Gaussian noise coexist. We determine the critical exponents, show that the convective regime is distinct from conventional Burgers hydrodynamics, and discuss how it could govern transient universal scaling in microscopic models of quantum active matter before a crossover to semi-classical dynamics.

title: Activation force dependence of the fluidization transition in supercooled active water
abstract: Using an activation model reproducing facilitation mechanisms, we found recently a fluidization transition in supercooled water triggered by the motion of a few active molecules. We investigate here the effect of the activation force on the transition. The activation force increases the probability for active molecules to overcome the energy barrier induced by caging. The induced molecular motions result in an intermittent loose structure leading to a decrease of energy barriers around the moving molecule, thus facilitating the motion of nearby molecules. Therefore we expect the force, if small enough, to increase the facilitation mechanism, and as a result cooperative motions induced by it. As a result the activation force permits to tune facilitation and cooperative motions in active glass-formers. We find an optimum force for cooperative motions that we evaluate to be around 3.5pN, a value in the range of protein motor forces. As expected for a phase transition we observe peaks of cooperative motions (dynamic heterogeneity) on the transition. This result shows that dynamical heterogeneity are the cooperative motions of physical importance for the transition.

title: JWST/MIRI Observations of Amorphous Silicates in Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
abstract: We present JWST/MIRI Low Resolution Spectroscopy (LRS) of 3I/ATLAS obtained post-perihelion at a heliocentric distance of 2.21 au. Our spectrum contains a prominent 10 micron silicate emission feature with a broad, smooth shape that is distinct from those commonly observed in Solar System comets. We model the spectrum using thermal emission from amorphous carbon, amorphous olivine, and amorphous pyroxene grains. Our models strongly favor a pyroxene-dominated, amorphous silicate composition and show a degeneracy between silicate grain size and the relative abundance of silicate and carbon dust. Across a set of representative models, the best-fitting crystalline abundance is zero, and we place an upper limit of 5.3% on the crystalline fraction of the silicates. We identify an emission feature near 6.83 microns that is consistent with aliphatic C-H-bearing material. The overwhelmingly amorphous silicate composition supports previous work that measured unusual volatile and isotopic composition in suggesting that the material incorporated into the object experienced little thermal processing and preserves information about the conditions in which this interstellar planetesimal formed.

title: The packing and covering number of trees are local
abstract: For a graph, its $r$-packing number is the size of the largest $r$-separated set and its $r$-covering number is the size of the smallest $r$-net. We show that the $r$-covering number and $r$-packing number are continuous in the fringe topology on locally finite trees. This recovers convergence results by Meir and Moon for e.g. uniform binary trees, uniform plane trees, uniform Polyá trees and random recursive trees, and proves new results for many other tree models, such as size-conditioned Bienaymé trees, simply generated trees, $m$-ary search trees, the minimum spanning tree of the complete graph and preferential attachment trees. Moreover, our formulation provides an intuitive interpretation of the limiting constant, that also provides an easy route for explicit computations in the case of size-conditioned Bienaymé trees. Our method relies on the definition of a canonical minimum $r$-net, and a relation between covering numbers and packing numbers due to Meir and Moon.

title: Relative distality and incidence bounds in positive characteristic
abstract: We prove Szemerédi-Trotter-type incidence bounds for algebraic relations in any field $F$ admitting a valuation with finite residue field. This includes $\mathbb F_q(t)$, $\mathbb F_q((t))$, and all finitely generated extensions of finite fields. Bays and Martin show that any algebraic $K_{d,s}$-free relation $E\subseteq F^k\times F^\ell$ admits a power-saving in the classical Zarankiewicz bound of Kővári, Sós, and Turán. Answering a question of the authors, we show that this power-saving is uniform in $F$: There is some $ε>0$ depending only on $d$ and the complexity of $E$ (and not on $F$) such that for $A\subseteq F^k$ and $B\subseteq F^\ell$, the number of edges $|E(A,B)|$ is at most $O(|A|^{1-ε}|B|^{1-\frac{1-ε}{d}}+|A|+|B|)$. For the case where $A$ is a set of points and $B$ is a set of lines in $F^2$ and $E$ is the incidence relation, we prove the explicit bound $O(|P|^{\frac{8}{9}}|L|^{\frac{5}{9}}+|P|+|L|)$. As the central ingredient of the proof, we introduce the model-theoretic notion of distality relative to a definable set. We begin developing this notion and prove that the theory of algebraically closed valued fields is distal relative to the residue field.
