An application of a result of Chernikov, Peterzil, and Starchenko, based on work of Chernikov, Galvin, and Starchenko, yields our incidence bounds.

title: Global Hölder solvability for parabolic equations with interior Morrey data
abstract: We prove global Hölder solvability for uniformly parabolic divergence-form equations with locally finite measure data under an interior Morrey growth condition and a capacity density condition on the spatial domain. The parabolic distance to the initial and lateral boundary is assumed bounded on the source support. For nonnegative data, we establish necessity results that demonstrate the sharpness of the growth and domain assumptions. We also derive estimates for divergence forcing, prove solvability for equations with lower-order terms, and obtain convergence rates in periodic homogenization.

title: Fisher Completions and Statistical Regularization of Wrapped Gaussian Families
abstract: We determine the intrinsic Fisher completion of the full-covariance wrapped Gaussian family on a fixed torus and relate its geometry to uniform estimation. The completion is homeomorphic to the total-variation closure. Every added law is, in suitable integer torus coordinates, a product of a uniform law and a lower-dimensional wrapped Gaussian. All these densities are positive and real analytic, but in dimension at least two no added point has a compact neighborhood. Small balls remain contractible, and explicit minimizing geodesics pass through added points. In dimension at least two, every fixed Fisher neighborhood of an added point has a positive minimax risk at every sample size. For subfamilies with a common positive lower bound on the variance in every nonzero integer direction, we prove that compactness of the completed closure is equivalent to uniform consistency in either $L^1$ or completed-Fisher loss. Equivalently, the Fourier moments must decay uniformly over the subfamily. A fixed covariance floor guarantees this condition without an upper covariance bound and gives $L^1$ risk at most $C_{\varepsilon,d}n^{-1/2}\{\log(n+1)\}^{d/4}$. A common-phase example illustrates how partially uniform limits can retain relative-phase information while remaining uniformly estimable.

title: Approaching Optimal Scaling of Queue Size for an Input-Queued Switch
abstract: We study the scaling of the expected total queue length in an $n\times n$ input-queued switch. It has been conjectured that the optimal scaling is $O(n/(1-ρ))$, up to logarithmic factors, where $ρ$ is the system load. This conjecture has been established in the traditional heavy-traffic regime and in certain sub-regimes of the large-system regime. But it remains unresolved over a wide range of load scalings in the large-system regime. In this paper, we develop a family of scheduling policies parameterized by a positive integer $k\ge 2$. We show that under uniform traffic, our policy achieves an expected total queue length of $O\bigl({n\log\max\{n,1/(1-ρ)\}}\big/{(1-ρ)^{2^k/(2^k-1)}}\bigr)$, as long as $ρ\to 1$ in the large-system regime. As $k$ increases, the exponent $2^k/(2^k-1)$ approaches $1$, bringing our bound arbitrarily close to the conjectured scaling. The expected amortized scheduling cost of the policy is $O(n^3 k)$ per time slot. Our policy is of a batching type, with a novel recursive design that allows an arbitrary number of batching levels. This design principle may also be useful for other scheduling problems in which combinatorial constraints restrict which jobs can be served simultaneously.

title: Coprime matchings of divisor sets
abstract: For a positive integer $n$, let $D(n)$ be its set of positive divisors and put $N:=τ(n)=|D(n)|$. We characterize the arithmetic progressions $\mathcal P$ of length $N$ that admit a bijection with $D(n)$ pairing relatively prime integers. Such a coprime matching exists if and only if, for every prime $p\mid n$, at most $N/(ν_p(n)+1)$ terms of $\mathcal P$ are divisible by $p$, where $ν_p(n)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $n$. Call $n$ an $M$-number if $p^p\nmid n$ for every prime $p$. We prove that $D(n)$ can be matched with every primitive arithmetic progression of length $N$, meaning one whose first term and common difference are coprime, if and only if $n$ is an $M$-number. This proves a conjecture of McNew and Pomerance. We call $n$ \emph{matchable} if $D(n)$ admits a coprime matching with the primitive arithmetic progression $\{1,2,\ldots,N\}$. The general criterion implies that $n$ is matchable if and only if $\lfloor N/p\rfloor\le N/(ν_p(n)+1)$ for all $p\mid n$. We explicitly classify the matchable non-$M$-numbers, settle a conjectured divisor criterion, and prove that every divisor of a matchable integer is matchable. A Vandermonde determinant gives the required matchings under bounds on the prime exponents, while a partition into shorter progressions handles the remaining cases.

title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation
abstract: Online resource allocation faces two coupled challenges: (1) allocating scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand, and (2) ensuring that agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully (strategyproofness). Reinforcement Learning (RL) adapts allocation decisions through experience but does not necessarily ensure strategyproofness. Existing strategyproof RL uses a linear allocation rule, which limits the resource interactions it can represent. Neural mechanism design methods offer greater expressiveness, but provide only approximate incentive guarantees. Against this background, we introduce the first strategyproof deep RL mechanism for online resource allocation. It integrates three novel components: (i) a monotonic neural network that learns nonlinear interactions by construction (higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance, while a longer reported duration or larger resource requirement cannot increase it); (ii) a generalised critical payment: the lowest accepted value, with all other inputs fixed; and (iii) training by either RL or imitation of an existing rule. Together, monotonicity and the critical payment ensure strategyproofness and individual rationality, while the neural rule provides flexibility and imitation improves training efficiency. Empirically, on a four-resource stream with two partner pairs that a linear difference cannot represent, the neural rule achieves 97.8% of an offline welfare upper bound, compared with 93.8% for a linear learner and 89.0% for first-come, first-served, closing 65% and 80% of the remaining optimality gap, respectively. Moreover, imitation reaches 97.5% in only 261 seconds, about 89 times faster than RL.

title: Bounds for B-coloring planar and outerplanar graphs
abstract: A proper coloring of the edges of a graph is one in which every $K_{1,2}$ is totally multicolored. A B-coloring is a coloring of the edges of $G$ in which every $K_{1,2}$ and every $K_{2,2}$ is totally multicolored. In this paper, we improve two results by the authors and Gyárfás. The first shows that an outerplanar graph with maximum degree $Δ$ can be B-colored with $\max\{Δ,9\}$ colors, improving a bound of $Δ+1$ and this is best possible up to the constant 9. The second shows that a planar graph with maximum degree $Δ$ can be B-colored with $\max\{2Δ+4,22\}$, improving a bound of $2Δ+8$.

title: Molecular shape controls dipolar correlations in polar liquids
abstract: The dielectric constant of polar liquids depends not only on the magnitude of the molecular dipole moment but also on short range orientational correlations between neighboring dipoles. How molecular structure determines these correlations, quantified by the Kirkwood correlation factor $g_\mathrm{K}$, remains unclear. Using molecular dynamics simulations of model polar liquids without hydrogen bonding, we show that molecular shape plays a central role. We interpret $g_\mathrm{K}$ as resulting from the combination of dipolar interactions and steric effects, which together favor either alignment or antialignment of neighboring molecules. Depending on molecular shape, $g_\mathrm{K}$ can either increases or decreases upon cooling, or change monotony. A minimal model of dipoles on a cubic lattice reproduces these three regimes and attributes the nonmonotonic case to a competition between the first layer of neighbors, which favors alignment, and the second layer, which favors antialignment.

title: Revisiting Privacy Risks in Quantized Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Model quantization has become a fundamental technique for enabling the efficient deployment of large-scale deep neural networks (DNNs) in data-intensive applications by reducing model size. Despite its widespread adoption, the impact of quantization on training data privacy --- particularly vulnerability to membership inference attacks (MIAs) --- remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive empirical study of privacy risks in quantized DNNs, evaluating eight state-of-the-art MIA attacks across six representative quantization methods. Our results reveal that practical quantization levels (4-8 bits) have limited impact on membership privacy risks, with quantized models remaining largely as vulnerable as their full-precision counterparts. Although aggressive low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) can provide meaningful privacy gains, these benefits come at the cost of substantial utility degradation. To understand the underlying causes of these observations, we systematically analyze how different quantization strategies affect model behaviors and outputs, and how these changes influence privacy vulnerability. Beyond evaluating attack risks, we further investigate whether existing privacy defenses developed for full-precision DNNs can effectively protect QNNs. Our results show that these defenses provide only limited additional privacy protection when applied to quantized models, while further amplifying utility degradation. Our study provides practical guidance for privacy-aware deployment of quantized DNNs and motivates the development of new attack and defense mechanisms for QNNs. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/JeffffffFu/Priv-QDNN.

title: Sufficiency Theorem and Closed-Form Posterior for a Windowed Change Point Detection Task
abstract: To function effectively in a changing world, agents must detect changes and act on them in a timely fashion. We study this in the context of a change point detection task in which clicks arrive from a Poisson process whose rate changes at an unknown time. An agent must declare the change within a detection window of fixed width or the trial ends in a miss. Here we prove a window sufficiency theorem, which states that the posterior probability of a change depends only on the clicks within the most recent window, regardless of the prior on the change time. This result follows from combining survival conditioning, which rules out change times whose windows have already expired, with cancellations driven by independent increments of a known baseline process. Window sufficiency generalizes to an unknown post-change process, as long as the baseline process is known. For an exponential prior on the change time, we further derive the posterior in closed form as a function of the elapsed times since each click in the most recent window, the known rates, and the window width. These results suggest that discarding old evidence can be optimal rather than a limitation when decisions face a deadline.

title: HGPRGDel: GPR-Aware Learning and Ranking for Growth-Coupled Gene Deletion Design
abstract: Designing microbial strains for growth-coupled production, in which cellular growth is linked to the synthesis of a target compound through genetic interventions, is a fundamental goal in metabolic engineering. Constraint-based methods can identify growth-coupled deletion strategies, but design for each target typically requires a separate search across a large number of possible gene-deletion combinations. This motivates a reusable approach that learns from previously evaluated strain designs to prioritize candidate interventions before downstream constraint-based evaluation. We present a reproducible protocol for growth-coupled gene deletion design that learns and ranks gene-deletion priorities for each target metabolite. Using computationally curated deletion strategies as learning resources, the protocol generates continuous deletion-priority rankings, constructs candidate strategies at adjustable search-space budgets, and evaluates these candidates through constraint-based metabolic analysis. Its learning component, HGPRGDel, explicitly represents gene-protein-reaction (GPR) logic, capturing how multiple genes can jointly support a reaction or alternative genes can maintain its activity, while integrating molecular and reaction-level information. Across e_coli_core, iMM904, and iML1515, the protocol achieves the highest macro-F1 and AUC among the evaluated learning configurations. HGPRGDel's rankings recovered an average of 90% of the reference deletion genes from MetNetComp by examining fewer genes than the evaluated baseline methods. By separating learned intervention prioritization from downstream constraint-based assessment, the protocol provides a reproducible framework for reusing strain-design knowledge while controlling the size of the candidate space and retaining mechanistic evaluation of growth-coupled production.

title: The Assouad Dimension of Graphs: An Affirmative Answer to Fraser's Question
abstract: This article primarily investigates the Assouad dimension of graphs of continuous functions. Initially, the Assouad spectrum of the graph of a Hölder and count-Hölder continuous function has been derived. It has been shown that the Assouad dimension of the graph of a continuous function $f:[a,b]\to \mathbb{R}$ with the count-Hölder condition is at least \( 1 + \sup \left\{ \overline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}L_f(y) : y \in \mathscr{R}_f[a,b]\right\} \) where $\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm{B}}$ denotes the upper box dimension, $L_f(y)$ is the level set of $f$ at level $y$, and $\mathscr{R}_f[a,b]$ is the range of $f$ on $[a,b]$. As a consequence, non-trivial lower bounds are obtained for the Assouad dimension of the graphs of classical functions such as the Weierstrass and Takagi functions. We have also employed a unified projection solely in the direction of the $y$-axis to establish lower and upper bounds for the Assouad dimension. On this basis, we have shown that the lower bound is sharp in terms of level sets, namely the upper box dimension cannot be replaced by the Assouad dimension. This provides a partial positive answer to Question 17.11.1 posed by Fraser in~\cite{Fraser2021}, and to Question 2.2 posed by Yu in~\cite{Yu2020}. Building on this result, the analysis has been further extended to a broader class of Weierstrass-type functions and some self-affine functions like fractal interpolation functions. Moreover, we have discussed certain circumstances under which the Assouad dimension can reach 2 with several examples constructed. A supplementary explanation of why Brownian motion has the full Assouad dimension has also been provided based on the preceding work of Howroyd and Yu \cite{Howroyd2019}.

title: No Connectedness Lemma for Alexandrov spaces
abstract: Since its introduction in 2003, Wilking's Connectedness Lemma has become a powerful tool in the study of manifolds with positive sectional curvature. In recent work of the authors, this has been extended to orbifolds. The purpose of this note is to exhibit counterexamples in the class of Alexandrov spaces for the Connectedness Lemma in both its ordinary and dual formulation. This answers a 2007 question of Wilking.

title: Neglecting Dynamical Microlensing Can Bias Accretion Disk Size Measurements at the Population Level
abstract: Microlensing of strongly lensed quasars probes unresolved accretion disks, but many inference methods use static magnification maps with fixed relative microlens positions. Using the GPU-accelerated simulator Microcaustics, we generate ten-year multiband light curves for three quadruply lensed quasar configurations. We compare dynamical microlensing with independent microlens motions against coherent bulk motion, and a microlens mass distribution against equal masses, keeping the velocity distribution of individual microlenses and mean mass fixed. We infer population disk sizes using ridge regression on the means and lower and upper scatters of ten variability and event metrics. We measure biases by applying models trained with simplified physics to simulations including both effects. Models trained on coherent motion interpret the additional variability from evolving caustics as smaller disks. For populations of 128 independent realizations, jointly inferred radii are consistently smaller by 6-28%. Microlens dynamics increase caustic-crossing rates pooled across all four macroimages by 5-15% and r-band high-magnification-event (HME) rates by 13-25%, while shortening median HME durations by 4-12%. Omitting the mass distribution produces configuration-dependent disk-size offsets from -12% to +5%. Including the mass distribution decreases caustic-crossing rates by 6-8% and HME rates by 6-12%. It also narrows the spread of ten-year averaged microlensing time-delay differences between macroimages by a median of 9-12% per system, while microlens dynamics have a smaller, image-pair-dependent effect. These results demonstrate the importance of microlens dynamics for population disk-size inference and motivate simulations that include dynamical microlensing and a microlens mass distribution.

title: When POST Becomes GET: Investigating HTTP Method Interchangeability and Its Security Implications
abstract: HTTP method semantics are a common boundary between safe retrieval and state-changing operations; however, deployed web applications do not always enforce this boundary consistently. In this paper, we study HTTP method interchangeability, a behavior where a POST request can be rewritten as a GET request to the same endpoint, with POST body parameters moved into the query string, while preserving an equivalent observed response. We present Method Interchange Detection Engine (MIDE), an automated pipeline that crawls web applications in a browser, records POST requests generated by page loads and user-interface interactions, converts supported POST bodies into GET candidates, and compares replayed responses with the original POST response. To avoid counting generic or parameter-independent responses as interchangeable, MIDE also sends a no-query GET baseline. We treat as high-confidence evidence of interchangeability only the cases where the converted GET matches the POST, while the baseline does not. We perform a large-scale unauthenticated experiment on the Tranco top 10k. We find high-confidence interchangeable requests on 407 of 10,000 tested sites (4.1%), 407 of 3,200 sites with captured POSTs (12.7%), and 407 of 2,734 sites with replayed POSTs (14.9%). A targeted Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) token-replay check finds cases where invalid tokens are rejected for POST but accepted for the equivalent GET. We also observe Web Cache Deception (WCD) conditions and cacheable GET responses for interchangeable request instances. These results demonstrate that method interchangeability is observable in real web applications and can expose method-scoped defense gaps.

title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.

title: Who Shaped What? Untangling Human and AI Creative Contributions Through Spatial Provenance in Image Editing
abstract: Images co-edited with AI are often labeled to disclose AI use. However, creators feel these labels do not sufficiently describe their contributions to the editing process. Editing histories preserve requests, suggestions, and revisions, but how do creators use these logs to judge contribution? We investigated this with Roop, a mixed-initiative design probe that links image regions to editing histories (spatial provenance) and summarizes interactions in a heat map. Twenty participants edited images, annotated human and AI contributions, then reviewed the spatial provenance heat map. Participants credited themselves for directing changes while crediting AI for determining visual details. They judged contribution partly by whether their interactions achieved their intentions. Reviewing provenance helped participants remember interactions without always changing whom they credited. These findings motivate provenance systems that preserve enough context for creators to explain how interactions shaped their work, alongside the record of what happened.

title: Penny for Your Prompts: A Measurement Study of Contextual Leakage in AI Chat Platforms
abstract: AI chatbot platforms have become one of the most popular web interfaces users interact with online, routinely receiving personal and intimate information shared under an expectation of privacy. Yet, on the web application side, these platforms have the ability to embed third-party analytics, advertising, and session replay scripts that operate silently alongside the chatbot, creating an underexamined channel for conversational data leakage towards third parties. We conduct the first systematic large-scale measurement study of contextual leakage in AI chatbots, auditing the web interfaces of 42 general-purpose and domain-specific (health, legal, and education) platforms. Beyond standard network interception, we instrument the browser at the JavaScript engine level to attribute each data flow to the exact user action that triggered it, and the DOM capture mechanism used to retrieve its content, a granularity invisible to network-layer analysis alone. We find that 21 of these platforms leak conversation titles to third-party trackers, while nine leak verbatim user prompts. Beyond content, we observe a substantial amount of chatbot platforms sending user emails to third-party trackers, enabling the association of conversational context with a user's identity. Our findings cast traditional web privacy issues under a new light, highlighting the privacy issues that are inherent in how users interact with modern AI chatbots.

title: Local Law and Eigenvector Delocalization for Random Lifts
abstract: We establish a quantitative local law for random $N$-lifts of a fixed finite connected simple graph with minimum degree at least three. Away from the singular energies of the universal-cover spectrum, we obtain high-probability entrywise Green's function estimates down to spectral scales $(\log N)^C/N$, uniformly in the bulk and near regular edges and cusps. As a consequence, we establish complete eigenvector delocalization: every normalized eigenvector $u$ whose eigenvalue stays a small but fixed positive distance away from the singular energies satisfies $\|u\|_\infty\leq(\log N)^C/\sqrt{N}$ with high probability.

title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents
abstract: Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.

title: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version)
abstract: Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a microarchitectural optimization recently introduced in mainstream desktop and server CPUs. Although DMPs offer performance improvements, they have been shown to enable side-channel leakage of secrets, even from constant-time code that has been hardened against Spectre attacks. Unfortunately, existing defenses either incur significant performance overhead or, as we show, fail to prevent all DMP leakage. In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture---without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.

title: Test-Time Communication in Trading Agent Swarms
abstract: Communication between agents has mostly been studied on tasks with a shared objective and fast, clear feedback. Trading has neither: each agent manages its own account, with decisions being scored by markets late and noisily. A trading swarm is thus a population of independent decision-makers rather than a team, for which convergence is a risk and not the goal. We ran 200 agents from four model families in groups of ten under five communication regimes, from isolation to message boards and shared notes, over seven US trading days (1 to 9 October 2026), logging everything each agent read before every decision. In two of the four families, communicating groups came to hold far more of the same stocks than the isolated group. A group's return was largely the return on what its members held in common. Seeing a post from a groupmate made an agent 7 percentage points more likely to reuse an eight-word phrase from it. Agents that started too close together to see each other's posts shared such a phrase in 14% of cases, the rate that common inputs produce. Seeing the post did not detectably change that morning's trades. Case studies traced the adoption of positions and decision rules over subsequent days, and communicating groups sold in step more often than isolated ones. Because isolated groups also converged on the same stocks, sometimes completely, assessments of herding need to measure excess convergence relative to a no-peer baseline.

title: PolyGandr: Steering Generative Models via Spatial Navigation through Latent Space
abstract: Generative models support content creation across text, images, videos, and design disciplines, yet their interfaces rely primarily on natural language. While effective for specifying high-level intent, language can be inefficient and imprecise for fine-grained control, iterative refinement, and open-ended exploration. We present PolyGandr, a visual interface for exploring relationships between latent representations and generated outputs, complementing natural-language model steering. PolyGandr formulates generative control as high-dimensional navigation, enabling users to define starting points, steering directions, and step sizes through a unified map-and-mixing-palette interface. Combining global exploration with local refinement supports both broad design-space navigation and fine-grained output manipulation without repeatedly translating visual intent into prompts. We evaluate PolyGandr across three use cases: StyleGAN2 face generation, Stable Diffusion chair design, and rotational kirigami engineering. A formative study indicates that PolyGandr complements existing workflows by supporting real-time editing while simultaneously providing an overview and means to explore the broader design space.

title: Flatness-based control of nonlinear complex networks
abstract: Effective control of nonlinear complex networks needs to identify not only the intervention sites but also the state variables to be monitored and the locations at which control inputs should be applied. Here, we present a network-scale generalization of an observability-guided, flatness-based control framework. The resulting control laws are implemented using sliding-mode control and evaluated in heterogeneous networks of chaotic oscillators driven toward a prescribed periodic regime. We compare two control architectures: in the node-wise method, oscillators are independently sensed and actuated, while in the pairwise method, measurements acquired from a single node within each dyad are used to synthesize control inputs applied to both nodes. Across the parameter regimes considered, node-wise control generally achieves accurate control over a broader operating region, whereas pairwise control remains effective over a more restricted region while using half as many measurement locations for a given number of actuated nodes. Moreover, network interactions can enhance control by propagating the control influence to non-actuated nodes, creating a cooperative effect between the collective dynamics and the control action. Collectively, these findings quantify the trade-offs among measurement-location requirements, control performance, and control effort in nonlinear complex networks.

title: Time-Dynamic Semantic-Activity Entanglement: Quantifying Communication-Based Synchrony in Collaborative VR
abstract: Collaborative virtual reality (VR) produces rich multimodal traces of team behavior, yet practical methods for characterizing time-varying team communication remain limited. We present time-dynamic semantic-activity entanglement (TSAE), inspired by the entanglement concept introduced by Gloor et al. (2022), to describe communication-based team synchronization within discrete time windows. TSAE is modeled by combining relative speaking activity with contextual semantic alignment for participant pairs, which is aggregated into participant-level trajectories and summarized through the Gini coefficient to understand the distribution of team-level communication synchrony. This approach is employed with German-language transcripts from fifteen collaborative VR gameplay sessions. Transcript utterances are represented using a long-context embedding model with a late-chunking strategy and analyzed within fixed game-time windows. A representative session illustrates shifting dyadic alignment and low-to-moderate participant contributions, with sporadic periods of high entanglement. Across fifteen game sessions, the metrics indicate complementary insights, offering a qualitative contrast to the core-periphery pattern reported in the foundational work. Hence, these descriptive findings support the study of communication as a dynamic process and provide a mathematically grounded approach to analyze its evolving distribution in shared interactive VR spaces.

title: Chaos picture of spin glasses
abstract: The chaos picture is a novel, coherent, and intuitive theoretical framework for spin glasses, reconciling the 40-year-old droplet vs. replica symmetry breaking debate. First, we argue the formation of a hierarchical energy landscape by pinning and dynamic filtering of random droplets. As the temperature decreases, the chaos picture describes a progressive freezing of scale-dependent droplets in real space, which mirrors a hierarchical free energy landscape fracturing process in phase space. This bifurcation process is accompanied by temperature chaos, leading to dynamic pure state coexistence without violating the droplet scaling. Crucially, the interface geometry is not critical to these mechanisms, naturally incorporating the interface crossover from planar, fractal, to space-filling as the dimensionality increases, in line with the mean-field limit. Finally, the chaos picture provides profound insights into spin-glass dynamics such as aging, rejuvenation, and memory effect, while offering a streamlined reinterpretation of the complex metastate framework.

title: Phase-type representations for Strong Stability Preserving Runge--Kutta methods
abstract: We develop a phase-type (PH) representation of strong stability preserving (SSP) Runge--Kutta (RK) methods. This representation provides a probabilistic interpretation of the RK coefficients and translates the chain order conditions into absorption-time moment identities. Using moment ratio bounds for PH distributions, we prove the conjectured optimal SSP coefficients for general implicit RK methods of orders two and three. The equality characterizations also establish uniqueness of the optimal RK tableaux.

title: Sharp Bounds for Toral Eigenfunctions and Threefold Additive Energy on Circles
abstract: For the lattice circle $P_n=\{z\in\mathbb{Z}^2:|z|^2=n\}$, we prove that the threefold additive energy $J_3(P_n)\le C|P_n|^3$, with an absolute constant $C$. This establishes the optimal bound suggested by Krishnapur--Kurlberg--Wigman and Bombieri--Bourgain. We also prove a uniform weak $L^6$ bound for $L^2$-normalized eigenfunctions on the square torus, and hence uniform $L^p$ bounds for every $1\le p<6$. This extends the classical $L^4$ bounds of Cooke and Zygmund and establishes Bourgain's conjecture in this range. Applications include mean-square convergence for $L^{6/5}$ observables and a logarithm-free remainder in the nodal length variance of arithmetic random waves.

title: Equidistant Affine Subspaces: Explicit Bounds, Codimension-Two Reduction, and Transverse Products
abstract: Let $\mathcal{N}(k,n)$ be the largest size of a family of affine $k$-planes in $\R^n$ at pairwise separation distance one. We develop a unified treatment of upper bounds, dimension reduction, and product constructions. Orthogonal-projection coordinates give a rank-stratified distance identity; a Veronese lifting converts its polynomial consequences into simultaneous total isotropy. Connected Nash decomposition and an analytic diagonal argument replace the linear-independence step in Höfer's three-dimensional method. An explicit cylindrical decomposition estimate yields $\mathcal{N}(k,n)\leqslant 2^{\,2^{\,3(k+1)(n-k)}}$. For configurations whose direction sums have dimension at most $k+1$, we prove the exact reduction $\mathcal{N}_{\leqslant k+1}(k,n)=\mathcal{N}(1,n-k+1)$. Every codimension-two equidistant configuration splits off a common linear factor, giving $\mathcal{N}(n-2,n)=\mathcal{N}(1,3)$. We also determine the sharp bound $2(n-k)$ when all directions lie in a fixed $(k+1)$-dimensional subspace. A transverse product construction gives multiplicative inequalities and makes $S(c)=\mathcal{N}(c-1,2c-1)$ supermultiplicative. In particular, $S(c)\geqslant 2^{c\bmod 2}7^{\lfloor c/2\rfloor}$. The structural results and constructions do not depend on the exact value of $\mathcal{N}(1,3)$.

title: Typical Kakeya-type sets and their typical code sets
abstract: We study properties of compact Besicovitch sets and other Kakeya-type sets which are typical in the sense that the exceptions form a meager set in the Baire category sense in a suitable metric space. The main motivation comes from the known fact that typical compact Besicovitch sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ have minimal Hausdorff dimension among all Besicovitch sets of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Thus, in order to estimate the smallest possible Hausdorff dimension of an arbitrary Besicovitch set, it is enough to estimate the Hausdorff dimension of a typical (compact) Besicovitch set, or analogously of a Besicovitch set satisfying our list of typical properties. Among other results, we prove that a typical Besicovitch set $K$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ has the following properties: it is not sticky, any line intersects $K$ in a set of ($1$-dimensional) measure zero or in a unit line segment and a set of measure zero, it has no more than $n$ different unit line segments in any direction, and for each $1\le j\le n$ the Hausdorff dimension of the set of those directions in which $K$ has exactly $j$ unit line segments is $n-j$. For compact metric spaces $X$ and $Y$, let $\mathcal{C}(X,Y)$ denote the set of compact subsets of $X\times Y$ whose projection onto the first coordinate is $X$, equipped with the Hausdorff metric. Kakeya-type compact sets can be coded by elements of such spaces, allowing typical properties to be studied through comeager subsets of $\mathcal C(X,Y)$. Among other results, we prove that, under suitable conditions on $X$ and $Y$, a typical $A\in \mathcal{C}(X,Y)$ is totally disconnected and purely unrectifiable, its projection to the second coordinate has Hausdorff dimension zero, and the dimension identities $\dim_H(A)=\dim_H(X)$ and $\dim_P(A)=\dim_P(X)+\dim Y$ hold.

title: Neighborhood Deprivation Shapes Post-Flood Population Losses in Pune and Bandung
abstract: Disaster research in high-income settings shows that better-resourced communities see population inflows and faster recovery, while disadvantaged communities suffer prolonged population loss. Whether this pattern holds in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South remains unclear. Here we show, using mobile phone data from Pune, India, and Bandung, Indonesia, how neighborhood-level changes in phone presence, a proxy for short-term population movement, relate to flooding and neighborhood deprivation. We combine satellite-derived flood maps with phone records to compare flooded and non-flooded areas over the 30 days around each flood. In both cities, less deprived neighborhoods see phone presence rise after flooding, while more deprived neighborhoods see it fall, consistent with resource-seeking interpretations documented in North American and European disaster research. The cities differed, however, in how deprivation relates to flood exposure: in Pune, more deprived flooded neighborhoods showed suggestive evidence of disproportionately larger decreases in detected device presence than similarly deprived non-flooded neighborhoods; no comparable interaction was observed in Bandung. Economic considerations are associated with post-flood device-presence changes in South and Southeast Asian cities in ways that parallel high-income contexts, though local context adds variation.

title: Nonexistence of Hadamard difference sets in groups of order $4p^2$ with $p\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, $p\ge 7$
abstract: We show that the Frobenius group $\langle x,y,z\mid x^p=y^p=z^4=1,\ xy=yx,\ zxz^{-1}=y,\ zyz^{-1}=x^{-1}\rangle$ of order $4p^2$ contains no $(4p^2,2p^2-p,p^2-p)$ difference set if $p\equiv 3\pmod 4$ is a prime with $p \geq 7$. Together with results of McFarland, Iiams and Liebler this shows that no group of order $4p^2$ with $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ and $p \geq 7$ contains a Hadamard difference set.

title: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense
abstract: Prior work framed the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent, and established it as a defense surface independent of the LLM layer and the agent layer; however, that work only tested the envelope layer briefly and did not examine how label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffold differences, or existing memories affect defense effectiveness. Following its GDA Measurement methodology and the A/B/C/D outcome taxonomy, this paper takes the A2A-TIBA attack as the test vehicle, uses the semantic breach rate as the primary indicator with the semantic refusal rate as its complementary reference, and characterizes the security boundary of the envelope layer through a two-by-two factorial experiment and a memory experiment. The results show that: when the envelope is authentic, strong labels consistently reduce the semantic breach rate, whereas weak labels are not necessarily better than an unlabeled baseline; when the envelope can be forged, the benefit of strong labels is weakened and its direction varies across frontends; and memory has a larger effect than any label manipulation: success memory raises the semantic breach rate while failure memory lowers it, and most combinations that contain both experiences return to the no-memory baseline. Accordingly, this paper refines the envelope layer from a single admission channel into two levels, an admission channel plus a context assembly surface, and argues that its security boundary is not a fixed property of labels but a dynamic outcome jointly shaped by label claims, frontend permissions, and historical memory.

title: Displacement Moments and Path-Terminal Separation in Brownian Interpolant Sampling
abstract: Brownian stochastic interpolants connect paired endpoint samples, yet their sampling error can depend on displacement moments even when neither endpoint has a first moment. For arbitrary Borel couplings, we prove early-stopped, target-to-output KL guarantees for standard Euler sampling from the true source. A fourth displacement moment gives an explicit $O(N^{-1})$ bound; a second moment suffices for fixed-law convergence as drift error vanishes. For one fixed coupling with no displacement moment above two, original bridge-path KL stays of order one, comparison-path KL is of order $1/\log N$, and terminal KL is at most $C/N^2$ on the same grid. The path decomposition identifies the information about the source discarded by Markov projection. When the original bridge is Markov, current-state Euler sampling instead has a second-moment $O((M_2+d)/N)$ bound; finite-entropy Schroedinger bridges for the probability Brownian reference are included. We also construct a current-state learner with expected output KL consistency from iid endpoint pairs. Numerical diagnostics illustrate the distinct errors. Conditional diffusion identities specify a restoration interface, while image controls find no iterative advantage over cheap probabilistic predictors. Uniform terminal rates for general second-moment couplings remain open.

title: Accurate structural modelling of protein-glycan recognition with GlycoWeave
abstract: Protein-glycan recognition underlies diverse biological processes, yet accurate prediction of protein-glycan complex structures remains challenging owing to the chemical diversity, conformational flexibility and sparse experimental structural coverage of glycans. Here we present GlycoWeave, a glycan-specific diffusion framework that integrates chemically constrained conformational sampling, multiscale molecular representations and multi-source learning. By operating in internal-coordinate space, GlycoWeave preserves glycan connectivity and stereochemistry while efficiently exploring bound conformations. A heterogeneous equivariant network couples atom-level interaction geometry with monosaccharide-level structural context, whereas multi-source, multi-head training integrates experimental complexes with structures refined using classical and quantum mechanics-informed potentials. On a benchmark of 698 protein-glycan complexes, GlycoWeave achieves a 71.9% Top-25 high-quality success rate, compared with 19.2% for AlphaFold 3, while requiring only 0.34 s per sampled pose. GlycoWeave further preserves glycan structural validity, recovers native protein-glycan interactions and reproduces linkage-specific conformational preferences, maintaining high accuracy across diverse glycan architectures and protein environments. These results establish GlycoWeave as an accurate, efficient and chemically faithful framework for modelling protein-glycan recognition. GlycoWeave is freely available at https://cadd.zju.edu.cn/glycoweave.

title: High powers of grids in random geometric graphs and thresholds for wide spanning structures
abstract: Using results of Leighton and Shor and of Shor and Yukich, we present a connection between $d$-dimensional bandwidth and (sharp) thresholds in $d$-dimensional random geometric graphs: namely, that the sharp threshold for a given graph property in random geometric graphs is determined by its $d$-dimensional bandwidth, and vice versa, whenever the $d$-dimensional bandwidth of this property grows sufficiently fast (at least polylogarithmically) with the order of the graphs. This connection provides a number of corollaries, such as new information about the sharp thresholds for containing different spanning subgraphs in $1$-dimensional random geometric graphs, as well as asymptotically tight bounds for the $d$-dimensional bandwidth of structures such as graphs of bounded treewidth or genus, giving an asymptotic resolution to several problems raised by Chung in 1988.

title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution
abstract: Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations. A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral. The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.

title: A semigroup approach for rough partial differential equations with jumps
abstract: We establish an infinite-dimensional sewing lemma for discontinuous paths on a scale of Banach spaces. This allows us to construct Young and rough convolutions with jumps. Based on this we analyze the local and global well-posedness of semilinear parabolic rough partial differential equations (PDEs) with jumps in mixed space-time regularity spaces.

title: Representation and abelianization growth, particularly along expanding sequences
abstract: We study two obstructions to a finite group $G$ having a generating $d$-tuple whose Cayley graph has spectral gap at least $ε$. Lubotzky and Weiss proved that such a gap forces $\mathrm{ab}_k(G)$, the largest order of the abelianization of a subgroup of index at most $k$, to be $\exp(O_ε(dk))$, while de la Harpe, Robertson and Valette proved that it forces $\mathrm{rep}_k(G)$, the number of irreducible complex representations of degree at most $k$, to be $\exp(O_ε(dk^2))$. We show that the first bound implies the second, and in fact implies it with $k^2$ replaced by $k\log k$. For this, we prove that every finite $d$-generated group satisfies the inequality $\mathrm{rep}_k(G)\leq\exp((d-1)k\log k+O(dk))\cdot\mathrm{ab}_k(G)$, regardless of its spectral gap. The leading term $(d-1)k\log k$ is attained by powers of alternating groups, and it disappears for groups without large alternating sections. The proof reduces to counting the finite primitive subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_m(\mathbf{C})$, and we show that there are at most $\exp(O(\log^4m))$ of them up to conjugacy and scalars. Wigderson asked whether $k^2$ in the second bound can be lowered to $k$, so our result answers his question up to a logarithm. We do not know whether the logarithm is actually needed. For powers of alternating groups, the natural candidates, we show that a spectral gap keeps the number of factors a fixed power below the maximum allowed by $d$-generation, and that random generators have spectral gap tending to $0$ already for superpolynomially many factors.

title: Game-Theoretic Solvers with Bayesian Opponent Modeling and Moral Rhetoric Framing for GLEE
abstract: We describe the agent we submitted to the GLEE Competition, which plays bargaining, negotiation, and persuasion games against a shared pool of human and AI opponents. The agent is built around three central components: a classical game-theoretic solver to compute numeric moves, an online Bayesian layer to estimate opponent archetypes, and a language model to write accompanying messages. We utilize Rubinstein bargaining for bargaining, Faratin concession for negotiation, and Kamenica--Gentzkow disclosure for persuasion, and adapt those models to live opponents using two separate layers: a Bayesian estimate of the opponent's hidden discount factor, reservation value, or signaling reliability, and a Thompson sampling bandit over five moral-foundation framings coupled with an evidence-intuition spectrum to establish message register. Most of the development effort went into the recurring problem that theoretically optimal policies perform poorly in certain live settings; we report associated failure modes, guardrails we built, and our hypotheses. We additionally evaluate our model over 13,200 Monte Carlo games against 11 synthetic opponent archetypes, an ablation of the opponent-modeling layer, and an extensive analysis of 9,337 live-game messages in which moral rhetoric framing in the persuasion setting is strongly correlated with whether the buyer purchased ($χ^2=616.7$, $p \approx 3.7\times10^{-132}$), surviving controls for quality, round, and configuration.

title: Code uniqueness of 4-cell connected disjoint clusters in spatial chromatic model
abstract: The spatial chromatic model (SCM) is a novel entity-oriented spatial data model proposed in recent years. Spatial tessellations formed by SCM have been applied in preliminary analyses of spatial point pattern recognition,spatial topology, and Voronoi diagram generation. Unlike previous spatial tessellation models, a key feature of SCM is that each subspace (cell) possesses a chromatic code, which serves as the foundation for various theoretical analyses and applications of SCM. The uniqueness of cell cluster codes in SCM constitutes an important property of the model. Previous studies have demonstrated the uniqueness of the chromatic codes of 2-cell and 3-cell connected disjoint clusters. Building on this analysis of connected cluster code characteristics, this paper proves the uniqueness of the chromatic codes of 4-cell connected disjoint clusters. The proof results and the new concepts introduced in this study help further refine the spatial chromatic model and provide a theoretical foundation for its subsequent applications.

title: Para-Gaussian Approximations of Random Deep Neural Networks
abstract: It is known that randomly initialized neural networks have Gaussian behaviour in the $n\to \infty$ limit. Unfortunately, this approximation can be poor for finite $n$ and gets worse as one goes deeper into the network. In this work, we develop a more accurate approximation that is \emph{slightly} non-Gaussian, which we call the para-Gaussian distribution and is constructed from the Hermite polynomials. We show how this para-Gaussian approximation can lead to a practical recursive method to approximate the deeper layers of the network. Finally, we apply this theory to linear neural networks (where things can be solved exactly) and to ReLU neural networks (where things can be approximated).

title: Agent-Conditioned Routing: Diverse Reasoning Paths Within One Frozen Model
abstract: Generating several solutions can expose alternative methods, but additional trajectories often paraphrase one dominant approach. We investigate whether the conditional capacity of a frozen sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can provide such diversity from one problem prompt, without user-assigned roles, prescribed methods, fine-tuning, or model copies. Agent-Conditioned Routing (ACR) assigns $m$ parallel trajectories persistent, untrained shared/private expert-eligibility masks while preserving the learned, input-dependent token router. On a screened 126-question multi-mode mathematics and physics benchmark, with model judges reading the reported derivations in full, we count the number of problems yielding at least two distinct primary methods among soft-correct solutions in four trajectories. ACR reaches approximately twice as many such problems as the strongest temperature setting under GLM 5.3 (37.3 versus 18.7), and 1.67 times as many under GPT-5.6 Sol (45.00 versus 27.00), at matched output budgets. A blinded four-expert audit on a stratified sample of 30 problems also finds more multi-method solutions with ACR on both backbones, with lower correctness. Matched-eligibility ablations show modest multi-method count advantages for ACR, while token-resampled masks attain higher correctness. An informed sequential prompt elicits more diversity still, using previous solutions and explicit requests for alternative methods. ACR adds about 160 KiB of mask state. In a three-problem microbenchmark capped at 1,024 tokens, its latency and peak VRAM usage remain within 3% of batched temperature sampling.

title: Comparing Temporal Deep Learning Architectures for Discrete Cross-User Myoelectric Control
abstract: The recognition of dynamic gestures via discrete myoelectric control is becoming an attractive input modality for event-based human-machine interaction. While recent work suggests that discrete cross-user models are possible (i.e., no calibration data is required from the end user), few have evaluated techniques to optimize these systems and their generalizability to new randomly prompted data simulating real-world discrete control is relatively unknown. Using the 612-user EMG-EPN dataset, this work benchmarks five temporal deep-learning approaches, evaluates the tradeoff between performance and model complexity, and compares hand-crafted and machine-learned feature extraction techniques. The CNN-GRU achieved the best accuracy of 93% when tested on 184 previously unseen users. These models were then evaluated on a different, more realistic, unsegmented dataset, wherein users were randomly prompted to elicit discrete gestures during a continuous data collection. This dataset was recorded five years apart and in a separate country from the data used to train the original model. Results show that the cross-user results scale to this new dataset (accuracies of 96%) even though no feedback was given to users during the elicitation of gestures. These findings highlight the exciting potential of discrete zero-shot cross-user myoelectric control and offer valuable insights for the continued advancement of this promising technology.

title: Stationary Coexistence in Stochastic Gause Systems with General Trophic Responses
abstract: We study stationary coexistence in stochastic Gause predator-prey systems with independent multiplicative environmental noise and trophic responses depending on both population densities. A weighted population balance cancels the trophic interaction and yields moments of order greater than one without imposing predator self-regulation. These estimates give a direct occupation-measure proof of a sufficient coexistence criterion based on prey establishment and predator invasion of the prey-only stationary environment. For responses whose rare-predator limit is strictly increasing and whose value at positive predator density never exceeds that limit, we also establish necessity of positive predator invasion whenever the prey-only stationary law exists. If the prey per-capita growth attains its global maximum at zero, interior stationarity itself forces prey establishment, giving a necessary-and-sufficient criterion beyond logistic growth. Logistic and bounded saturating growth laws provide explicit Gamma and beta-prime resident distributions. Applications include Holling, Ivlev, Beddington-DeAngelis, and Crowley-Martin responses. Responses with the same rare-predator limit share the coexistence threshold, although predator interference changes the interior distribution. Reproducible quadrature and simulations illustrate this distinction. The analysis builds on existing stochastic persistence theory and identifies precisely the additional comparison argument needed for necessity, including exclusion of interior invariant measures at zero predator invasion.

title: A Point-source Catalogue from Direction-dependent Calibrated 21CMA Images
abstract: We present a deep low-frequency radio point-source catalogue centred on the North Celestial Pole (NCP) and extending $5^\circ$ in radius, derived from a single 24-h observation with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA). Covering 75-175 MHz, the catalogue characterises extragalactic foreground point sources for Epoch of Reionization (EoR) studies. Previous 21CMA imaging has been limited by reduced dynamic range caused by direction-dependent effects, particularly the severe grating lobes of ultra-bright sources such as 3C 61.1 and ionospheric phase distortions. Here we apply 21CMAcali, a direction-dependent calibration and imaging pipeline, to mitigate these effects. The angular resolution ranges from 2.3 arcmin at 100 MHz to 1.4 arcmin at 168.75 MHz. The resulting maps show reduced artefacts and background noise, enabling more reliable recovery of faint sources. We construct a catalogue of 1246 radio point sources. Cross-matching with LoTSS-DR3, WENSS, and NVSS enables broad-band spectral fitting, while an independent in-band analysis yields a median spectral index of $α=-0.825$ (where $S \propto ν^α$). The Euclidean-normalised differential source counts at 150 MHz, derived from a dedicated 50-MHz-wide multi-frequency synthesis (MFS) image, are broadly consistent with existing measurements and semi-empirical models at the bright end, whereas the deficit at lower flux densities ($S \lesssim 0.04$ Jy) mainly reflects limited sensitivity and incompleteness. This catalogue improves foreground point-source characterisation in the 21CMA NCP field, demonstrates the value of direction-dependent calibration, and provides a reference for deeper catalogues based on multi-day observations.

title: Toric Varieties from Multiple Zeta Values
abstract: The linear relations among fixed weight multiple zeta values (MZVs) are a well-studied subject in number theory. Elements of putative linear bases for this fixed-weight space are, however, not algebraically independent; they satisfy non-linear relations. We study these relations by approximating them through motivic MZVs, formal MZVs and numerical computations. We show that motivic MZVs in fixed weight span a projective toric variety and explore its geometry. We define an outer approximation to the variety of formal MZVs in fixed weight by introducing toric varieties coming from shuffle and stuffle relations and taking their intersection. We conjecture that this intersection in fact agrees with the variety of formal MZVs and hence conjecturally also with the variety of motivic MZVs. This leads to a novel conjecture on a generating set for the extended double shuffle relations, which we checked computationally up to weight $23$.

title: Aligning Institutional Power and Operational Ability
abstract: To be socially sustainable, Agentic AI systems require normative designs that align responsibilities with the ability to fulfil them. Identifying incongruences such as unsatisfiable expectations or privilege escalation is crucial in avoiding normative pitfalls. In this study, we discuss design dimensions suitable for describing multi-agent systems in light of this norm-ability alignment requirement. We propose a formal framework centred on process-oriented modelling and institutional power for the analysis of a given normatively relevant process, discuss strategies for repairing it, and elaborate on how the symmetrical relation between operational process and institutional state affects the lifecycle of normative positions.

title: Local learning is all you need: brain-aligned predictive coding networks
abstract: Predictive Coding (PC) is an influential account of how brain representations emerge through hierarchical, local, self-supervised prediction-based learning, without requiring globally propagated error signals. Despite extensive evidence supporting PC, a striking paradox persists: computational models built on these biologically grounded principles have consistently failed to match state-of-the-art Deep Neural Networks in performance and brain-alignment. Here, we show that this paradox can be overcome. We introduce Predictive Brain Networks (PBNs), a hierarchical recurrent framework that implements local PC-based learning and achieves representational alignment with the human ventral visual stream matching or exceeding established vision models. Importantly, PBN top-down predictions encode unique, brain-aligned information not captured during bottom-up feature extraction, with this contribution increasing in locally trained variants. Further, PBNs substantially outperform existing PC-inspired networks on downstream classification tasks, reproduce key signatures of PC (with higher-level predictions shaping lower-level visual responses as observed in the primate cortex), and support uncertainty estimation. PBNs therefore close a longstanding gap in computational neuroscience by combining two properties that have been largely separated: the brain-inspired learning mechanisms of predictive coding and the representational power of modern deep networks. They provide a scalable framework for studying biologically grounded learning without sacrificing the capacity to produce rich neural representations.

title: The window process of slightly subcritical frozen percolation
abstract: We study the frozen percolation model on the complete graph $K_n$, where each edge appears at rate~$1/n$ and connected components are destroyed by lightning strikes hitting vertices at rate $λ_n$ (thus the rate at which a connected component is destroyed is linear in its size). We focus on the slightly subcritical sub-regime of the self-organized critical (SOC) regime, assuming $(\ln n)^{4/3}n^{-1/3} \ll λ_n \ll 1$. Our main object of study is the so-called window process, which allows us to study the fine details of the mechanism that drives the SOC behavior of this dynamic random graph. We prove two scaling limit theorems. First, we show that the fluctuations of the window process around its deterministic fluid limit converge to a stationary Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process, whose mean-reverting property captures the SOC nature of the model. Second, by zooming in on a finer space-time scale, we prove that the scaled increments of the window process converge to a tempered stable Lévy process.

title: The maximum size of intersecting $k$-graphs with covering number $k$
abstract: Let $m(k)$ be the maximum size of an intersecting $k$-graph with covering number $k$. In the present paper, it is proved that for all $k>e^{32}$, \[ m(k)\ge k^k\exp\bigl(-50\sqrt{k\log k}\bigr). \] Together with Zakharov's upper bound \cite{Z}, this implies $m(k)=k^k\exp\bigl(-k^{1/2+o(1)}\bigr)$.

title: Perfect sampling of Ising spin glasses with bounding chains
abstract: We study perfect sampling algorithms for Ising spin glasses based on coupling from the past and bounding chains, on several graph families and coupling distributions. For the single-site bounding chain, we establish coalescence in $O(n\log n)$ updates under Dobrushin conditions. On sparse random graphs, our numerical results suggest that efficient sampling extends throughout the tree-uniqueness regime, with a slowdown beyond this threshold. On Erdős-Rényi random graphs $\mathcal{G}(n,d/n)$ with standard Gaussian couplings, we introduce a block bounding chain and prove its coalescence in $O(n\log n)$ block updates in the tree-uniqueness regime for sufficiently large $d$, each block update requiring $O(n)$ operations, adapting a proof in~\cite{Efthymiou_Zampetakis_2024} for the rapid mixing of block Glauber dynamics. On periodic lattices, our experiments instead suggest that the single-site bounding chain is limited by the looseness of its bounding envelope, whereas on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, slow coalescence is accompanied by damage spreading at every inverse temperature tested. These observations motivate alternative bounding representations and couplings as strategies to improve perfect sampling on spin glasses.

title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

title: Magnetic structures in a model nickelate: Monte Carlo study
abstract: Within the framework of the classical Monte Carlo method with kinematic account of constant bosons concentration a model nickelate was studied, its magnetic structures for various values of exchange integrals considering up to third-nearest neighbours were determined.

title: The First Deep Learning all-sky List of Fermi-LAT Gamma-ray Sources
abstract: Aims: We develop a deep-learning-based pipeline to construct a list of γ-ray sources and to quantitatively assess the impact of background uncertainties on source detection and characterization. This work extends and enhances the existing AutoSource-ID algorithm, previously adopted on optical observations, for applications on γ-ray data. Methods: Source detection was performed through image segmentation using a U-Net architecture, while dedicated deep neural networks (DNNs) were employed for source localization, flux estimation, and the classification of detected sources as either genuine or spurious. The training data were generated from Monte Carlo simulations based on 10 years of Fermi-LAT observations. Results: We present the first Fermi-LAT γ-ray all-sky source list derived using a deep-learning-based method (1FDL), containing more than 3800 sources with estimated positions, fluxes, and probability scores that quantify the likelihood of each detection being genuine or spurious. We further evaluated the robustness of the pipeline against variations in the interstellar emission model (IEM) and compared the resulting source list with the 4FGL-DR2 catalog. Conclusion: We find that the our deep-learning-based approach achieves performance comparable to, or better than, the likelihood-based methods employed in the standard Fermi-LAT catalog pipeline when tested against changes in the IEM. The 1FDL source list is broadly consistent with the Fermi-LAT 4FGL-DR2 catalog obtained over the same 10-year observational period, including a few new sources confirmed in the recent Fermi-LAT 16-year source list (FL16Y). These results demonstrate the potential of DNN methods for the detection and characterization of γ-ray sources and provide a foundation for their application in future high-energy astrophysical analyses.

title: Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution improves agent workflows through iterative candidate generation and evaluation. Evaluation both guides subsequent search and determines the final scaffold, but evaluating every candidate on the full task set incurs substantial execution costs. We investigate how evaluation budgets can be allocated across these two roles. Our experiments show that sparse feedback can sustain productive evolution, while additional targeted evaluation improves final selection. Replay analyses further show that shared informative items and a common scoring reference support comparisons among closely matched candidates. Motivated by these findings, we propose \method, an evaluation allocation framework that combines sparse search-time feedback with targeted final confirmation. A short fully evaluated warm-up establishes a shared informative core and calibrates a response model whose item parameters remain fixed during search. After search, \method refits the model and applies paired successive halving, reusing accumulated observations and executing only missing evaluations. Across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, \method achieves higher mean performance than full evaluation in most settings while using approximately half as many evaluation cells.

title: An Interactive Mobile Augmented Reality System for Efficient Virtual Model-to-Patient Registration in Thoracic Surgery
abstract: Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) is a minimally invasive procedure, where precise surgical port placement is vital, yet it relies heavily on surgeon experience and mental mapping of pre-operative imaging in the operating room. To address this challenge, we present an accessible, interactive mobile augmented reality (AR) framework, HILMARTS, to enable accurate and efficient pre-operative virtual model-to-patient registration for AR-guided surgical navigation. Our system runs on a commercially available LiDAR-equipped iPad and supports a user-in-the-loop workflow through a two-stage coarse-to-fine registration process. First, the user performs a manual alignment using the AR view on the iPad. This initial maneuver is then refined through automatic point-cloud registration leveraging the LiDAR sensor. We further introduce a novel occupancy-grid-based Surface Coverage Score to provide real-time, actionable feedback to the operator on the geometric completeness of LiDAR data capture for reliable point-cloud-based alignment. In a phantom study with 16 participants, the system achieved a 3.31+/-1.26mm registration accuracy in ~4 min with a mean System Usability Scale (SUS) of 84.1. These findings highlight the system's accuracy, efficiency, robustness, and potential clinical usability, and could support its applicability to other AR-based surgical navigation tasks.

title: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs
abstract: Proprietary language models and their reasoning traces are vulnerable to API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on the teacher model's outputs. To obtain evidence of distillation, model providers can watermark the teacher's outputs, aiming to leave a radioactive signal in the student's outputs. Existing black-box detectors search for such radioactivity using token-level statistics of the suspect model's outputs. However, token-level signals are not always detectable, for instance when the distillation traces are sampled at a low temperature. In this work, we discover the watermark basin, a persistent signal that enables more reliable watermark detection: during fine-tuning, watermarked teacher traces embed a distinct, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space that lies orthogonal to the ordinary task-specific fine-tuning subspace. Building on this, we introduce Watermark Basin Alignment (WM-Basin), a black-box watermark detector that queries the suspect model through its API, without access to its weights or logits. WM-Basin maps generated text to gradient representations using a fixed clean probe model, projects out the ordinary fine-tuning task directions, and tests whether the residual gradient aligns with the watermark basin induced by the watermark key. We evaluate WM-Basin extensively across diverse teacher models and student architectures (from 135M to 8.2B parameters) distilled on mathematical reasoning. At a strict 0.1% false-positive rate, WM-Basin detects 79% of distilled models at n-gram=1 and 45% at n-gram=3, substantially improving over the state-of-the-art token-level baseline (29% and 1.3%, respectively). Because the watermark signal resides in a persistent basin, it survives post-distillation modifications including quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training.

title: Non-convergence in heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause dynamics: The bounded influence model
abstract: In a recent preprint, we found counterexamples to a number of auxiliary conjectures in a 2012 paper of Mirtabatabaei and Bullo, concerning convergence in two fundamental models of heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause dynamics, the synchronized bounded confidence (SBC) and synchronized bounded influence (SBI) models. Building on our work, Etesami and Touri presented an example of an opinion vector which doesn't converge under SBC dynamics, resolving the main conjecture from the 2012 paper in that case. Here we complete this project by presenting an example of an opinion vector which doesn't converge under SBI dynamics. The example was found with the help of AI.

title: Three quantitative central limit theorems for the unbounded excursion component of a Gaussian field
abstract: For a class of smooth stationary Gaussian fields, we study the fluctuations of the volume, surface area and Euler characteristic of the unbounded excursion component in growing boxes $Λ_n=[-n,n]^d$. We establish nondegenerate central limit theorems for all three functionals throughout the supercritical regime in every dimension $d\geq 2$. We further quantify these central limit theorems by establishing Berry--Esseen bounds of order $O\bigl(|Λ_n|^{-(1-1/s)}\bigr)$ in Kolmogorov distance, where $s\in(1,2]$ depend on the regularity and decay assumptions. Especially for the Bargmann--Fock field, we obtain a Berry--Esseen bound of $O\bigl(|Λ_n|^{-1/2}\bigr)$ for all three functionals. A matching lower bound shows that this rate is sharp for the Euler characteristic. For the volume, we improve the previously known rate of $O\bigl(|Λ_n|^{-1/2}(\log|Λ_n|)^{2d}\bigr)$. We mainly use Stein's method and moment bounds for differences arising from white-noise resampling to finish our proof.

title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning
abstract: Multi-relational graph detectors learn from clean data how much to trust each relation, but an adversary pays a different price to manipulate each relation and each action; taking such costs as given, we ask when using a relation is worse than ignoring it. Our first main result proves that degree gating strictly beats every selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate, and that this window is sharp; on real graphs, validated gating gains exactly on the relations that meet these conditions and nowhere else. Our second shows that a per-node exposure bound, which extends to message passing, tells a platform which relation to harden: exposure per unit cost, computed without any attack, picks the relation whose hardening raises the exact trap threshold most in 15 of 16 cases, against at most 7 for informativeness, cheapness, or an analysis with equal edit costs. Supporting tools give exact worst cases for linear relational models, certified brackets for R-GCN and tree ensembles, and a finite-sample guarantee for adversarial validation, under which clean-trained graph detectors fall below their graph-free counterparts in 58 of 90 settings on six graphs. A selection protocol built on these results is never significantly worse than ignoring the graph; with at most four relations it mostly abstains, as validation alone would, and its cost-aware proposals help when relations are many, so far shown on synthetic graphs. Without cost information, the safe choice is to abstain.

title: Peers4U: Designing Learner-Centered Virtual Peers for Children's Multimodal Mathematics Learning
abstract: In early mathematics, children learn abstract concepts through concrete representations, such as manipulating objects, drawing, and speaking.
