In comparison to the VERITAS double-pass image cleaning method, effective areas are increased at the lower energy range ($\sim$ 60 - 90 GeV) by a factor of up to $\sim$ 25. Energy thresholds are reduced by up to $\sim$ 22\%. Testing the method on Crab Nebula data resulted in an increased number of reconstructed excess events at energies < 1 TeV by a factor of up to $\sim$ 82. Finally, an increase in the differential sensitivity of VERITAS by a factor of up to $\sim$ 8 was observed at $\sim$ 20 GeV. With the addition of BDT-based $γ$/hadron separation cuts, the method improves the detection significance of a 20 hour Crab Nebula dataset, while excess event rates are enhanced by $\sim$ 16\%. In summary, the ONN image cleaning provides a reduced energy threshold and a higher rate of event reconstruction. The technique is especially advantageous for the analysis of gamma-ray sources presenting transient and soft spectra.

title: Quasiconformal distortion of the lower dimension and applications
abstract: We study the distortion of the lower dimension and lower spectrum of sets under quasiconformal mappings. As an application, we verify weighted Hardy--Sobolev inequalities in Euclidean domains arising as quasiconformal images of domains with sufficiently regular boundaries. The regularity in question is phrased in terms of estimates for either the Assouad or the lower dimension of the complement. We also provide dilatation-dependent classification results for certain planar open sets.

title: Minimal Reflected BSDEs and Superhedging of Irregular American Claims
abstract: We study the superhedging of American claims with an irregular optional payoff process $ξ$ over the full set $\mathcal{M}(X)$ of equivalent local martingale measures of a locally bounded market. We show that a process which is a strong optional supermartingale of class (D) under every $Q\in\mathcal{M}(X)$, with no bound from either side, decomposes as $S=S_0+\int H\,dX-A-C_-$, with a common integrand $H$, a right-continuous increasing process $A$ and a purely discontinuous increasing process $C$ given explicitly by the right jumps of $S$. For the robust Snell envelope this yields the superhedging duality $p_0(ξ)=\sup_{Q}\sup_τE^Q[ξ_τ]$ with an explicit optimal strategy and no regularity of $ξ$ in time. Unbounded payoffs are covered when $\{ξ_τ\}$ is uniformly integrable jointly over measures and stopping times, or when $|ξ|$ is dominated by a traded uniformly integrable martingale. For payoffs bounded below, the price is attained by wealth bounded below by a constant. For payoffs unbounded below this can fail, already in a complete market, and the price is attained once the constant bound is replaced by $-M$, with $M$ a traded martingale dominating $|ξ|$. In an incomplete Brownian market we study the associated reflected BSDE with an optional obstacle and a Lipschitz driver depending on the value. We prove existence and uniqueness of the minimal supersolution, a representation at stopping times, comparison and an equivalent dynamic minimality condition, for bounded data and for data dominated by a traded martingale. For a European-type obstacle, the Skorokhod conditions on the total regulator hold for some supersolution if and only if the terminal claim is attainable by a bounded wealth process; so in an incomplete market some data admit no supersolution satisfying them, while the right-jump regulator always satisfies its contact condition.

title: Monochromatic arm exponents for critical planar percolation
abstract: We determine the monochromatic three-arm exponent for critical planar percolation through the exact spectral threshold of an explicit positive integral operator family with elementary kernels, obtaining $ξ_3=0.76928375\cdots$. Unlike the monochromatic two-arm (backbone) event, the three-arm event can be obstructed by two distinct white clusters, so a Markovian exploration must retain the past connections. We introduce a two-point boundary observable that records these connections. Using the coupling between conformal loop ensemble (CLE) and Liouville quantum gravity (LQG), this observable satisfies a renewal equation in terms of quantum boundary lengths, and yields the explicit operator whose spectral information determines $ξ_3$. Our approach also gives an explicit spectral characterization of monochromatic $n$-arm exponents for all $n\ge4$.

title: Exploring the World of Lipids with Machine-Learned Coarse-Grained Models
abstract: Lipid bilayers are central to cellular organization and function, yet their atomistic modelling remains constrained by its high computational cost. While coarse-grained (CG) models can overcome this bottleneck, they are limited in accuracy due to the use of simplified functional forms based on molecular mechanics. Using a hybrid functional form combining physics-based terms with a graph neural network, we present implicit-solvent, machine-learned CG models for POPC. When trained on single-lipid data, the model recovers the atomistic conformational landscape. By adding short atomistic simulations of a small flat bilayer to the training data and combining force matching with a denoising objective, we train a model that accurately reproduces bilayer structure and dynamics, in closer agreement with the atomistic reference than existing models, like Martini3 and DryMartini. Beyond its training data, the model stabilizes curved geometries, including vesicles, and captures complex cooperative phenomena such as bilayer and vesicle self-assembly and pore sealing. While limitations remain, particularly regarding chemical transferability, our results establish machine-learned coarse-grained potentials as a promising path towards robust and accurate CG models of lipids and membranes.

title: Search and Verification for Strategyproof Facility Location on Metric Graphs
abstract: We study automated design of strategyproof (SP) mechanisms for randomized facility location on continuous metric graphs, with the objective of minimizing total distance. We develop methods for computing upper and lower bounds on the optimal approximation ratio achievable by SP mechanisms for a given graph and number of agents. For the lower bound, we propose a cost-preserving reduction to a finite domain that yields lower bounds for unrestricted SP mechanisms through linear programming dual certificates. For the upper bound, we introduce finite representations of mechanisms, called piecewise-linear attributions (PL attributions), that mix piecewise-linear deterministic mechanisms using affine weights on a triangulation of the report space. We show that for mechanisms represented by PL attributions, checking SP and an approximation guarantee reduces to finitely many quadratic nonnegativity tests over compact polytopes. With exact arithmetic and comparisons, each verification certifies the proposed property or returns locations where it fails. In addition, we introduce a strengthening of the incentive notion called strong strategyproofness. We show that for fixed component mechanisms and regions of a PL attribution, the strong strategyproofness requirement can be expressed by a finite number of linear constraints on the attribution coefficients. Using these theoretical results, we propose a heuristic procedure for computing an upper bound on the approximation ratio. We compute certified upper and lower bounds on several metric graphs and numerically evaluate the proposed search procedure. Lastly, we show that deterministic SP onto mechanisms on graphs are strongly strategyproof and admit PL attributions. Thus restricting attention to strongly strategyproof mechanisms admitting PL attributions loses no deterministic SP onto mechanisms.

title: Degenerate McKean--Vlasov SDE with Yamada--Osgood Coefficients and Arbitrary Modulus of Continuity in Wasserstein Distance
abstract: We establish the well-posedness of strong solutions for a class of degenerate mean-field stochastic differential equations with coefficients satisfying non-Lipschitz conditions. The diffusion coefficient is not required to be non-degenerate. Both the diffusion and the drift coefficients may depend on the law through the Kantorovich-Rubinstein metric with an arbitrary modulus of continuity. The drift and the diffusion satisfy a dimension-dependent Osgood-type condition, that becomes particularly sharp in dimension one. The proof combines the classical Yamada--Watanabe argument with Schauder's fixed-point theorem and does not rely on Gaussian estimates, allowing us to cover degenerate diffusions where such estimates are not available. This fills a gap in the existing literature.

title: A face polynomial invariant for embedded graphs
abstract: We introduce the face polynomial of a ribbon graph, a generating function for face numbers under the ribbon group action. It addresses the face-count case of the Ellis--Monaghan--Moffatt question on twisted duality. We derive deletion--contraction recursions and prove that this polynomial coincides with the vertex polynomial for \(\langleδ\rangle\), \(\langleδτ\rangle\), and \(\langleδ,τ\rangle\). We characterize monomial cases and obtain formulas and recursions for Euler-genus partial-twuality polynomials. For orientable graphs, we show that the partial-dual face polynomial has both parities whenever an edge exists, so the partial-dual Euler-genus polynomial has only even exponents.

title: von Neumann Stability Analysis of Braginskii MHD Thermal Conduction, Viscosity, Magnetic Diffusion, and Thermoelectric Effects and an Implementation in Athena++
abstract: Athena++ is a finite-volume astrophysical magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) code. As of writing, isotropic thermal conduction and kinematic viscosity, Ohmic resistivity, and ambipolar diffusion are present in the main branch. Here we present a fork of Athena++, ``Athena-Aniso''. It implements fully anisotropic thermal conduction (parallel, perpendicular, and the Righi--Leduc effect); anisotropic viscosity (all five Braginskii viscosity tensors); the Hall effect; and several thermoelectric effects (Peltier, Seebeck, Nernst, and Ettingshausen). These effects can be weighted by ionisation fraction in a partially ionised gas, with the neutral part diffusing isotropically. We have also added isotropic bulk viscosity. The Biermann battery is not implemented here. The dissipative terms have super-time-stepping support, while the non-dissipative terms are combined with the ideal MHD flux. A CFL condition for all terms is derived and implemented using von Neumann stability analysis. The dissipative terms are found to be stable under first-order time integration. The non-dissipative terms are found to be stable under third-order time integration. We additionally derive new signal speeds for a modified HLLE Riemann solver. These suppress grid-scale non-linear instabilities still present in the non-dissipative terms. The Nernst/Ettingshausen system is found to be ill-posed unless it is stabilised by both perpendicular thermal conduction and perpendicular magnetic diffusion. We derive a well-posedness criterion for this. We provide numerical tests of each implemented effect against derived analytical solutions.

title: Designing tunable hyperuniformity in random organization through nonlocal noise
abstract: Hyperuniform fluids suppress density fluctuations at large length scales, but microscopic protocols for designing their asymptotic scaling remain limited. Here we show how effective driving noise generated by particle dynamics can select the hyperuniform exponent while preserving ordinary diffusion and pairwise center-of-mass conservation of the organized particles. We establish this connection through two protocols based on biased random organization (BRO). First, a two-dimensional BRO layer is nonreciprocally coupled to a three-dimensional Brownian gas through density-dependent kick amplitudes. Bulk density fluctuations generate spatially nonlocal noise with a $q^3$ power spectrum in the adiabatic limit, producing $S(q\to0)\sim q^1$. Second, we introduce reciprocal kicks whose lengths follow a Pareto-like distribution, $P(\ell)\sim\ell^{-1-b}$. For $2<b<4$, the finite second moment supports ordinary diffusion, while the divergent fourth moment changes the long-wavelength noise spectrum to $q^b$. The corresponding fluctuating density field theory predicts continuously tunable hyperuniform scaling, $S(q\to0)\sim q^{b-2}$, supported by particle simulations. Together, these results connect targeted hyperuniform scaling to explicit microscopic dynamics and provide a physical basis for designing collective density correlations in nonequilibrium particle systems.

title: Toward Constant-Factor Maximin Share Guarantees for Subadditive Valuations
abstract: For $n$ agents and $m$ indivisible goods, an agent's maximin share (MMS) is the largest minimum bundle value she can obtain by partitioning the goods into $n$ bundles. Constant MMS approximations are known for additive, submodular, or XOS valuations, but whether such a guarantee exists for general subadditive valuations remains open. We advance this question in two directions. For general subadditive valuations, we exponentially improve the guarantee from $Ω(1/\log\log n)$ to $Ω(1/\log^* n)$, where $\log^* n$ is the iterated logarithm. We then seek constant MMS guarantees under additional structure on subadditive valuations by studying $q$-partitioning valuations: every partition of a bundle into at most $q$ groups admits nonnegative group prices that sum to the bundle's value and whose sum on any collection of groups is at most the value of their union. This hierarchy ranges from subadditivity at $q=2$ to XOS for $q\ge m$. We give the first study of MMS in the intermediate classes and prove constant guarantees whenever $q/n$ has a fixed positive lower bound, including $1/6$ for $q\ge n$ and $1/4$ for $q\ge2n$. For XOS valuations, we further improve the universal guarantee from $4/17\approx 0.2353$ to $5/16=0.3125$. For subadditive valuations, we prove a bidding amplification theorem that gives an exponential bound on each agent's probability of receiving less than half her MMS, while satisfying her budget in every outcome. For $q$-partitioning valuations, we give a scalar criterion that converts bounds on the value lost from disjoint deletions within a bundle into bounds on potential losses, even when an agent contributes zero below the target bundle value. For XOS valuations, we prove a reservation theorem that selects goods for integral assignment together with auxiliary additive valuations and accounts for the loss in rounding.

title: Operational Thresholds for Long-Range Entanglement in Quantum Networks
abstract: Quantum networks distribute entanglement between distant nodes by combining many short entangled links using local quantum operations. These operations only succeed probabilistically, yet existing percolation-based theories of entanglement transmission treat them as perfect. We approach the problem through statistical physics, using a stochastic generalization of concurrence percolation to determine how reliable local operations must be for long-range entanglement to remain possible. On hierarchical $(U,V)$-flower networks, which permit full analytical control across network scales, we derive an exact renormalization recursion for the probability that an end-to-end entangled connection survives. For the $(2,2)$-flower this yields a closed-form operational phase boundary, $η_p = 2 - \frac{32}{27}η_s$, where $η_s$ and $η_p$ are the success probabilities of the series (entanglement swapping) and parallel (purification) operations, respectively. At this boundary the survival probability jumps discontinuously from $0$ to $S_\infty = 3/(4η_s)$. Numerically propagating the full distribution of end-to-end concurrence yields a second threshold in the initial link quality, which varies continuously with operational reliability. Above both thresholds the large-network state is binary: the connection either fails outright or approaches a perfect Bell pair. Our results thus reveal a two-threshold structure for long-range entanglement, in which operational reliability and initial link quality can compensate one another. Operational success rates therefore emerge alongside initial link quality as a primary design constraint for scalable quantum networks.

title: Odd-ordered Cayley graphs satisfy Erdős--Gyárfás
abstract: Erdős and Gyárfás conjectured that every graph with minimum degree at least three contains a power-of-two-length cycle. We prove every Cayley graph of odd order satisfies the conjecture. As a corollary, we find that Cayley graphs of finite nilpotent groups satisfy the conjecture as well.

title: Rank-metric intersecting codes
abstract: Intersecting codes are codes in which any two nonzero codewords share a common nonzero coordinate, and they have been extensively studied due to their applications in communication theory, cryptography, and combinatorics. Recently, geometric interpretations have provided new insights into intersecting codes, both in the Hamming metric and, more recently, in the rank metric for linear codes. In this paper, we introduce and study matrix rank-metric intersecting codes. By defining the support of a matrix as its row space, we extend the notion of intersecting codes to the matrix rank-metric setting. Using the slice space associated with the generator tensor of a rank-metric code, we derive a geometric characterization that is equivalent to the intersecting property. This characterization generalizes the known results for linear rank-metric intersecting codes and highlights both analogies and differences with the linear case. In particular, it yields bounds on the parameters of intersecting codes, one of which is sharp and differs from the one in the linear case, together with first constructions. We then consider codes that are closed under multiplication, i.e. matrix algebras. In this setting, the intersecting property can be read off from the algebraic structure, namely the Jacobson radical and the socle. This provides a simple and flexible way to construct many intersecting codes, including codes that do not satisfy the classical sufficient condition on the minimum distance.

title: The Maximum Second Zagreb Spectral Radius of Trees, Unicyclic Graphs and Bicyclic Graphs
abstract: The second Zagreb matrix of a graph $G$ is $Z(G)=D(G)A(G)D(G)$, where $D(G)$ and $A(G)$ are the degree matrix and the adjacency matrix of $G$. For many degree-based weighted adjacency matrices, the trees, unicyclic graphs and bicyclic graphs with the largest spectral radius have a vertex adjacent to all others, and Mei et al. conjectured this for every such matrix on unicyclic graphs. Jiang et al. showed that $Z(G)$ is a counterexample. We prove that, for $q\in\{0,1,2\}$ and every $n\ge4$, the connected graph of order $n$ and cyclomatic number $q$ maximizing the spectral radius of $Z(G)$ is unique, and is obtained from two adjacent vertices with $q$ common neighbours by attaching $n-q-2$ pendent vertices to them as evenly as possible. The only exceptions are the star for $q=0$ and $n\le7$, and the triangle with one pendent vertex at each vertex for $q=1$ and $n=6$. This confirms a conjecture of Jiang et al.\ and all three parts of a conjecture of Shen and Shan for this matrix, with best possible thresholds on $n$. For $n\ge8$, the maximum value is $\lfloor (n+q)^2/4\rfloor+(n+q)/2+7q-2+O(1/n)$, whereas the star gives only $(n-1)^{3/2}$. A key tool is a determinant criterion that reduces spectral comparisons to sign conditions on explicit polynomials.

title: Ablating Design Choices for Protein Ensemble Generators Across Structural Regimes
abstract: Generative models of protein conformational ensembles inherit much of their design from structure prediction for folded proteins. Ordered and disordered proteins, however, occupy distinct structural regimes, and we investigate how design choices hold up across them. Using a minimal C$α$ flow-matching model, we ablate choices of architecture, sequence conditioning, rigid-body alignment and training source, and evaluate each variant against experimental SAXS and NMR chemical-shift data partitioned into ordered, disordered, multi-domain and transitional proteins. Mixture-of-experts routing, a static pair representation and a disorder probe have no detectable effect, a smaller protein language model performs worse on ordered proteins but not on disordered ones, and alignment in the loss degrades agreement with SAXS. Replacing coarse-grained simulations of disordered proteins with fragment-assembled ensembles improves agreement with chemical shifts at a cost to SAXS, while an equal mixture of the two keeps most of the gain at a smaller cost. This points to the training data, rather than the architecture, as the main constraint.

title: From Random Advection to Transport Noise and the LU Framework for the Navier--Stokes Equations
abstract: We consider the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations in a smooth bounded domain in dimension two or three, with Dirichlet boundary conditions, when the velocity is advected by a rapidly varying stationary Markov process $\eps^{-1}m(t/\eps^2)$. The fast field may be spatially inhomogeneous. We prove that, when $\eps\to0$, the laws of the large-scale velocities are tight and that their limit points are martingale solutions of the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations with transport noise in the form of the location uncertainty framework. The limiting equation contains in particular a noise which is described in terms of the covariance of the fast advection. Under a symmetry assumption on the temporal correlations of the fast field, the noise is Stratonovich and an advection by the Itô--Stokes drift appears. The proof relies on perturbed test functions, which we use both for the uniform energy bounds and for the identification of the limit. We have to adapt this method and add the Stokes operator to the Poisson equation associated to the fast advection in order to use fewer regularity assumptions and obtain correctors which satisfy the boundary conditions.

title: A Low-Diameter Nash-Williams--Tutte Theorem
abstract: The Nash-Williams--Tutte theorem characterizes the existence of $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees by a condition on every vertex partition. We prove that, for simple graphs, the same condition guarantees $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees, each of diameter $O(n/δ)$ and with $O((n/δ)\log(δ+1))$ internal vertices, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $δ$ is the minimum degree. Both bounds hold simultaneously for every tree, with absolute implicit constants independent of $k$, and each is asymptotically optimal in general. Our proof is constructive and yields a randomized algorithm with expected running time $\tilde{O}(n^5)$. We derive applications to short edge-disjoint routes and weak linkages, small Steiner trees, and survivable networks with short paths. The joint bounds also yield low-diameter spanning Eulerian subgraphs and short tours for postman and general routing problems.

title: The Power of Interaction in Locally Edge-Private Subgraph Counting
abstract: We study (non-induced) subgraph counting under interactive local edge differential privacy (LEDP). Given a fixed pattern graph $H$ with $k$ vertices, $\ell\ge1$ edges, and $q$ connected components, our goal is to approximately count its copies in an arbitrary $n$-vertex undirected graph while preserving edge privacy. We give two complementary accuracy guarantees. First, for every $H$, we give Linear Noise Cancellation (LNC), a two-round $\varepsilon$-LEDP algorithm with additive error and root mean square error both $O(n^{k-3/2}/\varepsilon^\ell)$ on every $n$-vertex graph. For fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, this improves the optimal noninteractive additive error for triangles by a factor of $\sqrt n$ and gives the same improvement in worst-case root mean square error for all cliques on at least three vertices. To our knowledge, this is the first separation between interactive and noninteractive LEDP subgraph counting, showing that a single additional round can improve worst-case accuracy polynomially. Second, we determine how accuracy improves when the graph has maximum degree at most a public bound $d$. Our Predict and Correct (PC) framework gives an $(\ell+2)$-round $\varepsilon$-LEDP algorithm with additive error $O(n^{q-1/2}d^{k-q-1}\log^{3\ell-2}n/\varepsilon^\ell)$. For connected patterns, its polynomial factor is $\sqrt n\,d^{k-2}$, giving sublinear error on constant-degree graphs at fixed privacy. We prove matching lower bounds in $n$ and $d$, up to logarithmic factors at fixed privacy, even under arbitrary interaction and approximate privacy with sufficiently small $δ$. At $d=Θ(n)$, the lower bound also establishes the optimality of LNC's dependence on $n$.

title: A Short Proof and Generalization of the Rainbow Cycle Theorem and Improved Bounds for Binary Even-Query LCCs
abstract: A \emph{rainbow cycle} in a list-edge-colored graph is a cycle where no color appears more than once. We give a short and simple proof of a result of [ABSZZ] showing that a properly edge-colored $n$-vertex graph with average degree $Ω(\log n\log\log n)$ always contains a rainbow cycle, and generalize it to weighted graphs with edges list colored with list size at most $\ell$ and where the total weight of all edges containing a given color $i$ incident to a vertex is at most $Δ$, showing that $Ω_\ell(Δ\log n\log\log n)$ average degree guarantees a rainbow cycle. Using the reduction of [AG26] and the new generalized rainbow cycle theorem, we prove that for $r\geq 3$, every binary linear $r$-query locally correctable code $E:\mathbb{F}_2^k\rightarrow \mathbb{F}_2^n$ satisfies $k\leq \tilde{O}(n^{1-2/(r-1)})$ by showing a rainbow analogue of the odd $r$-LDC lower bounds of [BHKL25,JM25], closing the gap between the best known lower bounds for odd- and even-query binary linear $r$-LCCs.

title: Haptic Shared Control for Multi-Robot Systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems offer significant advantages in terms of flexibility and redundancy, enabling the efficient distribution of complex tasks among multiple robots. However, their deployment requires advanced control strategies to ensure optimal cooperation between autonomous agents and human operators. We propose a modification of the global connectivity maintenance algorithm to incorporate measurements taken in agent's local frame, using sensors with limited fields of view. This algorithm, responsible for the autonomous behavior of the multi-robot system, is combined with different adaptive supervision strategies, allowing the user to exert control at varying scales over the entire group. (i) Single Agent Control (S): The operator directly controls a single robot, (ii) Pinning Control (P): The operator imposes constraints on multiple robots to influence the group, (iii) Centroid Control (C): The operator acts on the system's center of mass to steer the entire fleet. In conjunction with the connectivity maintenance algorithm, these methods ensure compliance with inter-agent constraints while providing haptic feedback to the user regarding the system's connectivity state. The effectiveness of these approaches was evaluated through a user study, comparing performance with and without haptic feedback across multiple scenarios tailored to the different control modes.

title: Faster Planar Diameter using Pseudoline Envelopes
abstract: We give an improved algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter that runs in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ time. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ time algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter of Gawrychowski, Kaplan, Mozes, Sharir, and Weimann [SIAM J. Comput. 2021] and the recent $\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})$ time algorithm for unweighted undirected planar diameter of Fredslund-Hansen, Mozes, and Weimann [SOSA 2027]. The main new result is an improved data structure for computing the farthest vertex when given feasible planar distances to the vertices on the outer face. The critical insight is the fact that normalized distances to the vertices of a face behave like pseudolines, for which we can leverage range searching and upper envelope data structures. Using the farthest vertex data structure, we are able to compute all vertex eccentricities and diameter in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$.

title: Long-time Brownian dynamics of hard and sticky colloids by geometric projection
abstract: Particle-resolved colloid simulations are often limited by the fastest microscopic time scale retained in the model, which can be many orders of magnitude shorter than the collective process of interest. This is especially restrictive for aggregating colloids, where explicit near-contact potentials force the time integration to resolve the rapid positional relaxation of bonded pairs within narrow attractive wells. Here we introduce an overdamped constraint-based Brownian dynamics method that replaces the time-resolved integration of stiff near-contact forces by a geometric projection step. After each free Brownian update, hard-sphere exclusion, sticky bonds, and hard-wall interactions are enforced by projecting the particle positions onto the constrained configuration set. The method preserves hard-sphere structure and diffusion, recovers the aggregation kinetics of sticky hard spheres, and extends the physical time reached at fixed computational cost by one to two orders of magnitude relative to the explicit-potential simulations tested here. This acceleration makes Brownian-dominated, low-Péclet electrophoretic deposition accessible to particle-scale simulations, revealing a pathway in which the suspension first densifies and only subsequently develops a bonded network. Implemented as a LAMMPS fix, the framework provides a modular route to long-time Brownian simulations of dense constrained colloidal systems.

title: The integer spectrum of a superintegrable quantum field theory
abstract: In our previous article CMP 407 (2026) 131, we explored the rich algebraic structures arising from a specific quantum many-body Hamiltonian quartic in the bosonic creation-annihilation operators. This Hamiltonian originated from the works of Gérard and Grellier on classical turbulent energy transfer in a Lax-integrable setting, and its quantum version respects hierarchies of polynomial conservation laws all of which possess purely integer spectra, as does the Hamiltonian itself. The latter feature, known from numerical studies, has previously remained unproved. Here, we present an elementary solution of the quantum Gérard-Grellier Hamiltonian. The eigenstates are labelled by partitions and the corresponding eigenvalues admit simple explicit expressions in terms of the principal hook lengths. The key ingredient in this construction is a specific basis we introduce, inspired by the classical multisoliton coherent states, in which the Hamiltonian is upper-triangular. The expressions for the eigenvalues then immediately follow, while the full eigenbasis can be recovered via a Gram-Schmidt procedure.

title: For You, Not for Everyone: Bystander-Aware Delivery of Critical Feedback in Robot Tutoring
abstract: Robots in shared settings may expose information intended for an individual user to nearby bystanders. Robot tutoring makes this concern particularly salient: critical feedback is directed at an individual learner, yet bystanders may overhear or see it. To address this, we compared context-invariant and context-adaptive robot behaviors in a between-subjects study with 40 participants. Following an initial phase without a bystander, a bystander entered the setting. Participants then received two scripted critical feedback messages concerning their pronunciation and handwriting, independent of their actual performance. With the context-invariant behavior, the robot tutor delivered both messages aloud. With the context-adaptive behavior, the robot tutor scanned for the bystander, turned its body and display away after detecting them, gave a spoken attention cue, and presented the same feedback messages silently on its display. Participants rated the robot tutor higher in perceived privacy awareness and perceived social competence in the context-adaptive condition than in the context-invariant condition, while evidence for reduced experienced embarrassment was inconclusive. These findings inform the design and evaluation of robots that respond to bystander presence by adapting how they communicate potentially sensitive information.

title: BaCon: Band-Concentrated Exponential Random Graph Models
abstract: Exponential-family random graph models ERGMs provide a parametric interpretable framework for modeling real graphs including the Web and social networks Fitted ERGMs may suffer from degeneracy matching observed graph statistics in expectation does not guarantee that the observed graph and similar ones are highly probable under the fitted distribution We introduce Band-Concentrated ERGMs BaCon a framework that avoids degeneracy by imposing a probabilistic constraint requiring at least $1-δ$ of the distribution probability mass to lie on the set of graphs with statistics within an $\varepsilon$-tolerance band around the observed statistics BaCons maximumentropy distribution still belongs to the exponential family while including a factor checking for inclusion in the tolerance band We derive the exact Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rule for this target and use a practical stochastic approximation procedure with a smoothed band membership during fitting Experiments on social networks across increasingly challenging model specifications show that BaCon substantially increases the probability mass assigned to graphs whose statistics are close to the observed ones while remaining estimable for specifications where standard ERGM estimation fails These results demonstrate that probability mass constraints are a principled way to mitigate degeneracy while retaining the benefits of exponential-family graph models

title: Basic Reproductive Numbers in Host-Parasite Systems with Demographic Bistability
abstract: The basic reproductive number, $\mathcal{R}_0$, is widely used to determine whether an infectious disease can persist in a population. However, its interpretation may become unclear when the underlying disease-free demographic dynamics exhibit multiple types of stable attractors. In this study, we investigate how demographic bistability between fixed points and periodic cycles affects the calculation and interpretation of $\mathcal{R}_0$. We consider two discrete-time host-parasite models with infection: a tick-host model motivated by Borrelia burgdorferi transmission and a Nicholson-Bailey host-parasitoid model with intraspecific competition and infection. For each model, we calculate reproductive numbers associated with different disease-free attractors using the next-generation operator method and compare their invasion thresholds. In the tick-host model, the reproduction number calculated on the stable demographic cycle differs from that calculated at the positive coexistence fixed point, resulting in parameter regions where infection can invade at one demographic attractor but not the other. In contrast, in the host-parasitoid model, the host-driven invasion threshold is necessarily the same at the positive coexistence fixed point and on the host-only periodic cycles. These contrasting results demonstrate that demographic bistability alone does not necessarily produce attractor-dependent invasion thresholds. Rather, the effect of demographic dynamics on invasion depends on the structure of pathogen transmission. In particular, a complete host--vector--host transmission pathway can allow differences between demographic attractors to alter the invasion threshold. Our results emphasize the importance of considering both demographic dynamics and transmission structure when interpreting $\mathcal{R}_0$ in populations with multiple stable disease-free states.

title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response
abstract: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.

title: The ALMA survey to Resolve exoKuiper belt Substructures (ARKS) XII. Constraints on large bodies embedded in discs
abstract: The ALMA survey to Resolve exoKuiper belt Substructures (ARKS) presents detailed constraints on structure and properties of a sample of 24 debris discs at millimetre wavelengths, including measurements of vertical thicknesses for a subsample of discs. We estimated sizes and total masses of large bodies that feed collisional cascades producing the observed millimetre dust in 11 ARKS discs with a well constrained vertical thickness. Separately, we estimated the sizes and total masses of large bodies that could be gravitationally stirring these discs, assuming that such stirring is the origin of the vertical thickness. We used a semi-analytic particle-in-a-box collisional model and a semi-analytic model of stirring through gravitational scattering. We accounted for the dependence of collisional damping efficiency on the average collision velocity. We find that planetesimals feeding the collisional cascades are less than 20 km in size, while the total masses in the planetesimals are lower than 200 M$_\oplus$. There is a good agreement between minimum disc masses inferred from millimetre and infrared observations. The hypothetical stirrers are always larger in size than the planetesimals, but they do not necessarily contain most of the disc mass. In agreement with previous work, the observed dust masses can be explained by steady-state collisional models with reasonable disc masses. The measured vertical scale-heights can be explained by gravitational stirring from embedded large bodies of reasonable properties. However, more advanced models are needed to address the observed non-Gaussian vertical profiles, along with the dependence of disc scale-height on particle size and stellocentric distance.

title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
abstract: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.

title: Nonintegrability theorem on perturbed integrable Hamiltonian dynamical systems with two independent resonances
abstract: In this paper we establish a new theorem for nonintegrability of a perturbed, autonomous, two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian dynamical system with two independent resonances, based on a criterion which utilizes the well-known theorem of Poincaré and a Lie-series symplectic transformation. We also make certain assumptions and suggestions as to when the theorem holds and when it does not.

title: Deep Neural Operator Learning for stochastic heat equations and applications
abstract: In this paper, we establish a universal approximation theorem for solution operators of semilinear stochastic heat equations in spatial dimension \(d\ge2\), extending deep neural operator approximation results to SPDEs with distribution-valued Gaussian forcing. A smooth Fourier cutoff reduces the forcing to finitely many measurements, while Besov and Schauder estimates control the resulting solution error. The finite-dimensional solution map is then approximated by ReLU branch networks together with grid-based trunk functions, yielding explicit bounds on the numbers of forcing measurements and trunk functions and approximation in every finite stochastic moment. For linear equations, the reduction coincides with truncation of the first Wiener chaos. Lastly, as an application, we prove a high-probability local-in-time approximation theorem for stochastic Navier--Stokes equations, with finite measurements of both the initial condition and forcing and an explicit sensing rate.

title: Linear Equivalence of Full Weight Spectrum Cyclic Orbit Codes
abstract: We determine the linear-equivalence classes within the two families of full weight spectrum one-orbit cyclic subspace codes. This solves the second open problem posed by Castello, Polverino and Zullo [J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 212 (2025) 106005]. For the first family, the criterion is a fractional linear transformation over $\F_q$ followed by a power of $q$-Frobenius. For the second family, it is an affine transformation over $\F_{q^2}$ together with a power of $q$-Frobenius. We use polynomial spaces over finite fields, the linear-isometry theorem for cyclic orbit codes, and trace duality. The arguments include parameters belonging to proper subfields of the ambient field.

title: Local Visibility Roadmaps in Continous Multi-agent Path Finding
abstract: We address the problem of smooth continuous multi-agent path finding (SC-MAPF), where agents move in a continuous environment along smooth curves in continuous time. The paths for individual agents are searched in local visibility roadmaps that consider obstacles and other agents. A new algorithm is proposed in this work, which combines the previous algorithm CE-CBS for high-level search with any-angle path finding for local single-agent planning, where agents are to avoid obstacles, both static and other agents. The new algorithm is tested and compared to CE-CBS, the algorithm building individual paths using RRT$^*$, and SMT-CCBS algorithm, an algorithm for MAPF$_R$. Experimental results show various advantages of the new algorithm over CE-CBS and SMT-CCBS in comparable settings.

title: Residual Attribute Leakage Is an Interface: Auditing Privacy Evaluation After Text De-identification
abstract: A privacy evaluation of de-identified text asks a language model (the adversary) to guess a person's protected attribute. We introduce a prior-normalised clipped leakage score of its confidence gain on the true value and audit the conclusions drawn from it. Each verdict depends on an evaluation interface (the queried person, answer options, prior, adversary model and scoring rule), which we vary on fixed releases of three corpora. In a stress test, an editor that writes the opposite-sex form at the same spans a redaction editor would redact misleads the adversary about most people, yet ranks first among editors scored on the same MedQA entries under this score, as under attack accuracy and proper scoring rules read as privacy. A relabelling-invariant reading of AUC ranks that editor sixth of eight, and a rule-aware adversary recovers the attribute from the same text. On ordinary releases most verdict changes are gains or losses of separability; of six choices varied over all pairs, only the adversary reverses comparisons (5 of its 124 changes), and the query can target the wrong person. SACC, a traceable editor we build as the instrument, lets us ablate two editing principles and show where its advantage does not hold.

title: The Complexity of Continuous Contract Design over Polymatroids
abstract: We study optimal contracts when an agent allocates continuous effort subject to polymatroid capacity constraints. Effort produces a linear expected reward and incurs a cost. With binary outcomes and limited liability, the principal chooses a single reward share. For linear costs, an optimal contract can be computed in polynomial time. For quadratic costs, the agent has a unique best response computable by polynomially many submodular minimizations, yet optimizing the principal's share is NP-hard even for explicitly represented cut-based rank functions. With $n$ activities, the best-response path can have $2^{n-O(\log n)}$ breakpoints even when each reward coefficient and each rank value is an integer representable in $O(n\log n)$ bits. The construction also answers a question of Allman, Lo, and McCormick on polynomial bit length for source-sink monotone two-parameter minimum cuts. Despite this complexity, an optimal contract for quadratic costs always exists with a share of at most $1/2$. Consequently, $O(1/\varepsilon)$ best-response computations suffice for a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation. For rational quadratic costs on explicitly described rational polytopes containing zero, this gives a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. More generally, a share of at most $1/p$ suffices for continuous convex costs homogeneous of degree $p>1$, on any compact convex action set containing zero. For general convex costs with an exact value and bounded-subgradient oracle, we obtain an oracle approximation scheme using approximate best responses and a supplied lower bound on positive welfare.

title: Exponential decay for the two-dimensional Heisenberg model
abstract: In this work, we prove exponential decay for the spin correlation of the spin $O(\mathsf{N})$ model for $\mathsf{N}\geq3$ at every inverse temperature $ β>0 $. In particular, our work confirms Polyakov's prediction in 1975 on the Heisenberg model, i.e., the case of $\mathsf{N}=3$. To this end, we investigate a generalized $O(\mathsf{N})$ model where $ \mathsf{N} $ is a positive \emph{real number}, as follows: we sample a loop soup on the metric graph (say of a box) with intensity $ \tfrac{\mathsf{N}}{2} $ subject to the conditioning that the local time at each lattice vertex is $β$, and then for each loop we independently assign it to copies $1\leq \mathsf{i}\leq \lceil\mathsf{N}\rceil$ such that it is assigned to copy $\mathsf{i}$ with probability $ \tfrac{1}{\mathsf{N}} $ for $ 1\leq \mathsf{i}\leq \lfloor\mathsf{N}\rfloor $. Then, by Lupu's isomorphism theorem, we can construct a spin field by assigning a random sign to each loop soup cluster in each copy independently, such that the field coincides with the spin $O(\mathsf{N})$ model when $\mathsf{N}$ is an integer. We then establish exponential decay for every real-valued $\mathsf{N}>2$. Our result reveals an underlying mechanism for exponential decay, which emerges as soon as $\mathsf{N}>2$ (i.e., as soon as beyond the range of the XY model) and does not necessarily rely on the rotation symmetry in the sphere $ \mathbb{S}^{2} $.

title: Modelling lock-in of AI adoption through skill erosion
abstract: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills required for future work. We study a model in which individuals tend to imitate successful peers, while their independent skills grow with practice and erode with reliance on AI. Because each agent's skill reflects their history, non-users and AI users develop different skill distributions, which we derive exactly. Skill erosion can produce bistability and hysteresis between a low-adoption, high-skill state and a high-adoption, low-skill state. When agents rarely change behaviour at random, the two transitions are asymmetric. A single AI user spreads through a population of experts only if AI-assisted work earns more than expert work, whatever the timescale of skill adaptation. A single non-user, by contrast, can lead an AI-dependent population back to independent work only if they regain enough skill before returning to AI, which becomes easier the more persistent behaviours are. As AI improves, adoption can jump abruptly, and a sufficiently long increase in its benefit, such as a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value. Skill erosion thus creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

title: Best-of-Many-Worlds MMS Allocation for Chores with Sublinear Disposals
abstract: We study randomized allocations (lotteries) of indivisible chores under additive costs and introduce the notion of MMS1, which requires each agent's bundle to satisfy the maximin share (MMS) bound after the removal of at most one chore. Our main result establishes that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery in whose support every allocation is MMS1 and all but $o(n)$ agents satisfy MMS. Consequently, every realized allocation can be made MMS by disposing of at most $o(n)$ chores. The proposed framework further achieves ex-ante proportionality alongside ex-post $4/3$-MMS, $o(n)$-AMMS, or $1$-out-of-$d$ MMS for $d=(1-o(1))n$. These guarantees substantially improve upon state-of-the-art bounds for MMS allocation for chores with disposal or subsidy, best-of-both-worlds fairness, approximate AMMS, and ordinal MMS approximations.

title: Automaticity of structural defects in fixed points of block substitutions
abstract: We study structural defects in fixed points of block substitutions, building on arXiv:2604.12637 and providing its technical supplement. We develop an automata-based framework to characterize their occurrence and derive verifiable combinatorial criteria. We also introduce simplifications for the construction and analysis of these automata, including tensor-product decompositions, that clarify the mechanisms underlying structural defects and their emergence.

title: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing
abstract: Leakage-resilient cryptography protects secrets against side-channel attacks, in which a physical implementation reveals partial information about its internal state. A fundamental primitive in this area is a leakage-resilient storage, which allows a secret to be stored in a way that remains secure even if an adversary learns some information about the storage's internal state. A popular approach represents a secret as the inner product of two $n$-bit vectors, called shares. The shares are stored and processed separately by two parts of the implementation, called the left and right parties. Because leakage accumulates over time, the shares must be refreshed repeatedly. We prove that a simple refresh, in which the left party multiplies its share by a uniform invertible matrix $M$ and the right party multiplies its share by $M^{-1}$, is secure under continual local leakage. After $T$ refreshes, each allowing at most $λ$ bits of leakage per party, the transcripts for two stored secrets are at statistical distance at most $C\cdot T\cdot 2^{6λ-n/9}$ for an absolute constant $C$. We also obtain a Boolean-circuit compiler with statistical privacy error at most $C\cdot S\cdot 2^{18λ-n/27}$ for $S$ operations and at most $λ$ bits of local leakage per party per operation. The guarantee covers repeated stateful evaluations with adaptively chosen public inputs, with $S$ counting all operations across invocations. Thus, for polynomial-size circuits, a constant leakage fraction is tolerated with share length depending only on the security parameter. We formalize the refreshing bound, the composition and compiler guarantees, and the expected-work bounds in Lean 4. Our results also provide efficient simulation: the leakage can be reproduced from the public inputs and the circuit outputs alone, with expected polynomial overhead.

title: Asymptotics for partitions over the Fibonacci numbers and related sequences, II
abstract: In a recent paper of the same title, we considered nondistinct partitions of integers over the Fibonacci sequence and related linearly recurrent sequences. In this paper, continuing this story, we apply the same method, but consider distinct partitions. In particular, let $q_F(m)$ denote the number of ways of writing $m$ as the sum of distinct Fibonacci numbers. It is well-known that, while $q_F(m)$ behaves wildly, its partial sums behave in a more structured way. In particular, Kempton showed that the function $N^{-\log 2/\log\varphi}\sum_{m\leqslant N}q_F(m)$ is asymptotically logarithmically-periodic. In this paper, we improve on this result by providing an explicit error term. Additionally, we prove the analogous result for a class of more general linear recurrent sequences.

title: On Douglas' conjecture for $m$-Kronecker quivers
abstract: We prove Douglas' conjecture for $m$-Kronecker quivers for each $m \geq 3$ on the normalized logarithms of Euler characteristics of moduli spaces. Also, we state a log-concavity conjecture on Euler characteristics near slope one for the 3-Kronecker quiver.

title: Robust Aggregation of Quantile Statistics: from Median to Interval
abstract: Quantile-based summaries, such as prediction intervals and medians, are commonly used in economic forecasting, climate science, and public health. For highly skewed samples, experimental evidence suggests that estimates of the mean can be biased toward the median, whereas estimates of the median are relatively accurate. This motivates aggregating explicitly elicited quantiles rather than reported means. We study robust aggregation of quantile reports for bounded outcomes under squared loss, minimizing worst-case regret relative to an omniscient Bayesian aggregator who knows the information structure and observes all private signals. Without restrictions on the information structure, no rule improves on the constant forecast at the range midpoint in worst-case regret. We therefore consider weak substitutes, a diminishing-returns condition on the value of information, and characterize optimal aggregation rules under this condition. For central prediction intervals with common nominal coverage $α$, the optimal rule, which we call regularized simple average for prediction intervals, shrinks the average reported interval midpoint toward the range midpoint, with a weight determined by $α$ and the number $n$ of experts. This optimal rule strictly improves on the constant baseline in worst-case regret when $α<1/\sqrt{n}$; at or above this threshold, the constant rule is optimal. The optimal worst-case regret is minimized at a unique interior coverage level, revealing a nonmonotonic relationship between coverage and aggregation performance. For median reports, regularized simple average for medians similarly shrinks the average reported median toward the range midpoint, assigning weight $1/n$ to the reported average and strictly improving on the constant baseline in worst-case regret for every finite $n\ge2$.

title: Bankruptcy Rules for Strategic Agents
abstract: Bankruptcy rules are rules for dividing an insufficient estate among people with different claims. Existing rules assume that the claims are publicly known. When this is not the case, claimants have a strong incentive to claim more than they are due, as bankruptcy rules give larger allocations to claimants with larger claims. A remedy often used by legal systems is to make over-reporting costly by requiring evidence and imposing penalties. But this remedy also increases the legal expenses of proving true claims, which might result in under-reporting. Encouraging true reporting requires fine-tuning of the legal costs. This paper incorporates the costs of supporting both true and false claims into the bankruptcy model. Claimants incur costs for the true and false parts of their claims, with false claims costing at least as much per unit as true claims. The goal is to set cost rates that induce claimants to report their true entitlements, neither more nor less. Whether this is possible depends on the allocation rule. The proportional and constrained equal awards rules cannot guarantee truthfulness at any positive true-claim cost rate; the same holds for constrained equal losses with at least three claimants. For $N\ge2$ claimants, the rule TAL-1/N from the parameterized Talmud family induces truthfulness exactly when the true-claim cost rate is at most 1/N and the false-claim cost rate is at least 1-1/N. This rule is optimal in the sense that its truthful cost region contains that of every piecewise smooth allocation rule: it gives the legal system the maximum possible flexibility in setting the legal costs. For two claimants, TAL-1/2 (aka Contested Garment rule) uniquely attains this optimal region.

title: Real-Space renormalization for the drawups and drawdowns of stochastic trajectories: universality classes for diffusion processes and random walks via the scale function
abstract: For one-dimensional diffusion processes with arbitrary diffusion coefficient $D(x)$ and Ito force $F_I(x)$, we analyze the statistical properties of the renormalized trajectories at scale $Γ$, where one keeps only the alternating sequence of local minima and local maxima that are separated by drawups and drawdowns of amplitude bigger than $Γ$. The elementary RG-step between $Γ$ and $Γ+d Γ$ thus amounts to eliminate the drawups and drawdowns of amplitude $Γ$, a real-space-RG-procedure that is well-known for Brownian trajectories in the context of the Strong-Disorder-RG approach applied to the disorder landscape of random models. The main result is that the universality classes are determined by the scale function $s(x)$ satisfying $D(x) s''(x)+F_I(x) s'(x)=0$ that governs the exit probabilities from an interval : all the diffusions sharing the same scale function $s(x)$ have the same statistics of renormalized trajectories, even if their initial microscopic trajectories are completely different. The simplest universality classes for diffusions on the whole line $x \in ]-\infty,+\infty[$ and on the half-line $x \in ]0,+\infty[$ are illustrated with several examples of processes, with or without steady states: Cauchy, Student, Bessel, Fisher-Snedecor, Geometric Brownian. This framework concerning diffusion processes is then adapted to discrete-time and to continuous-time random walks on the one-dimensional lattice with arbitrary nearest-neighbor jump probabilities or rates.

title: Stochastic synthesis and degradation of arbitrary diffusive processes
abstract: Target search processes are often carried out by diffusive elements that are introduced and removed at random times, causing fluctuations in the number of searchers in the system over time. For instance, proteins are synthesized and degraded stochastically in the cell, and susceptible to react with specific binding sites during their lifetime. Here we derive the density profile generated by non-interacting particles subject to stochastic synthesis and degradation (SSD) at constant rates, given a source location and an arbitrary propagator for the single, non-degrading particle. We also study the first-passage properties of these many-searcher processes, which can be deduced from the knowledge of the first-passage time distribution of a single particle. We analyse the behaviours of the characteristic reaction time and of the mean first-passage time in the limits of small and large rates. Taking into account the costs associated with synthesis leads to the existence of an optimal synthesis rate. We further generalise these results to bursty synthesis, when production events involve more than one particle at a time, as often observed in cell biology. The mean first-passage time in these situations can be significantly reduced at low synthesis or large degradation rates, as it is divided by the mean burst size in these regimes. The results presented here are applied to one-dimensional Brownian searches. Some general connections between SSD and resetting processes are pointed out as well as important differences, since SSD is associated with a distinct queueing protocol.

title: Space-Time HWI Inequalities and the Wasserstein Current for Kinetic Equations
abstract: We prove a space-time analogue of the HWI inequality of Otto-Villani for controlled kinetic equations with a semiconvex confining potential. It bounds the time-averaged relative entropy by spatial and conditional velocity transport distances, the velocity Fisher information, an intrinsic action of the path, and a boundary term given by the time endpoint values of the Wasserstein current. The key step is a differential comparison inequality for the Wasserstein current, which captures the transfer of dissipation from velocity to position. Along the Langevin semigroup, this inequality yields a kinetic evolution variational inequality involving the second time derivative of the squared spatial Wasserstein distance and a damping term. Under a compatible spatial Talagrand's transport inequality, we obtain a boundary-free space-time logarithmic Sobolev inequality on every interval $[0,T]$, $T>0$, with the optimal $T^{-2}$ short-time scaling of the constant. As a consequence, we also establish entropy decay for every friction coefficient and every initial density of finite entropy, with optimal cubic order at short times and exponential decay at long times.

title: Geometric Bin Packing Beyond Convexity: Approximation Schemes without Augmentation
abstract: We study the geometric bin packing problem for simple polygonal regions, i.e., non-degenerate, connected, rational regions, in the minimum number of unit-square bins, allowing only translations. We even consider packing general non-convex objects, possibly with holes, where we can then pack smaller objects. Previous schemes cover squares (MOR'06), circles and other $L_p$-balls (Algorithmica'16), sufficiently skewed rectangles (Algorithmica'23), and convex fat objects with a constant number of distinct shapes under resource augmentation (arXiv'24, WAOA'23). The result for circles and other $L_p$-balls needs bin augmentation to obtain rational packing realizations. For restricted classes of $L$-shaped polygons, Gerlach et al. (SoCG'26) give constant worst-case guarantees, while for general non-convex objects, bounding-box reductions give just approximation factors that depend on fatness. Against this background, we present a general framework that provides asymptotic polynomial-time approximation schemes (APTAS) for bin packing of any fixed class of simple polygonal regions satisfying just two assumptions. First, covering any object by the grid cells intersecting its interior in any sufficiently fine square grid, relative to the object's bounding box, increases its area by at most a small fraction. Second, the class can be partitioned into a constant number of sequences such that each object in a sequence can be translated to fit inside every preceding object. In particular, certain classes of star-shaped polygons and more general polygonal regions, including some with simple holes, satisfy both assumptions. In addition, our framework does not require a bound on the objects' boundary complexity. We emphasize that our results require no bin augmentation whatsoever and yield explicit, exact rational packings of polynomial encoding length for all input objects.

title: AI for eGovernance: Leveraging Language Technologies For Digital Inclusion
abstract: The Kenyan government has invested heavily in the digitisation of public service delivery, in line with the Kenya Digital Master Plan 2022-2032. The national eGovernment platform, eCitizen, hosts services that are vital to citizens' livelihoods, including business registration, youth enterprise lending, digital literacy and tax filing. However, the platform faces digital inclusion challenges that limit equitable access for marginalised groups, particularly youth in rural areas and persons with disabilities. This exclusion is driven by a language barrier, since the platform is primarily in English with limited Swahili support, and by a text-only interface that excludes low-literacy and visually impaired users. This paper reports findings from six one-on-one interviews and an eleven-person roundtable discussion across four platforms essential to youth livelihoods: Ajira Digital, Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) iTax, Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) and the Youth Enterprise Development Fund (YEDF). Drawing on these findings, on Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 principles as a design lens for diagnosing eCitizen's accessibility gaps, and on comparator models such as Estonia's Bürokratt and India's Bhashini, the paper proposes a human-centred, systems-minded framework for embedding generative AI and language technologies into eCitizen, including text simplification, neural machine translation, text-to-speech and speech-to-text. The paper argues that, when deployed responsibly with appropriate human oversight, these interventions could meaningfully improve access to government services for linguistically excluded citizens. It also emphasises that AI alone cannot overcome the broader structural barriers, including unemployment and educational inequality, that shape digital exclusion.

title: Extracting System Prompt of LLM Services in Complex (Agentic) Settings: Hierarchical Optimization and Reliable Evaluation Metrics
abstract: System prompt is a critical intellectual property of large language model (LLM) services. To analyze its leakage, prompt extraction attacks have been extensively studied. However, we validate that existing attacks substantially degrade on recent LLM services, whose complexity has evolved in both the prompt itself and system-level constraints. Specifically, (1) system prompts become longer and more structured to contain pre-defined tool schemas, execution logic, safety guardrails, etc., and (2) only the final post-processed outputs (e.g., agent's actions) but not the raw textual response can be observed. In this paper, we address the above increased complexity by proposing Extraction with Hierarchical Optimization (ExtraHerO), which (1) decomposes the prompt extraction into a hierarchical reconstruction process with a pre-defined structural prompt template, and (2) iteratively updates the adversarial query with guidance of feedback-template differences to observe diverse outputs. In particular, we monitor the information gain of attack optimization to early stop or reset it for a good trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency. We also find that existing evaluation metrics for prompt fidelity can be misleading because they do not account for structural information. Therefore, we rely on global textual similarity and prioritize structural keywords. Moreover, we introduce a system-level metric, adversarial utility, to measure the help of prompt extraction for real-world downstream attacks. Experimental results demonstrate the consistent superiority of ExtraHerO, with average improvements of 12.5\% (fidelity), 2.3\% (functionality), and 6.0\% (adversarial utility) on chatbots, and 12.2\%, 34.3\%, and 30.5\% on agents.

title: Disruption limits around triaxial bodies and implications for ring-bearing minor bodies
abstract: The classical Roche limit is often used as a boundary between ring-dominated and satellite-dominated regions, although it is derived for a self-gravitating fluid satellite orbiting a spherical primary. This assumption is poorly suited to ring-bearing minor bodies, which are often triaxial. Here, we compute the equilibrium figures and disruption limits of inviscid fluid satellites orbiting triaxial primaries, modelling their gravity fields through J2 and C22. The primary's oblateness and equatorial asymmetry shifts the disruption limit outward relative to the classical Roche limit, with C22 dominating the correction at sufficiently high values, which require highly oblate primaries. The disruption location also depends on the primary's orientation, defining a radial disruption region rather than a single limit in non-double-synchronous systems. Increasing orbital inclination shifts the limit inward, significantly so only at high inclinations. Symbolic regression provides an empirical expression for the disruption limit around triaxial primaries, which we apply to ring-bearing minor bodies. The correction is most relevant for Haumea and Chariklo, whereas the rings of Chiron and Quaoar located beyond the classical Roche limit remain outside the disruption region for realistic particle densities. This indicates that treating the disruption limit as a strict boundary between ring-dominated and satellite-dominated regions is an oversimplification, since the long-term survival of a ring also depends on collisional evolution, particle properties, and resonant confinement driven by the primary's non-axisymmetric gravity field.

title: Who Is Doing the Thinking? Characterising Human Agency in First-Year Students' AI Interactions
abstract: When students use generative AI to produce their work, the learning process becomes invisible. Established frameworks such as Bloom's taxonomy then classify the cognitive level of what the AI produced, not what the student contributed. We propose the Human Agency Depth Taxonomy (HADT), a preliminary six-tier taxonomy that classifies the engineering contribution a student makes in a prompt, independent of the AI's output. HADT combines three dimensions: contextual bandwidth, engineering abstraction and student agency. We applied HADT to 962 prompts from 105 students' structured AI Journals in an AI-permissive, first-year software engineering course of 145 students, and examined how agency changed over ten journalled weeks. Most prompts (84.2%) carried some student contribution beyond delegation. Agency tracked the development lifecycle. Architecture-discovery prompts dominated the requirements phase (48% of turns) and fell to 5-12% from week 9, while prompts analysing existing systems rose during build and verification (odds ratio 2.88, with turns clustered by student). Two-thirds of the variance in tier lay within students, so agency depended more on the phase of work than on the student. A turn-level rise in delegation in deadline weeks did not hold once turns were clustered by student. Explicitly specifying constraints on the AI's output was rare throughout, which we interpret as a knowledge bottleneck for novices rather than a gap in instruction. We discuss implications for course and assessment design, and for using HADT as a formative lens on how students engage with AI.

title: On the Onsager--Machlup functional of the infinite-dimensional angular central Gaussian distribution and related measures
abstract: The Onsager--Machlup functional of a probability measure is a generalisation of the negative logarithm of the probability density function, defined precisely using the ratios of masses of balls in the limit of vanishing radius. It plays an important role in several areas of applied mathematics because its minimisers can be understood as modes of the measure. We show that the Onsager--Machlup functional of the angular central Gaussian measure on the unit sphere of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space---i.e., the radial projection of a centred Gaussian measure with covariance operator $C$---is constant on the finite-dimensional sphere spanned by the eigenvectors of leading eigenvalue under $C$, and takes the value $+\infty$ elsewhere. We discuss the consequences of this extreme concentration of mass for maximum a posteriori estimation in Bayesian inverse problems with an angular central Gaussian prior.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Submodular Trajectory Rewards
abstract: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning with decoupled dynamics and a monotone submodular reward function over joint trajectories. Due to the non-additive reward, an optimal policy may depend on the history of all agents. This dependence makes exact optimization exponential in the horizon and the number of agents. To overcome this challenge while retaining theoretical guarantees, we introduce pre-window curvature $c_m$, which quantifies how states visited more than $m$ steps earlier reduce current marginal gains. Using this curvature to control the error from restricting the policy of each agent to depend only on its last $m+1$ states, we propose a greedy algorithm that exploits the decoupled dynamics to optimize local policies sequentially. For fixed $m$, the algorithm achieves a $\frac{1-c_m}{2-c_m}$ approximation guarantee up to estimation error, and its computation time is polynomial in the number of agents and the horizon. We recover the known $1/2$-factor approximation for time-additive rewards and obtain an approximation factor no smaller than the known total-curvature bound for a single agent. We formulate multi-agent traffic monitoring as an example of this framework and evaluate our algorithm on it.

title: Logarithmic Comparison-Query Complexity for EF1 Allocations
abstract: We study the comparison-query complexity of computing allocations that are envy-free up to one item (EF1) for $n$ agents with heterogeneous additive preferences over $m$ indivisible items. In this model, the algorithm may only query which of two bundles an agent prefers, without ever observing numerical valuations or costs. Prior work established $O(\log m)$ query bounds for at most three agents, leaving open whether query complexity logarithmic in $m$ is achievable for every fixed $n \ge 4$. We resolve this open question in the affirmative: for every fixed $n\ge2$, we design algorithms that compute EF1 allocations using $O(\log m)$ comparison queries, matching the known $Ω(\log m)$ lower bound. Our results hold for both chores with nonnegative costs and goods with nonnegative valuations.

title: Nonlinearity-Induced Suppression of Dissipation in Bath-Coupled Floquet Topological Insulators
abstract: Topological insulators can host chiral, disorder-robust edge states that dissipate energy when coupled to an external bath. We show that nonlinear interactions enable all-optical control over edge-state dissipation in a laser-written Floquet topological insulator periodically coupled to a photonic bath. Although moderate nonlinearity enhances dissipation due to mode mixing, increasing the nonlinear strength to an optimal value dramatically suppresses dissipation by forming highly localized traveling edge solitons. These results establish engineered system-bath coupling and nonlinear interactions as a route to suppress dissipation of chiral topological edge transport.

title: Stochastic interpretation of the Water Waves equations
abstract: The aim of this article is to derive a stochastic interpretation of the Water Waves equations, based on the location uncertainty principle (LU). Next, these equations are used to infer simpler models from scaling limits, such as the Saint-Venant, Boussinesq and Serre-Green-Naghdi ones. Once adapted to the stochastic setting, these models have been successfully implemented numerically, and we show several experiments to assess their properties -- for example the breaking of the wave symmetry, and the influence of time correlated noises.

title: Critical amplitudes of the Baxter-Wu model from MCPA and Wolff simulations: free-exponent and fixed-exponent fits
abstract: The two-dimensional Baxter-Wu model belongs to the universality class of the four-state Potts model. Exact expressions are available for its energy, specific heat, magnetization, and polarization amplitudes. We use these results as a benchmark for evaluating two simulation algorithms and two approaches to extracting critical amplitudes. Microcanonical population annealing (MCPA) and the sublattice-freezing Wolff algorithm yield highly consistent estimates for the energy and order parameters when applied to lattices of comparable size. According to the exact Joyce series, the local effective exponent does not stabilize at a constant value but instead undergoes a monotonic drift. This behaviour stems from corrections to scaling, which can be expressed as a series in the cube root of the reduced temperature. As a result, these corrections decay relatively slowly, with the leading term being of relative order $|t|^{2/3}$. When performing a fit with a free exponent on an automatically identified plateau, this drift gets incorporated into the estimated exponent, introducing a substantial bias in the derived amplitudes. In contrast, a fit that fixes the exponent to its exact value and explicitly accounts for the analytic correction series delivers a close match to the known exact amplitudes. Using this refined fitting approach, we obtain estimates for the susceptibility amplitudes and the universal amplitude ratios. These values are in good agreement with predictions from form-factor calculations. Additionally, we numerically determine the leading correction coefficient for the polarization.

title: Limits to research in astrophysics
abstract: Fundamental physics faces several intrinsic limitations, such as the finite speed of light in vacuum, the absolute zero temperature, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and so on. At the same time, the material resources necessary to conduct research in astrophysics, such as energy, fresh water, and rareearth elements, are also limited in both quantity and extraction capabilities, a concept often referred to as planetary boundaries.
