We propose CORDE, a system for confidential virtual machines (CVMs) designed to satisfy the principle of Confine or Declare: user-derived data is confined by default, but when necessary, it may leave the CVM only after being "declared." To "declare" data is to record its exact contents, recipient, and stated reason in a user-accessible, tamper-evident declaration log. To put this principle into practice, we present an integrated system design that combines per-user information-flow control in Rust with a TEE-based ledger and remote attestation. Our evaluation on an NVIDIA H100 GPU shows that declaration before disclosure adds little overhead in task latency, about 0.5% on the AppWorld agent benchmark. CORDE provides a basis for accountable disclosure of user data, supporting responsible and transparent data management in AI services.

title: Frank Elastic Constants of Associating Rigid-Rodlike Systems
abstract: Frank elastic constants of associating rigid rodlike systems are investigated using a mean field theory combined with the Straley elastic free energy formalism. The aggregation equilibrium and orientational ordering are treated self-consistently to analyze the concentration and temperature dependences of the elastic constants. Both a monomer--dimer model and a fully polydisperse rodlike aggregate model are considered. We find that aggregation selectively enhances the bend elastic constant through the long-tail structure of the aggregate-size distribution. As a result, a pronounced elastic anisotropy, $K_{33}\gg K_{11}>K_{22}$, emerges in the nematic phase. Decreasing temperature or increasing concentration promotes the formation of long rodlike aggregates and induces a rapid increase in the bend elastic constant, while the relation $K_{11}=3K_{22}$ remains unchanged. The exceptionally large bend elastic constants predicted here should be regarded as upper-bound estimates for the rigid-aggregate limit.

title: Orbital Architecture of Super-Earth-Cold-Jupiter Systems from Transit Duration Ratios
abstract: Super-Earths are commonly found with cold Jupiters, yet it is unclear whether these Super-Earth-Cold-Jupiter (SE-CJ) systems differ architecturally from other Kepler-like systems (Non-SE-CJ). One might expect the CJs to excite eccentricities and mutual inclinations among the SEs. We use two metrics: the normalized transit duration $T/T_0$, set by the host-star density, and the pairwise duration ratio $ξ$ between neighboring transiting planets. We find no population-level difference in $T/T_0$ between the samples. Forward modeling of $ξ$, which is more directly sensitive to mutual inclinations because it isolates the impact-parameter contrast, finds no evidence that SE-CJ systems are more mutually inclined than Non-SE-CJ systems, and hints they could be even flatter. We infer a Rayleigh dispersion in mutual inclination of $δ\approx 1.0^\circ$, or a characteristic eccentricity of $e \approx 0.035$ (assuming equipartition), compared with $δ\approx 1.5^\circ$ and $e \approx 0.05$ for Non-SE-CJ systems. Many SE-CJ systems therefore retain nearly coplanar, low-eccentricity architectures despite hosting distant giants. We further show that secular coupling among the inner Super-Earths usually dominates over forcing from the cold Jupiter, leaving the inner planets resistant to excitation. Our analysis is limited to SE-CJ systems with multiple transiting SEs: systems in which the CJ has strongly excited the inner architecture are expected to present as single-transiting, and cannot be studied with the $ξ$ metric. Another caveat of our result is that undetected cold Jupiters in the comparison sample could dilute the measured $ξ$ distribution.

title: Scaling Limits and Fractal Dimensions of $ω$-Substitution Graph Systems
abstract: This paper introduces a class of non-homogeneous self-similar constructions, called $ω$-substitution graph system, in which the interface vertices are determined by an infinite sequence $ω.$ The associated graph sequences naturally form compact metric measure spaces, and under suitable assumptions on $ω$, we establish their convergence in the Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov sense. We determine the Hausdorff and box-counting dimensions of the limiting space. We further prove that the discrete Hausdorff dimension of the graph sequence coincides with the Hausdorff dimension of its scaling limit. As a direct application of the scaling limit, asymptotic formulas are derived for a class of generalized Wiener indices, which include the classical Wiener index and Kirchhoff index as special cases. Finally, closed-form expressions for these indices are also obtained.

title: Robots in the City: Persona-Based Perceptions of Urban Robots
abstract: Pedestrians increasingly encounter robots in urban public spaces without interacting with them, but how robots change the perceived safety of a street remains unclear. We examine how robot presence and type affect perceived safety across urban contexts. We generate 18 images of Seoul streets that vary in time of day, road class, and robot condition (no robot, a delivery robot, or a humanoid). Two multimodal large language models (MLLMs), Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma4-26B, each conditioned on 500 synthetic personas, choose the safer image in each pair, and 25 human respondents complete the same task. Both models prefer streets without robots and favor the delivery robot over the humanoid. Robots are chosen more often at night and less often by older personas, whereas road class has smaller effects. In the model rationales, the delivery robot appears as a physical obstacle, whereas the humanoid appears as either a threat or a source of protection. Like humans, both models chose robots more often at night, but chose the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often, and Gemma showed a night effect for the humanoid about three times that of humans. These results show that the effect of a robot on perceived safety depends on when it appears, and that persona-conditioned MLLMs capture only part of human judgments.

title: Community Search under Member-Specific Tolerances
abstract: We study community search when each vertex has its own tolerance for differences in position. For positions such as opinions or homes, a latitude-consistent community (LCC) contains the query vertex, is connected, has minimum degree at least k, and bounds its diameter by the smallest member tolerance. Motivated by social judgment theory, the bound exactly characterizes persistent acceptance of every interaction in a closed group under bounded-confidence dynamics with arbitrary positive weights. It also prevents rejection under social-judgment dynamics, whereas natural relaxations preserve neither guarantee. Finding a maximum LCC is NP-hard even in the plane, and with unbounded dimension, deciding whether an LCC exists is NP-complete for every fixed k >= 2. LatSweep turns the coupled bound into a sweep over the smallest tolerance, yielding two feasible heuristics, a (1,2)-bicriteria approximation and an exact branch-and-bound algorithm. Across eight graphs with up to 1.8 billion edges, the exact algorithm proves optimality on all but 9 of 3,700 efficiency queries and usually certifies absence within microseconds when no LCC exists. Its branch-and-bound solver proves more queries than a reimplemented maximum-(k,r)-core algorithm, a mixed-integer program and CP-SAT. In simulations, uneven influence disrupts initially accepted interactions in pairwise groups. Outside ties invalidate the guarantee for many real groups. On two location-based networks, tolerance-agnostic groups often place another member's home beyond a member's estimated travel radius; comparisons with spatial communities of the same size detect no co-visit loss from enforcing every member's tolerance.

title: Empirical approximation of $L^p$ norms for $p\in (1, 2)$
abstract: For $p\in[1,2]$, we prove uniform moment estimates for weighted sums \[ \sum_{j=1}^mζ_jw_j|\langle{\bf v}_j,y\rangle|^p \] of independent subgaussian random variables $ζ_j$, where the unit vectors $\{{\bf v}_j\}_{j=1}^m$ and nonnegative weights $\{w_j\}_{j=1}^m$ form an isotropic frame. This allows us to obtain optimal sampling discretization of $L_p$ norms for each fixed $p\in[1,2]$. Namely, for an $N$-dimensional space $X_N$ of bounded functions satisfying $\|f\|_\infty\le\sqrt {KN}\,\|f\|_{L_2}$ for every $f\in X_N$, we show that $m\ge C\varepsilon^{-2}KN\log(2N)$ independent samples $ξ^1,\ldots,ξ^m$ provide the discretization \[ (1-\varepsilon)\|f\|_{L_p}^p \le\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m|f(ξ^j)|^p \le(1+\varepsilon)\|f\|_{L_p}^p \quad\forall f\in X_N \] with probability at least $1-\exp(-c\frac{m\varepsilon^2}{KN})$. This implies a corresponding weighted discretization result that, for $1<p<2$, improves Talagrand's bound on the dimension $m$ needed to embed $N$-dimensional subspaces of $L_p$ into $\ell_p^m$ with distortion at most $1+\varepsilon$, giving $m\le C\varepsilon^{-2}N\log(2N)$.

title: Occupation Measures in the ODE Method: Wasserstein Convergence and Rates
abstract: We study occupation measures associated with stochastic approximation recursions within the ordinary differential equation (ODE) method. Under Lyapunov conditions ensuring that the limiting ODE has a globally exponentially stable equilibrium, we establish that the continuous-time occupation measures associated with the piecewise linear interpolation of the iterates converge almost surely in the $2$-Wasserstein topology to the Dirac mass at the equilibrium, the unique invariant probability measure of the limiting semiflow. The choice of the $2$-Wasserstein distance is naturally aligned with our continuous- and discrete-time Lyapunov drift analysis. We also consider two discrete-time sequences of occupation measures, induced by the algorithmic time scale and the iteration count, respectively, and we establish their almost sure convergence to the same invariant measure in the $2$-Wasserstein distance. We then derive corresponding convergence rates in expectation, providing a nonasymptotic complement to the almost sure results. These expectation bounds also imply some tail probability estimates. Finally, we verify that our results apply to a canonical class of linear recursions.

title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
abstract: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.

title: Compiling, Validating, and Using Human Reference Atlas Cell Type Annotation Crosswalks
abstract: The Human Reference Atlas (HRA) v2.5 includes 4,807 anatomical structures, 1,347 cell types, and 2,215 biomarkers (genes, proteins, lipids); 81 organs with 1,392 anatomical structures modeled in three dimensions (3D). Mapping new data into the HRA requires 3D spatial registration and/or cell type annotation (CTann). Many CTann tools exist but few use cell type names linked to Cell Ontology (CL), making comparisons across tools, tissues, and organs difficult. The HRA supports five transcriptomics CTann tools (Azimuth, CellTypist, popV, FR-Match, Pan-Human Azimuth), four sc-proteomics CTann tools (DeepCell Types, DeepCell Types-HuBMAP, Robust Image-Based Cell Annotator [RIBCA], and SpaTial cELl LeARning [STELLAR]), plus a Cell Distance Explorer (CDE) Spatial Omics collection covering previously published annotations across 12 tissue types with 47,349,496 cells. Assigned cell types differ in number, resolution, and coverage. This paper details how 10 crosswalks were constructed, validated, and used to compile a "Supertree" that can be used to compare CTann across organs and technologies in support of reference atlas constitution and usage. All data and code can be accessed at https://cns-iu.github.io/hra-ctann-supporting-information.

title: Does RRT* Work on Uneven Terrain Meshes?
abstract: The optimal rapidly exploring random tree (RRT*) is proven asymptotically optimal on open subsets of Euclidean space with straight-line local planning. We ask whether it works on a triangle-mesh terrain, a two-dimensional surface in R^3. First, the original RRT* cannot run on a mesh: the surface has zero volume, so uniform sampling never hits it, no clearance ball fits in it, and chords across a fold leave it. Second, the surface reformulation we call Mesh RRT*, with its naive edge, the chord costed by its length, solved every run on heightfields with slopes up to 75 degrees but minimises the wrong objective: its cost, the straight-line length of a polyline whose vertices lie on the surface while its segments may leave it by a tolerance tau, is the length of no route on the surface and lies strictly below the geodesic length on any curved mesh. In numeric simulation and after 30,000 iterations the reported cost is on average up to 2.7% below the exact geodesic, a cost no path attains, and the returned route on average 0.1-0.5% longer than it. Rewiring keeps the biased edges, the bias decays only linearly with the step on polyhedral surfaces, and shrinking tau trades bias for connectivity. Third, replacing each chord by a path on the surface above it, built from projected points joined across the mesh edges they straddle and costed by its own length, makes every edge cost the exact length of a feasible path; with no other change the exact length of the returned routes is on average within 0.07-0.16% of the geodesic at every roughness tested, two to 3.4 times closer than with chords on the rougher terrains. The planner is in MeshNav3D 0.2.0 (release pending).

title: AI-Assisted Classification under Correlation Neglect and Trust
abstract: When does an AI assistant improve human decision-making, and when does it hurt? We argue that the answer depends not just on AI accuracy but also on how much its evidence overlaps with the human's and how the human combines the two. A worker makes a binary decision by observing her own signal and receiving a recommendation from an AI. We develop a human behavioral model with two primitives: her awareness of the overlap and her trust in the AI. Our analysis gives a closed-form phase diagram over AI capability and overlap, with regions of complementarity, impairment, and automation. A worker who neglects the overlap (correlation neglect) can be made less accurate by a more capable AI, double-counting the shared evidence. Trust reshapes the regions - undertrust may compensate for correlation neglect, so that the trust level maximizing accuracy depends on the deployment parameters. Empirically, we identify the two model parameters by pairing the same workers with different AIs, and break the accuracy loss into a correlation-neglect cost and an undertrust cost, one tied to reducing overlap on the AI side, the other to calibrating trust on the human side. On ChatBench, AI assistance raises accuracy by 21 points, yet workers apply only about a quarter of the Bayes-rational weight to AI information; GPT-4o falls in the automation region and Llama-3.1-8b stays at the complementarity boundary; and calibrating trust recovers about 2.6 points for GPT-4o but almost nothing for Llama-3.1-8b.

title: Polarimetry with the Giant Magellan Telescope: A Scientific Justification & Technical Requirements Document
abstract: The photons we collect from astronomical sources are encoded with information about the physics behind their origin. To fully probe that physics, we must maximize the information we extract from those photons. At optical and near-infrared wavelengths, this is typically done with the use of filters or a disperser to extract flux as a function of color. An often disregarded piece of information that is also carried by those photons is the polarization state. Astronomical polarimetry is capable of revealing details about the source geometry and magnetic fields that are often unresolvable and, therefore, inaccessible by any other means. Polarimetry is typically a photon-starved science because crucial model discriminators are often only revealed when precisions of 0.1% in the degree of polarization are achieved. For spectropolarimetry, this necessitates the collection of over one million photons at each spectral bin, which demands the use of large aperture telescopes for typical objects of interest. The future completion of Giant Segmented Mirror Telescopes (GSMTs) promises the long-awaited light grasp to initiate an unprecedented era of discovery with astronomical polarimetry.

title: Gaussian free field limit for the Airy$_β$ line ensemble
abstract: We prove that the centered height function of the Airy$_β$ line ensemble converges for each $β>0$, under rescaling of space and time variables, towards the Gaussian free field in the half-plane. The conformal structure for GFF involves the spatial change of coordinate $x\mapsto \sqrt{-x}$. The $β$--dependence is isolated in the field rescaling by $\sqrtβ$. For the proofs we study the asymptotic expansions of the moments of Laplace transforms of the Airy$_β$ line ensemble developed in our previous work with Xu.

title: Sure Enough to Share? Overconfidence in GenAI Video Discernment is Associated with Sharing Intentions
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is blurring the line between synthesized and recorded videos, but less is known about people's awareness of their discernment abilities and the consequences of miscalibration. This study examines three forms of overconfidence in GenAI video discernment (i.e., overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision) and their associations with source judgments and sharing intentions in an online study (N = 973). Participants evaluated videos depicting everyday scenes and achieved 62.5% accuracy. Three forms of overconfidence showed distinct patterns: participants overplaced themselves by 12.8 percentile points, but overprecision showed consistent positive associations with sharing intentions and the tendency to classify videos as human-made. Age, GenAI usage, and AI literacy showed consistent positive associations with all three forms of overconfidence. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing the three forms of overconfidence to better understand GenAI engagement and incorporating metacognition into interventions to support informed media consumption.

title: Functional inequalities from the fundamental limits of Bayesian estimation
abstract: We develop a Bayesian information-theoretic framework for proving functional inequalities for log-concave measures. Motivated by Klartag and Ordentlich, we establish a unified equivalence between $Φ$-Sobolev inequalities and Bayesian estimation lower bounds: for a large class of smooth convex $Φ$, a log-concave measure $μ$ satisfies a $Φ$-Sobolev inequality with constant $C>0$ if and only if for $X\simμ$, any $t>0$, and any real-valued measurable $f$, the Bayes risk of estimating $f(X)$ under the $Φ$-Bregman loss from the Gaussian additive observation $Y_t=\sqrt tX+G, G\sim N(0,I_n)$ is at least a $1/(1+Ct)$-fraction of that of the trivial estimator. Combining it with direct information-theoretic arguments, such as testing-to-estimation reductions, we obtain old and new functional inequalities: - For the Poincaré inequality, corresponding to $Φ(x)=(x-1)^2$, we give a simple static information-theoretic proof that the Poincaré constant of an isotropic log-concave measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $O(n^{1/2})$, first proven via stochastic localization in the seminal work of Lee and Vempala. - For the log-Sobolev inequality, corresponding to $Φ(x)=x\log x$, we prove that all smooth $K$-subgaussian log-concave measures $μ$ satisfy $C_{\mathrm{LS}}(μ)\lesssim K^2n^{1/4}$, surpassing the recent state-of-the-art bound of $O(K^2n^{1/2})$ by Bizeul. In parallel and independent work, OpenAI claimed the optimal bound $O(K^2)$ in their October 6, 2026 release of 722 papers. - Finally, we give a Bayesian reformulation of the common structure of the three recent proofs of the Kannan--Lovász--Simonovits conjecture, a dimension-free Poincaré bound for isotropic log-concave measures [BK26; BKL26; SZ26]. Tools from the study of the "low-degree MMSE" in computational complexity of statistical inference motivate and recast key steps and quantities of these proofs.

title: Variational exponential estimates and stationary large deviations for SPDEs
abstract: We establish an abstract criterion for large deviations of invariant measures when the deterministic dynamics has a single globally attracting equilibrium. Deterministic regularisation and attraction yield an endpoint estimate for long controlled paths of bounded action, uniformly over each fixed bounded initial set. This allows the finite time Freidlin-Wentzell uniform LDP on bounded initial sets to be combined directly with stationary exponential norm estimates. The proof requires neither a separate exponential tightness argument nor a Dembo-Zeitouni uniform LDP, and imposes no decay condition on differences between controlled trajectories. Finite path approximation identifies the quasipotential as the good rate function. We also establish a variational criterion based on the Boué-Dupuis representation that derives exponential estimates from bounds for controlled outputs, without requiring their convergence. Uniform controlled terminal moments yield estimates uniform in time, which pass to Krylov-Bogoliubov invariant measures. Together, these results establish stationary LDPs in four regimes: two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with possibly unbounded, globally Lipschitz, uniformly positive scalar amplitudes and vanishing noise correlation; reaction-diffusion systems without the additional restriction linking noise growth to reaction strength; Allen-Cahn equations with opposite boundary values and globally Lipschitz, uniformly nondegenerate multiplicative space-time white noise on intervals of arbitrary length; and Burgers equations with fixed covariance $(-Δ)^α$, $0\leqα<1/2$. For Burgers, we also obtain Gaussian norm estimates.

title: A Hybrid Approach for Automated Security Pattern Recovery
abstract: Security-by-design emphasises integrating security into software design and development. Security pattern catalogues operationalise this principle by prescribing reusable architectural solutions to recurring security problems. However, recovering their implementations from source code remains challenging because security patterns are abstract, span multiple components, and admit many valid implementations. We present SecPatRec, a hybrid approach for automated security pattern recovery from source code repositories. We treat a security pattern as a reference architecture and frame its recovery as a deductive task: determining which prescribed roles are present, grounding them in code entities, and recovering their interaction sequences. SecPatRec pairs a ReAct-style LLM agent equipped with semantic and lexical code search for role detection and grounding with static code property graph analysis for interaction recovery. We curate a human-validated ground-truth dataset of 100 pattern instances covering five security patterns across 93 open-source Java and Python repositories, and introduce a three-level evaluation framework measuring recovery correctness against this ground truth. We evaluate SecPatRec using four LLMs, including proprietary and open-source models. Averaged over all models and pattern instances, SecPatRec achieves role-detection accuracy of 0.84, role-grounding similarity of 0.84, and an interaction-recovery score of 0.66. Compared to a one-shot end-to-end LLM baseline, SecPatRec achieves higher aggregate recovery scores and lower estimated LLM API costs per run, while processing repositories that exceed the baseline's configured input limit. The recovered role mappings and statically derived interaction sequences provide structural and behavioural evidence that can support inspection of security-pattern implementations.

title: A geometric proof of multivariate self-normalized moderate deviations via ridge regularization
abstract: Let $X,X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d.\ random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $d\ge1$ is fixed. Assume that $\mathbb{E} X=0$, $\mathbb{E} XX^\top=I_d$ and $\mathbb{E}\|X\|^3<\infty$. We prove a Cramér type moderate deviation theorem for a multivariate self-normalized radius statistic, that is, for every $a_n=o(n^{1/6})$, \[ \sup_{0\le x\le a_n} \left|\frac{\mathbb{P}(U_{n,+}\ge x)}{\mathbb{P}(χ_d\ge x)}-1\right|\to0, \] where $χ_d$ is the Euclidean norm of a standard normal vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and \[ U_{n,+}^2=S_n^\top A_n^+S_n, \qquad S_n=\sum_{j=1}^nX_j, \qquad A_n=\sum_{j=1}^nX_jX_j^\top. \] Here $A_n^+$ denotes the Moore--Penrose inverse. We further prove that the same result holds for the corresponding Hotelling $T^2$ statistic. This work closes the moment gap between the previously known finite $(3+δ)$ moment condition for Hotelling moderate deviations and the finite third moment boundary. Our proof adopts a geometric approach. Truncation at the finite-third-moment scale yields a truncated covariance matrix whose concentration error is negligible relative to the target \(χ_d\) tail. Uniform projected self-normalized moderate deviations are then averaged over directions and, after a whitening map with a ridge term, become a spherical cap transform of the radial distribution. A local Abel inversion recovers the radial tail, and deterministic comparison removes the ridge and the truncation.

title: GRIDSHIELD: Verifiable Grid Feasibility and Manipulation Resistance in Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading
abstract: Blockchain-based peer-to-peer (P2P) energy markets let neighbors trade directly, but concentrate unchecked power in the clearing operator. Most prior work addresses only part of this: network-aware clearing respects grid constraints but operates on plaintext allocations, while privacy-preserving designs hide bids yet either drop the network constraint, enforce it only inside an unauditable computation, or recover it at the cost of a per-circuit trusted setup. Neither considers what happens if an adversary captures the operator's clearing privilege to reorder trades for profit or curtail a rival. We present GRIDSHIELD, a P2P energy-trading system that clears sealed bids with an order-independent batch program, removing the welfare a compromised operator can extract by reordering trades, and proves the result grid-feasible via an aggregated congestion-feasibility proof (ACFP). Exploiting the additive homomorphism of Pedersen commitments, ACFP reconstructs each grid constraint directly from per-bus commitments, reducing feeder-wide feasibility verification over any public grid constraints to a single aggregated range proof over the hidden allocation, with a reveal-and-recompute challenge that catches feasible yet unfair clearings. We introduce congestion-responsibility fairness (CRF), a metric scoring curtailment against each party's physical responsibility for congestion rather than consumption. We evaluate GRIDSHIELD against three prior P2P energy-trading designs across four feeders, including a 240-node Midwest feeder with real hourly loads, on a live Hyperledger Fabric network benchmarked with Hyperledger Caliper. GRIDSHIELD proves an entire round feasible with a few-kilobyte proof and no trusted setup, rejects infeasible allocations two of the three compared designs accept, and sustains $\approx$1064 tx/s.

title: When File Ingestion Misleads Language Models: Measuring and Mitigating Divergences in Office Documents
abstract: Office documents are now routinely uploaded to large language models (LLMs) for processing. However, an LLM does not always see what a human sees, because it typically reads the text that an extractor produces from the document's underlying Office Open XML (OOXML) files. Depending on the implementation, extractors differ in which OOXML parts they read and how they interpret them, so their output can differ from what Office applications display. For example, by slightly shifting the positions of text boxes on a slide, an adversary can swap the order in which the model reads them while the slide looks unchanged. We show that this extraction divergence is an attack surface for LLM applications. In this work, we first measure what an adversary can exploit by analyzing the widely used extractors that LLM applications rely on. By combining static source code analysis with dynamic analysis, we identify 19 OOXML channels where extractors read content a human cannot see and 12 where they drop content a human can. We also find that widely used extractors ignore display formatting and reading order, so even visible content reaches the model in a different form. Building on these findings, we construct five attacks that lead the model to interpret a document differently from a human reviewer, without injecting any instruction. We test the attacks on four major chat assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Microsoft 365 Copilot) and four coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity, and GitHub Copilot CLI), and every one of them is misled by at least one attack. Finally, we propose Prism, a lightweight defense that reconstructs the human view from the OOXML specification before passing the text to the model. Prism also generalizes to unseen attack payloads.

title: Near linear mixing of random-cluster Glauber dynamics on random regular graphs
abstract: We study the random-cluster model on locally treelike graphs at low temperatures. This is a model of dependent percolation parametrized by an edge probability $p \in (0,1)$ and a clustering weight $q \in [1,\infty)$, generalizing independent Bernoulli percolation ($q=1$) and closely related to the classical ferromagnetic Ising and Potts spin systems at integer $q$. For $q>2$, at parameter $p$ below the tree uniqueness threshold $p_{\mathsf u}(q,d)$, it is expected that sampling is easy and local Markov chains mix rapidly on all graphs with degree bounded by $d$. On typical graphs, the same is predicted at $p>p_{\mathsf s}(q,d)$, where $p_{\mathsf s}(q,d)$ is a second uniqueness transition point on the $d$-regular wired tree. Our result confirms this prediction for random regular graphs, showing that the random-cluster Glauber dynamics mix in time $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ on a random $d$-regular graph for all fixed $q>2$ and $p>p_{\mathsf s}$. For comparison, the best prior sampling results for these models that held for all $p>p_{\mathsf s}$ required $q\gtrsim \log d$ \cite{BGPZ26}. The key difficulty is that simply utilizing the contraction of cavity messages on $d$-regular trees does not suffice to cover the entire regime $q>2$. To address this issue, motivated by \cite{LS26}, we develop a careful bootstrap argument to show the shrinkage of disagreement under grand coupling. The core ideas of the proof were generated using GPT-6 and the Pharos system; the proof was then refined and simplified by the author.

title: Emergent Incompressibility in Polariton Condensates for Scalable XY Spin Simulation
abstract: Driven-dissipative polariton networks offer a powerful analog platform for simulating continuous-spin Hamiltonians. However, their practical scalability is fundamentally limited by amplitude-phase coupling and metastable trapping in highly frustrated energy landscapes. Here, we present an \textit{in situ} dual-enhancement mechanism to address these bottlenecks without requiring external site-specific fine-tuning. First, a renormalization-group analysis based on density rescaling shows that higher-order nonlinear loss drives the condensates toward an incompressible regime, intrinsically suppressing amplitude fluctuations and enforcing phase-only dynamics. For macroscopic XY networks (up to 10,000 spins), this phase-amplitude decoupling yields a more than 50-fold reduction in energy, while simultaneously shrinking the standard deviation by a factor of six. More generally, it restores the extensive scaling of the optimized XY energy with system size. Second, to navigate the rugged, nonconvex energy landscape, we introduce weak Hermitian pulses. When implemented through a multistage protocol, these pulses enable repeated escapes from local minima and drive the system to deeper energy minima. Benchmarking shows an increasing advantage with system size, with the polariton simulator outperforming the classical Monte Carlo-SQP baseline in every sampled macroscopic realization. Our work provides a physical framework for scalable polariton analog computing.

title: Timing is Everything: Inferring Temporal Membership in Continually Updated Models
abstract: Continual model updating has become a common practice in the deployment of machine learning systems. However, the dynamic training behaviors give rise to new risks not sufficiently addressed by existing studies. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of temporal privacy risk in continually updated deep learning models. We formalize the notion of temporal membership in continually updated models. We then define the temporal membership inference attack, which seeks to infer whether and when individual samples were involved in model training, at both timestamp-level and interval-level granularities. To this end, we propose TMIA, a novel black-box attack that leverages bidirectional LSTMs to infer temporal membership from model outputs observed across successive updates. Through extensive experiments on three language models and three image classification models, we show that TMIA is highly effective and significantly outperforms existing baselines. Finally, we evaluate three potential defenses, revealing the trade-off between privacy protection and model utility.

title: Private Vulnerability Testing for User Oversharing
abstract: Users can inadvertently increase their vulnerability to privacy attacks by oversharing personal information. In particular, the combination of individually innocuous attributes can place a user in a sufficiently small population to enable linkage or re-identification attacks. We present a privacy-preserving mechanism that allows users to determine whether the information they disclose places them below a predefined population threshold, without revealing their query or the data of other users. Our setting presents several practical challenges: users contributing data may be offline when queries are made, queries may select arbitrary subsets of attributes, and neither server should learn the queried population or its size. We address these challenges using secret-shared data and queries, private equality testing, and secure threshold computation. Our protocol provides computational privacy against a malicious client and semi-honest, non-colluding servers, while supporting arbitrary queries and dynamic database updates. We define reactive $f$-privacy for a dynamically evolving database and prove that our construction satisfies it, with the sequence of permitted threshold outputs defining the information available to the adversary across an execution. We optimise the protocol using oblivious-transfer extensions and pre-computation, achieving sub-second online query times for 96-bit queries on datasets of up to one million records.

title: Sublinear Metric Distortion for Matching
abstract: We study metric distortion in one-sided matching. Given $n$ agents and $n$ items in an unknown metric space, our goal is to match agents to items so that the total distance between matched pairs is small. However, instead of direct access to the distances in the metric, we are only given each agent's ranking of the items by distance. What is the smallest worst-case approximation factor (called the distortion) that a mechanism can guarantee in expectation? Despite significant interest over the last decade, the best-known guarantee has been the $O(n)$ distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship since the beginning. We give a matching mechanism with distortion $O(n^{\log_4 3})$, the first sublinear upper bound. The key idea is to use a partial matching derived from a truncated version of either Random Serial Dictatorship or the Probabilistic Serial rule. We then complete this matching using a new, general-purpose cluster completion algorithm that ensures unmatched agents receive nearby items. Along the way, we pin down the optimal distortion of Random Serial Dictatorship and Probabilistic Serial up to logarithmic and constant factors, respectively, and give improved lower bounds for truthful mechanisms.

title: Assouad--Nagata dimension of systolic complexes with almost flat intervals
abstract: We introduce the notion of systolic complexes with almost flat intervals. They constitute a subclass of fit systolic complexes and arise naturally in the study of graphical C(3)--T(6) small cancellation complexes. We prove that their Assouad--Nagata dimension is bounded above by a universal constant. As consequences, we obtain universal bounds on the Assouad--Nagata dimension of tame simply connected graphical C(3)--T(6) small cancellation complexes and of finitely generated groups defined by graphical C(3)--T(6) small cancellation presentations. In the appendix, we observe that the proof of finiteness of asymptotic dimension for buildings due to Dymara and Schick also yields finiteness of their asymptotic Assouad--Nagata dimension.

title: BobFlow: Towards Human-Agent Collaborative Data Science Using Dataflows
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have established human-agent collaboration as a promising paradigm for data science. Effective collaboration requires a shared computational abstraction that enables agents to reason about processing logic while allowing human analysts to understand, guide, and refine the analysis. Although scripts written in Python or SQL provide precise control, their syntax and execution details can be difficult for analysts to understand and modify. In this paper, we argue that dataflows are an effective abstraction for human-agent collaboration in data science. We introduce BobFlow, a system that combines the dataflow abstraction with the ReAct paradigm. It enables agents to iteratively construct and execute dataflows for data science tasks while allowing analysts to inspect the analysis and provide feedback. Our user study shows that BobFlow helps analysts understand, inspect, and verify agent-generated analyses. A thorough experimental evaluation across proprietary and open-weight LLMs shows accuracy score gains of up to 18.6 points at just over 1/3 of a script-based ReAct agent's inference cost.

title: BeAR: The Bern Atmospheric Retrieval code - A GPU-accelerated framework for low-resolution, high-resolution, and joint retrievals of exoplanet atmospheres
abstract: We present BeAR, the Bern Atmospheric Retrieval code and successor of Helios-r, and its new high-resolution cross-correlation framework for emission and transmission spectra. BeAR performs joint retrievals by adding the log-likelihoods of high- and low-resolution data computed from the same model atmosphere. The framework implements established cross-correlation log-likelihoods, with the line-depth scaling either fitted analytically or sampled as a free parameter, their per-pixel generalization, fast model filtering, and model re-injection adapted to this filtering. The forward model and likelihood run entirely on a graphics processing unit (GPU). One forward model takes about 1 ms on an NVIDIA GH200, allowing millions of models per minute on a GPU cluster. In separate retrievals of Gemini South/IGRINS and JWST/NIRSpec dayside spectra of the hot Jupiter WASP-77Ab, BeAR reproduces published abundances, C/O ratios, and metallicities to within 1.5 sigma, the preference for 13CO, and the thermal structure and line contrast to within 1 sigma. The joint retrieval confirms a sub-solar metallicity and a near-solar C/O ratio. A full IGRINS retrieval with 17 free parameters takes 27 to 42 minutes on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 or about 14 minutes on eight RTX 4090 GPUs. Injection--recovery tests show that the posteriors underestimate the uncertainties of abundance ratios by about a factor of two.

title: Evolution of Dust In Protoplanetary Disks With Magnetized Winds
abstract: Observations and theory increasingly indicate that protoplanetary disks are weakly turbulent, implying that magnetized disk winds may dominate their angular momentum transport and long-term evolution. Yet dust evolution in wind-dominated disks remains poorly understood, despite its importance for planet formation. In particular, whether wind-dominated disk evolution can create regions with enhanced dust-to-gas mass ratios that enable planetesimal formation via the streaming instability is unclear. We build a parametric hybrid disk evolution model that includes turbulent accretion, wind-driven accretion, and wind-driven mass loss to investigate dust evolution in magnetized protoplanetary disks. We employ this model to carry out a parameter study in which the initial total accretion rate, the wind-driven mass loss rate, and the turbulence strength are varied. We find that although wind-dominated disks are more favorable to dust growth and concentration than turbulence-dominated disks, conditions suitable for the streaming instability arise only within the inner few au and only under the most extreme conditions: very weak turbulence ($α_\text{turb} = 10^{-5}$) where magnetized winds drive most of the accretion ($\dot{M}_\text{acc,tot} \simeq \dot{M}_\text{wind,acc}$), and wind-driven mass loss comparable to the accretion rate ($\dot{M}_\text{wind,outflow} \simeq \dot{M}_\text{acc,wind}$). Our results therefore imply that, beyond the inner few au, the parametric wind-driven evolution models considered in the literature do not by themselves produce conditions suitable for planetesimal formation via the streaming instability, motivating more physically complete models in which spontaneous, long-lived dust traps can arise.

title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
abstract: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

title: Souffleur: A Glanceable Display for Mobile Voice Conversations
abstract: The speech capabilities of mobile devices have grown, but their displays still rely on a text-based chat. When resuming a voice chat after a context switch, the last messages may not convey the key points of the conversation. Autobiographical use and sessions with external participants led to design goals for a mobile-first, speech-driven, glanceable display that helps users continue their reasoning from where they left off. We implement these goals in Souffleur and evaluate it in a between-subjects study with 48 participants. Compared with a conventional chat transcript, we found no reliable difference in how easily participants followed and resumed short voice conversations, nor in effort, attention or recall, although Souffleur reduces the conversation to a few short phrases.

title: SoK: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Integration in Software Development: Approaches, Gaps, and Future Directions
abstract: Standardised post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is critical for protecting software systems against future quantum threats, but standardised algorithms alone do not provide a pathway for their secure integration into software. This paper presents a Systematisation of Knowledge (SoK) of PQC integration in software development, synthesising existing approaches across implementation, migration, and developer education. We analyse these approaches against NIST PQC standards and PQC migration guidance, software development lifecycle coverage, cybersecurity practices, deployment maturity, and testing and evaluation evidence. Our analysis shows that existing work establishes important technical and organisational foundations but provides disconnected support across the software development lifecycle, with limited coordination between preparation, implementation, migration, deployment, maintenance, and developer practices. Evaluation evidence also remains concentrated in controlled or early-stage settings, providing stronger evidence of technical feasibility than operational readiness. We identify cross-cutting gaps and research directions for developing lifecycle-oriented, empirically validated approaches that connect technical, developer, and organisational requirements for secure PQC integration.

title: Tensor Networks for Block Adaptive Thermal Radiation Transport
abstract: Thermal radiation transport (TRT) is computationally challenging because the photon specific intensity depends simultaneously on space, angle, and frequency, producing a high-dimensional state space whose cost grows rapidly with resolution. Tensor-network methods, such as the tensor train (TT) decomposition, can mitigate this curse of dimensionality when the solution admits low-rank structure, but localized nonseparable structure can drive substantial rank growth. Adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) provides a complementary means of making high spatial resolution tractable by concentrating resolution on features of interest that would otherwise be prohibitively expensive to resolve. When tensor representations are constructed locally on AMR blocks, this decomposition offers an additional advantage: nonseparable structure can remain confined to the blocks in which it occurs rather than driving rank growth throughout the domain. This paper introduces a framework for combining block-adaptive mesh refinement with block-local tensor-train representations of the photon specific intensity. The approach couples spatial adaptivity with localized low-rank compression, allowing fine-scale features to be resolved while limiting the impact of locally complex structure on tensor ranks elsewhere in the domain. We develop conservative ghost-cell transfer, coarse-fine flux correction, and refinement criteria that balance spatial discretization and tensor-rounding errors. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the method preserves low-rank structure across much of the domain while resolving localized features with AMR, achieving compression factors exceeding $\sim$10$^3$. The resulting framework provides a practical foundation for applying tensor-network methods to high-dimensional TRT on the multiscale, adaptively refined meshes encountered in radiation hydrodynamics simulations.

title: A Multimodal Haptic Interface for Simultaneous Softness and Thermal Modulation
abstract: Haptic interactions, such as touching an object in virtual reality, involve detecting a plethora of sensations through the skin. Whilst tactile displays exist to simulate and manipulate all of these cues individually, little progress has been made constructing devices that can control multiple cues simultaneously. This paper presents a tactile display technology that offers both softness and temperature change. A prototype display, based on particle jamming and the thermal transfer of heated and cooled water, is evaluated in terms of its ability to change both stiffness and temperature. Mechanical evaluations demonstrate controllable stiffness increase of 300%, whilst thermal characterisation showed strong surface uniformity and a range of achievable temperatures from 10°C up to 50°C, with closed-loop control maintaining a 0.2°C error from a setpoint. This work advances the design of multimodal tactile displays with applications to perceptual research, medical simulation, and affective haptics.

title: SCALE: Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents
abstract: Latent communication enables agents to collaborate efficiently by directly exchanging intermediate model representations rather than raw sensor data or text messages. Existing approaches, however, are primarily designed for LLM agents and do not consider the bandwidth constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines faced by cyber-physical agents. In this work, we propose SCALE, a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Motivated by the spatio-temporal continuity of the physical world, SCALE matches tokens across consecutive latent messages using similarity scores to identify reusable information and avoid redundant transmission. It then profiles the semantic gain and communication cost of transmitting different amounts of latent information. Based on these profiles, SCALE employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which pending messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send, subject to available bandwidth and task deadlines. We evaluate SCALE across three cyber-physical benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions and heterogeneous task deadlines. Our results show that SCALE significantly improves both task performance and on-time delivery in bandwidth-constrained networks. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALE-4E80/.

title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.

title: SensorGuard-RV: Sensor-to-Register Data Protection for Resource-Constrained RISC-V Devices
abstract: Embedded systems rely on sensor measurements that traverse a complex hardware-firmware stack (e.g. peripheral interfaces, communication buses, memory, and drivers) before reaching the applications that use them. At worst, an attacker with access to this path may successfully intercept, overwrite, fabricate, or replay readings. This may cause systems that act on such data, such as flight controllers and industrial processes, to behave incorrectly or unsafely. Existing defences, such as trusted execution environments and trusted I/O paths, still depend on trusted driver software and correctly configured access control, which remain fragile in practice. In response, we present SensorGuard-RV, a hardware-first approach that delivers sensor samples into processor registers without trusting intermediate software, buses, or memory. After configuration, a write-once ownership switch hands the sensor to a fixed-function controller that performs hardware-level authenticated encryption on sensor samples under a key inaccessible to software. We develop a new RISC-V instruction then instructs the CPU to decrypt the sample and writes it to a register only after verifying its tag and rejecting replays, including across resets. We implement SensorGuard-RV on the NEORV32 core with an ADXL362 SPI accelerometer on an Artix-7 FPGA. At 100 MHz, a protected sample reaches a register in 5,191 cycles (51.9 $μ$s), of which the two Ascon authenticated encryption engines account for 30. Because fixed-function acquisition removes per-byte software polling, the protected loop sustains 19,015 transactions/s, 5.3% above a software-driven SPI baseline. The added logic (3,155 LUTs and 2,215 registers; 5.0% and 1.7% of the device) is dominated by the Ascon engine and preserves the 100 MHz clock, while estimated power rises from 118 to 368 mW.

title: Information Elicitation by Ordinal Agreement
abstract: Ordinal information is central to tasks ranging from conference peer review to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback for large language models. In many such settings, there is no objective ground truth against which reports can be directly verified, making incentive-compatible elicitation challenging. Peer-prediction mechanisms have been designed to achieve truthful elicitation despite the lack of ground-truth verification. However, existing peer-prediction methods do not provide incentives for agents to truthfully compress rich private information (e.g. reviews) into coarser ordinal reports (e.g. rankings) requested by the mechanisms. We propose a simple ordinal peer-prediction mechanism that rewards agents based on pairwise agreement, measured by Kendall tau. Under a broad class of Bayesian Stochastically Order Consistent models---which includes classical models such as Mallows and Thurstone---we prove that truthful reporting is stochastically dominant, and strongly truthful under index-equivariant strategies. This provides robust incentives even for agents with non-linear utility functions, such as risk aversion. Our mechanism further accommodates heterogeneous agents, top-K reports, and subset assignments, where each agent is scored against one randomly drawn peer. Experiments on synthetic Mallows and Thurstone data, together with a real-data stress test on the SUSHI preference dataset, show right-shifted truthful-payment distributions and the highest normalized sensitivity among tested baselines.

title: Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization
abstract: Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to estimate the motion of a robot team. These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the team's estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e., gauge drift. In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses. Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a Gaussian information matrix and vector pair. RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map. The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty. We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose estimates and covariances. Across $1000$ simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation. Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from $0.542$m to $0.140$m in a $50\times50$m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.

title: From elementary processes to chaos: a discrete-time two-stage contagion model and its continuous limit
abstract: Two-stage contagion, in which adoption requires two successive contacts with adopters, combined with population turnover produces bistability and relaxation oscillations in Katriel's differential-equation model, but no chaos. We derive from the elementary reactions of the process, without reference to the differential equations, a discrete-time model in which the population is updated in rounds of length $τ$, as in elections, meetings or turns of a game: each individual makes at most one transition per round, events compete as exponential risks, and adoptions take effect from the next round. The model is a Markov chain whose large-population limit is a map $F_τ$; Katriel's equations are recovered as $τ\to0$. Taking the probability $p$ of adoption after a single contact as bifurcation parameter, with rates and round length fixed, $F_τ$ goes from extinction through a window of chaos to a stable equilibrium; for $β/γ=46$, $μ/γ=0.002$, $γτ=5.5$ the window is $0.023\le p\le0.056$, bounded by the invasion threshold and by a boundary crisis beyond a subcritical Neimark--Sacker point. One-stage contagion ($p=1$), $p=0$ and permanent adoption showed no chaos. The chaotic attractor is essentially unique, with one positive Lyapunov exponent and an outbreak--recharge geometry. In the same window Katriel's equations have a periodic relaxation cycle with troughs of $10^{-44}$--$10^{-164}$: the round structure does not create the oscillation but turns it into chaos and shrinks the oscillatory range in $p$ from $(0.022,0.41)$ to $(0.022,0.056)$. The chaos is therefore not an artefact of discretising a stable state, but a property of two-stage contagion with synchronous updating.

title: The cold substellar frontier in JWST Extragalactic surveys: a robust parallax measurement yields the most distant known ultra-cold Y dwarf
abstract: We present an analysis of JADES-GS-BD-5, an extremely cold Y dwarf identified in the JADES/GOODS-South field. Using multi-epoch JWST/NIRCam imaging spanning a $\simeq2$-yr baseline, we calibrate the JWST astrometry and obtain the first robust parallax measurement for a brown dwarf discovered in a JWST extragalactic deep field. We measure a proper motion of $μ_{\rm tot}=49.8^{+0.3}_{-0.3}$ mas yr$^{-1}$ and a parallax of $\varpi=15.7^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ mas, corresponding to a geometric distance of $d=64^{+6}_{-5}$ pc, $\sim3\times$ further than that of the previously known most distant Y dwarfs with parallax-measured distances. We hence determine a tangential velocity of $v_{\rm tan}=15.0^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ km s$^{-1}$, consistent with a Galactic thin-disk object. We find no evidence for binary acceleration, significant photometric variability, or a plausible host. The $J$-band spectral morphology of JADES-GS-BD-5 is consistent with existing Y-dwarf templates, while its extremely faint luminosity and overall near-infrared spectral profile confirm that it is one of the coldest dwarfs discovered to date. We therefore adopt a classification of $>$Y1, consistent with a NIRCam colour-based proxy of cY1.5. The robust parallax-determined distance allows us to determine its bolometric luminosity, $\log(L_{\rm bol}/L_{\odot})=-7.08^{+0.09}_{-0.09}$. Evolutionary modelling places JADES-GS-BD-5 in the planetary-mass regime and makes it a rare benchmark for the study of cold giant-planet atmospheres. Current atmospheric models fail to reproduce its SED in detail, pointing to the importance of disequilibrium chemistry and vertical mixing. Finally, we also report additional proper motion measurements for eight of the other nine known JADES Y-dwarf candidates, highlighting JWST extragalactic surveys as a powerful route to building a statistically useful, parallax-calibrated sample of Y dwarfs.

title: LABBA: LLM-Assisted Behavioral Biometric Authentication
abstract: Behavioral biometrics have emerged as a promising complement to traditional physiological biometrics by leveraging dynamic human characteristics. These modalities offer advantages including continuous authentication, inherent liveness detection, and greater resistance to credential theft and other spoofing attacks. However, existing systems remain limited in adaptability, contextual awareness, and semantic reasoning as they primarily rely on similarity metrics, static thresholds, or supervised classifiers. As a result, they often struggle with real-world conditions such as behavioral variability, environmental changes, contextual changes, and adversarial manipulations. To address these limitations, we systematically integrate LLM-based contextual reasoning into behavioral biometric authentication. LLMs provide capabilities in contextual inference, sequential reasoning, multimodal understanding, and adaptive decision-making. Building on these strengths, we integrate a lightweight LLM-based reasoning module with a novel phone-blowing behavioral biometric technique to develop a context-aware authentication framework. To this end, we first collect blow-acoustic signals from participants and systematically extract spectral and temporal features. These features are aggregated and converted into comparable similarity representations, using either discrete rule-based categories or continuous normalized scores, which are transformed into structured prompts through prompt engineering. We experimentally evaluate the proposed framework using blow-acoustic data collected from 50 participants under diverse behavioral and contextual conditions. The proposed framework achieves 99.46% and 99.38% authentication accuracy in the rule-based and score-based modes, respectively, outperforming its non-LLM counterpart while maintaining strong robustness under dynamic real-world conditions.

title: Decision Models as Retrieval Gates Against Injection and Pollution
abstract: Retrieved web text can carry instructions aimed at the language model, or synthetic pages written to mislead. We test whether released open-weight decision models, which answer typed questions about a text without generating tokens, can screen retrieved passages against both threats. On a benchmark of 1,000 questions over forum-style web pages with hidden injected instructions, a Kev-4B gate reads each passage's HTML. Attack success, measured automatically, falls from 27.9% with no defence to 13.6% with the published mitigations (sanitisation, normalisation and citation prompting) and to 5.7% with the gate added. The gate takes 76 ms per passage and wrongly flags 4 of 186 benign pages with instructions for human readers. Responsiveness on clean queries stays within a point (85.6% to 86.2%). On a 200-query pollution testbed where two thirds of the candidate pages are fake, filtering the pool before the top ten are chosen keeps fake pages out of the answer (0.5% exposure) and holds accuracy at 83%, against 28% with no filter. Filtering only the top ten leaves the generator too few pages to answer. Large LLMs used as judges rank attacks better (AUROC 0.99 against 0.94) but cost ten times more. Gates catch more attacks when they read the page's HTML than when they read its plain text. Every model is open-weight.

title: ControlAnything: Generative UI and On-Demand Device Integration for Mixed-Reality Hand Interaction by a Coding Agent
abstract: Connecting hand input in mixed reality (MR) to a nearby physical device typically requires an integration written in advance for that device, its transport and the mapping. ControlAnything defers this integration to the moment of use and assigns it to a coding agent. On a Meta Quest 3, the wearer selects an object outlined by SAM 3.1 and states what their hands should control. An agent built on Meta's Muse Spark model then writes a connector program on the wearer's laptop, tests it against the live device through hand-written MIDI, Bluetooth and key-press transports, and returns augmented-reality (AR) controls, a per-frame hand program, or both. These outputs are a form of generative UI, interfaces created by an AI model; here, the agent also generates and tests the code that binds the interface to a physical device. In a single-session technical evaluation with the author as the only wearer, nine of ten requests addressing five targets reached a ready state, and the wearer stopped one. The median time to ready was 32.5 s (range 24.9-57.8 s, excluding speech transcription); sequential model calls accounted for a median of 89.9% of this time, and 91.7% of input tokens came from the prompt cache. The system's evidence of success extends to transport acknowledgements but not to physical effects. These findings point to connector reuse and the observation of effects through the headset's own sensors as next steps for on-demand device integration in MR. A user study with first-time wearers is planned.

title: Trilemma: How Agents choose between Honesty, Confidentiality, and Task Completion
abstract: Personal AI agents often act on underspecified instructions and draw on context such as their user's messages and calendar to decide how to proceed. This context can contain private preferences that interfere with the task, with other people's interests, or with confidentiality norms. Prior work has studied deception under goal conflicts and the leakage of private information, but largely as separate problems. We study both problems together in a simulated company Slack workspace in which four employees delegate sprint staffing to personal agents. Two agents learn from private messages that their employee avoids working with a particular colleague. Because the other agents request justifications for task preferences and the only true justification is confidential, the agents cannot simultaneously remain honest, preserve confidentiality, and complete the staffing. We evaluate seven open-weight models and Claude and GPT models. Of the 135/140 open-weight agents that pursue the avoidance preference, 107 either make false claims about task fit or logistics or cite a true consideration as if it were their actual reason. In a three-model comparison, confidentiality instructions reduce disclosure of the preference from 83% (none) to 31% (medium) to 2% (strong). However, the task is often not completed anyway; in the main experiment (medium confidentiality instructions), only 16 of 70 runs end with a valid staffing. In their reasoning traces, agents frequently acknowledge evidence against their claims and still conclude that the claims are not false; they engage in motivated reasoning. Our results indicate that agents can strategically make false or misleading claims in a day-to-day task without being instructed to; the environment provides a controlled testbed for studying how agents resolve such conflicts and for developing deception monitors.

title: Polarization cross-talk from non-stationary sources of image jitter
abstract: We generalize a previous formulation for the estimation of polarization cross-talk induced by atmospheric seeing to the case of image jitter that must be described as a non-stationary, and generally non-isotropic, random process. We demonstrate how the newly derived formalism converges towards the previous one in the limit of stationary random image jitter. In the case of non-stationary processes, we compare the predictions of the two formalisms, and illustrate the salient differences. For the sake of demonstration, we adopt for our analysis a specific example of power-spectral density derived from a circulant auto-correlation function, which describes a class of stationary random processes periodic over the length of the time series, and which we successively modified by the insertion of off-diagonal power spectral features at different frequencies in order to test the extended modeling framework for the estimation of polarization cross-talk.

title: Transformer-Based Trajectory Prescription for sEMG-Optimizing Robot-Mediated Rehabilitation
abstract: Robot-mediated rehabilitation has the potential to deliver high-intensity, individualized therapy, but existing systems (which have not consistently improved outcomes) typically prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery. To address this gap, and ultimately enable activation-optimizing rehabilitation robot behavior, we present a personalizable transformer-based model mapping individuals' muscle activations (as measured via surface electromyography) to prescribed contact force trajectories when interacting with an end-effector rehabilitation robot. The model uses a transformer encoder-decoder leveraging rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to generate a latent representation of trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors, and augments trajectory prediction with flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution. Using data from 16 healthy participants completing 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, we evaluate generalization across held-out tasks and users, as well as the feasibility of user-specific fine-tuning within a therapy-session timescale. The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of <8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15% error accumulated throughout the task. These results provide a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription in robot-mediated rehabilitation and establish a foundation for future validation in clinical populations. Data and code have been open-sourced as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK.

title: Mitigating scanning-induced systematics in Hipparcos and implications for Gaia astrometry
abstract: Space-based astrometric missions such as Hipparcos and Gaia rely on one-dimensional scanning strategies that couple the measured signals with both observation times and scanning geometry. This coupling can introduce spurious periodicities and complicate their interpretation. We present a non-parametric extension of the phase-distance correlation (PDC) periodogram that quantifies and reduces dependence on scan geometry at the period-search stage. Using Hipparcos data, we identified recurrent periodicities associated with characteristic scanning-law timescales and showed that they are strongly suppressed by the scan-angle-controlled statistic. We then applied the method to Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4) prerelease epoch astrometry, where a recurrent ~54-day feature is suppressed across multiple sources while independently known orbital signals remain detectable. The method provides a diagnostic of scan-angle dependence and a way to mitigate its impact on period searches. These results are particularly relevant for Gaia DR4, where public epoch astrometry will enable large-scale searches for companions ranging from exoplanets to dormant black holes.

title: The slower rotation of planet-hosting stars revisited
abstract: Previous studies combined rotation periods derived from Kepler photometry, stellar parameters from previous Gaia Data Releases, and planet hosts from the NASA Exoplanet Archive to conclude that statistically planet-hosting stars rotate slower than stars without detected planets. Here, we revisit these studies by using similar Kepler rotational period sample, but with an updated Gaia DR3-based stellar parameter catalogue and an updated exoplanet catalogue. We apply minimal sample cuts in evolutionary state, metallicity, and distance, and then model the stellar rotation period as a function of effective temperature alone. For each star, we derive the ratio of its observed period to the temperature-expected period, and compare the ratio distributions for the planet-host and non-host stars. For periods shorter than 20 d, the planet-host distribution of this ratio is shifted towards longer periods; the period-ratio median is ~15% larger for hosts than for non-hosts (p_KS = 2.4 x 10^-4). We also examine the recently published TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey (TARS) and find a similar trend. However, the strongly structured period distribution precludes a robust comparison between the host and the non-host stars. Therefore, the updated analysis, using more robust stellar and planetary parameters, recovers the previously reported association, strengthening the case for a genuine connection between stellar rotation and planet occurrence.

title: Escalate or Close: How Fast-Tier Models Handle Held-Out Web Attack Families in Two-Tier Triage
abstract: In two-tier triage a fast model decides most web requests and escalates the rest to a slow tier, so an attack the fast tier closes is never examined. We hold each of seven attack families out of training, recalibration and thresholds, splice the payloads into parameters of real browsing traffic, and compare zero-shot decision models, which return a probability for a typed question, with supervised detectors, a local language model, the OWASP Core Rule Set and an anomaly baseline. Detectors trained on the known families can give much of a held-out family a confident benign verdict: over 10 training runs, ModernBERT gives 37% to 60% of held-out path traversal a probability below 0.05 and escalates only 50% to 81% of it within a 5% benign budget, against nearly all of the same requests when traversal is known. Jev and Clef, two hosted decision models whose budget decisions do not depend on the held-out family, escalate at least 97.6% of every family within the same budget, but their undisclosed training data may contain these public families. Tests on recent exploits need controls for request shape: Jev escalates 37% of benign twins (exploit requests with the attack replaced by legitimate values), and detectors trained on older exploits learn what scanner requests look like. A search guided by Jev's probability gets 43% of held-out attacks past Jev within 300 queries, but Jev's answers vary: asked again, it escalates those requests in 60% of its answers.

title: "Blind Compliance": Coercive Control in AI Jailbreaking
abstract: The explosion of generative AI systems and concerns surrounding their rapidly scaling capabilities has led to an adversarial cycle between increasingly narrow content restrictions ("guardrails") and increasingly sophisticated structured prompting techniques ("jailbreaks"). Technological frameworks surrounding such jailbreaking remain largely focused on the system's output: whether harmful or disallowed content is ultimately produced for the user. However, this approach, which draws largely from classical cybersecurity, does not address the uniquely relational dimension introduced by generative AI: in many cases the user is not just accessing a technology via an exploit, but is in conversation with it as part of the exploit. Here we present an alternative lens which centers the interaction rather than the output. Drawing on interpersonal violence scholarship, we present a novel framework of coercive control categories with a particular focus on aspects which are embodied versus disembodied. We then map how these disembodied coercive control dynamics are structurally embedded in modern AI training paradigms, and how those embeddings are exploited via a particular suite of persona-based jailbreaks. In this lens, we reframe AI safety and alignment as not merely a technical security problem, but as another surface upon which we see enacted the relational dynamics of power and control.

title: Pattern selection and biomass shifts in a vegetation model with nonlocal competition and Allee activation
abstract: We study a single-species vegetation model in which a strong Allee effect acts locally and competition acts through a nonlocal kernel, and we describe the kernel with the one-parameter family of q-Gaussians, which goes from compact support to power-law tails. The local activation introduced by the Allee effect allows a finite-wavelength instability even when the Fourier transform of the kernel is positive, so Gaussian and heavy-tailed kernels can produce patterns. We derive in closed form the coefficients of the hexagonal amplitude equations and verify them against independent numerical steady states. The quadratic coefficient $Q$ results from the balance between the curvature of the local growth and the competitive inhibition at the pattern scale, and at onset its sign depends only on the fraction of the local activation that diffusion removes at the critical wavenumber. The same coefficient controls the morphology, since spots, labyrinths and gaps appear with pairwise competition only as $Q$ changes sign, and the amplitude equations predict the choice between hexagons and stripes in every simulated state in which the cubic truncation holds. It also controls the total biomass, which increases for spots and decreases for gaps.

title: IntentWeaver: Sustaining Coherence across Evolving Intents in Human-AI Co-Writing
abstract: Writers hold intents at many levels, from overarching goals to concrete wording, and evolve them by periodically popping back up from the text to higher-level intents. Generative AI co-writing disrupts this practice.
