abstract: Mapping behavioral intelligence in malware analysis reports to ATT&CK techniques supports threat analysis and defense, but reliable identification remains challenging. Supporting evidence is often scattered across long, heterogeneous reports, while closely related techniques share behavioral cues and differ only in subtle but decisive details. While large language models (LLMs) can use external knowledge to interpret reports, they may assign techniques based on plausible associations rather than sufficient evidence. We present MEvince, a knowledge-constrained LLM reasoning framework for report-level malware technique identification. Its core is a shared behavioral representation connecting report observations to technique definitions. This representation is built through agentic mining of technique documentation and supports two online stages: 1) primitive-guided extraction uses behavioral primitives to structure LLM-extracted observations, link them to source passages, and group dispersed evidence; 2) evidence-aligned retrieval matches this evidence to technique profiles through the same concepts, retaining likely candidates and confusable alternatives for LLM comparison of distinguishing behaviors. Controls at both stages validate evidence references and check technique-specific requirements. The representation also supports adaptation without parameter updates, where offline agentic audits diagnose concept weaknesses and refine extraction or retrieval policies. We evaluate MEvince against 11 baselines spanning four method families using a dataset of 610 public malware reports referenced by MITRE ATT&CK. MEvince improves exact-ID F1 over the strongest baseline by 17.4%, and its concept-guided retrieval increases gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%. With a small adaptation set, offline refinement yields further gains and outperforms baselines that update model parameters.

title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
abstract: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. We report a preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks comparing free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. Signing is what defeats in-transit tampering: an unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. On identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits: the residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing. A preregistered pre-signing injection attack confirmed this boundary: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna), and the signature then authenticated the corrupted manifest. Signing protects requirements in transit, not at extraction; the extraction step is the trust boundary.

title: AMORT-V1: Checkpointed Post-Quantum Attestation for Industrial Controllers
abstract: Programmable logic controllers often remain deployed for decades, making post-quantum attestation a long-term requirement. Prior measurements of OpenPLC attestation show that post-quantum signing can consume 88--99% of round-trip latency and that durable state can further limit throughput. We introduce AMORT-V1, a checkpointed attestation protocol that moves public-key signing and durable commitment from individual reports to periodic checkpoints. An ML-KEM epoch establishes per-device evidence keys, devices authenticate reports with MACs, and the controller commits ordered evidence through hash-chained Merkle checkpoints signed with ML-DSA or SLH-DSA. Because shared MACs do not provide transferable proof of device origin, AMORT-V1 adds a device-held disclosure chain whose keys are released after checkpoint commitment. We validate the protocol with a 27-case attack matrix, 149 differential-test vectors, and a seven-node Raspberry Pi 5 testbed with five physical OpenPLC provers. Checkpointing reduces controller cost by 90 times relative to per-report ML-DSA without durable logging and by 878 times when durable logging is required. Transferable device-origin verification costs 2.95micro sec per report, while controller-side scaling to 10,000 identities requires 6.18 micro sec and 155 octets per report. AMORT-V1 also supports rollback-resistant restart through TPM-backed monotonic state without placing durable hardware operations on the per-report path.

title: Polynomial-Time Approximate EFX for Chores via Flow and Matching
abstract: We study approximate EFX allocations of indivisible chores under nonnegative additive costs. Exact EFX allocations need not exist in general. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a complete $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX allocation for any rational $0<\varepsilon\leq1$, improving the previous approximation guarantee from a factor depending on the number of agents to a constant. The algorithm extends to EF$k$X, achieving a $(2+1/k+\varepsilon)$-approximation for every integer $k\geq1$. For instances with relatively few chores, the polynomial-time BRBI algorithm gives stronger guarantees. It finds exact EF$k$X allocations when $m\leq2kn$ and achieves a factor of at most $2-1/k$ when $m\le(3k-1)n$. In particular, $k=1$ and $m\leq2n$ give exact EFX. We further show that the approximation factor \(2+1/k\) is asymptotically tight for our main algorithm. We also construct a four-agent, ten-chore instance in which every complete allocation has EFX approximation factor at least $11/10$, improving upon the $20/19$ lower bound for submodular costs even under additive costs.

title: Stable dissipative topological solitons in media with even-order dispersion
abstract: The formation and dynamics of dissipative solitons are governed by the interplay of dispersion and nonlinearity, alongside the gain-loss balance. While it is known that dispersion orders beyond the conventional second order support stable solitons, the possibility of the creation of dissipative topological solitons in this setting was not explored. Here, we reveal a class of stable dissipative solitons enabled by the pure-high-even-order dispersion (PHEOD), with dispersion orders m=4, 6, 8, and 10. The resulting dissipative topological solitons (DTSs) and moving topological solitons (MTSs) are dark-type structures featuring a zero-amplitude point that separates two CW backgrounds with opposite signs. In particular, the PHEOD solitons feature oscillatory tails, which are not present in the conventional dark states. The linear-stability analysis confirms full robustness of the PHEOD-supported DTSs and MTSs. We also explore collision dynamics of MTSs, whose repulsive interactions are inelastic, leading either to rebound, accompanied by emission of dispersive radiation, or complete fusion. These findings establish PHEOD as a means for the generation of new species of dissipative solitons, and broaden the variety of nonlinear modes available to experimental studies in nonlinear optics.

title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ less time and 1.55$\times$ lower cost per completed task.

title: MP-DualNet: A Dual-Branch Deep Learning Approach for Magnetopause Boundary Detection Using Simulated SXI Images
abstract: The Earth's magnetopause is a key boundary governing solar wind-magnetosphere coupling. The Solar wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer (SMILE) mission will provide global soft X-ray imaging of the magnetosphere through solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission, offering a new opportunity for remote sensing of magnetopause dynamics. However, the limited field of view (FOV) and variable observation geometry of the Soft X-ray Imager (SXI) pose challenges for reliable magnetopause detection. In this study, we develop MP-DualNet, an end-to-end dual-branch deep learning framework for automated magnetopause detection from simulated SXI observations. The framework jointly performs coarse localization to determine magnetopause visibility and relative position within the FOV, and fine-scale boundary localization through pixel-level segmentation. The model is trained and evaluated using line-of-sight magnetopause envelope maps derived from global hybrid simulations under different solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field conditions. The results demonstrate stable and consistent performance, with a classification accuracy exceeding 0.94 and a segmentation IoU above 0.97. For the test set, the mean absolute angular displacement from the reference boundary was 0.488 degrees. The model maintains robust performance across a wide range of noise levels and generalizes well, as demonstrated by its application to an independent storm event. These results indicate that MP-DualNet provides a reliable and generalizable approach for magnetopause detection in SXI observations, supporting future 3D reconstruction and space weather studies in the context of the SMILE mission.

title: Preliminary Goniopolarimetric Simulations for Space Weather Radio (SWARA) Polarimeter
abstract: Goniopolarimetry is a technique that measures the direction-of-arrival (DoA) using the polarization properties of the incident electromagnetic (EM) waves. This study aims to incorporate the technique of Goniopolarimetry for our proposed polarimeter, Space Weather Radio (SWARA) Polarimeter, to provide early warnings for space weather or solar events. We have performed preliminary simulations for a tri-monopole antenna configuration. The behaviour of the tri-monopole antenna with varying signal-to-noise (SNR) ratios along the field-of-view (FOV) was investigated using simulations. The angular localization error (ALE) variations, along with SNRs, were simulated to quantify the sensitivity of the Goniopolarimetric algorithm to galactic background noise. Future work will focus on determining the optimum effective length of the individual monopoles to maximize sensitivity and localization accuracy while ensuring efficient impedance matching with the receiver. The optimized antenna will be evaluated under realistic plasma environments through electromagnetic and plasma simulations to investigate the influence of plasma parameters.

title: Prospects for detecting hot-Jupiter tidal decay through transit timing with the mission Earth 2.0
abstract: Orbital decay of hot Jupiters provides a unique opportunity to probe tidal dissipation in star-planet systems. However, despite extensive observational efforts, only one hot Jupiter, namely WASP-12b, currently exhibits conclusive observational evidence for orbital decay. Expanding this sample is therefore crucial for establishing a statistical understanding of tidal interactions in planetary systems. Long-term transit timing variations (TTVs) provide a direct observational probe of orbital decay induced by tidal dissipation between a hot Jupiter and its host star. The Earth 2.0 (ET) mission will revisit the original Kepler field, delivering high-precision transit timing measurements and extending the observational baseline to approximately 24 years (2009--2033). In this work, we aim to assess the capability of ET to detect orbital decay in hot Jupiters previously observed by Kepler. We generate four years of simulated ET light curves based on the expected photometric precision and observing cadence of the mission and analyze them jointly with archival Kepler and TESS observations. Using these combined datasets, we perform long-term TTV analyses and predict the achievable precision for measuring orbital period variations. We find that ET can substantially improve the precision of orbital decay measurements in hot Jupiter systems by a factor of 7.2. Assuming the stellar tidal quality factor inferred from previous observations, ET is expected to detect orbital decay in three additional hot Jupiter systems. The expanded sample of hot Jupiters with measured orbital decay will establish ET as a powerful probe of tidal dissipation in star-planet systems, providing tighter constraints on stellar tidal quality factors and new insights into the tidal evolution of hot Jupiters.

title: First broadband search for fixed-polarization dark photon dark matter with GigaBREAD
abstract: We present the first search for fixed-polarization dark photon (DP) dark matter in the 44-52$μ\mathrm{eV}$ mass range, corresponding to 10.7-12.5GHz. GigaBREAD is a room-temperature broadband dish antenna experiment in which DP convert to ordinary photons on a cylindrical metallic emission surface and are focused onto a radio-frequency receiver. Previous searches, including GigaBREAD and several other dish antenna searches, have assumed randomly polarized DP dark matter. However, vector dark matter produced by a misalignment-like mechanism may retain an approximately fixed polarization, leading to sidereal modulation of the detector response as the Earth rotates. We reanalyze the GigaBREAD data using a polarization-matched likelihood that accounts for the time-dependent projection of a fixed DP polarization onto the detector axis. We find no evidence for a fixed-polarization DP signal and set upper limits on the kinetic mixing parameter at the level of $χ\sim10^{-12}$. These limits are about $20\%$ better than a naive limit obtained by rescaling the previous GigaBREAD limit under the fixed-polarization assumption.

title: Structured Quantum Hardness from Unstructured Assumptions
abstract: Whether useful structured hardness can arise from unstructured assumptions is a fundamental question in complexity and cryptography. The longstanding Bennett-Gill question asks whether $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ remains hard relative to a random oracle; [GIKKLS, STOC 2023] recently gave a conditional affirmative answer in the classical setting. We establish the quantum analogue: if $\mathsf{UP}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}$, then $\mathsf{NP}^{O}\cap\mathsf{coNP}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{BQP}^{O}$ with probability $1$ over a random oracle $O$. Beyond extending the classical result, this separation has a distinctly quantum significance: Shor's algorithms defeat canonical number-theoretic hardness candidates, while lattice assumptions and other leading post-quantum cryptographic assumptions do not directly supply hard languages with two-sided classical certification on every input. Our conditional oracle separation provides evidence that such structured quantum hardness can nevertheless arise from unstructured sources. Complementing this result, we rule out fully black-box quantum reductions of worst-case quantum hardness in $\mathsf{NP}\cap\mathsf{coNP}$ to post-quantum injective one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation. This barrier excludes a broad class of black-box approaches to deriving structured quantum hardness from generic cryptographic primitives, providing partial evidence that the non-black-box techniques in our first result are essential.

title: No Significant Rotation of the Spiral Structure in the IM Lup Protoplanetary Disk
abstract: Spiral structures are often observed in protoplanetary disks, but their origins remain uncertain. Yoshida et al. (2025) reported a pattern speed consistent with local Keplerian rotation for the $m=2$ spiral in the dusty disk around IM Lup using multi-epoch ALMA observations, supporting a gravitational instability (GI)-driven origin. However, recent studies revise the disk geometry of IM Lup, motivating a reassessment of its spiral pattern speed. In this study, we reanalyze the disk geometry of the same multi-epoch data using visibility-based continuum emission modeling. The inferred disk geometries differ from those adopted in previous studies by a few degrees but are consistent across epochs and with recent independent estimates based on gas emission analyses. The revised geometries yield weaker residuals and more physically plausible radial spiral phase profiles. Unlike previous studies, our remeasured spiral pattern speeds are consistent with zero rotation within the uncertainties. We conclude that the previously reported Keplerian-like motion can be explained by a mismatch in the adopted disk geometry, which affects the spiral phases measured in Band 6 (2017, 2019) and Band 7 (2024) differently. In addition, we identify a tentative large-scale one-armed spiral-like structure extending beyond the known $m=2$ spiral, which may provide clues to additional perturbations, such as an embedded planet or late-stage infall. Future high-resolution Band~6 observations with a longer time baseline will be essential for more accurately determining the spiral pattern speed.

title: Dynamic Watermarking and Action-Conditioned Latent Dynamics for Secure Vision-Based Controllers
abstract: Replay attacks are difficult to detect in vision-based control systems because previously recorded observations can remain plausible while the physical system follows a different trajectory. This paper develops an adaptive dynamic-watermarking framework for detecting replay attacks against vision-based controllers. A private Gaussian watermark is added to the nominal control input, and a control input-conditioned latent dynamics network (LDN) predicts the corresponding evolution in a compact latent space learned from image observations. Attack evidence is obtained from the discrepancy between the predicted latent response and the latent representation of the received image observation. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the watermark covariance using the latent state and detector confidence, thereby balancing attack detectability, watermark energy, and control distortion. A Lagrangian penalty on task-specific safety costs is included during training to limit the adverse effect of the excitation. The framework is evaluated on a vision-guided UR5 manipulation task in which the robot reaches a target while avoiding a moving human arm under nominal and replay-attacked observations.

title: Breaking the Modality Barrier: Multimodal Fusion With Missing Modalities for Cybersickness Prediction
abstract: Cybersickness is a major barrier to comfortable VR use, and reliable prediction often requires multiple physiological and behavioral sensors. However, existing models typically assume a fixed set of modalities, making them vulnerable when sensors are unavailable and difficult to generalize across datasets with different sensor configurations. We adapt a transformer-based model that handles arbitrary sensor combinations without imputing missing data. Anchor-based contrastive learning maps heterogeneous sensor embeddings into a shared latent space using eye tracking as the anchor modality, while masked self-attention excludes unavailable sensors during fusion. We evaluate our approach on three publicly available cybersickness datasets: VR.net, SIM21, and Blur-Rollercoaster, collected using different VR systems and sensor configurations. Across single-sensor dropout conditions, prediction error changes by less than 0.09 MAE. Joint training across all datasets achieves 0.51 MAE and 0.63 Pearson correlation, substantially outperforming single-dataset models. These results demonstrate robust and generalizable cybersickness prediction across diverse VR systems.

title: Designing with Cinematic Language: An Intent-Driven Approach to Human-AI Video Clip Co-Creation
abstract: Generative video models have made video creation more accessible, yet creators still struggle to translate high-level narrative intentions into coherent cinematic expressions. Existing systems primarily rely on prompt refinement or expose isolated camera controls, leaving a gap between what to express and how to film it. We present CineAssist, a human-AI co-creation system that treats cinematic language as an interactive design medium connecting creative intentions with executable video controls. We construct a Cinematic Language Design Space and an annotated dataset from 107 filmmaking sources and 1,436 film clips, linking communicative intentions to cinematic parameter values. CineAssist combines a multi-agent workflow for intent alignment and strategy recommendation with an interactive cinematic editor and a context-sensitive preference learner for user-controlled personalization. We evaluate the system through three studies examining end-to-end usability, cinematic quality, and preference evolution. Results show that CineAssist facilitates efficient, controllable, and personalized intent-driven cinematic video creation.

title: Design of Multi-UAV Cooperative Deep Semantic Autoencoders for Communication Networks
abstract: Driven by the rapid development of the low-altitude economy, Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks have become increasingly important for executing tasks such as search, rescue, and monitoring. However, under bandwidth-constrained scenarios, UAV networks still face significant challenges in task execution efficiency and intelligent processing capabilities. To address these issues, we propose Multi-UAV Cooperative Deep Semantic Autoencoders (MC-DSA) for communication networks. The architecture comprises one Task UAV (T-UAV) and multiple Support UAVs (S-UAVs), which jointly enhance communication efficiency and data-processing capability via semantic communication and cooperation. Specifically, we introduce a semantic matching and source selection mechanism, enabling the proposed MC-DSA to handle low-quality images while ensuring effective utilization of high-quality images. The T-UAV broadcasts a task query, and each S-UAV computes the semantic similarity between its local image and the query. Communication links are established only when the similarity exceeds a predefined threshold. The training algorithm optimizes network parameters through gradient descent, improving semantic feature extraction accuracy. The testing algorithm evaluates UAV collaboration efficiency and communication quality. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with benchmarks, the proposed MC-DSA improves image semantic segmentation accuracy while maintaining task execution efficiency. As a result, it reduces redundant transmissions and offers an effective solution for multi-UAV communication networks.

title: Breaking $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$ via Adaptive Neuron Clustering in Cryptanalytic Model Extraction
abstract: Cryptanalytic model extraction poses a fundamental threat to deep learning model confidentiality by enabling precise parameter recovery with theoretical guarantees of functional equivalence. To counter this growing threat, $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$ (NeurIPS 2025) was proposed as the first dedicated defense against cryptanalytic extraction and remains the only defense believed to be effective to date. It encourages neurons to learn similar weights so that they switch activation states together, making their individual contributions harder to distinguish. However, we notice that neurons with similar weights need not switch activation states together under small perturbations. Instead, weight similarity can cause the original clustering rule to merge signatures from distinct neurons when only a subset of their normalized weight coordinates agree. Motivated by this observation, we introduce $\mathsf{SimBreak}$, an adaptive clustering rule that breaks the weight-similarity defense of $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$. $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ estimates a relative scale from all jointly observed weight coordinates and uses the same scale to test both weight direction and bias consistency. Across six protected fully connected networks trained on MNIST, $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ raises target layer signature recovery from $0\%$ to $100\%$, with a maximum relative recovery error of $2^{-22.27}$. Our work challenges the use of neuron weight similarity as a sufficient basis for protection and establishes adaptive evaluation as essential to assessing cryptanalytic extraction defenses.

title: Slide to Report: Continuous Reporting Symptom-Specific Cybersickness in VR
abstract: Cybersickness is often assessed during VR exposure through discrete overall sickness, which cannot capture specific symptoms or their changes over time. Post-exposure questionnaires such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire provide symptom-specific measures but cannot be collected during immersion. We investigate whether separating cybersickness into three symptom-specific dimensions -- nausea, oculomotor discomfort, and disorientation -- during immersion provides more informative continuous measurements. We conducted a between-subjects study with 52 participants in a VR-rollercoaster, comparing a three-slider interface with a single-slider interface. Concurrently, participants also completed an auditory Simon task to measure attention. We additionally collected multimodal set of physiological signals, including GSR, ECG, PPG, eye and head tracking. Results show that each slider correlated most strongly with its corresponding SSQ subscale, whereas the single slider correlated with all SSQ subscales. Using three sliders did not significantly affect usability, workload, or attention. We publicly release the multimodal dataset to support future cybersickness research.

title: Current frontiers in mobility and well-being
abstract: Human mobility has a profound impact on social structure and collective behavior, which allows individuals to reshape group structures in response to strategy information, acting as a double-edged sword for cooperative behavior. It can both disrupt existing cooperative communities and enable individuals to escape adverse environments and seek high-quality interaction partners. This paper surveys current research progress on the impact of mobility on cooperation within the framework of evolutionary game theory, focusing on specific mechanisms of passive escape, dynamic self-organization driven by active choice, and the core trade-off between migration costs and speed. Mobility, an individual's spatial response to local strategic information that turns location into strategic advantage, influences cooperative evolution by altering interactive information and environmental feedback, consequently affecting sustainable social well-being, such as collective benefits. Under specific conditions, this self-interested behavior at the individual level can foster macrosocial harmony, embodying the unity of individual rationality and collective cooperation. Furthermore, we also discusses inter-layer migration and information routing mechanisms in multilayer networks and extends the perspective to human-machine hybrid systems where mobile agents with information regulation capabilities can serve as information supernodes. Our paper aims to provide a unified framework for understanding mobility as a combined physical and informational driving force in the evolution of cooperation.

title: Exact $\ell_p$-CVP via Euclidean SVP in Polynomial Space
abstract: We give a randomized, rank-preserving reduction from exact $\ell_p$-CVP to exact Euclidean SVP for every integer $p\ge2$. For rational inputs of bit length $\ell$ on full-rank lattices $L\subset\mathbb R^N$, the reduction uses $(Cp)^N\poly(p,\ell)$ oracle calls and additional bit operations, where $C$ is an absolute constant. It uses $\poly(p,\ell)$ working space outside the oracle, and all oracle queries have rank $N$ and $\poly(p,\ell)$ bit complexity. For $p=2$, the reduction transfers polynomial-space exact SVP algorithms to exact CVP with $2^{O(N)}\poly(\ell)$ time overhead. Instantiating it with the SVP algorithms of Kannan and of Feng, Gao and Liu yields randomized polynomial-space CVP algorithms running in time $N^{N/(2e)+o(N)}$ and $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$, respectively. For every fixed integer $p\ge3$, the same reduction yields exact $\ell_p$-CVP algorithms for arbitrary rational targets either in randomized time and space $2^{O(N)}$, or in randomized time $N^{N/(4e)+o(N)}$ and polynomial space. These algorithmic bounds are up to polynomial factors in $\ell$. The reduction performs local search sequentially over the cosets of \(2L\), where \(L\) is the input lattice, while tracking the excess of the current objective value over the optimum. Within a coset containing a closest vector, midpoint inequalities bound the unknown correction in terms of this excess, which in turn allows us to construct many short corrections that reduce the excess bound by a factor of four. A counting argument shows that these improving corrections form a sufficiently large fraction of the lattice points in a known search region, and a sparsification-based sampler assigns sufficiently large probability to every nonzero vector in that region, using at most one SVP call per sample. For \(p\ge3\), the same framework is extended using a diagonal weighted norm computed from the current point.

title: Take It From Here: Evaluating Coding Agents On Project Takeover
abstract: Coding agents increasingly collaborate on long-term projects. When taking over a project, they need to recover currently applicable requirements from the interaction history and update them in response to new requests. However, most coding benchmarks do not include long interaction histories, and some evaluations that consider history still do not cover the full process from requirement reconstruction to project delivery. We therefore provide agents with the interaction history, current request, and pre-request project environment, ask them to make the requested changes, and assess takeover performance through delivery tests. Across six model-harness configurations and 37 targets eligible for executable validation, the mean complete-delivery rate under Full History is only 4.95%. We then use requirement atoms to independently diagnose a larger set of takeover targets, examining relevant information identification, pre-request state reconstruction, and current request processing. We further supply correct pre-request or target states to examine the remaining difficulties in requirement processing and project modification. The diagnostics show that none of the six configurations produces fully correct post-request requirement states, and a case illustrates omission of previously recovered constraints during updating. With correct target states supplied, the mean complete-delivery rate is 8.11%, with build and regression pass rates of 96.40% and 90.99%, but target-test success remains 9.01%. These results show difficulties in both forming target requirement states and implementing supplied targets in existing projects. Based on these findings, we introduce ReqMemBench, which combines requirement diagnostics with delivery validation to support systematic evaluation of project takeover.

title: Using Structure Functions to Characterize Protoplanetary Disk Velocity Residuals
abstract: Protoplanetary disks, the birthplace of planetary systems, are highly dynamic environments. High angular and spectral resolution observations have revealed non-Keplerian motions in nearly every source studied, indicative of (magneto-)hydrodynamical instabilities or planet-disk interactions. However, these velocity perturbations rarely exhibit ordered structure, limiting our ability to attribute them to a specific mechanism. We propose the second-order structure function as a tool for recovering structural properties of velocity perturbations in the presence of significant noise. Using morphological models, we demonstrate how easy-to-calculate heuristics and parametric model fits together identify structure in noisy data and recover its properties, including correlation lengths, their radial scaling where genuinely present, and the anisotropy. We further outline a workflow to de-noise the data and to build a matched null model against which inferences are compared. Applying the framework to one numerical simulation each of the gravitational, magneto-rotational and vertical-shear instabilities, we recover their structure at high significance and the structural heuristics separate all three pairs, with the gravitational and vertical-shear instability simulations remaining the hardest to distinguish once observationally degraded. As a demonstration on real data, 12CO observations of TW Hya reveal azimuthally elongated velocity structure that persists once the large-scale m=1 component is removed. We also delineate where a Gaussian description breaks down for coherent features such as spiral arms, and how inclination affects the recovered heuristics. The methodology is implemented in the eddy package and provides a foundation for statistically characterizing turbulent velocity structure in high-resolution disk observations.

title: VREgo: Consumer VR Headsets for Learning Robot Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations
abstract: VREgo trains manipulation policies from demonstrations recorded on consumer VR headsets; we instantiate it with EgoKit on one such headset, the PICO 4 Ultra. On-device head and hand tracking and stereo object localisation allow the operator to begin a demonstration at the table. We adapt HumanEgo's preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds per recording, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes. We evaluate policies in simulation on two tabletop tasks recorded by one operator. For cube placement, we compare PICO and Project Aria recordings of the same 41 layouts. With 40 training demonstrations, the PICO policies placed the cube on the tray in 67, 74, and 60 of 100 evaluation layouts across three training seeds. The corresponding Aria results were 73, 78, and 0. For a two-stage stacking task recorded with the PICO alone, the baseline placed the block on the tray in 94 of 100 layouts and met the end-of-episode criterion for both placements in two. In one diagnostic episode, repeated replanning deferred release beyond the eight executed steps. Demonstration replays also showed that the open gripper could displace the cube before grasping it. After adapting the training trajectories and adding task-specific execution rules that use simulator object positions, the system met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four evaluation noise seeds. The same 100 layouts informed rule development and evaluation. VREgo is available at https://vrego.chuange.org/.

title: Quadratic Extractors
abstract: A quadratic source is a random variable $X\sim\mathbb{F}_2^n$ generated by applying $n$ quadratics to a hidden uniform string. Previously, the best-known explicit extractor for this model required min-entropy roughly $k=n-\sqrt{\log n}$. In this paper, we give an explicit construction for min-entropy $k=\mathrm{polylog}(n)$. Even for the special case of $2$-local sources, where each bit of $X$ depends on two hidden uniform bits, achieving an entropy requirement below $k=\sqrt{n}$ was an important open problem. This is because such sources provably cannot be reduced (in a black-box manner) to our most powerful general-purpose seedless extractor, known as a sumset extractor. Our new extractor bypasses this barrier, providing the first explicit construction to go beyond sumset extraction.

title: Coordinated Space and Ground Monitoring of Accretion Bursts in a Protoplanetary Disk: MIRI and iSHELL observe the long-term modulation of gas within a small inner disk cavity
abstract: DQ Tau is a TTauri eccentric binary with pulsed accretion bursts regulated by its $\sim 16$-day orbital period. We have monitored this system with seven instruments from ground and space over 40 days. We present results on molecular gas variability from nine JWST-MIRI and nine IRTF-iSHELL epochs over three sequential accretion bursts with accretion luminosity pulses increasing by factors of $\sim 9$-80. A fundamental new measurement from this analysis is the line broadening of CO (from iSHELL) and H$_2$O (from MIRI) lines, which we use to estimate Keplerian radii and their variability in parallel to the line luminosity. This unprecedented dataset clearly shows that the molecular emission does not react like HI and the 5-$μ$m continuum with each accretion burst: the line luminosity and width of all hot molecular gas tracers decrease over $\sim30$-35 days, consistent with an emitting region decreasing in temperature and mass as it recedes to larger radii within the $\sim 0.2$-0.4 au inner cavity perturbed by the binary. The infrared molecular spectrum of DQ Tau is affected more by disk dynamics then by chemical changes triggered by variable accretion, supporting model expectations for chemical relaxation timescales that are much longer than the duration of these accretion bursts ($\gg 10$ days). The variability observed in all tracers in this study is consistent with a scenario where gas mass builds up near the disk edge to modulate the burst peak intensity and gas density in the inner cavity every $\sim4$-5 orbital periods. The origin of this modulation is still unclear.

title: Probabilistic counting of labelled trees with prescribed vertical edge profile
abstract: The vertical edge profile of a labelled plane tree $t$ is the collection of integers counting the number of oriented edges from label $i$ to label $j$ for every possible pairs of labels $(i, j)$. In a previous work by the second author, it was shown that a process constructed from the vertical edge profile forms a Markov chain for a wide class of models of random labelled plane trees where edge label increments are constrained to lie in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$. The purpose of this paper is twofold. First, we continue the study of Markov properties of the vertical edge profile. In particular, we derive general formulas for the transition kernel and the initial distribution of a class of Markov chains related to the vertical edge profile. Second, we apply these results to the probabilistic enumeration of trees with a prescribed vertical edge profile. These applications yield a unified probabilistic derivation of several enumeration formulas. In particular, we recover some results established Bousquet-Mélou and Chapuy for binary trees and Cayley trees. These enumeration formulas admit a remarkable factorized form, already noted in previous works. The probabilistic methods developed here explain this phenomenon by showing that these factorizations arise naturally from the Markov structure underlying the vertical edge profile.

title: Chvátal's Toughness Conjecture for Dense Almost Regular Graphs
abstract: Chvátal's toughness conjecture asserts that there is a constant $t_0$ such that every $t_0$-tough graph on at least three vertices is Hamiltonian. Most partial results on this conjecture concern graphs with a restricted structure, such as chordal graphs and $H$-free graphs for small linear forests $H$. We confirm the conjecture with $t_0=4$ for dense almost regular graphs, without any structural assumption: for every $α>0$, there exist $\varepsilon>0$ and $n_0$ such that every $4$-tough graph $G$ on $n\ge n_0$ vertices with $δ(G)\geαn$ and $Δ(G)-δ(G)\le\varepsilon n$ is Hamiltonian. This result also bears on a conjecture of Bollobás and, independently, Häggkvist from the 1970s that every $k$-connected $D$-regular graph on $n$ vertices with $D\ge n/(k+1)$ is Hamiltonian. This conjecture is false for every $k\ge4$, even for large $n$. Our result shows that its conclusion holds for all large $n$ when $k$-connectivity is replaced by $4$-toughness, and that the degree condition can then be weakened to $D\geαn$ for an arbitrarily small fixed $α>0$. We also construct $3/2$-tough regular non-Hamiltonian graphs of linear degree, showing that the constant $4$ cannot be replaced by $3/2$.

title: Sets of reach $R$ are $\operatorname{CAT}\left( 1/R^2\right)$
abstract: Positive reach underpins many results in computational geometry and topology. It is used for triangulation criteria, topological inference, and manifold learning. The geometric properties of these sets have therefore been studied intensely. In this paper we focus on the intrinsic metric properties of sets of positive reach. In particular we give an elementary proof of the fact that (closed) sets of reach at least $R$ are $\operatorname{CAT}(1/R^2)$. This fact was established earlier by Alexander and Bishop, using quite significant machinery. The fact that a space is $\operatorname{CAT}(1/R^2)$ offers many advantages, such as the uniqueness and continuity of sufficiently short geodesics, the existence of Fr{é}chet means and by extension the Rips based homotopy reconstruction of Hausmann is available.

title: Exact local spectral thresholds for loose and tight Hamilton cycles in $3$-graphs
abstract: For an $n$-vertex $3$-uniform hypergraph $H$, let $σ(H)$ denote the minimum adjacency spectral radius of its vertex links. We determine the exact thresholds for $σ(H)$ that force loose and tight Hamilton cycles for all sufficiently large admissible orders, and give constructions showing that each bound is best possible. The loose threshold is $(1+\sqrt{13})n/8+O(1)$, with two forms according to $n$ modulo four. The tight threshold is $2n/3+O(1)$, with four forms determined by $n$ modulo three and, when $3\mid n$, modulo nine. The resulting spectral conditions and the corresponding minimum vertex degree conditions do not imply one another. For loose cycles, we combine fractional packing stability and absorption with exact completion near a space barrier. For tight cycles, spectral stability and rooted sampling reduce the problem to three extremal configurations. We resolve these configurations by controlling the spectral loss caused by missing triples and constructing short paths that extend to Hamilton cycles, including in the presence of exceptional vertices.

title: A proof of the Theta conjecture
abstract: We prove the touching refinement of the Theta conjecture of Interdonato and Iraci, giving a formula for $Θ_{e_\ell}Θ_{e_k}\nabla E_{d,j}$ as a weighted sum over parking functions with decorated rises and valleys and touch number $j$. Summing over $j$ gives the Theta conjecture. As corollaries, we prove the valley Delta conjecture of Haglund, Remmel, and Wilson and its generalized version proposed by Qiu and Wilson. Our proof compares algebraic and combinatorial recurrences using an extension of the plethystic substitution $X\mapsto(q-1)X$ to quasisymmetric functions. The algebraic recurrence follows from an endomorphism constructed by D'Adderio, Interdonato, Iraci and Pagaria on the Dyck path algebra of Carlsson and Mellit. The combinatorial recurrence is obtained by introducing signed labels and deleting the main diagonal. The two recurrences have the same initial conditions, which identifies the corresponding generating functions.

title: Sampling Colorings on $G(n, d/n)$ via Glauber Dynamics
abstract: We study the mixing time of Glauber dynamics for sampling uniformly from the proper $q$-colorings of sparse Erdős-Rényi random graphs $G(n,d/n)$. Our main result establishes that with probability $1-o(1)$ over the draw of $G$, Glauber dynamics is rapidly mixing for every $q\geq d+d^{1/2+\varepsilon}$, given any fixed $0<\varepsilon\leq1/2$ and any sufficiently large fixed $d$. In particular, the surplus of colors above $d$ is sublinear and close to $\sqrt{d}$. The achieved color range therefore approaches the tree uniqueness threshold and improves over the previously best achievable number of colors $q > 1.763 d$ due to Efthymiou, Hayes, Stefankovic, and Vigoda [SODA 2018]. Moreover, our mixing-time bound is $O(n^{2+o_d(1)})$, and hence almost quadratic as $d\rightarrow\infty$. Our proof is based on establishing a spectral gap for block dynamics resulting from a suitable decomposition of $G(n,d/n)$ into blocks and singleton vertices, ensuring that every high-degree vertex is encapsulated within a block. Our main technical contribution is a novel way of establishing rapid mixing of block dynamics via an integrated Bochner-Bakry-Émery approach, which we expect to have applications beyond sampling colorings. We further devise a new block decomposition of $G(n,d/n)$ that strengthens and simplifies similar constructions used in previous work. Finally, to compare block and Glauber dynamics, we establish a novel recursive separator decomposition of tree-like blocks, together with a coupling argument that avoids the need for nearly uniform color marginals at vertices adjacent to hubs. This comparison argument might be of independent interest.

title: Avoiding short progressions in Euclidean Ramsey theory II
abstract:
Recently, Currier, Moore, and Yip developed a general framework for constructing colorings avoiding prescribed monochromatic arithmetic progressions in Euclidean Ramsey theory. Writing $\ell_m$ for an $m$-term arithmetic progression with unit spacing, they proved $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,\ell_{20})$ and $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,α\ell_{6889})$ for every $α>0$. We refine and simplify their framework, proving $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,α\ell_{22})$ for every $α>0$. We further establish $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,α\ell_{21})$ except possibly for four values of $α^2$, and $\mathbb E^n
ot	o(\ell_3,α\ell_{17})$ for all but finitely many $α>0$. Our approach also recovers several earlier results and avoids some technical arguments used in previous works.

title: Induced packing treewidth III. Branch decompositions
abstract: The notion of induced packing treewidth aims to unify classes defined by forbidden induced subgraphs or induced minors with classes defined by the existence of certain structured tree decompositions. In this paper, we introduce induced packing branchwidth, a branch-decomposition analogue of induced packing treewidth. For a graph $H$, the induced $H$-packing branchwidth of a graph $G$, denoted by $\branchpi_H(G)$, is the minimum, over all branch decompositions of $G$, of the largest number of pairwise anticomplete induced copies of $H$ that cross one displayed cut. For $H=P_2$, it equals sim-width. We prove several structural properties of graphs of bounded $\branchpi_H$, for various choices of $H$, including $χ$-boundedness, polynomial degree-boundedness, and metric properties.

title: Edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles in the McKay--Miller--Širáň graphs $H_q$ for every prime power $q\geq 3$
abstract: Motivated by Hamilton cycle problems and applications to collective communication, we study edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles in the McKay--Miller--Širáň (MMS) graphs. The MMS graph $H_q$ (indexed by a prime power $q$) is a highly symmetric graph arising from finite fields. For every prime power $q\geq 3$, we prove that the MMS graph $H_q$ contains $\big\lceil\frac{q-1}{2}\big\rceil$ edge-disjoint Hamilton cycles. This resolves a problem of Li, Wang and Zheng, who established the result for prime $q$ and for $q=4$. Our construction uses graph lifts over finite fields and joins the components of lifted Hamilton cycles by adding edges within vertex fibres. The resulting cycles can be constructed using $O(|E(H_q)|)$ finite field operations, comparisons, and elementary list operations. As an application, these cycles provide edge-disjoint spanning rings for parallel ring-all-reduce algorithms on MMS networks.

title: Sufficient conditions for spanning trees with bounded total excess in tough graphs
abstract: Let $G$ be a connected graph and $T$ a spanning tree of $G$. The toughness of $G$ is defined by $t(G)=\min\Big\{\frac{|S|}{c(G-S)}:S\subseteq V(G), c(G-S)\geq2\Big\}$ for $G\neq K_n$. A graph $G$ is said to be $t$-tough if $t(G)\geq t$. The size, the adjacency spectral radius and the signless Laplacian spectral radius of $G$ are denoted by $e(G)$, $ρ(G)$ and $q(G)$, respectively. The $k$-excess of a vertex $v$ in $T$ is defined as $\max\{0,d_T(v)-k\}$. The total $k$-excess $\mbox{te}(T,k)$ is defined by $\mbox{te}(T,k)=\sum\limits_{v\in V(T)}{\max\{0,d_T(v)-k\}}$. A tree $T$ is called a $k$-tree if $d_T(v)\leq k$ for every $v\in V(T)$, namely, the maximum degree of a $k$-tree is at most $k$. It is obvious that $T$ is a spanning $k$-tree if and only if $\mbox{te}(T,k)=0$. This paper investigates a generalization of spanning $k$-trees using a concept called total $k$-excess and puts forward three lower bounds based on $e(G)$, $ρ(G)$ and $q(G)$ in a connected $\frac{k}{k(k-2)+b+3}$-tough graph $G$ to guarantee that $G$ has a spanning tree $T$ with $\mbox{te}(T,k)\leq b$, where $k\geq3$ and $b\geq0$ are two integers. As corollaries, we obtain three sufficient conditions for a connected $\frac{k}{k(k-2)+3}$-tough graph to has a spanning $k$-tree.

title: Cut Conditions, Integrality, and Obstructions for Directed Multiflows
abstract: In contrast to the max-flow/min-cut theorem for single-commodity flows, the cut condition is necessary but not sufficient for the existence of directed multiflows, even with only two commodities. Poremba and Shepherd (IPCO 2023) conjecture that the cut condition is sufficient for all capacities and demands on a directed two-commodity topology if and only if it contains neither of two specific topologies as a relevant minor. We prove this conjecture. As a consequence, the fractional and integral flow-cut gaps of every directed two-commodity topology coincide and are either 1 or 2. We then investigate stronger necessary conditions for multiflow feasibility and their implications for integrality. We introduce a hierarchy of five conditions, ranging from the classical cut condition through conditions based on blocking edge sets and binary edge lengths to the linear programming dual characterization of fractional feasibility. The corresponding classes of sufficient topologies are strictly nested. We extend the Nagamochi-Ibaraki theorem: whenever one of the first four conditions is sufficient on a topology, integral capacities and demands satisfying that condition admit an integral multiflow, computable in polynomial time. Finally, we prove that recognizing topologies on which any of these four conditions is sufficient is coNP-complete, even for two commodities.

title: Piercing a Chessboard with Restricted Slopes
abstract: Is it true that for $n\geq 3$, $n-1$ lines are needed to pierce every cell of an $n\times n$ board? This problem was independently rediscovered several times: Alkauskas (1998), Harel-Ackerman-Pinchasi (2012, without claiming the $n-1$ bound), Bárány-Frankl (2021). However, apparently the first to pose it was T. Keller (Honolulu, Hawaii), in 1980, in the problem section of The American Mathematical Monthly. In this note, we give an affirmative answer to Keller's problem when all lines have slopes in $(-\infty,-1]\cup(0,1]$.

title: Upper bounds on all-terminal reliability polynomials in terms of cycle basis lengths
abstract: Let $G=(V(G),E(G))$ be a connected multigraph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. The all-terminal reliability polynomial of $G$ can be written as $R_G(q)=(1-q)^{n-1}\sum\limits_{i=0}^{d}H_iq^i$ where $d=m-n+1$ is the cycle rank, each edge fails independently with probability $q\in[0,1]$, and $H_0,\ldots,H_d$ are the associated coefficients. A cycle basis, which consists of cycles that form a basis of the cycle space of a graph, is an important tool for characterizing its cycle structure. The structural properties of cycle bases, together with the associated length optimization problems and construction algorithms, have been extensively studied. In this context, Colbourn posed the following open problem, which concerns upper bounds on the reliability coefficients in terms of cycle-basis lengths: For all-terminal reliability, is it true that if $G$ has a cycle basis containing cycles of lengths $c_1,\ldots,\allowbreak c_{m-n+1}$, then $H_i \le\sum\limits_{\substack{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m-n+1\},|I|=i}}\prod\limits_{j\in I}(c_j-1)$? In this paper, we establish a result that resolves this open problem.

title: Odd realisation numbers of rigid graphs
abstract: Determining the number of realisations of a rigid graph for a specific choice of edge lengths is a fundamental problem in discrete geometry. Gortler, Healy and Thurston showed that the number of real realisations of a generic framework is always even or equal to one. Despite being rare, there do exist graphs whose number of complex realisations is odd and not equal to one. In this article, we exhibit two necessary conditions for a rigid graph to have an odd realisation number other than one. We also provide an infinite family of rigid graphs with an odd realisation number other than one.

title: Cube tilings, partition counters, and the Calkin--Wilf and Kepler trees
abstract: A tiling of the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ by translates of the discrete cube $K_d=\{0,1\}^d$ cuts every translate $K_d+x$ into subcubes. We study the function $\ell(x)$ counting these parts. Its sum over every translate of $K_d$ equals $3^d$, for an arbitrary translation set. For lattice tilings with a triangular basis we obtain a dimension-reduction formula, and we describe every cocyclic lattice by a single normalized congruence. Along a cyclic generator, the counter of a signed bidiagonal lattice is a row of Stern's diatomic sequence; pairs of counter values realize the Calkin--Wilf tree, and complementary binary words realize the Kepler tree. For the binary lattice, the translated counter labelings of the cube carry generating face partitions, supplied by the tiling itself, which force the levels of the Kepler tree, and every nontrivial face partition has a unique lamination direction. Using finite Fourier analysis we prove that the ordered cyclic profile determines a standard cocyclic cube tiling lattice up to coordinate reflections. For lattices tiling by discrete boxes we determine exactly when the analogous statement holds.

title: Globally Simple Heffter Arrays $H(n;k)$ with $k \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$
abstract: Heffter arrays are combinatorial structures that can be used to construct orthogonal cyclic cycle decompositions of complete graphs. A square Heffter array $H(n;k)$ is a partially filled $n \times n$ array with $k$ filled cells in each row and column. Its entries are distinct and nonzero, form a half-set of the group $\mathbb{Z}_{2nk+1}$, and sum to zero in every row and column. If the natural orderings of the rows and columns of an array are simple, the array is called globally simple. The globally simple property guarantees the orthogonal cycle decompositions constructed from the Heffter array consist of simple cycles. While existence results are known for most congruence classes of the parameters $n$ and $k$ modulo 4 for square globally simple Heffter arrays $H(n;k)$, the existence for $k \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$ has remained largely open. In this paper, we present a construction for globally simple integer Heffter arrays $H(n;k)$ covering all admissible values of $n$ when $k \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$. This settles the existence question across all congruence classes.

title: A criterion for the set of subsums to be a Cantorval for a certain class of multigeometric series
abstract: The paper studies the topological structure of the set of subsums (incomplete sums) of multigeometric series of the form $\frac{k_1}{s} + \frac{k_2}{s} + \ldots + \frac{k_m}{s} + \frac{k_1}{s^2} + \frac{k_2}{s^2} + \ldots+ \frac{k_m}{s^2} + \frac{k_1}{s^3} + \frac{k_2}{s^3} +\ldots$, where $k_1, \ldots, k_m, s \in \mathbb{N}$. In terms of graph theory, necessary and sufficient conditions are established for the set of subsums of a given series not to be a finite union of closed intervals, as well as necessary and sufficient conditions for this set to contain an interval. As a consequence of these statements, a criterion for the set of subsums to be a Cantorval is obtained. An example of applying the criterion to a series whose Cantorval property was previously unknown is given. A more general object of study of topological properties is the set of numbers whose representations in a numerical system with a natural base and a redundant alphabet are subject to restrictions on the use of digits. It is for this object that the above statements are proved.

title: Hilton's Conjecture on Uncomplemented Incomparable Families
abstract: A family ${\mathcal A}\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ is \emph{uncomplemented} if it contains no set together with its complement. Families ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t$ are \emph{strongly incomparable} if every set in one family is incomparable with every set in another family. In 1976, Hilton conjectured that if ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ are uncomplemented and strongly incomparable, then $$\sum_{i=1}^t |{\mathcal A}_i|\le 2^{n-1}.$$ We confirm this conjecture by a matrix rank argument that encodes incomparability and uncomplementedness in the same matrix, which is quite different from the earlier methods on this problem. We also study weak incomparability, in which the same set may occur in different families. Goldwasser, Hilton and Zheng conjectured an upper bound in this setting and claimed that their conjecture is equivalent to Hilton's conjecture. We give counterexamples to their conjecture for every $t\ge3$ and identify the error in the claimed equivalence. We then propose a replacement conjecture and confirm it when $t$ is large. The upper bound $2^{n-1}$ in Hilton's conjecture can be attained if some families are allowed to by empty. It is natural to consider the maximum size of $\sum_{i=1}^t |{\mathcal A}_i|$ for uncomplemented and strongly incomparable families ${\mathcal A}_1,\ldots,{\mathcal A}_t\subseteq 2^{[n]}$ when all families are required to be non-empty. Denote this maximum number by $M(n,t)$. We show that \[ 2^{n-1}-1\le M(n,t)\le 2^{n-1} \] for $n\ge3$ and $3\le t\le n$.

title: A Rooted Structure Theorem for $5$-Connected Graphs and $K_6^-$-Minors
abstract: Jorgensen conjectured that every $6$-connected graph with no $K_6$-minor is apex. For a $6$-connected graph containing a $K_4$ on vertices $a_1,\dots,a_4$, being apex is equivalent to $G-a_i$ having a planar embedding with the other three roots on a common face for some $i$, so that for such graphs the conjecture becomes a rooted planarity statement. Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas showed that the failure of the corresponding three-rooted planarity is witnessed by a legless tripod. We introduce a four-root structure, called a frame, that extends this certificate, and prove a structural theorem: every $5$-connected graph containing a frame rooted at four prescribed vertices contains a subgraph of one of five explicit types, denoted $A$--$E$. This theorem does not depend on the edges among the roots. As an application, we show that when the four roots span a $K_4^-$, each of the five configurations yields a $K_6^-$-minor. Together with a planar argument for the case without a frame and an induction based on a theorem of Kawarabayashi, this gives a proof that every non-planar $5$-connected graph contains a $K_6^-$-minor. This statement also follows from a recent theorem of Lo; our proof is independent and is driven by the rooted structure theorem, whose method we expect to apply to Jorgensen's conjecture with other target configurations.

title: The strong cylinder conjecture over prime fields
abstract: Let $p$ be prime and let $S\subseteq\mathbb F_p^3$ have $p^2$ points, with every affine plane meeting $S$ in a multiple of $p$ points. We give a self-contained argument that $S$ is a union of $p$ parallel lines.

title: Permutons
abstract: Permutons are limit structures for large permutations. Intrinsically, a permuton is a familiar mathematical object: a probability measure on the unit square with uniform marginals. The compact space of permutons completes the set of permutations of all sizes under a natural topology; each permuton is not only a limit of permutations but also a generator of random permutations. Since their (relatively recent) discovery as a tool for understanding the behavior of large (possibly random) permutations, permutons have proved remarkably fruitful, with dozens of fascinating connections to combinatorics and probability. We review the fundamentals of permutons, sometimes providing new, shorter proofs, and give an account of some of their myriad applications. The survey concludes with a long list of open problems. An extensive -- but not comprehensive -- bibliography is appended.

title: Good colorings of doubled triangles and a conjecture of Schwartz
abstract: A good coloring of a sphere triangulation is a black-and-white coloring of its faces such that, at every vertex, the numbers of black and white faces differ by a multiple of~$3$. Good colorings correspond to proper vertex $4$-colorings. For a good coloring with fold count $\mathrm{f}$ (the number of black-white edges) on a triangulation with $F$ faces, R.~E.~Schwartz introduced the Eisenstein isoperimetric ratio $η=\mathrm{f}^2/F$. For triangulations with degree sequence $6,\dots,6,2,2,2$, he proved that $η\ge3$ and conjectured that every such triangulation has a good coloring with $η$ below a universal constant. These triangulations are indexed by the nonzero Eisenstein integers~$β$. We study the family $\T(n)$ given by $β=n$, a positive integer, which consists of the doubled equilateral triangles of side~$n$. We prove that every good coloring of $\T(n)$ has at least $3n$ folds, so $η\ge9/2$, and that this bound is attained for every~$n$. Thus the minimum of $η$ on this family is exactly $9/2$, and Schwartz's conjecture holds for it. We also prove that subdividing a good coloring of $\T(β)$ gives a good coloring of $\T(nβ)$ with the same value of $η$. Consequently, Schwartz's conjecture holds in general if and only if it holds for primitive Eisenstein integers.

title: Equality in the direction bound over prime fields
abstract: Let $p$ be prime. We prove that a noncollinear set of $2m+1\le p$ points in $\AG(2,p)$ determines exactly $m+2$ directions if and only if, up to an affine transformation, it consists of the origin and a coset of a multiplicative subgroup of order $m$ on each coordinate axis. Thus equality is possible precisely when $m\mid p-1$. This extends the Lovász--Schrijver classification for $2m+1=p$.

title: Spectral conditions for the existence of $\{K_2,\{C_k\}\}$-factor in $t$-tough graphs
abstract: For $t>0$, a graph $G$ is called $t$-tough if $|S|\geq t\,c(G-S)$ for every $S\subseteq V(G)$ with $c(G-S)\geq2$, where $c(G-S)$ denotes the number of components of $G-S$. Toughness is closely related to the existence of Hamiltonian cycles and factors in graphs. Chvátal [Discrete Math. 5 (1973) 215--228] conjectured that there exists a constant $t_0>0$ such that every $t_0$-tough graph of order at least three is Hamiltonian. Bauer, Broersma and Veldman [Discrete Appl. Math. 99 (2000) 317--321] constructed $(9/4-\varepsilon)$-tough graphs without a Hamiltonian path for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon>0$. For the weaker requirement of a $2$-factor, Enomoto et al. [J. Graph Theory 9 (1985) 87--95] proved that every $2$-tough graph of order at least three has a $2$-factor and that the toughness threshold $2$ is best possible. A graph $G$ is said to have a $\{K_2,\{C_k:k\geq3\}\}$-factor if and only if $G$ contains a spanning subgraph consisting of components that are either cycles or single edges. A $\{K_2,\{C_k:k\geq3\}\}$-factor can be viewed as a combination of a $1$-factor and a $2$-factor, motivating the study of such factors in tough graphs. In this paper, we establish sharp sufficient conditions in terms of the adjacency spectral radius, the distance spectral radius, and the distance signless Laplacian spectral radius for a $t$-tough graph to have a $\{K_2,\{C_k:k\geq3\}\}$-factor.

title: Five-Entropic Matroids Are Quinary
abstract: A finite matroid is representable over a field if its elements can be assigned vectors over that field such that the rank of every subset equals the dimension of the span of its vectors. For an integer q >= 2, a matroid is q-entropic if there exists a random vector indexed by its ground set, with each coordinate taking values in a common q-element alphabet, such that the entropy of every marginal subvector equals the rank of the corresponding subset multiplied by log q. It remains open to determine for which values of q every q-entropic matroid is representable over a field. For q=2 and q=3, representability over F_q has long been known. More recently, it was established that every 4-entropic matroid is representable over F_4 and that the 6-entropic matroids are precisely the regular matroids, that is, those representable over every field. We settle the previously unresolved five-symbol case, proving that a finite matroid is 5-entropic if and only if it is representable over F_5. For the nontrivial implication, we use Matúš's equivalence between entropic and partition representations. We show that a degree-five partition representation induces, on each embedded U_{2,4}-minor, an F_5-linear representation after coordinatewise relabeling, with a rescaling class independent of the chosen linearization. Using the foundation presentation of Baker and Lorscheid, we verify the compatibility relations among these local classes and thereby obtain a global F_5-representation.

title: A Cameron-Goethals-Seidel-Shult theorem for marked graphs
abstract: The classical Cameron-Goethals-Seidel-Shult theorem characterizes graphs with least eigenvalue at least $-2$ in terms of generalized line graphs, exceptional graphs, and root systems. In this paper, we establish a marked graph extension of this theorem. For a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and a binary vector $\mathbf{b}\in\{0,1\}^n$, we completely characterize all marked graphs $\mathbf{G}=(G,\mathbf{b})$ such that $λ_{\min}(A(G)+\mathbf{b}\mathbf{b}^\top-J_n)\ge -2$, where $J_n$ denotes the all-ones matrix of order $n$. Using representations by finite root systems, we show that every irreducible marked graph satisfying the above inequality is represented by either the root system $B_n$ or the exceptional root system $E_8$. This leads to a complete structural characterization in terms of irreducible marked graphs, namely induced subgraphs of extended generalized line graphs, the marked graph $(2K_1,\mathbf{0})$, and exceptional graphs with all vertices marked. In the special case $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{j}$, our characterization reduces to the original Cameron-Goethals-Seidel-Shult theorem. The root system $B_n$ and extended generalized line graphs play the roles occupied by $D_n$ and generalized line graphs in the classical theory. We further apply the characterization to graphs whose second largest eigenvalue is at most $1$, showing that every $-2$-markable graph satisfies this spectral condition.

title: The minimum forcing number of graphs and involutory weighted adjacency matrices
abstract: Let $G$ be a graph with a perfect matching. The minimum forcing number $f(G)$ of $G$ is the smallest size of a matching in $G$ that is contained in exactly one perfect matching. For the $d$-hypercube $Q_d$ ($d\geq 2$) Diwan (2019) determined $f(Q_d)=2^{d-2}$ by using a linear algebraic method, and Mohammadian (2022) generalized this method and showed that $f(G\square K_2)=n/2$ when a bipartite graph $G$ admits order $n$ and an involutory weighted adjacency matrix over a field $\mathbb F$, where $\square$ denotes the Cartesian product. In this paper, we further prove that if $\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}\neq 2$, then $\frac{n}{2}\le f(G\mathbin{\square} P_k)\le \frac{n}{2}\lceil\frac{k}{2}\rceil$ for every $k\ge 2$, where $P_k$ is the $k$-vertex path; this recovers Mohammadian's result when $k=2$, and the lower bound is attained for $k=3$. Moreover, we extend this method to non-bipartite graphs. Recursively constructing the adjacency matrix of the folded hypercube $FQ_n$ over the binary field $\mathbb F_2$, we prove that $f(FQ_n\mathbin{\square} K_2)=2^{n-1}$ for every even $n$. Combined with Mohammadian's result for odd $n$, this establishes the same formula for all $n\geq 1$.

title: Homomesy of tropical $T$-systems for pairs of simply laced Dynkin diagrams
abstract: For a pair of simply laced Dynking diagrams $X$ and $X'$, we prove Chin's homomesy conjecture on the number of red and blue mutations in a period of the tropical Zamolodchikov $T$-system associated to $(X, X')$ using Nakanishi's dilogarithm identity.

title: Binary Belief Propagation Fixed Points: Finiteness, Rigidity, and Topological Complexity
abstract: A fixed finite binary Ising model has only finitely many admissible complex belief propagation fixed points, even at degenerate parameter values. Families of positive fixed points obtained by varying external fields can nevertheless have nontrivial topology. We study this distinction through the external-field projection. For a fixed field, we prove finiteness by bounding the pole orders of the magnetizations on a hypothetical complex solution curve. The generic degree on the support graph then bounds the total local multiplicity. A graph has a single smooth real line as its full positive response for every choice of positive couplings, base field, and strictly positive sweep direction exactly when it contains no two vertex-disjoint connected subgraphs of cycle rank at least two. Two such subgraphs suffice to create a circular component. For a plane obtained by varying two vertex fields, connected simple bipartite cubic graphs with one uniform coupling and a universal bound on the fixed fields realize every genus. The minimum number of vertices grows logarithmically in the genus, by a matching algebraic upper bound on Betti numbers. Finally, we certify the complete field discriminant of an eighteen-vertex product model and recover its torus component's genus from the counts of distinct roots on all field cells. The three main theorems, including the logarithmic size bounds, are formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib.

title: Online Graph Coloring: Competitive Ratios Separating Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms
abstract: We study online coloring, focusing on the competitive ratio. The best previously known results were (1) a lower bound of $Ω(n / \log^2 n)$ for both deterministic and randomized algorithms by Halldórsson and Szegedy (1994), (2) an upper bound of $O(n / \log n)$ for randomized algorithms by Halldórsson (1997), and (3) an upper bound of $O(n / \log \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025). In this paper, we improve these results as follows: 1. A new lower bound of $Ω(n / \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms. 2. A new upper bound of $O(n (\log \log n)^2 / \log^2 n)$ for randomized algorithms. 3. A new upper bound of $O(n / (\log \log n)^{2-\varepsilon})$ for deterministic algorithms for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. For randomized algorithms, we nearly close the gap between the lower and upper bounds; the remaining gap is only $O((\log \log n)^2)$. We establish the asymptotic separation between randomized and deterministic online graph coloring. Against an oblivious adversary, a polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio asymptotically smaller than any deterministic algorithm can guarantee, even with unlimited computation.

title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.

title: Artificial Currency and Separate Selling: A 3-Approximation for Consumer Surplus
abstract: We study the allocation of indivisible items to buyers with additive values drawn from independent distributions. The objective is consumer surplus net of burnt payments. We consider artificial-currency mechanisms: buyers receive personalized budgets of a currency worthless outside the mechanism and use them to bid across items. The better of separate selling and artificial-currency mechanisms provides a 3-approximation to optimal consumer surplus. The guarantee holds at every Bayes--Nash equilibrium, without equilibrium selection. Both branches are necessary: either alone may capture only a vanishing share of the optimum. The proof decomposes benchmark surplus into a stable part captured by artificial currency and a variation covered by separate selling.

title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
abstract: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

title: Annular Counterexamples and Skew-Shape Block Identities
abstract: We establish four connected results on weighted order ideals, cluster coefficients, and block-statistic enumerators. First, we give a counterexample to Theorem 14 of Kang, Lee and Lim (European Journal of Combinatorics, 2026): in the rank-two annular cluster model, a single bridging-lamination coefficient row produces $1+q^2$, contradicting the asserted unimodality. We identify the unsupported initial case in their published induction. Second, we refute their log-concavity Conjecture 1: the same gap example violates log-concavity, and a further single-curve computation gives the full-support polynomial $1+2q+7q^2+10q^3+9q^4+4q^5+q^6$, which also fails log-concavity. Third, we establish the skew-shape block-statistic identity proposed in Kahane's Conjecture 4.4 (arXiv:2607.11225v1) for arbitrary finite skew Young diagrams, under an explicitly specified root-exclusion convention. Its proof combines commuting tableau-transfer matrices, a connected-block inverse kernel, and finite polynomial differential equations; the corresponding mathematical statements have Lean 4/Mathlib formalizations. Fourth, we derive a bivariate block refinement whose coefficients are nonnegative after shifting the order parameter by one and, when necessary, multiplying by a monomial in the weight parameter. We specify the correction to the printed root convention, confirmed by Kahane in correspondence, and the geometric sign and specialization conventions clarified by the relevant authors for the annular examples.

title: Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
abstract: Foundation models trained on large unlabeled corpora develop emergent capabilities, tasks that go beyond the training objective.
