Dust polarisation observations therefore provide constraints on CR scattering in clouds, connecting scattering to cloud-scale transport at energies accessible to $γ$-ray observatories.

title: Integration by parts and DLR equations for SPDEs on the whole line
abstract: We study a stochastic reaction-diffusion equation on the whole real line, driven by space-time white noise, with a possibly nonlocal diffusion operator, such as a fractional Laplacian, and a coercive potential with polynomial growth. On the whole line, unlike on bounded intervals, its invariant measures cannot be described by an explicit density with respect to a Gaussian measure. We set the equation in suitable weighted spaces and show that invariant and infinitesimally invariant measures coincide, as do reversible measures and solutions to an integration-by-parts formula. We then show that the reversible measures are exactly the Gibbs measures defined through the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle equations, without any moment condition, thanks to a priori estimates that also yield a Fernique-type theorem, uniform with respect to translations. In this way, we connect the Da Prato-Zabczyk approach to invariant measures of SPDEs with the DLR approach from statistical mechanics to Gibbs measures. Finally, we prove the existence of a reflection positive reversible measure and, in analogy with the one-dimensional long-range Ising model, we show that the reversible measure is unique, ergodic and translation invariant when the kernel of the nonlocal operator has a finite first moment, while it can be non-unique, for suitable double-well potentials, when the kernel has a power-law decay with infinite first moment.

title: You Can Have It All: Small sparse induced-universal graphs for minor-closed classes
abstract: We show that, for every fixed proper minor-closed graph class $\mathcal{G}$ and every positive integer $n$, there exists a graph $U_n$ with $n^{1+o(1)}$ vertices and edges such that every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{G}$ is isomorphic to an induced subgraph of $U_n$. This result generalizes and unifies the results of Dujmović et al. (J. ACM 2021) on induced-universal graphs and the results of Esperet, Joret, and Morin (J. London Math. Soc. 2023) on sparse induced-universal graphs from planar graphs to all proper minor-closed graph classes. It simultaneously improves the previous bounds for the number of vertices in induced-universal graphs (previously $O(n^2)$ obtained as a corollary of a result of DeVos et al. (J. Comb. Theory, Ser. {B} 2004) and a result of Gavoille and Labourel (ESA 2007)) and the number of edges in subgraph-universal graphs (previously $O(n^{3/2})$ by Babai et al. (Theory and Practice of Combinatorics 1982)).

title: A stochastic chemical system in contact with reservoirs
abstract: In this paper we analyse the behaviour of a non-reversible stochastic chemical system obtained as an approximation of a stochastic chemical system in which the concentration of some chemicals is higher than the concentration of the other chemicals. The master equation associated with this approximated system is characterised by a discrete part, modelling the reactions among chemicals that have low concentration, by a transport term and a diffusion term. The transport-diffusion terms describe the fluctuations in the concentration of abundant chemicals. The model contains a second order term is of order ε, that describes the fluctuation in the concentrations of the abundand substances. We prove that the master equation has a spectral gap that is independent on $ε$ and we analyse in detail the asymptotics of the solution to the master equation as $ε\to 0$.

title: The Monophonic Directed Convexities
abstract: Graph Convexity is a topic with many papers in the literature, especially on the $P_3$, geodesic, and monophonic convexities in undirected graphs. Regarding directed graphs, Erd{\H o}s et al. in 1972 and Chartrand and Zhang in 2000 obtained the first results on the $P_3$ and geodesic convexities for directed graphs, respectively. In this paper, we start the investigation of monophonic convexity on directed graphs. We define two convexities, the monophonic and the strong monophonic directed convexities, related to the minimal and the induced directed paths, respectively. We show that deciding whether a set is convex is polynomial-time solvable in the monophonic convexity, but coNP-complete in the strong monophonic convexity. For both convexities, we prove that the hull number is NP-complete even in DAGs. Regarding the monophonic convexity, we prove that the hull number is polynomial time solvable in tournaments, but the interval number is NP-complete in tournaments and also in bipartite oriented graphs.

title: Affine Springer fibers, Cherednik algebra modules and Hilbert schemes: torus link case
abstract: For a pair of positive integers $M,N$ with GCD $d$, we relate the bigraded $S_N\times S_d$-Frobenius characters of the homology of the positive part of a homogeneous affine Springer fiber for $\mathrm{GL}_N$ of slope $M/N$ to a direct sum of the associated graded of minimal supported modules of type $A_{N-1}$ rational Cherednik algebra at the same slope, and to the equivariant K-theory of a coherent sheaf on the Hilbert scheme of points on the plane. For the first object, we use the Hessenberg paving of Goresky-Kottwitz-Macpherson; for the second and third objects, we resort to an explicit Hodge module on $\mathfrak{sl}_N$. The bridge between them is a non-coprime shuffle theorem of Kim-Oh.

title: Benchmarking large language models for parameter-level structural identifiability classification in epidemic ODE models
abstract: Structural identifiability determines whether unknown parameters can be uniquely recovered from ideal model outputs, making it a prerequisite for interpreting parameter estimates. We evaluated whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably provide preliminary structural identifiability classifications for epidemic models. We constructed a retrospective benchmark of 88 scenarios from 14 of the 27 studies considered, encompassing 696 parameter-level formal reference classifications from published results or Julia-based symbolic analysis. Scenarios were evaluated using Domain-Aware and canonically relabeled ("Domain-Anonymized") prompts, with ten runs per configuration and prompt condition. Six configurations completed all scheduled responses, yielding 83,520 parameter-level decisions for the primary comparison. GPT-5.5 Instant and GPT-5.5 Thinking Medium had the highest accuracies among complete configurations (88.71% and 88.07%). Canonical relabeling improved both configurations and attenuated their performance decline in scenarios with many unknown parameters or state variables, although effects differed across model families. Locally identifiable parameters were the most difficult class (highest strict recall among complete configurations: 42.00%), although the local reference set was small. In multivariable analysis, each additional unknown parameter reduced the odds of correct classification (OR 0.881; 95% CI 0.852-0.910), whereas additional observed outputs increased them (OR 1.666; 95% CI 1.503-1.846). Exploratory evaluations indicated strong performance for GPT-5.5 Thinking High and Claude Opus 5, despite incomplete coverage. LLMs may generate preliminary hypotheses or flag cases for formal review, provided outputs are checked against published results or formal symbolic methods. They should not be used to certify the structural identifiability of a complete model.

title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
abstract: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.

title: A counterexample to the strong version of the union of uniform closed balls conjecture in dimensions three and higher
abstract: Fifteen years after its formulation and following its recent proof in the plane, we show that the strong version of the union of uniform closed balls conjecture fails in every dimension $n\geq 3$. For every $n\geq 3$, $r>0$, and $\varepsilon>0$, we construct a compact set $S\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying the interior $r$-sphere condition and containing a point that belongs to no closed ball of radius $(1/2+\varepsilon)r$ contained in $S$. Consequently, the known universal radius $r/2$ is optimal in every dimension $n\geq 3$, even for compact sets, whereas the optimal radius in the plane is $r/\sqrt{3}$. The construction uses simplices with coincident circumcenter and incenter and yields an exact formula for the largest radius of a contained ball covering the center; the regular simplex recovers the original example motivating the conjecture.

title: Coxeter cubes on the graph associahedron and separable elements
abstract: A Coxeter cube is a Boolean lattice inside a finite Coxeter group $W$ such that every square is a Coxeter square in the sense of Dyer and Wang. A Coxeter cube of full dimension based at the identity, which we call a based cube, is the same as a partition of the positive roots into inversion sets with one simple root in each block. These partitions were studied by Dimitrov, Gigliotti, Ossip, Paquette and Wehlau under the name of fine decompositions, and by Hohlweg and Pons as partitions of $w_0$. We show that the based cubes of $W$ form a point configuration in the graph associahedron $K(Γ)$ of the Coxeter diagram $Γ$ of $W$. The vertices of $K(Γ)$ are the based cubes whose blocks are parabolic. Every other based cube lies in the interior of an edge or of a cubical face, and we count the based cubes on each edge using the Coxeter arrangement. We also characterize the elements of $W$ that occur as vertices of based cubes. For the cubes at the vertices of $K(Γ)$ these are exactly the separable elements of Gaetz and Gao, and for arbitrary based cubes they satisfy a similar condition.

title: The elliptic Hall algebra and the combinatorics of affine Springer fibers
abstract: For coprime positive integers $m,n$ and $k\ge1$, we study the symmetric functions $e_k[-X^{m,n}Y]\cdot1$ arising from the elliptic Hall algebra action. We identify their $ω_X$-transforms with the normalized bigraded Frobenius characteristics computed by Boixeda Alvarez--Hameister--Ma for the torus-equivariant Borel--Moore homology of the positive parts of homogeneous affine Springer fibers. We introduce cyclic LLT polynomials and determine their monomial expansions, yielding explicit monomial formulas for these elliptic Hall algebra expressions in terms of cyclic parking functions. These results extend the affine Springer fiber identity and monomial formula of Carlsson--Mellit from integral slopes to arbitrary positive rational slopes.

title: An Empirical Study on CVE-based Vulnerabilities Propagation from one System to another System (IntraProject vs InterProject)
abstract: Vulnerabilities in applications, including browsers, media players, online services and document readers, etc. are often exploited and cause a serious damage. The vulnerabilities could exist in your system maybe because of some coding errors, design oversights, outdated software, AI generated codes or maybe transferred from another system during development (e.g., code clones). The propagation of software vulnerabilities is a critical concern in cybersecurity. This study examines the root cause problem of vulnerabilities propagation with experiments. We analyzed the propagation of CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) based vulnerabilities within and between different software projects (IntraProject vs. InterProject). We performed several experiments on CVE based vulnerability dataset (retrieved from NVD source) by using our vulnerability detection tool (SQVDT). In the results, we discovered similar patterns of vulnerable code in several very famous recently used software, including latest version of Linux, Android operating systems, and in thousands of open source projects available on GitHub. We found several very high severity level (CVSS) vulnerabilities that propagated from one system to another system, just because of copy/paste (reuse) the code. Furthermore, we performed an empirical evaluation and verification of these vulnerable patterns that propagated to other systems by also considering the frequency of their propagation. Finlay, we recommended the impact of these vulnerabilities propagation on the interconnected systems.

title: Zero-sum Ramsey numbers of forests and complete bipartite graphs
abstract: For a graph $G$ and an integer $m\ge2$ dividing $e(G)$, where $e(G)$ denotes the number of edges of $G$, the zero-sum Ramsey number $R(G,\mathbb Z_m)$ is the least $N$ such that every $\mathbb Z_m$-labeling of $E(K_N)$ contains a copy of $G$ whose edge labels sum to zero. Bialostocki and Dierker (1990) [4] conjectured that $R(F,\mathbb Z_{e(F)})/R(F,2)\to1$ uniformly over all forests $F$ as $e(F)\to\infty$, where $R(F,2)$ is the two-color Ramsey number, and Caro (1991) [9] conjectured that $R(tG,\mathbb Z_t)=t(|V(G)|+d)-d$ for $t\ge2$ disjoint copies of $G$, where $d=\operatorname{def}_t(G)$ is the defect. We disprove the first conjecture by an infinite family of trees. Building on the work of Caro and on his joint work with Provstgaard, we obtain infinitely many counterexamples to the second conjecture, and we determine the zero-sum Ramsey numbers of a class of graphs: for powers of two $q\ge2$ we characterize all $s,k\ge1$ satisfying $R(K_{s,kq},\mathbb Z_q)=s+kq$, and we prove $R(mK_{q,q},\mathbb Z_m)=2qm+m/\gcd(m,q)-1$ for every $m\ge2$.

title: Geometric regulation of stress-limited growth on surfaces
abstract: We analyze a model for microbial communities growing on surfaces in which individual growth is inhibited by collective growth-induced pressure. Asymptotic and numerical solutions on the sphere and homogenization of periodic surfaces show surface geometry can be tuned to either slow or accelerate growth. We use these insights to identify classes of surfaces for which the growth rate can be made arbitrarily small or arbitrarily close to the stress-free growth rate. These results show stress-sensing is coupled to surface curvature and topography at scales much larger than the individual, and provide design principles for controlling the growth of stress-sensitive microbial communities.

title: Uneven Self-Reported AI Use: An Embedded Case Study Across Eleven Teams in a Software Organization
abstract: This paper presents a descriptive, embedded single-case study examining self-reported AI use within a software organization. The study draws on 98 structured interview records collected across 11 teams, using ten standardized team-level instruments (n = 65) and one instrument with distinct response anchors (n = 33). Among respondents assessed using standardized instruments, 36 of 65 (55.4%) reported AI-use frequency scores of 4 or 5 on a five-point scale. Team-level proportions varied from 20.0% (1/5) to 71.4% (5/7). A record-level cross-tabulation revealed limited awareness or understanding of organizational AI policies across both frequency groups: 86.1% (31/36) of respondents scoring 4-5 and 96.6% (28/29) of those scoring 0-3 reported either no policy awareness or uncertainty about policy details. In the group assessed using the distinct instrument, 31 of 33 respondents (93.9%) scored 4 or 5. Although the pooled proportion reached 68.4% (67/98), differences in response anchors limit direct comparability, making the standardized-instrument results the primary analytical reference. Interviewer-recorded observations provide qualitative context on reported practices and constraints but do not support estimates of their prevalence or causal explanations for differences in AI-use frequency. The findings characterize AI-use patterns and policy awareness within the interviewed sample, without supporting inferences about organization-wide adoption, policy compliance, or the effectiveness of AI use. The study contributes an empirically grounded organizational case and an explicit account of the methodological boundaries of cross-team comparisons using heterogeneous interview instruments.

title: Where are the shortest-path nodes in spatial networks?
abstract: To predict the spatial distribution of shortest-path nodes, we propose a Gaussian estimate of the shortest-path node probability $π_{uv}(w)$, the probability that a node $w$ lies on a shortest path between a source $u$ and a destination $v$. According to the Gaussian estimate, three variables affect the shortest-path node probability $π_{uv}(w)$ and combine into one variable, the standardized detour $X_{uvw}$. In our simulations of hard and soft random geometric graphs in Euclidean, hyperbolic and spherical space, the standardized detour $X_{uvw}$ alone approximately determines how fast the shortest-path node probability $π_{uv}(w)$ decreases as the node $w$ moves away from the geodesic between the source $u$ and the destination $v$. We find and explain that, when the hopcount variance $σ^2(H_{uv})$ is very small, the shortest-path nodes have a discrete spatial distribution, a quantized distribution of shortest-path nodes. We further extend the study to spatially inhomogeneous networks, for which we propose a method to find the shortest-path nodes.

title: Response of Circular Binaries to Monochromatic Gravitational Waves
abstract: The exchange in specific orbital energy between a test particle in a Keplerian binary orbit and a continuously incident linearized gravitational wave (GW) is considered. Analytical expressions for the rate of change of energy, semi-major axis and mean motion of the test particle are derived. Numerical solutions illustrate a resonance effect betwen the GWs frequency and the particle's initial orbital frequency. We distinguish between bounded short-period oscillations and resonant libration. The effect of the GWs angle of incidence with the particle's orbital plane is also considered. Using an illustrative high GW strain we show that changes to the eccentricity are bounded while inclination exhibits small linear growth for an initially flat, circular orbit. Long coherence requirements linit the observational significance of GW resonance to astrophysical systems with very short orbital periods.

title: Limits of Cell Sensing in Observer-Absorber Assemblies
abstract: Absorption improves concentration sensing for an isolated cell by suppressing rebinding correlations. We study how that local advantage competes with collective depletion in assemblies of cells coupled through the shared diffusion field. We introduce an observer--absorber model for permeant ligands sensed and consumed intracellularly with finite volumetric uptake rate $κ$ that continuously interpolates between Berg--Purcell monitoring and perfect absorption. For a single spherical cell, monitoring correlations, uptake statistics and optimal joint estimator are obtained analytically, and we characterize the transition between using observer and absorber information for sensing. In this case, all sensing strategies improve monotonically with $κ$. For arbitrary cell assemblies, we show that the long-time sensing problem can be reduced to solving for just two steady-state quantities for each cell: the mean internal concentration $\Cbar$ and its local sensitivity $\Tbar=-\partial_κ\log\Cbar$. In multicellular systems, uptake shortens rebinding memory, but it also depletes the signal available to neighbors. We reveal geometry-dependent optima for absorption rates, with Pareto fronts arising from competing objectives, as well as pure observing, pure absorbing, and partially absorbing regimes.

title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
abstract: Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

title: Energetic costs of reaching the physical limits of sensing
abstract: Cells sense chemical gradients by absorbing ligand molecules, a nonequilibrium process that necessarily produces entropy. But how many molecules must a cell absorb, and therefore energy dissipate, to approach the physical limits of sensing? We derive closed-form expressions relating gradient sensing uncertainty to the number of absorbed molecules, which we link to entropy production. Unlike concentration sensing, which depends only on the total count, gradient sensing must resolve the angular asymmetry of the absorbed flux, adding a bounded dipole-contrast factor set by how strongly the cell absorbs. In the strong-signal regime, cells approach peak chemotactic alignment while absorbing a small fraction of the diffusion-limited uptake, with the required number of uptake events set by the relative concentration change across the cell. Re-analysis of Dictyostelium chemotaxis places the cell at 0.25% of that limit with a minor metabolic load, suggesting that sensing is limited by counting noise rather than by energetic cost.

title: GARD: Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense against Backdoors in Multimodal Contrastive Learning Models
abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning models such as CLIP are vulnerable to backdoor attacks with diverse trigger structures, ranging from localized patches to globally distributed perturbations, with recent attacks increasingly optimizing these triggers in the representation space. Existing post-hoc defenses based on clean fine-tuning may leave backdoors active, while trigger-inversion methods depend on accurately estimating the attack target and trigger. We observe that backdoored encoders exhibit structure-dependent representation sensitivity: global perturbations preferentially expose distributed backdoors, whereas local patch perturbations are more effective for localized backdoors. Based on this observation, we propose Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense (GARD), a target- and trigger-agnostic post-hoc defense. GARD optimizes complementary global and local adversarial probes to maximally displace clean-image representations, and then realigns the perturbed representations with detached clean anchors while preserving image-text alignment. The resulting model requires no additional computation at inference time. Across six visual backdoor attacks and two CLIP visual backbones, GARD reduces the attack success rate below 1% in all 12 evaluated attack-backbone combinations while maintaining competitive clean accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of adversarial representation probing for repairing backdoored multimodal contrastive encoders.

title: Davenport Constants of High-Dimensional Integer Sets
abstract: The Davenport constant of a finite set of integer vectors is the maximum length of an irreducible zero-sum sequence over that set. For nonempty sets closed under negation, it equals the largest $\ell_1$-norm of a Graver basis element of the matrix formed by those vectors. We study extremal and average-case versions in growing dimension, with applications to integer programming. For integer cubes $[-R,R]^d \cap \mathbb{Z}^d$ and the sign cube $\{-1,1\}^d$, totally unimodular encodings improve on the upper bounds from direct circuit decomposition, while random perturbations of Hadamard matrices give new lower bounds. A key ingredient is a uniform affine Bernoulli variant of Nguyen and Wood's surjectivity theorem. In every sufficiently large dimension the sign-cube lower bound is $d^{d/2}2^{-d-o(d)}$, and the integer-cube lower bound is $R^d d^{d/2}2^{-o(d)}$ uniformly for polynomially bounded integer radii. For random sign-cube sequences of even length conditioned on summing to zero, we prove a sharp threshold from irreducibility to reducibility at $d\log d/\log 4$, far below the extremal scale. For fixed $p$ and $R$, we determine exact exponential rates for lattice $\ell_p$-balls when $p=1$, $R\geq3$, or $2\leq p<\infty$, $\lfloor R^p\rfloor\geq3$. For each fixed integer $k\geq3$, we determine the exponential rate of the worst-case $\ell_1$-distance from an optimal LP vertex to the nearest integer optimum in standard-form programs with ternary matrices having at most $k$ nonzero entries per column.

title: Integrability of the horizontal mean curvature near characteristic points in the Heisenberg group
abstract: We investigate the local integrability of the horizontal mean curvature near characteristic points of surfaces in the first Heisenberg group. We prove that, for every embedded surface of class $C^{2,α}$, with $α>0$, the horizontal mean curvature is locally integrable with respect to (any) Riemannian surface measure, without any assumption on the structure of the characteristic set. We further establish that the horizontal unit normal belongs to $BV_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and characterize its $W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity in terms of the vanishing one-dimensional Hausdorff measure of the characteristic set. Finally, we answer an open question by Danielli, Garofalo and Nhieu by constructing a $C^2$ surface with a unique characteristic point whose horizontal mean curvature fails to be locally integrable, thus showing that the additional Hölder regularity cannot, in general, be replaced by $C^2$ regularity.

title: Mesoscopic derivation of predator-prey dynamics via diffusive fast-reaction asymptotics: cross-diffusion and fear effects
abstract: We propose a kinetic derivation of a spatial predator-prey model with cross-diffusion interactions and a Beddington-DeAngelis functional response. At the mesoscopic level, we divide the two populations into distinct behavioral states: prey can be active or hidden in a refuge, while predators can be either searching or handling. The microscopic state of each subpopulation is described in terms of group size and a continuous directional velocity variable, with state transitions governed by suitable Boltzmann-type interaction operators. By combining a diffusive scaling with a slow-fast formulation of the kinetic reaction operators, we formally derive a macroscopic reaction-cross-diffusion system for the total population densities of prey and predators. The limiting model consistently recovers the Beddington-DeAngelis functional response along with its associated nonlinear diffusion terms. Crucially, the kinetic upscaling yields a predator-dependent prey growth term taking a logistic form with an effective carrying capacity. This carrying capacity depends non-monotonically on predator density because prey redistribute between active and refuge states. Since density-dependent competition acts separately within these behavioral states, intermediate predator levels reduce aggregate crowding and thereby increase the effective carrying capacity of the total prey population. Overall, our derivation provides a mechanistic link connecting predator-induced behavioral shifts, refuge use, and macroscopic cross-diffusion.

title: Euclidean Ramsey Theory for Lines and Finite Configurations
abstract: A classical question in Euclidean Ramsey theory, posed by Erdős, Graham, Montgomery, Rothschild, Spencer, and Straus, asks which finite configurations $X\subset\mathbb E^2$ must appear in blue under every red--blue coloring of the plane having no red pair of points distance one apart. For $m \ge 2$, let $\ell_m$ denote the line of $m$ points with consecutive points distance one apart. Tsaturian showed that $\ell_5$ is unavoidable; we improve this to $\ell_7$. Additionally, we show that in every three-coloring of the plane in which two colors contain no $\ell_2$, the third color must contain an $\ell_3$. To conclude our discussion on lines, we prove several related results on two-colorings of higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces where both colors avoid longer lines. Our methods also extend to other point configurations. In any two-coloring of the plane in which one color contains no $\ell_2$, we show that the other color must contain both a regular pentagon of side length one and a unit square together with its center. We also prove that every two-coloring of three-dimensional space contains either a monochromatic unit square or a monochromatic noncoplanar tetrahedron with four edges of length one and two of length $\sqrt{2}$. Our proofs combine Székely's averaging inequalities for distance-avoiding sets with the Fourier-analytic and linear-programming methods of de Oliveira Filho and Vallentin, together with a theorem on rotation-invariant measures from OpenAI's recent work on the Hadwiger-Nelson problem.

title: Cohesive granular piles with controlled volume fraction
abstract: Experimental procedures involving wet granular media expose the sample to variation of its organization across different measurements, leading to non reproducible results. Rigorous control over the preparation process and a thorough understanding of the microstructure of the granular heap are key parameters to manage results dispersion from one experiment to an other. In this study, we present a protocol to prepare large samples of wet grains in a cylindrical container. Quantitative results are presented showing the effectiveness of the protocol regarding : the accessibility of different granular materials with different volume fraction $φ_0$ and the reproducibility of this said density obtained experimentally in the same experimental conditions. In addition, X-ray scans were performed using a micro-CT scanner to dive into the microstructure of the carefully prepared piles. Results show a small variation between the bulk density $φ_0$ and the local one $φ$, underlining the homogeneity in the samples. On top of that, several scans made in the same medium at different heights confirm the homogeneity across a given sample.

title: Mechanical pairing and self-assembled chains of non-convex granular rotors
abstract: We experimentally and numerically demonstrate the self-assembly of granular rotors into chain-like structures. The rotors are non-convex rigid bodies with rotational activity. We first investigate the interaction between two rotors and we establish an attractive interaction controlled by the ratio of the rotational activity to the noise and also dependent of the rotors geometry. We then show that the cohesive state between spinner pairs leads to robust chains that can be either initially set or spontaneously obtained by self-assembly.

title: Memory of Initial States in Long-Time Dynamics Revealed by Non-Gaussianity
abstract: In quantum dynamics of few-body observables in quadratic systems, information about the initial state is retained in long-time averages, as captured by the generalized Gibbs ensemble. Here, we show that this memory extends beyond the averages to temporal fluctuations around them. By generating a manifold of non-Gaussian initial states and quantifying their non-Gaussianity via the corresponding entropy, we find that the magnitude of temporal fluctuations is a smooth function of the initial-state non-Gaussianity. This relation explains the qualitatively different scaling of fluctuations observed after quantum quenches: exponentially small fluctuations for non-Gaussian initial states and polynomially small fluctuations for Gaussian initial states. Therefore, our results identify non-Gaussianity as a key to uncovering initial-state memory beyond long-time averages.

title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid
abstract: Recent work identified spatially localised midplane stress structures as the building blocks of chaotic behaviour in pressure-driven parallel shear flows of viscoelastic fluids. Such coherent structures are thought to originate from a linear centre-mode instability of the laminar state. In the absence of inertia, however, the Oldroyd-B and FENE-P constitutive models predict that this instability is confined to ultra-dilute polymer solutions and very large Weissenberg numbers in channel flow, while no purely elastic instability has been reported in pipe flow. Here, we study numerically the linear stability of channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) fluid and find a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both geometries across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers. Since the sPTT and FENE-P models have identical steady rheology and laminar profiles, their contrasting predictions indicate that the existence of the centre-mode instability is governed by the transient rheological response of the fluid. Our results suggest that the purely elastic centre-mode instability should be observable under realistic flow conditions. They also offer a means of discriminating between constitutive models.

title: CUVE: Making Supervised Classification more Accessible through Visualization
abstract: We present CUVE, an interface that enables people to build classifiers by generating visualizations that are interpretable by both humans and learning algorithms (the Visualization as Intermediate Representation approach). This UI enables users to create supervised classifiers and to visually investigate how to improve them and how they carry out their function. A preliminary study investigates the usability of our prototype and compares it with a traditional text-based programming interface.

title: BODYinTRANSIT-Lab: A Multimodal Dataset for Investigating Sensory-Driven Transformations in Body Perception and Affective Experiences
abstract: Multimodal datasets that combine synchronised behavioural and physiological signals with subjective affective and body perception measures are still rare. This limits both the understanding of embodied experience and the development of computational models that infer subjective states from sensor data. We introduce BODYinTRANSIT-Lab, a multimodal dataset that addresses this gap by capturing affective, perceptual, and behavioural responses to the Footsteps Illusion. In this closed-loop paradigm, participants perform walking tasks while receiving real-time manipulated auditory feedback of their own footsteps intended to alter perceived body weight. The dataset comprises synchronised recordings from 101 participants recruited through systematic stratification by eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level. BODYinTRANSIT-Lab combines full-body kinematics with electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, and electrodermal activity. Its annotations capture both immediate and post-trial experience, including within-trial perceived-weight ratings, post-trial assessments of body feelings and affective experience, 3D avatar body visualisations, and quantitative body maps. Psychological, behavioural, demographic, and social measures provide further information about factors that may influence individual responses. We provide a deep learning benchmark that uses walking kinematics to classify relative affective valence and perceived weight within subjects. On within-session, segment-level splits, the baseline model achieved mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight. The BODYinTRANSIT-Lab dataset provides an experimentally controlled resource for cognitive neuroscience and affective computing research, with potential applications in affect-aware interactive systems, health and well-being technologies, and creative embodied experiences.

title: And yet it moves - or does it? Spurious drifts at equilibrium
abstract: When diffusion depends on the state of a system, the drift measured from its trajectories contains a spurious part unrelated to forces. At equilibrium, particles can then appear to sediment, repel each other, even rotate - the same way whether the movie is played forward or backward. Drifts are conditional averages, not currents: they carry meaning only together with a consistently inferred diffusion tensor. Paired with the wrong one, they make passive particles look active. I show how to infer spurious drifts from trajectory moments alone, enabling thermodynamically consistent inference.

title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
abstract: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable

title: From Bias to Positionality: A critical grammar for Large Language Models
abstract: Bias has become a default lens for understanding what machine learning systems do and how we should relate to them. Bias is at root a deviation from a standard; in decision making systems we can supply a standard from outside: a law, a protected attribute, a benchmark, a statistical property. However, even there, biased is often used as a shorthand, without stating what the position taken is - a silent ``relative to''. In a general use of language models, nothing supplies the standard: there is no decision to audit and no counterfactual output, so the shorthand fails. We argue that positionality -- the located, articulated, owned and contestable position from which anything is said -- is the better grammar for the question these models now force: who is speaking, from where? Against the vendors' answer of nowhere and the seductive possibility of everywhere, we argue that when a model is taken as-if speaking, it speaks from somewhere, and this means positionality can describe models, and the way they are believed beyond their warrant, even though they are not accountable speakers. A model's positionality is laminar -- laid down across corpus, tuning, system prompt, application and the live conversation. We separate three sets of factors: the positionality of a model's creators, the behaviour they intend for it, and the behaviour it enacts, and situate current work within this matrix. This lets us highlight what each stratum inherits from the one below, with ruptures and collapses where that inheritance is disavowed. We then return to where models speak from, and discuss the implications for how models are made, read and held accountable.

title: Treewidth versus Hadwiger number: Graph classes with dominated balanced separators are quasi-linearly treewidth-Hadwiger bounded
abstract: In a hereditary graph class $\mathcal{G}$, the treewidth of a graph in $\mathcal{G}$ is bounded by a function of the size of a largest clique minor of the graph if and only if the class $\mathcal{G}$ excludes some planar graph as an induced minor. Campbell et al. (arXiv 2024) conjectured that such a bounding function can always be chosen to be linear. We verify this conjecture for several classes of graphs (including even-hole-free graphs) and show that if a hereditary graph class $\mathcal{G}$ has dominated binary-weighted balanced separators, then the bounding function can be taken to be in ${O(h \log h)}$, where $h$ is the Hadwiger number. We say that $\mathcal{G}$ has dominated binary-weighted balanced separators if, for every ${G \in \mathcal{G}}$ and every $\mathsf{w} \colon V(G) \to \{0,1\}$, there is a set ${D \subseteq V(G)}$ of bounded size so that deleting the closed neighbourhood $N_G[D]$ of $D$ leaves each component with at most a fixed fraction of the total weight of $G$. Our result reduces the quasi-linear weakening of the conjecture of Campbell et al. to a conjecture of Gartland and Lokshtanov stating that every graph class excluding a planar graph as an induced minor admits dominated binary-weighted balanced separators.

title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
abstract: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.

title: Random Laguerre tessellations in hyperbolic space
abstract: We introduce Laguerre tessellations in hyperbolic space as a weighted generalization of Voronoi tessellations and a hyperbolic analogue of Euclidean power diagrams. We present geometric and analytic constructions and establish conditions under which a collection of weighted points generates a well-defined tessellation. For Poisson point processes of weighted points, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions on the intensity measure ensuring that the resulting diagram is almost surely a tessellation. We then prove that hyperbolic Poisson-Laguerre tessellations are stable under intersections with totally geodesic subspaces, with an explicit transformation of the intensity measure. As applications, we identify the Poisson-Laguerre tessellations arising as sections of hyperbolic Poisson-Voronoi and ideal Poisson-Voronoi tessellations. In particular, the latter have unbounded cells, while their proper totally geodesic sections have bounded cells almost surely.

title: Isolation Is Not Confidentiality: Security Boundaries of Geometric Access Control in RAG
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on vector databases containing documents governed by different access-control policies. Recent search-preserving geometric approaches enforce such access control by structuring the embedding space so that transformed embeddings, which we call protected representations, remain retrievable without exposing information across policy boundaries. We provide a unified security analysis of this paradigm, covering policy isolation, representation confidentiality, query forgery resistance, and policy-membership hiding. We consider both a curious cloud service provider observing the protected representations stored in the vector database and a curious user holding aligned pairs of original embeddings and protected representations. Evaluating the available implementations of the works proposing these geometric transformation mechanisms across three encoders, we find that geometric transformations preserve retrieval utility and provide strong policy isolation, but do not provide the other security properties. A curious user can recover the original embeddings from a few hundred pairs and forge policy-compatible queries at a higher cost that grows with encoder dimension for secret per-policy transformations. Moreover, policy-dependent geometry can leak policy membership even when unauthorized retrieval is prevented. These results show that policy isolation, confidentiality, forgery resistance, and membership hiding are distinct security objectives.

title: Gorenstein dimensions for stable Auslander algebras of Nakayama algebras
abstract: Let $A$ be a Nakayama algebra and $\underline{\mathrm{Aus}}(A)$ its stable Auslander algebra. We introduce a new homological invariant, called the finitistic Gorenstein dimension, which coincides with the classical Gorenstein dimension whenever the latter is finite, and compute this invariant for $\underline{\mathrm{Aus}}(A)$ when $A$ has infinite global dimension. Combined with an accompanying criterion for the finiteness of the Gorenstein dimension of $\underline{\mathrm{Aus}}(A)$, our results provide a complete description of this dimension and verify the Gorenstein Symmetry Conjecture for this class of algebras. Furthermore, we show that the finitistic Gorenstein dimension of $ \underline{\mathrm{Aus}}(A) $ is also left-right symmetric, is explicitly related to the finitistic dimension of $A$, and can be attained among the injective dimensions of the projective $ \underline{\mathrm{Aus}}(A) $-modules corresponding to simple $A$-modules. Our proofs rely on computing injective dimensions in terms of distances in the coresolution forest of $A$, a combinatorial structure closely related to Ringel's coresolution quiver.

title: Energy Dissipation Along Trajectories and Wasserstein Gradient Flow of Aggregation-Diffusion Equations
abstract: In this work, we established the Wasserstein gradient flow structure of nonlinear Fokker-Planck equations on bounded domains involving both nonlinear diffusion and nonlocal interaction effects. Our approach is based on stochastic analysis. More precisely, we investigated the associated stochastic differential equation (SDE) with normal reflection at the boundary from a trajectorial perspective and derived a semimartingale decomposition of the corresponding energy process. This decomposition leads to a trajectorial energy dissipation identity, which, together with the characterization of the metric derivative, allows us to establish the Wasserstein gradient flow structure of the aggregation-diffusion equation.

title: Triviality of metric fibrations over locally finite metric graphs
abstract: In this note, we give a direct proof that every metric fibration over a geodesic metric space locally modeled on finite metric stars is isometrically isomorphic, over its base, to the $\ell^1$ product of its base and a fiber. Neither compactness nor completeness of the base is assumed. We also construct a nontrivial example over a closed interval with a truncated metric, showing that the local star condition alone does not imply the conclusion.

title: Sharp Proximity Bounds for Integer Programs with Few Rows
abstract: We study the proximity between an optimal vertex of a standard form linear program with constraint matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}$ and an optimal integer solution. When $m = 2$, we prove the sharp infinity-norm bound $Δ-1$, where $Δ$ is the largest absolute maximal minor of $A$. When $m = 1$, we express the difference between an optimal LP vertex and an optimal integer solution as a nonnegative combination of certain generators in the kernel of $A$ with a bounded coefficient sum. This implies sharp proximity bounds for all norms when $m=1$. Combining this representation with its known counterpart for Hilbert bases due to Sissokho, we develop techniques that transfer results from $m=1$ to $m=2$. Along the way, for $m=2$, we prove that such a representation exists for an extended Gomory group relaxation and obtain the sharp infinity-norm bound $Δ$ for Graver basis elements. We also present a new short proof of Sissokho's result and lower bounds on the proximity for all $m$ and $Δ$.

title: Thermodynamics of words
abstract: We introduce the word thermalization hypothesis according to which in a literary work there are effective interactions between words that drive them to thermalization where their word frequency distribution is the same as for the phenomenon of Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation. In this concept, the different words play a role of classical oscillators (particles) and their word frequencies, or related tokens, are analogous to certain filling factors over energy state levels. The thermalization process is characterized by the conservation of total system energy, or total number of words/tokens, and total probability norm, or total number of different words. We apply this approach to analyze 16 literary works, including Bible, complete works of Shakespeare, and data from American National Corpus. We show that for these cases the effective system energy is very low and thus there is the RJ condensation phenomenon with a big fraction of total probability concentrated at the lowest energy states corresponding to a big fraction of rare words appearing only once or twice in the whole text. Such a RJ condensation is observed for light propagation in multimode optical fibers and other physical systems. We relate the thermalization of words to the recently proposed wealth thermalization for households in world countries. The economy concepts of Lorenz and Pareto curves, and also Zipf curves, are applied to the word frequency distributions of the selected 16 cases and it is shown that the thermalization theory gives a strikingly good description of real data.

title: ScaleBrain: A Scale-Consistent Framework for EEG Foundation Models
abstract: Foundation models pre-trained on large unlabeled electroencephalography (EEG) corpora have emerged as a transformative paradigm for Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications. Recent EEG foundation models have shown that multi-scale representations derived from fixed-length patches can improve EEG representation learning. Existing frameworks commonly construct temporal scales through feature-level operations. However, these operations leave the correspondence between learned features and scale-specific characteristics of the original EEG signals implicit. Moreover, when the self-supervised objective is not aligned with the multi-scale input representations, information at some temporal scales may receive insufficient supervision during pre-training. In light of this, we propose ScaleBrain, a scale-consistent pre-training framework that explicitly coordinates multi-scale representations of EEG from both the model input and optimization objective sides. Specifically, ScaleBrain introduces multi-scale EEG tokenization to represent the same EEG segment through analysis windows with different temporal spans and shared temporal anchors, and pairs these representations with scale-specific reconstruction to align with the multi-scale input structure and provide supervision across temporal resolutions during self-supervised learning. We further develop an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism to contextualize the fused multi-scale representation along spatial and temporal dimensions. Extensive evaluations on six public BCI benchmarks against 12 representative baselines show that ScaleBrain achieves the highest mean Balanced Accuracy on five datasets and ranks third on the remaining one, with only 5.0M parameters, demonstrating strong performance and favorable parameter efficiency.

title: Where do we Jam? - The Impact of Real and Virtual XR Spaces on Musical Creativity, Co-Presence, Affect, and Flow
abstract: Extended Reality (XR) technologies can place musicians in virtual, mixed, or real environments during networked music performance (NMP). To examine how NMP applications in XR should be positioned on the reality-virtuality continuum, we conducted a laboratory study (N = 28) comparing a simulated NMP experience in Virtual Reality (VR) with one in Augmented Reality (AR). In both conditions, musicians saw their remote partners in real time as 3D point clouds rendered with an optimized Gaussian Splatting shader. While VR allowed participants to select and customize fully virtual 3D environments, AR showed a pass-through view of the laboratory environment. We measured creativity support, flow, involvement, co-presence, and affect, and complemented these data with qualitative interviews on participants' preferences and requirements for creative environments. Our results show that participants felt significantly more involved by the immersive XR experience in VR than in AR. Positive affect, flow, and creativity support were strongly correlated in both conditions, whereas involvement correlated with flow and creativity support only in VR. Qualitative findings showed substantial variation in participants' preferences for AR or VR and also regarding the design of creative virtual environments. Together, these findings suggest that the surrounding environment is a critical design dimension in networked Musical XR, shaping collaborative musical experiences beyond merely representing remote collaborators and mitigating communication latency. Future XR-mediated NMP systems should therefore treat the surrounding space as an integral component of the collaborative musical experience, rather than as a mere visual backdrop. At the same time, they should support experiences across a broad spectrum of the reality-virtuality continuum to accommodate highly individual user requirements.

title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn
abstract: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.

title: Analytic Two-Radius Model for the Zero-Shear and High-Frequency Viscosity of Colloidal Suspensions
abstract: Nearly hard-sphere colloids are stabilized by short-range repulsions that set their effective size and equilibrium microstructure. Their hydrodynamic interactions, in contrast, are set by the no-slip surface. Since these two do not necessarily coincide, there are potentially two effective radii that control their dynamics in different ways. Yet it is commonplace to model and analyze such suspensions with a single effective radius, which merges these different physics. Two-radius models, in which a hard, solvent-permeable shell surrounds a no-slip core, have been proposed to improve the description of these suspensions. Their rheology is known exactly at pair level, but at higher concentrations their zero-shear viscosity has been obtained only with semi-empirical expressions, which do not recover the exact pair result. Here, we close this gap with a theory for the zero-shear and high-frequency viscosity of these two-radius models. By keeping pairs out of near contact, the shell lowers the high-frequency viscosity, as our Stokesian dynamics simulations confirm, and shifts the zero-shear viscosity from hydrodynamic toward thermodynamic stress. We apply our theory to experiments on charge- and sterically stabilized colloids from the literature and find that it accurately describes the measured viscosities. We discuss the benefits of fitting data to a two-radius model compared to a single-radius one. To facilitate this fitting in future work, closed-form expressions are provided that cover the full range of shell thicknesses and volume fractions.

title: On $q$-Ary $t$-Designs from Codewords of Every Nonzero Weight in Linear Codes and Their Duals
abstract: The paper investigates when the codewords of every nonzero weight in a linear code form a $q$-ary $t$-design and how to generalize the property to its dual code. We reduce the verification of this property to a prescribed range of low weights. Specifically, for MDS codes, we show that the $q$-ary $2$-design property at every nonzero weight is equivalent to that at any fixed nonzero weight. As an application, we prove that the codewords of every nonzero weight in a $[q+1,3,q-1]_q$ MDS code and its dual hold $q$-ary $2$-designs if and only if $q$ is even. We also establish a duality principle. When $t\le\min\{d,d^{\perp}\}$, the codewords of every nonzero weight in a linear code form a $q$-ary $t$-design if and only if the same property holds for its dual code. We then investigate narrow-sense antiprimitive BCH codes $\mathcal{C}_{(q,q+1,δ,1)}$ and their duals. For $q=2^m$ and $δ=2^r$ with $1\le r<m$ and $\gcd(r,m)=1$, the codewords of every nonzero weight in these codes form $q$-ary $2$-designs. Furthermore, for $δ=4$ and $q=2^{m}$ ($m\ge4$), we establish that the minimum-weight codewords of $\mathcal{C}_{(q,q+1,4,1)}$ form a $q$-ary $2$-design if and only if $m$ is odd.

title: Gradient Inversion through Linear and Affine Subspace Constraints
abstract: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine-learning model without directly sharing their local datasets. However, as prior works have shown, the gradients exchanged during training may reveal sensitive information about client data. Most existing attacks usually optimize dummy inputs to match the true client gradients (Gradient Inversion Attacks), while some attempt to reconstruct them based on the observation that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer are a linear combination of its inputs. In this work, we extend this observation by showing that aggregate gradients from an FC layer with the correct scaling are actually an affine combination of its inputs. We evaluate a gradient inversion attack that leverages either known linear-subspace information or its affine-subspace counterpart at each FC layer to improve reconstruction accuracy. Our results show that subspace-based methods can substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings. We further demonstrate that moderate overestimation of the batch size can generally improve or preserve reconstruction quality, even when the true batch size is unknown. We additionally examine reconstruction under gradient perturbations introduced by a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, providing insight into the effectiveness of the considered formulations under noisy conditions.

title: Rheology of Parametric Odd Materials
abstract: The design and control of rheological properties in active systems are crucial for developing functional materials with novel properties. While significant attention has been devoted to odd viscosity and odd elasticity, comprehensive odd rheological models remain scarce. Here, we introduce and characterise a platform-agnostic odd viscoelastic material, where complex responses arise from parametric control of internal rotational degrees of freedom and are triggered by coupling between normal and shear stresses. Such control can be achieved through either parametric driving or a parametric nonlinear feedback. We further show that this coupling can induce rotation-driven fluidisation, transitioning the material from an elasticity-dominated to a viscosity-dominated regime. Lastly, we show that the interplay between odd and even sectors enhances the nonlinear material response under large-amplitude oscillatory shear (LAOS). The findings outline a route to Floquet-engineered metafluids with programmable, non-reciprocal rheology.

title: Comparing WeChat and Telegram MiniApp Security Architectures: Toward Cross-Platform Analysis
abstract: MiniApps are increasingly central to super-app ecosystems, yet architectural differences complicate the transfer of security analysis techniques across platforms. Existing WeChat analyzers rely on packaged applications and platform-specific APIs, limiting their direct applicability to Telegram's web-based MiniApps. We present a qualitative comparison of WeChat Mini Programs and Telegram MiniApps, grounded in official documentation, prior research, and manual analysis of a specific Telegram Android source revision. Using a shared taxonomy of security controls, assets, and threat sources, we examine execution environments, communication paths, and trust boundaries. WeChat provides a dedicated MiniApp runtime; Telegram combines web execution with host controls. Both retain developer responsibilities for backend authentication and resource authorization. Two worked examples derive requirements for cross-platform analysis: distinguishing credential roles and validation boundaries, and associating host capabilities with concrete execution contexts and permission handlers. These findings inform future automated analysis without ranking the ecosystems by security or claiming validated vulnerability detection.

title: On the minimum number of entries in a set of maximal mutually orthogonal partial Latin squares
abstract: In superimposed form, a set of $k\ge2$ mutually orthogonal partial Latin squares of order $n$ is said to be maximal if no additional $k$-tuple may be inserted into any empty cell without violating orthogonality or the Latin property. For $k=2$ and $n\ge 21$ it is shown that the minimum number of filled cells in such a square is $\lceil n^2/3 \rceil$. Likewise for $k=3$ and $n\ge 44$ the minimum number of filled cells is $\lceil n^2/4 \rceil$ or $\lceil n^2/4 \rceil+1$, depending on the residue of $n$ modulo 4. In each case it is shown that the extremal systems are essentially those produced by a construction presented in the paper. A similar result is obtained for all $k\ge4$ for minimal systems that have a certain balance property, and it is conjectured that for sufficiently large $n$, even without this balance property, the extremal systems always correspond to those produced by this construction.

title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. It combines (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, (2) a 2D product taint lattice $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trust}} \times \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sens}}$ and a workspace provenance ledger that prevents secret laundering across disk, (3) deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and (4) bytecode certificates, split-horizon audit logs, self-healing security test synthesis, and an adaptive UserWikiManager. Across $N=252$ fixtures ($120$ attack, $120$ benign, $12$ kill chains), a live local LLM judge (qwen3:4b) refuses $98.3\%$ of benign work at $142.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ latency, whereas Ring 0 achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ in $12.7\,μ\mathrm{s}$ ($11{,}200\times$ faster). In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy misses $4/12$ kill chains ($\mathrm{ABR}=0.667$) and coarse Boolean taint blocks $83.3\%$ of benign workflows, while our 2D product lattice achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ at $\approx 20\,μ\mathrm{s}$ per step.

title: Triangle Factors in the Semi-Random Graph Process
abstract: The semi-random graph process is a single player game which starts with an empty graph on $n$ vertices and in each round the player is offered a random vertex and connects it to a vertex selected according to some strategy $\mathcal{S}$. The goal is, in as few rounds as possible, to arrive at a graph that satisfies some graph property $\mathcal{P}$. The main contribution of this work is to show that there is a strategy $\mathcal{S}$ which creates a $K_3$-factor in at most $2.929329 \, n$ rounds w.h.p.

title: Rank Reversals in Efficient Vectors for Pairwise Comparisons
abstract: Studied are the orders among alternatives given by efficient vectors for a reciprocal matrix A. The focus is upon: 1) existence of efficient vectors with a given order and 2) discrepancies between the ranking for a pair of alternatives resulting from an efficient vector and from the corresponding entry of A, called rank reversals. We use matrix intervals in which the consistent matrices built from efficient vectors lie. The existence of efficient vectors (or those from constituent convex subsets) with a rank reversal at a given position is characterized. The minimum number of rank reversals for a reciprocal matrix among all weight vectors is described and it is shown that there is an efficient vector that has this number of rank reversals. A way to construct such a vector is given. The order transitive and the uniformly ordered reciprocal matrices are shown to be, respectively, the matrices for which there is an efficient vector with no rank reversals and the matrices for which all efficient vectors have no rank reversals. The effects on rank reversals of addition and deletion of alternatives are also discussed. Using numerical experiments, the frequencies of rank reversals in certain formulaic weight vectors are given.

title: AVCC: Audio-Visual Conversation Corpus for Turn-Taking Prediction with a Human Benchmark
abstract: } Predicting who will speak next, and when, is a prerequisite for conversational agents and social robots that take turns without waiting for silence. Multiparty next-speaker prediction (NSP) has been studied on corpora with per-speaker sensors, each with its own event definitions. No public benchmark covers the single camera and microphone a robot has, and no model has been compared against how well people perform the same prediction. We turn AVCC, a 31-hour audio-visual corpus of two- and three-speaker online conversation recorded with a single static camera and microphone, into a public NSP benchmark. We add a speaker-disjoint seven-video test partition with 865 hold and 865 shift events at mutual-silence gaps, word-level forced-aligned transcripts for the whole corpus, and a human reference benchmark collected at the same events. We score an audio-only Role-Relative VAP model (RoleVAP) and the multimodal MuVAP model. Labels, transcripts, per-response human data, and the scripts that reproduce every number are released.

title: Data-driven regional traffic simulation from heterogeneous mobility sources
abstract: Regional traffic simulators increasingly combine mobile-phone, road-sensor and GPS data, but what each source contributes is rarely clear. We present an agent-based simulator of daily traffic in Emilia-Romagna, Italy: phone data give trips and their timing, half of the road sensors set the traffic level, all sensors correct it locally, and GPS traces guide route choice. We measure what each source adds against predictors without simulation, on sensors kept out of parameter calibration in winter 2020 and partly shared with it in summer 2021; as these sensors informed some modelling choices, the evaluation is not fully independent. Total traffic is within 1% of observations in winter and 10% in summer, and the simulator ranks roads better than a road-type predictor (Spearman 0.67-0.68 against 0.41-0.48, winter). GPS improves this ranking, sensors improve local estimates, and timing comes mostly from the demand. Single-road errors remain similar to those of simple predictors, and the test of specific origin-destination pairings was underpowered and inconclusive. These findings provide a practical framework for assessing the contribution and limitations of heterogeneous data sources in regional traffic simulation.

title: Data4Cyber: Labeled Cyber-Physical Datasets for Distribution-Grid Management Systems Under Representative OT Attacks
abstract: Cyberattacks against power systems increasingly exploit industrial communication and control dependencies arising from distributed energy resources (DER), remote management, and market-based incentives. Progress on intrusion detection is constrained by a lack of public datasets that align operational technology (OT) network telemetry with physical measurements and control context. Data4Cyber is a labeled cyber-physical dataset recorded in a laboratory distribution management system (DMS) for self-consumption optimization with photovoltaic generation, battery storage, controllable loads, and substation metering. It captures synchronized process measurements, controller context, price incentives, and packet captures (Modbus/TCP and MQTT) across one benign baseline and six attack scenarios spanning protocol-semantic Modbus manipulation, man-in-the-middle (MitM) false-data injection, and MQTT price manipulation. Its fixed 1 s time base, phase-resolved labels, and state-oriented representation support temporally blocked stateful-detector evaluation. Baseline results show that high recall alone is insufficient: several detectors achieve sensitivity through alarm saturation. Context-driven attacks require process-aware interpretation rather than single-channel thresholding.

title: Tailoring Optimization Approaches with Domain Knowledge in Industry Process for Meta-heuristic Development
abstract: The paper presents an Industry Process for Meta-heuristic Development (IPMD) schema, a systematic methodology for applying meta- and hyper-heuristic applications to optimization problems. In this context, we present a case study of Balancing Non-dominated Tournament Genetic Programming (BNTGP) applied to solve two NP-hard multi-objective optimization problems: routing (Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows) and scheduling (Multi-Skill Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem). The BNTGP method is based on a metaheuristic design. Its genetic programming-based representation makes BNTGP a hyper-heuristic, as it enables the exploration of a search space of heuristics for solving problems in general. The resulting heuristic can then be applied across a set of problem instances.

title: On Monotonicity in Mean Field Games Induced by Discount Factor Transformations
abstract: This paper is devoted to the well-posedness of a class of infinite horizon discounted Mean Field Games (MFGs) problems, where both an exponential discount and a so-called cheap control factors are present simultaneously, and scale in a possibly different way. We introduce a new class of transformations of variables, at the level of both the MFG PDE and the corresponding FBSDE systems. We then show how these transformations reveal a new mechanism that generates semiconvexity estimates for the value function and ensures the existence of mean field equilibria, as long as the parameters land in a suitable regime, that we quantitatively describe. This new mechanism demonstrates furthermore how discount factors lead to a source of strong displacement monotonicity for the Lagrangian, without any initial monotonicity assumptions on the running costs. Consequently, in such regimes of parameters uniqueness of solutions manifests. Our approach uses a Lagrangian point of view, which lets us treat general non-separable Lagrangians and both deterministic and idiosyncratic noise driven models in a transparent, unified way. For a specific class of quadratic Lagrangians, using turnpike-type methods, we further obtain an exponential contractivity estimate for the mean field equilibria.

title: Transforms between multivariate Laguerre and Meixner polynomials and their applications to gateways
abstract: We establish gateways in both directions between the Laguerre process and a discrete Markov process for every inverse temperature $2θ\geq 1$. Here, a gateway is an intertwining relation between Markov processes with continuous and discrete state spaces. A key ingredient is a pair of generating function identities that relate two double generating functions for multivariate Meixner polynomials to a single and a double generating function for multivariate Laguerre polynomials, respectively. These identities reveal a close relationship between the two families of polynomials and yield integral transforms that underlie the gateway relations. Gateway relations provide a means of transferring properties between continuous and discrete processes. As an application, we derive the Feller-Dynkin property and the uniqueness of the invariant distribution for the Laguerre process from the corresponding properties of the discrete process.

title: Safety and Connectivity Certificates for Finite-Time Formation Transitions
abstract: Finite-time formation transitions are useful for coordinating multi-agent systems in time-critical missions, but convergence to a prescribed formation in finite time does not guarantee collision avoidance or communication connectivity during the transition. Existing approaches address finite-time coordination and safety-constrained formation control, yet explicit connections between disagreement during transitions, formation geometry, and coupling-gain selection need to be developed for certifying safe maneuvers. This paper develops a disagreement-based framework for certifying transient safety and connectivity during finite-time tracking of arbitrary prescribed formation trajectories. Local feedback guarantees exact finite-time tracking with a graph-independent settling-time bound, while a graph-dependent disagreement bound is used to derive sufficient geometric conditions for collision avoidance and connectivity preservation. These conditions further yield an offline coupling-gain selection rule based on the available geometric clearance. Numerical simulations illustrate the trade-off between convergence rate and control effort as the coupling gain increases. They also demonstrate the effectiveness and conservatism of the proposed certificates.

title: Domain-Invariant and Language-Model-Assisted Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks on Keyboards
abstract: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) recover typed text from the sound of keystrokes, using only a commodity microphone and no access to the victim's device.
