Our findings suggest that the value of oversight tools for coding agents lies less in making developers trust the agent and more in helping developers feel confident in their own evaluation of agent-made changes. We discuss implications for visual tools that support code comprehension and human oversight in AI-assisted software development.

title: C$_2$ Swan, CH and CN emission, surface temperature and luminous efficiency of the Hayabusa2 sample-return capsule from ground-based spectroscopy
abstract: The Hayabusa2 sample-return capsule entered the atmosphere over South Australia on 5 December 2020 at 12 km/s. A slitless spectral video, taken from the ground with a hand-tracked consumer camera, shows the capsule alone from 80 to 49 km. In the first ten seconds of heating the shock layer emits the CN violet system, the CH A-X band and the C$_2$ Swan bands, the latter for the first time in remote observations of a capsule entry. C$_2$ ($T_{\rm rot}\approx9200$ K, $T_{\rm vib}\approx7800$ K) and CN (about 7000 K) are far hotter than the surface. C$_2$ and CH disappear while the heat flux is still rising and CN persists, which we relate to the early pyrolysis of the carbon-phenolic ablator and to the changing boundary-layer chemistry. The colour temperature of the heat shield rises from 2720 to 3080 K, in agreement with airborne results. The radiated energy is one to two orders of magnitude below that of natural fireballs, because the light comes from the hot surface rather than from ablation vapour. A faint persistent train lights up about 1 s after the passage and fades within a few seconds, probably chemiluminescence in the cooling wake.

title: RiskLens: Human-Informed Incident Transfer for AI Risk Evaluation
abstract: As AI capabilities advance, early-stage teams need better ways to judge whether historical incidents transfer to new products, demanding support beyond static risk checklists or one-off ideation tools. We present RiskLens, a human-AI workflow with an interactive system built around a live crawl, refreshable ranker, and extensible, human-informed schema. RiskLens analyzes 2,034 AI incidents and 10,443 AI products to rank transferable incidents using a feature schema spanning technical, operational, and user-facing attributes and supports an interface that presents ranked incident evidence, generated scenarios, risk metrics, and mitigation suggestions. In a study with 21 AI-familiar participants, users surfaced evaluation criteria that we added as 13 human-informed dimensions, including harm categories, failure mechanisms, and vulnerable groups. The feature-based model outperformed a generic baseline with an 86.2% win rate, and remained stable on a twenty-month future holdout; after human-informed schema expansion, the updated model outperformed the same baseline on 91.4% of pairs.

title: Decisions at the end of the world
abstract: International treaties are often described as tigers without teeth, failing to secure compliance or change outcomes. Cooperation also depends on how states maintain the rules they have already made -- especially where no sovereign stands above the states. Here we map more than six decades of decision-making under the Antarctic Treaty, linking submitted proposals to recorded responses and tracing how instruments act on earlier ones. Shared references tie decisions together across the agenda. Recurring revision concentrates in specialised histories, above all the management of protected areas, beyond what activity, popularity and reference age predict. Periodic administrative reviews retire outdated instruments in bulk, joining otherwise separate histories without coordinating policy across subjects. Binding Measures build overwhelmingly on earlier Measures, with little direct succession from non-binding Resolutions. Distinguishing these layers shows how a shared rule system is sustained by consensus, and provides a basis for comparing cooperation across global commons.

title: Strong error estimates for finite element approximations of the stochastic Burgers--Huxley equation with multiplicative noise
abstract: This paper is concerned with strong error estimates for fully discrete finite element approximations of the stochastic Burgers--Huxley equation with multiplicative noise. We use the implicit Euler--Maruyama scheme for time discretization and continuous piecewise linear finite elements for spatial discretization. Moment bounds and exponential integrability estimates are established and used with the discrete stochastic Gronwall inequality to derive error estimates in full expectation. Sub-second-moment error estimates are first obtained in the discrete maximum-in-time $L^2$-norm and the discrete $L^2$-in-time $H^1$-norm. Second-moment error estimates in the discrete maximum-in-time $L^2$-norm are then established using a higher-moment argument. The convergence rates are of order $k^{1/2}$ in time and $h$ in space, with the spatial rate being optimal in the $H^1$-norm. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to examine the convergence rates and the influence of multiplicative noise on the solution.

title: The graph $a$-Turán theorem
abstract: We prove analogues of Turán's theorem and the Erdős--Stone theorem for graph $a$-numbers. The $i$th $a$-number $a_i(G)$ equals the $i$th rational Betti number of the real toric manifold associated with the graph associahedron of $G$. We show that the Turán graph $T_r(n)$ maximizes every $a$-number among $K_{r+1}$-free graphs on $n$ vertices. We also show that for any fixed graph $H$ with at least one edge and each fixed $i\geq1$, the limiting extremal density of the $i$th $a$-number among $H$-free graphs depends only on the chromatic number of $H$. Since $a_1(G)$ is the number of edges of $G$, these results recover the two classical theorems in degree one and extend them to higher $a$-numbers.

title: $(r,s)$-Designs in the Nonbinary Johnson Scheme: Constructions and Linear Codes
abstract: Using factorizations of complete graphs, we determine the existence conditions for $(2,1)$-designs in the nonbinary Johnson scheme where each $3$-element subset appears exactly once as a support. Furthermore, by utilizing large sets of Steiner triple systems, we construct designs with index $1$ that cannot be obtained from the known construction combining block designs and orthogonal arrays. For linear codes, we express multiplicative character sums over specified nonzero coordinates as sums over the codewords of the dual code. Using this identity along with the rank of a matrix formed by Krawtchouk polynomials, we provide a sufficient condition for the set of all codewords of a given weight to form an $(r,s)$-design. In this matrix, we can utilize not only the rows corresponding to weights absent from the code, but also the rows corresponding to weights for which the set of codewords already forms a design. Moreover, let $q>2$ be a prime power, and let $0 \neq C \subsetneq \mathbb{F}_q^n$ be a linear code with exactly two nonzero weights. For $t \geq 2$, the set of all codewords of weight $w \geq t$ forms a non-empty $(t,t)$-design if and only if the dual minimum distance is at least $t+2$. Consequently, this provides a negative answer to the Wu--Zhou problem concerning two-weight codes with a dual minimum distance of $3$.

title: Self-Consistent Microscopic Description of the 146Sm Half-Life for Early Solar System Chronology
abstract: The extinct \textit{p}-process radionuclide $^{146}$Sm, decaying to $^{142}$Nd, is a key short-lived chronometer for the formation and early evolution of terrestrial planets and planetesimals. However, there has been a long-standing discrepancy in both the experimental measurements and the theoretical evaluations of the $^{146}$Sm half-life. To address this, a self-consistent microscopic framework for $α$ decay is developed in this work, in which the $α$ particle is treated as a four-nucleon quartet. Its formation amplitude in the nuclear interior is constructed from a coherent superposition of multiple pure single-particle configurations weighted by the pairing occupation amplitudes. Coupling this shell amplitude to the $α$ cluster that survives in the low-density surface region yields a self-consistently determined two-state (shell~$\oplus$~cluster) preformation weight and effective potential. The calculated half-lives for the neighboring emitters of $^{146}$Sm are in good agreement with the measured values. Cross-validation over the neighboring emitters reproduces each excluded half-life without any nucleus-specific adjustment, and yields $^{146}$Sm predictions consistent to within $\pm 6\%$ of the resulting half-life $T_{1/2}=75.1^{+6.1}_{-5.6}$~Ma. This provides a solid calibration for theoretical studies of the early solar system.

title: Quantum Cost of Emptiness in a One-Dimensional Bose Gas
abstract: The probability $P_0(R)$ of an empty interval of radius $R$ probes the far tail of density fluctuations in the thermodynamic ground state of the repulsive Lieb--Liniger gas. Here $ρ$ is the bulk density and $c$ the repulsion. As $\ell = ρR \to \infty$ at fixed $γ= c/ρ> 0$, we find $-\log P_0 = f(γ)\ell^2 + B(γ)\sqrt{\ell} - \frac{1}{4}\log\ell + O_γ(1)$, with no linear term and $B = 2ζ(3/2)\sqrt{f/(πγ)}$. Exact Gaussian completion of the auxiliary-field determinant reduces the leading collective response to an electrostatic slit problem, yielding $f(γ)$ in elliptic integrals. Its dipole polarization tail drives auxiliary scattering returns whose local density saturates while the active rapidity range expands as $\sqrt{R}$, producing the square-root boundary cost. The full return spectrum and the occupied-rapidity endpoints together fix the $-1/4$ logarithmic coefficient. Through the contact identity, widening the void probes a dense healing scale at the boundary whose growing characteristic occupation supports an emergent classical-field description even in a strongly interacting bulk.

title: Agentic Dashboards: A New Design Paradigm for Visual Analytics
abstract: Visual analytics systems traditionally combine analytical methods and interactive visualizations into a fixed application specified at the design phase. Coding agents offer a flexible approach: experts could conduct analysis through natural-language instructions. We envision an agentic dashboard as a persistent visual analytics workspace where an agent makes decisions about analytical methods, views, and their coordination within a designer-defined decision space. This approach shifts part of the visualization designer's role from engineering a fixed interface to defining the decisions an agent may make at runtime. We illustrate how such a dashboard could operate with current capabilities and propose criteria for evaluating its behavior and potential failures. As analytical workflows become more fluid and agent-mediated, visualization can help experts maintain awareness, coordinate with agents, and exercise judgment.

title: SEC: One-Share Everywhere-Short Secret Sharing from Lossless Expanders
abstract: We introduce SEC, an expander-code-based ramp secret sharing scheme over $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, particularly suitable for lattice-based distributed cryptography. It is everywhere-short: bounded secret coefficients yield bounded share coefficients, and the integer reconstruction vectors have bounded entries. Moreover, each participant receives exactly one share, regardless of the number of parties and the privacy and reconstruction thresholds. This improves on prior schemes with bounded share coefficients and bounded entries in the integer reconstruction vectors, in which the number of sub-shares or shares per participant grows either with the number of parties and the threshold or with the security parameter. The construction rests on a coding-theoretic observation: in the bi-adjacency matrix of a lossless bipartite expander, unique-neighbor peeling completes every sufficiently small set of columns to a square unimodular submatrix. We prove correctness, everywhere-shortness, and linearity, and give a publicly computable entrywise bound on the reconstruction vector our algorithm returns for each authorized set. For privacy, we introduce hard-core local leakage resilience, which strengthens the leakage-resilience notion of Nielsen and Simkin (EUROCRYPT 2020) to protect a hard-core function of the secret, and we prove that SEC satisfies it against correlated multi-query local leakage under the MatrixHint-MLWE problem, which admits a reduction from the standard MLWE problem. For $n=60$ participants and security parameter $κ=128$, SEC achieves privacy threshold 6 against $2^{64}$ leakage queries and empirical reconstruction threshold 46. The ideal entropy-coded secret and share sizes are about 3.5 KiB and 6.4 KiB, respectively.

title: Antipodal paths: a short proof by counting intersections
abstract: We give a short elementary proof of Norine's antipodal-coloring theorem: every red--blue edge coloring of a hypercube in which antipodal edges have opposite colors contains a monochromatic path joining antipodal vertices.

title: Stretched bilayer-cytoskeleton links hold echinocytes in a model splenic slit
abstract: Stored red blood cells become echinocytes, growing spicules before losing membrane; the spleen clears the resulting small, spherical cells. Whether spicules alone hinder splenic passage is unknown. Shape and area change together. In a two-component model whose shrinking cytoskeleton raises spicules, we drove a discocyte and stage I to III echinocytes of equal area and volume through a model splenic slit. The pressure drop needed to pass rose with stage; stage III echinocytes were held at 37 to 50 times the pressure drop that passed the discocyte. Bilayer-cytoskeleton links stretched near full extension held these cells; lengthening them about twofold released a held cell. Capillary-sized channels, as in our device, separated the stages far less. Of the shape classes in stored blood, the model held at high pressure drops only storage-induced microerythrocytes, which perfused human spleens clear most. Spicules, besides membrane loss, may decide which stored cells the spleen retains.

title: Optimal feature selection for firewall log analysis using Machine learning and Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithms
abstract: Firewall log classification is important to monitor network traffic. Machine learning classifiers using network-related features have shown good results for this task, but high-dimensional features slow down classification. In this paper, we apply feature selection using bee swarm optimization with Q-learning-based local search (QBSO-FS) to the UCI Internet Firewall Data Set, together with random forest (RF), k-nearest neighbor (KNN), and Bernoulli naïve Bayes (Bernoulli NB) classifiers. The first version of this preprint selected and evaluated feature subsets on the same 5-fold cross-validation of the full data set, which contains 12.8\% exact duplicates; the reported scores are therefore optimistically biased. In this extended version, we re-evaluate the method with a leakage-free protocol: the data are split into training, validation, and test sets, features are selected using the validation set only, and accuracy and macro-averaged scores are measured once on the untouched test set, for both the raw data and a deduplicated, preprocessed version. On a single stratified split, QBSO-FS selects 5--7 features. The selected subsets clearly improve Macro-F1 over all features for KNN on both data sets and for RF on the deduplicated data (by 8--19 percentage points). For RF on the raw data and for Bernoulli NB, the differences (0.2--1.5 percentage points) may not hold for a different split. RF with 7 selected features reaches 99.90\% accuracy and 94.88\% Macro-F1 on the deduplicated data. On the same split, this exceeds our re-implementations of the deep neural network configurations of previous studies and the feature subset selected by particle swarm optimization in one of them, while the run time saved on this low-dimensional data set is small. These results suggest that the method can support automatic firewall log analysis, while evaluation over multiple splits remains future work.

title: Anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior driven by dichotomous Markov noise in a quantum Ising chain: Generalized stochastic resonance in the defect density
abstract: The anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior may arise under noise, adding a noise-induced contribution to the defect density beyond the conventional Kibble-Zurek term. Most investigations of such behavior have so far been restricted to Gaussian noise. For Gaussian colored noise (GCN), the power spectrum dictates a monotonic variation of this term with the correlation time. Here, we focus on dichotomous Markov noise (DMN), a prototypical non-Gaussian colored noise, in the quantum Ising chain. We show that the noise-induced defect density, taken as the response function, exhibits generalized stochastic resonance: it is nonmonotonic in the correlation time, growing in the fast-noise regime and decreasing in the slow-noise regime. This resonance stems from the anomalous AKZ behavior in the slow-noise regime, where the DMN-induced trend is nonmonotonic, in contrast to the monotonic GCN case. The underlying mechanism lies in the sparse realizations of DMN in the slow-noise regime, a feature not captured by the power spectrum. Our work thereby reveals a fundamental distinction between Gaussian and non-Gaussian noises in the nonequilibrium critical quench dynamics of the quantum Ising chain.

title: Sharp Bounds for Near-Maximizers of Gaussian Processes
abstract: For a centered Gaussian process $G$ with continuous sample paths on a compact metric space $T$, a continuous drift $f: T \mapsto \mathbb{R}$, a noise level $σ>0$, and $ε\ge 0$, let $A_ε$ be the set of points at which $f+σG$ is within $ε$ of its maximum. Writing $\mathbb{E}\sup_TG$ for the expected supremum of $G$, we prove that the expected squared diameter of $A_ε$ in the canonical pseudometric of $G$ is at most $8ε\mathbb{E}\sup_TG/σ$ and that the expected maximal squared distance from a point of $A_ε$ to an exact maximizer is at most $4ε\mathbb{E}\sup_TG/σ$. The constants cannot be improved uniformly over index sets, processes, and drifts, and no logarithmic factor in $ε$ appears, unlike in bounds integrated from tail estimates. At $ε=0$ the bounds give the almost sure uniqueness of the maximizer in the canonical pseudometric without nondegeneracy assumptions. Given this uniqueness, both bounds follow from a bound with constant $2$ on the mean square of the largest increment of an independent copy of $G$ from an exact maximizer to a point of $A_ε$. The proof rests on an identity for the mean squared support function of the $ε$-subdifferentials of a smooth convex function at a standard Gaussian vector, obtained from two Gaussian integrations by parts.

title: A Polynomial Bound on Split Rank
abstract: We prove that the split rank of a rational pure-integer polyhedron is polynomially bounded in its input length, resolving a conjecture of Basu, Conforti, Di Summa, and Jiang. If the defining system has dense binary encoding length $L$, then $O((L+1)^9)$ split rounds suffice to reach the integer hull in arbitrary dimension.

title: On subgroup regular sets in generalized Cayley graphs
abstract: A subset $D$ of the vertex set of a graph is called an $(a,b)$-regular set if each vertex in $D$ has exactly $a$ neighbors in $D$, and each vertex outside $D$ has exactly $b$ neighbors in $D$. A proper subgroup $H$ of $G$ is called an $(a,b)$-regular set of $(G,α)$ if it is an $(a,b)$-regular set of $GC(G,S,α)$ for some generalized Cayley subset $S$ of $G$ induced by the involutory automorphism $α$. This paper investigates subgroup $(0,b)$-regular sets in generalized Cayley graphs. We first obtain some necessary and sufficient conditions for a proper subgroup of a group $G$ to be a $(0,b)$-regular set of a generalized Cayley graph. In particular, we show that a proper normal subgroup $H$ of $G$ is a $(0,b)$-regular set of $(G,α)$ if and only if $H$ is a perfect code of $(G,α)$ for some odd integer $b,$ which generalizes the result in [F.S. Seiedali, Z. Akhlaghi, B. Khosravi. Generalized Cayley graphs and perfect code. Discrete Math. 2026]. Furthermore, for connected generalized Cayley graphs with $α$-normal generalized Cayley subsets, we characterize subgroup $(0,b)$-regular sets via equitable partitions.

title: Learning memory forces and bounding frequency errors in fractional Kuramoto grids
abstract: Missing history creates two different demands on a forecaster for a fractional grid: predicting frequency accurately and reconstructing memory well enough to bound the prediction error. We connect these demands through the hereditary force that remains after an integral observation correction. A compact decoder retains the directions most relevant to that force, and an exact decomposition separates omitted directions from coefficient error. A response-trained linear predictor and neural refinement learn the coefficients for frequency prediction. A separate force reconstruction supplies the reference for a nonlinear energy bound for the specified finite relaxation model, accounting for numerical propagation defects and the difference between the reference and point forecasts. For the outage transients studied here, refinement improves on the linear predictor across the time steps and memory parameters tested. Replacing the noisy origin states reveals why this gain can coexist with greater memory reconstruction error: the learned correction partly compensates for observation error. Separating prediction from reconstruction enables frequency bounds in cases where the point predictor alone cannot support them. A critical radius compares calibrated uncertainty with the angle margin available along the reference trajectory, explaining both issuance and abstention. Under jointly exchangeable calibration and test events, the calibrated guarantee bounds the marginal probability of issuing an invalid envelope. Together, these results connect uncertainty about history outside the observation window to frequency forecasts and explicit conditions for bounding their errors.

title: Chimera states in a network of firefly oscillators
abstract: We investigate chimera-like states in a network of identical firefly oscillators with nonlocal delayed coupling. For a uniform communication delay, the network exhibits a breathing phase-frequency chimera, characterized by the coexistence of frequency-locked and frequency-drifting populations and an oscillating incoherent-domain width. We then introduce heterogeneous pairwise communication delays to investigate a numerical analogue of the Sarfati-Peleg phenomenon observed in natural firefly swarms. In this regime, a recurring collective chorus coexists with character oscillators that flash persistently before or after the chorus. Cycle-resolved delay maps, role rasters, character probabilities, and spatial covariance diagnostics demonstrate the persistence and collective organization of these chorus-character roles. Although the uniform-delay and heterogeneous-delay states represent different forms of partial synchronization, the same firefly-oscillator framework supports both regimes. Finally, we construct a reduced analytical description in terms of a chorus-relative delay field and a memory field. The local dynamics is organized around a saturated subcritical pitchfork structure, producing a stable chorus equilibrium together with two stable character equilibria. The reduced model therefore provides a phenomenological description of the tri-stable chorus-character organization and its characteristic delay scale. Our results show that heterogeneous delayed interactions among identical relaxation oscillators can generate persistent temporal identities analogous to those reported in synchronous firefly swarms.

title: Core nonemptiness for $2/3$-convex games
abstract: We study the core of $2/3$-convex games, a class of transferable-utility (TU) games that generalizes convex games, which requires at least two of any three distinct coalitions satisfy the supermodular inequality. We show that every $2/3$-convex game admits a marginal worth vector in the core, and hence has a nonempty core. Our proof is constructive and yields a linear-time algorithm for finding such a core allocation. We also show that $2/3$-convexity does not imply permutational convexity in general, while the implication holds under an additional superadditivity condition on pairs of singletons. As an application, we introduce a TU model motivated by the OSCE's consensus-minus-two procedure and show that the resulting game is $2/3$-convex but need not be convex.

title: A One-Sided Chord Trim of Wetzel's Sector Covers Unit Arcs
abstract: Wetzel conjectured, and Panraksa and Wichiramala proved, that the circular sector of radius one and angle $30^\circ$ contains a congruent copy, reflections allowed, of every arc of length one. We show that half of its arc is not needed: replacing the arc between the angles $15^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ by its chord gives a convex cover of area $π/24+(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)/8=0.2603092\ldots$. As in the proof for the sector, we place an arc in two supporting wedges. A sum of support, cap and radial inequalities, with vector coefficients summing to zero, shows that an arc with no copy in the trimmed sector is longer than one. One two-parameter family of configurations is checked by rational interval arithmetic; programs and data are supplied. No chord that starts below $3.6^\circ$ gives a cover. We also reduce the inclusion-minimality of the trimmed sector to two families of cuts.

title: Proliferating against the current: how multistep branching nucleation can sort microtubule polarity in the spindle
abstract: The spindle, which segregates chromosomes during cell division, is a paradigm of cytoskeletal self-organization: a highly ordered structure that persists for hours is assembled from dynamic microtubules that branch, grow, slide, and turn over within tens of seconds. Its microtubules point inward, with minus ends clustered at the poles and plus ends extending toward the chromosomes at the center of the structure. In large meiotic spindles this arrangement is puzzling, since microtubules nucleate near the chromosomes and grow at their plus ends much faster than motors slide them backward. One would therefore expect the plus ends, rather than the minus ends, to radiate outward. Here, we propose a resolution to this seeming paradox through a kinetic model that integrates the core filament-level processes. When branching complexes assemble with a sufficient delay, for instance through several sequential rate-limiting steps, they accumulate on old microtubule lattice sites near the backward-sliding minus ends of mother microtubules. Each generation is then born farther back than the last, so the self-renewing population drifts toward the minus ends even though each filament's center advances toward its plus end. For the sliding and growth velocities measured in Xenopus egg extract spindles, a multistep mechanism requires at least four rate-limiting steps. The kinetic theory has a surprisingly amenable structure: the filament length configuration variable can be eliminated exactly, yielding a finite space-time hierarchy, and the direction of population drift follows from a general criterion comparing the mean lattice age at branching sites with the ratio of plus-end advance to sliding speed.

title: "We Are the Dirty Hands": Reimagining an Ambient Intelligence Care System with Professional Caregivers
abstract: While ambient assisted living (AAL) sensing systems offer promise for aging in place, their impacts on professional caregivers are overlooked. We conducted two collective speculation workshops (N=24) with personal health aides (PHAs, n=18) and certified nursing assistants (CNAs, n=6) to examine the ethical implications and value tensions of a care system with ambient intelligence (CSAI), our conceptualization of an AAL. Participants anticipated different implications across care roles and settings. PHAs anticipated additional responsibilities from CSAI, including learning how it operates and supporting older adults in its use. CNAs, who had greater access to workplace resources and protections, similarly noted that CSAI could create additional work. Participants also identified tensions around visibility, as sensing could support caregivers by documenting difficult working conditions while simultaneously making their behavior more vulnerable to misinterpretation. Through their modifications and surfaced discussions, we propose design guidelines for AAL systems, such as integrating context-aware sensing.

title: Asymptotic analysis of infinite-server queues driven by a Cox process with squared Bessel arrival intensity
abstract: This paper introduces a model for infinite-server queues driven by a Cox process with stochastic intensity given by a squared Bessel (BESQ) process. Exploiting the affine structure of the underlying dynamics, we derive a closed-form expression for the joint moment-generating function (MGF) of the arrival intensity, the number of customers in the system, and the integral of the number of customers in the system over a time interval. The asymptotic properties of the model are also analysed. We establish laws of large numbers, central limit theorems, large deviation principles, and moderate deviation principles for several quantities of interest. More precisely, these results are obtained for three important settings: cumulative occupancy over a finite time interval, system occupancy under a diverging long-run mean arrival intensity, and the superposition of independent infinite-server queues with Cox-BESQ arrival intensities. Numerical experiments illustrate the associated rate functions and demonstrate the effectiveness of the resulting rare-event approximations.

title: Counting doubly labelled trees and one-component networks
abstract: A phylogenetic network is one-component if the child of every reticulation is a leaf. This class of networks has been widely used as building blocks in the combinatorial study of phylogenetic networks. We establish a bijection between one-component networks on $k$ taxa and rooted binary multi-labelled trees in which every label occurs exactly twice. Using this bijection and Burnside's lemma, we derive a closed formula and a two-term recurrence for the number of one-component networks. We further obtain explicit formulas for counting one-component networks with a prescribed number of reticulations.

title: Null designs and switching in polynomial spaces
abstract: Null designs are finite point configurations with real weights whose polynomial moments vanish up to a given degree. In Godsil's framework of polynomial spaces, we give elementary proofs of sharp lower bounds on the number of points in the Euclidean and spherical cases. We characterize the spherical null designs attaining the bound and give explicit formulas for their weights. We then study how null designs can be used to replace part of a weighted design while preserving its polynomial moments. We give conditions ensuring nonnegative weights and apply the minimum-size classification to switching on circles. Examples on spheres and in Hamming and Johnson spaces illustrate these results, including a replacement between noncongruent spherical $5$-designs that preserves equal weights and the number of points.

title: Between Niti and Nyaya: A Society-Centered Framework for AI Governance
abstract: Governments are making decisions about AI before they can measure its public effects, and those decisions determine whether a person can learn that AI influenced an outcome, challenge it, and see it corrected. Research has documented what AI governance produces: principles, strategies, registers, and audits. However, we lack shared language for understanding AI policy while it is still being made. We introduce the Society-Centered AI Governance Framework, which gives policymakers, researchers, and the public a way to assess instruments in any jurisdiction by whether a person can get notice, challenge a decision, and see it corrected. It reads a jurisdiction's instruments together by date and binding status, separates an agency duty from a right a person can invoke, and traces which later instrument must enforce each commitment. We evaluated it in North Carolina using interviews with nine AI Leadership Council members, conducted before and after the state's 2026 AI roadmap, and a provision-level reading, with human-reviewed model-assisted coding, of 49 AI governance documents from 19 states. For the state's own AI systems, we find visibility-first governance: visibility duties are in effect, notice exists as an agency duty with no right a person can invoke, and AI-specific challenge and correction remain advisory. The roadmap assigns owners and dates to the missing protections, so the gaps are documented but not yet closed. Recent federal preemption proposals focus on AI development, so recourse for a state's own systems is likely to remain a state decision. We identify "legitimacy before protection" as a testable risk of visibility-first governance and name the milestones that would test it. More broadly, judging AI policy by who can act on what it makes visible lets the field assess recourse while policy is still forming, before harm occurs.

title: MRxD: A Usage-Pattern Framework for Mixed-Reality Cross-Device Interaction
abstract: Mixed reality (MR) cross-device experiences often combine MR headsets with non-immersive devices such as laptops, tablets, and phones. Yet such cross-device design remains challenging because users must coordinate workflows across heterogeneous devices with different roles. This motivates our focus on usage patterns: recurrent ways in which people distribute and coordinate work across devices. Through a systematic analysis of 238 MR cross-device papers, we developed MRxD, a usage-pattern framework organized around three dimensions: user attention, task relatedness, and cognitive symmetry. Using these dimensions, we identified six usage patterns and synthesized the design strategies commonly used within each pattern. We further investigated the framework's application in design practice through a workshop (n=6) and the results suggest that MRxD can guide pattern-based design exploration and identify blind spots. We further discuss how usage patterns may shift or combine, and outline research gaps and design implications for future MR cross-device systems.

title: The ZTF Variability Archive (ZVAR): Initial Data Release (DR1)
abstract: The Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) has observed the northern sky observable from Palomar Observatory since March 2018, accumulating a median of a thousand photometric measurements across $gri$ for each of more than a billion sources. Among these billions of objects are millions of periodically variable stars, active galactic nuclei, stellar remnants, and substellar objects. We describe the initial data release (DR1) of the ZTF Variability Archive (ZVAR) which provides image difference forced photometry, candidate periods, and variability metrics for approximately 1.3 billion sources in ZTF having an identification in Pan-STARRS1 DR1 (PS1). The data cover the 5.37 year interval between March 2018 and July 2023. ZVAR is sensitive to periods between 5 minutes and 2.7 years. We also describe tools for accessing the ZVAR data.

title: Contiguity of unions of perfect matchings and random regular uniform hypergraphs
abstract: For fixed integers $s\ge3$ and $r$ satisfying $\log(r!)>\frac{r(s-1)}s\log r$, the union of $r$ independent uniform perfect matchings of the complete $s$-uniform hypergraph is mutually contiguous to the uniform simple $r$-regular $s$-uniform hypergraph, as $n\to\infty$ through multiples of $s$. In particular, $r=\lceil e^s\rceil$ suffices. The main input is the sharp entropy inequality for random permutations of Bristiel and Caputo. It proves the global maximization needed for the second moment of the number of complete factorizations. The remaining calculation, including its lattice factor, matches the short-cycle contribution required by small-subgraph conditioning.\\ This is an expanded version of a proof provided by ChatGPT-Astra.

title: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution
abstract: LLM agents apply approval settings, such as whether to ask before a consequential tool call, through instructions in their system prompt, and operators keep these settings confidential by restricting access to prompts and responses. Audits check whether an agent obeys its setting, not whether a neighboring process can infer which setting is deployed. PolicySniff infers an agent's approval-policy state through shared-GPU execution. A co-resident attacker that knows the candidate settings and the task first profiles both settings, then times only its own GPU kernels while the agent processes the task. The policy prefix is cached before capture, so the attacker observes processing of a task suffix that is identical under both settings. On an eager sparse mixture-of-experts runtime, where each selected expert runs as separate work, a frozen and blinded study identified the deployed setting at 94.17% balanced accuracy on its primary estimand. Across all authorization conditions, accuracy was 88.82% on tasks for which both settings produce the same decision and 91.98% on tasks where they differ. Hardware replays of expert routing show that its temporal density and layer-and-bucket alignment carry the policy information. Behavioral compliance does not imply configuration confidentiality: deployments that keep their approval setting private should measure its distinguishability on the serving runtime and enforce authorization outside the model.

title: the limit point set of real roots of random polynomials: a resolution of erdős problem 521
abstract: We resolve Erdős Problem~521 by proving that the normalized real-root count $N_n/\log n$ of Rademacher polynomials almost surely has no limit. More generally, consider the Kac polynomials \[ P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}ξ_jx^j \] with i.i.d.\ real coefficients of mean zero, variance one, and a finite absolute exponential moment. Let $N_n$ denote the number of distinct real roots of $P_n$. We prove that, almost surely, \[ \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{N_n}{\log n}=\frac1π, \qquad \limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{N_n}{\log n}=\frac1π+C_*, \] and the set of subsequential limits is exactly \[ \left[\frac1π,\;\frac1π+C_*\right]. \] Here $C_*>1/π$ is a constant uniquely determined by an equation. The lower-limit identity remains valid under the weaker assumption that $\mathbb{E}|ξ_0|^{2+δ}<\infty$ for some $δ>0$.

title: Conditional Gaussian Limits and Character Laws for Randomized Symmetric-Group Representations
abstract: Let $ρ_n$ be a real orthogonal representation of the symmetric group $S_n$ of dimension $d_n\to\infty$, let $σ_n$ be a uniform random permutation, and let $O_n$ be an independent Haar-orthogonal matrix. We study the linear statistics $\operatorname{Tr}(A_nO_nρ_n(σ_n)O_n^T)$ for deterministic real test matrices $A_n$ normalized only in Frobenius norm, which allows tests that isolate individual entries. Conditionally on $σ_n$, the statistic has mean $s_nχ_n(σ_n)$, where $χ_n$ is the character of $ρ_n$ and $s_n=d_n^{-1}\operatorname{Tr} A_n\to s$. We show that the centered statistic has conditional Gaussian limit $N(0,1-s^2)$ for every such test if and only if the trivial and sign constituents of $ρ_n$ occupy $o(d_n)$ dimensions, and that this limit is asymptotically independent of every convergent $σ_n$-measurable observable. The key input is a tensor-square estimate, based on the Frobenius-Schur identity and the minimum degree of non-linear irreducible representations of $S_n$, which shows that this single condition controls both normalized traces needed in the Haar-conjugation argument. For the uncentered statistic, convergence in distribution of $χ_n(σ_n)$ to a law $Ξ$ is necessary and sufficient for every test statistic to converge to $sΞ+\sqrt{1-s^2}G$, with $G$ standard Gaussian and independent of $Ξ$. For every irreducible sequence with $d_n\to\infty$, finitely many entries scaled by $\sqrt{d_n}$ have independent standard Gaussian limits. Finally, we compute $Ξ$ explicitly for diagrams with a fixed first-row tail, their transposes, and diagrams with sublinear largest hook, answering in these cases a question of Tsou.

title: Enumerating Pyranim Isomorphisms
abstract: We study a Nim-adjacent poset game, where chips are arranged in a pyramid and two players take turns removing chips that do not currently support chips to the upper-left and upper-right; upon removing this chip, all supported chips above are also removed. Play continues until the final chip is removed. We use a bijection between the game states, Dyck paths, and unit interval graphs to count the number of possible game states up to isomorphism.

title: Fault Injection Attacks on Q-Learning: Analysis, Vulnerabilities, and Countermeasures
abstract: Hardware fault injection attacks threaten machine learning systems, yet their impact on reinforcement learning (RL) has received little attention despite the use of RL in safety-critical applications. This paper presents a security analysis of Q-Learning implementations under voltage and clock glitching attacks on a ChipWhisperer platform, evaluating five variants: Standard, Robust, Resilient, Linear, and Deep Q-Learning. In standard Q-Table implementations, faults corrupt reward computation, action selection, and Q-value updates during learning, and change the selected action during inference. Robust Q-Learning does not prevent these attacks: NaN and infinite values injected during learning persist in the Q-table, and its greedy policy uses the same code as standard Q-Learning. This paper also evaluates a Resilient Q-Learning variant that applies triple modular redundancy with majority voting. It corrects corruption of a single Q-table copy, but inputs shared by the copies, such as the reward, and the voting code itself remain outside its protection. The analysis extends to Linear and Deep Q-Learning, where faults corrupt stored weights during learning and change actions during inference. Moving beyond benchmark environments, this work evaluates an online traffic light controller in a microscopic traffic simulator, where a single injected infinite value degrades accumulated vehicle waiting time by 148x while corrupting under 4% of the Q-table, and where triple modular redundancy corrected the faults injected in our tests, although glitching could still halt the device. Altogether, this work provides a basis for understanding and securing RL deployments against fault injection attacks.

title: Congruences Modulo 16, 32 and 64 for a Restricted Overpartition Function
abstract: Let $\overline{t}^{(3)}(n)$ denote the number of overpartitions of $n$ in which consecutive parts differ by a multiple of $3$ unless the larger part is overlined, and the smallest part is overlined unless it is divisible by $3$. Using dissections of theta functions, we establish two infinite families of congruences modulo $32$ and $64$. We also obtain two residue formulas modulo $16$ and use them to derive four further infinite families of congruences modulo $16$. In particular, for every positive integer $M$ and nonnegative integer $n$, the residue of $\overline{t}^{(3)}(M^2(18n+12))$ modulo $16$ is $8$ if $6n+4$ is a square and $0$ otherwise.

title: Gradient Flows over Convex Bodies for Learning Optimal Regularizers
abstract: We consider the question of describing gradient flows over the collection of convex bodies. This is motivated by foundational questions arising in inverse problems. Suppose we wish to solve an ill-posed inverse problem using regularization techniques. Can we learn an optimal choice of a convex regularizer directly from prior data? Given a numerical algorithm that computes such an optimal regularizer, is there a principled manner for describing the evolution of its iterates? The objective of this paper is to lay the foundation towards answering these questions. To this end, we consider a criterion of an optimal regularizer based on seeking a convex body that minimizes the expected gauge evaluation with respect to a prior data distribution subject to a volume constraint. The formulation is initially nonconvex, but admits hidden convexity by passing to its polar. We characterize the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions that certify global optimality. We also analyze the $L^2$-gradient flow as well as a minimizing movement scheme with the Hausdorff penalty. Our results show that the objective gap decays exponentially along the gradient flow and we obtain dimension-dependent rates for both the objective gap and distance to the optimal body for the Hausdorff scheme. Finally, we apply the KKT conditions to identify explicit optimal convex bodies. For data where the optimal nonconvex regularizer is the $\ell_p$-quasinorm, $p \in (0,1)$, the optimal convex regularizer is the volume-normalized $\ell_1$-ball. For data described by paired basis atoms, the optimal convex regularizer is the polar of a shifted zonotope.

title: The lower boundary of the $\{K_2,K_{p},K_{q}\}$-profile
abstract: We determine the asymptotically sharp minimum number of $q$-cliques that appear in any $n$-vertex graph with $γn^2$ edges and $δn^{p}$ $p$-cliques for $q>p>2$. The question of determining the minimum number of $r$-cliques that appear in any $n$-vertex graph with $γn^2$ edges was previously resolved by Razborov for $r=3$, Nikiforov for $r=4$ and Reiher for all $r\geq 5$. For all $r\geq 3$, the minimum is attained by a complete multipartite graph where all parts are equal except for one that can be smaller or by a limit of such graphs. Very recently, Ma, Wang and Zhu as well as Li, Liu and Zhang showed that the same construction is also a minimizer for the number of $r$-cliques when the number of $s$-cliques is fixed for any $2\leq s<r$. A minimizer in our setting is the disjoint union of the same complete multipartite graph with an independent set. This establishes the lower boundary of the three-dimensional $\{K_2, K_p, K_q\}$-profile.

title: A global rigidity criterion for Coxeter $3$-polytopes
abstract: We give a combinatorial condition ensuring global projective rigidity of simple hyperbolic Coxeter $3$-polytopes. As an application, we prove that every right-angled Löbell polytope is globally rigid.

title: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records
abstract: The CoordX Protocol carries signed and encrypted entries between parties. It proves who wrote each entry and who had permission to write it. It does not say what an entry means. That task belongs above the protocol layer. This paper describes the CoordX type system, the layer that gives entries a meaning. A type is a short document that says how to read one part of a shared record: which entries count, what each position means, what a party may do there, and what a party must do next. The type system has two key properties. It is trustless: a type is an ordinary signed object fixed by its digest, and every party evaluates it for itself over entries that the CoordX Protocol has already verified. No party has to trust a server, a registry or another party's software. It is swappable: a type names the interpreter it is written for, so many interpreters, of different capabilities and designs, can be used side by side in one record. We describe how to write type schemas, and we define the expressive power of the schema language. Payloads form a regular language. Entry structure forms a regular tree language. Every rule and every computed value is a total function in the primitive recursive class, so evaluation always halts. We compare this with KQML, FIPA-ACL and CBCL, and we relate it to language-theoretic security.

title: SwarmSafe-Delta: Isolating Message Effects on LLM Agent Safety
abstract: When a tool-using LLM agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether an upstream message changed the executor's action. We introduce SwarmSafe-Delta, a paired executable protocol that freezes upstream computation, varies real, hidden, and format-matched placebo delivery, and scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets. Across four models and constructed optional tasks, real delivery at $N=4$ produces 21.4% risky-world violations, versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 percentage points). Real delivery also improves benign task success, illustrating that suppressing communication sacrifices utility. In a second regime constructed to require an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. These effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates. Exploratory action-level analyses show that the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution; model differences also largely track these message compositions. The contribution is a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol rather than a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.

title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents
abstract: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. Across all evaluations, Intent Profile-based protection outperforms all profile-free baselines on the primary metric. On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%). On more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajectories, where ground truth comes from environment state, profile-based post-execution detection reaches 0.949 AUROC versus AlignmentCheck 0.909, 0.897 with raw agent configuration and 0.843 without context. Profile-based input alignment improves protection success by 7 points over DataFilter with a comparable benign utility. These results suggest that an agent's intended purpose can serve as a useful security reference for detecting and mitigating deviations from its deployed role and operational boundaries.

title: A thermodynamically consistent, fully compressible, fluctuating hydrodynamics model of a Cahn Hilliard binary fluid mixture
abstract: We derive, from first principles, a thermodynamically consistent set of fully compressible fluctuating hydrodynamic equations for a Cahn-Hilliard binary fluid mixture, in isothermal and non-isothermal form and for symmetric and non-symmetric mixtures. The derivation uses the GENERIC formalism, with the friction operator constructed from flux fluctuations following Jelic and Ottinger, so that deterministic and stochastic fluxes derive from the same operator and correlation matrix and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem holds by construction. We show that the momentum equation must use the total mass density, that the Cahn-Hilliard variable is the mass fraction, and that the diffusion flux must be driven by the specific, not the volumetric, exchange potential. We derive a generalized Korteweg tensor for square-gradient energies in density and composition, and show that the reversible pressure tensor of the non-isothermal model is fixed by the degeneracy condition, producing a thermal capillary stress when the interfacial free energy has an entropic part. Thermodynamic consistency is proved in full: Jacobi identity, positivity and degeneracy, local energy conservation with interstitial-working fluxes, a local entropy balance, Soret-Dufour reciprocity, and Einstein statistics of the linearized equations. The final equations are written in conservative form for finite-volume discretization, and closed-form static and dynamic structure factors are given for all models as analytic benchmarks. An appendix shows that the same models follow from classical irreversible thermodynamics with the Helmholtz or Gibbs free energy; this route is unique for isothermal flows and has a gauge freedom in the non-isothermal case that GENERIC removes.

title: Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). Near-infrared processing and data products
abstract: The Euclid near-infrared processing function (NIR PF) converts the raw observations acquired by the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) into calibrated images and source-level products. Following the first implementation delivered with the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1), the NIR PF has been revised for the first major Euclid Data Release (DR1), with improvements to detector-level processing, calibration, image reconstruction, and quality control. The DR1 processing includes observations covering more than $1900\,\rm{deg}^2$ and has produced $71\,659$ calibrated near-infrared (NIR) images. We assess the performance of the processing chain through extensive astrometric and photometric validation. The astrometric solution reaches an average root-mean-square (RMS) of 10 mas, remaining below 20 mas for 99% of the dithers in all three NISP bands. Temporal variations in the instrumental throughput are typically corrected to a level of 2 mmag RMS, while the relative photometric accuracy reaches 0.9% for sources brighter than 19 mag in $Y_\mathrm{E}$, $J_\mathrm{E}$, and $H_\mathrm{E}$, and the residual spatial variations of the photometric calibration across the focal plane are at the level of approximately 10 mmag for the entire sample. Despite some remaining limitations, the DR1 NIR imaging products are consistent with the required astrometric and photometric performance over the large area covered by this release.

title: Even Loose Proximity Constraints Make Makespan-optimal Unlabeled Multi-agent Pathfinding Hard
abstract: We study \textsc{$r$-Connected Unlabeled Multi-agent Pathfinding} ($r$CUMAPF), a variant of MAPF where interchangeable agents have a proximity range $r\in \mathbb{N}$, and agents must form a single group in a given graph $G$ through limited-range communication at all times. The problem arises in fundamental applications such as self-reconfiguration and platooning, while standard MAPF does not capture proximity constraints. For the problem of finding a makespan-optimal solution, prior work shows \NP-hardness for $r=1$ and polynomial-time solvability when $r$ is sufficiently large; the complexity for the intermediate case $2\le r$ is largely unknown. To narrow this gap, we show that finding a solution to $r$CUMAPF with makespan at most $2$ is \NP-hard for $2\le r= O(|V|^{1-\varepsilon})$, where $0<\varepsilon\le 1$ is a fixed constant and $|V|$ is the number of vertices. As a consequence, we show that the labeled analogue of $r$CUMAPF is also \NP-hard under the same condition.

title: Strategic Repayment and Latent Fragility in Financial Networks: Why Banks Withhold Payable Liquidity
abstract: A network in which every bank pays in full can nevertheless admit a self-fulfilling settlement freeze under the same balance-sheet fundamentals. Thus, observing full repayment does not establish the uniqueness or robustness of the payment equilibrium. We derive this result from a precautionary-liquidity choice: banks may delay otherwise feasible payments to insure an interim funding need, trading a positive settlement-discipline cost against the marginal value of retained cash. The optimal reserve is a critical quantile of future liquidity requirements, and the repayment rule nests Eisenberg-Noe maximal feasible clearing exactly. Counterparty underpayment both reduces current cash and raises desired reserves. We characterise network amplification and the conditions for coexistence, including a homogeneous two-bank GPD frontier in which interbank exposure and maximum funding pass-through enter through one dimensionless index. A two-date settlement accounting rule distinguishes payment timing from ultimate default. The main result concerns equilibrium coexistence; the conditional best-response adjustment diagnostic does not assign selection probabilities.

title: Evaluating Authorization and Trust Boundaries in Agentic Orchestration Frameworks
abstract: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, and multi-agent collaboration, introducing security risks at orchestration boundaries. These risks depend on how identities are represented, operations are authorized, and instructions or information propagate between components. We evaluate LangChain, LangGraph, AutoGen, and OpenClaw through twelve experiments mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications using a common LLM (gpt-4o-mini). The experiments cover prompt injection, unauthorized resource access and command execution, memory poisoning, and inter-agent trust and identity attacks. Adversarial inputs induced unauthorized tool invocation, while tool chaining, stale filesystem validation, encoded instructions, and inter-agent delegation exposed weaknesses in authorization across component boundaries. Memory poisoning showed that untrusted state can influence responses, a risk distinct from conventional access-control violations. In the evaluated protected configurations, explicit authorization, controlled capability assignment, filesystem containment, and execution safeguards prevented specific unauthorized operations. The findings emphasize preserving authorization and information-trust boundaries throughout agentic workflows rather than treating framework capabilities or model-level instructions as sufficient security guarantees.

title: Odd faces as a parameter for maximum independent set in embedded graphs
abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for finding a maximum weight independent set in a graph embedded in a surface of bounded genus and with a bounded number of vertex-disjoint odd faces. In particular, we obtain an algorithm for graphs with an even-faced embedding in a torus and for planar graphs with a bounded number of odd faces, answering a question of Thomassé (2018) and a question of Choi, Gorsky, Kim, McFarland, and Wiederrecht (2025) respectively. We reduce the original problem to finding a minimum cost non-negative integer circulation with homology constraints in the dual of a certain double cover of the original graph.

title: Stream of Belief: Eliciting Collective Intelligence through Latent Belief Dynamics
abstract: In this work, we view multi-agent reasoning as a process of seeking a collective equilibrium of implicit belief dynamics and introduce Stream of Belief (SoB), where agents maintain continuous latent beliefs and iteratively refine them through communication and reflection. Our method seeks a collective belief state of a multi-agent system where further communication induces no meaningful information propagation. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the generalization of SoB across tasks and model families. More Broadly, our results suggest a new perspective on scaling multi-agent reasoning from belief dynamics.

title: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated via truthful evidence in open channel
abstract: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. These findings expose a cognitive route to rumour amplification and support monitoring inferred relationships before agent-generated conclusions guide public decisions.

title: Full-Cover and Non-Overlapping Uni-domination in Graphs: Bounds and Complexity
abstract: A vertex is uni-dominated by a set $S \subseteq V(G)$ if exactly one vertex of $S$ lies in its closed neighborhood, and the uni-domination number $\mathrm{ud}^*(G)$ is the largest number of vertices a single set can uni-dominate. The graphs admitting an efficient dominating set are those with $\mathrm{ud}^*(G) = n$. Hedetniemi and Rall asked for the largest constant $c$ with $\mathrm{ud}^*(T) \geq c \cdot n$ for every tree $T$ of order $n$. We answer their question: the constant is $4/5$, and a set attaining it can be computed in linear time. This set is moreover a dominating set. Recall that an efficient dominating set satisfies two requirements at once: it dominates every vertex, and it dominates no vertex twice. Our set satisfies the first one, which leads us to study $\mathrm{ud}^*$ under each of the two requirements separately, giving the Full-Cover variant $\mathrm{ud}^*_0$ and the Non-Overlapping variant $\mathrm{ud}^*_+$. The two behave very differently: on arbitrarily large graphs $\mathrm{ud}^*_0$ may remain bounded by a constant, whereas $\mathrm{ud}^*_+$ always grows with the order. We present bounds for both, and show that the associated decision problems are polynomial for constant thresholds and NP-complete for the thresholds $\lceil \sqrt[c]{n} \rceil$ and $4\sqrt{n}$, respectively, the latter even on split graphs. Finally, we show that neither of the two parameters bounds the other.

title: Symmetric Chemical Reaction Networks: Realizations and Steady States
abstract: We investigate symmetric chemical reaction networks and their steady states. From classical equivariant dynamical systems and network theory it is known that the mass- action ODE of any symmetric chemical reaction network is equivariant. For symmetries that permute the species, we prove that any equivariant mass-action ODE is realized by a symmetric chemical reaction network and construct a sparsest such realization. We apply the half-degree principle to show that a symmetric CRN that has a steady state also has one with few distinct coordinates.

title: No complete set of mutually unbiased bases in dimension ten contains the Fourier pair or three product bases
abstract: With computer-assisted proofs that $\mathbb{C}^6$ admits at most three mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) now available, $\mathbb{C}^{10}$ is the smallest dimension in which it is unknown whether a complete set of $d+1=11$ MUBs exists; only three MUBs are known. We prove that every triple of mutually unbiased product bases of $\mathbb{C}^2\otimes\mathbb{C}^5$ is strongly unextendible: no vector is unbiased to all three bases. Consequently no set of four MUBs in dimension ten, and in particular no complete set, contains three product bases. This settles the case $d=2\times5$ anticipated by McNulty, Pammer and Weigert; it was known only for the Heisenberg-Weyl triple. The proof covers all ten equivalence classes with explicit Nullstellensatz certificates modulo one prime on $91$ charts of $\mathbb{P}^9\times\mathbb{P}^9$ for each class ($910$ in all), transferred to characteristic zero by a projective reduction lemma, together with an independent rank certificate for eight of the ten classes. We also prove that the pair formed by the standard and the Fourier basis of $\mathbb{C}^{10}$ is contained in no set of four MUBs. Exactly $3040$ rays are unbiased to both bases (this confirms the count found numerically by Führ and Rzeszotnik), each of them is unbiased to at most eight of the others, and every triple formed by the pair and a third MUB is strongly unextendible. For this we certify $34,940$ cyclic $10$-roots in Krawczyk uniqueness boxes, decide unimodularity exactly through an involution, and prove completeness by a four-dimensional interval branch-and-bound obtained from the Chinese-remainder splitting $\mathbb{Z}_{10}=\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_5$.

title: A Polynomial Time Algorithm for Finding a Minimum 5-Partition of a Submodular Function
abstract: Given a real-valued submodular function on a finite ground set, the minimum $k$-partition problem asks for a partition into $k$ nonempty parts minimizing the sum of their function values. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for $k=5$. The idea follows directly from the previous $k=4$ result, where there is precisely one obstruction for generalizing it to $k=5$. We show the special case can be handled by reasoning about a restricted family of $3$-partitions.

title: Intransigence or compromise: concatenated opinion dynamics with voting feedback
abstract: In this paper, we study opinion evolution in a sequence of Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) models, concatenated so that the final opinions of each model serve as the initial opinions of the next. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. With the state-dependent switching of stubbornness, the dynamics are not guaranteed to be contractive. We show that, over any fixed strongly connected network, the opinions always converge. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.

title: Gorenstein toric Fano $d$-varieties have Picard ranks at most $2d$
abstract: We show that the Picard rank of $d$-dimensional Gorenstein toric Fano varieties is at most $2d$. This generalizes Batyrev's conjecture of Picard ranks for smooth toric Fano varieties, which was proved by Casagrande for all $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial Gorenstein toric Fano varieties. The convex-geometric proof is a generalization of Casagrande's proof and Eikelberg's theory of non-$\mathbb{Q}$-factorial toric Picard groups, with key ideas from work of Debarre, Øbro, Fujita and the first author. The proof was found using ChatGPT 6.1.

title: Centralizers in Catalan Monoids
abstract: Fix a chain $X_n=\{1<\cdots<n\}$, where $n$ is a positive integer. The Catalan monoid $\mathcal{C}_n$ consists of all decreasing and order-preserving transformations of $X_n$, with function composition as the operation. For $β\in\mathcal{C}_n$, its centralizer is $C(β)=\{α\in\mathcal{C}_n:αβ=βα\}$. We characterize the elements of $C(\varepsilon)$, $C(μ)$, and $C(β)$, where $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{C}_n$ is an idempotent, $μ\in\mathcal{C}_n$ is a nilpotent, and $β\in\mathcal{C}_n$ is a general element. For an idempotent $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{C}_n$, we derive formulas for the cardinality of $C(\varepsilon)$, as well as formulas for the numbers of idempotents and nilpotents of $C(\varepsilon)$. We relate indexing sets arising in these formulas to Dyck paths and Narayana numbers. For a nilpotent $μ\in\mathcal{C}_n$, we present algorithms that construct $C(μ)$, its subset of idempotents, and its subsemigroup of nilpotents, thereby determining their cardinalities. We also describe the nilpotents whose centralizers consist only of idempotents, of nilpotents together with the identity, or of nilpotents and idempotents. We extend these descriptions to arbitrary elements of $\mathcal{C}_n$. To obtain our results, we represent $β\in\mathcal{C}_n$ as a sequence $\langle T_1,\ldots,T_m\rangle$ of rooted trees. The sets of vertices of the trees form a partition of $X_n$. Each tree is level-ordered, which means that it can be drawn in such a way that moving from the root down, level by level, from left to right at each level, we pass through an increasing sequence of consecutive elements of $X_n$.

title: CoopDistill: Equilibrium-Guided Multi-Agent Policy Distillation for Cooperative Driving
abstract: Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency. Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) explores alternatives through interaction, but coordinated learning and safe execution remain challenging. Their integration nevertheless faces challenges in exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and execution reliability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation framework. A potential-game (PG) formulation provides a fixed-path longitudinal reference, around which a residual MARL policy learns longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path corrections. A hard-case curriculum concentrates experience on interactions that PG leaves unresolved or substantially delayed. A comparative rollout selector evaluates the joint consequences of learned corrections against PG before choosing the executed action. Experiments in merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios compare CoopDistill with six baselines at four connected automated vehicle penetration levels. Relative to PG, success improves by 2.1--27.1 percentage points and delay decreases by 7.3--27.3\%, with no observed collisions. Code is available at https://github.com/FanGShiYuu/CoopDistill

title: OpenMAS-GApp: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Domain-Adaptive Multi-Agent Application Construction
abstract: Constructing multi-agent system (MAS) applications across domains requires translating diverse requirements into executable systems, involving task decomposition, agent and tool selection, and execution organization. Existing studies have explored individual aspects of MAS construction, including agent generation, architecture design, workflow generation, and component selection. However, these methods are often developed and evaluated independently, using different task specifications, component resources, and execution settings. This makes it difficult to compare their construction capabilities or determine how they can be applied to different domains. To address this problem, we propose OpenMAS-GApp, a One-for-All benchmark for MAS application construction across diverse domains. It standardizes task inputs, component resources, construction interfaces, and execution environments to support MAS construction under consistent conditions. Within OpenMAS-GApp, we provide Graph Harness as a reference construction method that derives task dependencies, selects compatible agents and tools, and organizes their interactions into executable graphs. We evaluate construction methods across 19 benchmark datasets under 20 evaluation settings spanning four application types and four professional domains.

title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations
abstract: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

title: Projective planes with abelian collineation groups of type (F) are Desarguesian
abstract: We use prime ideal factorization and residue class fields of cyclotomic integer rings to prove that every abelian direct product difference set is classical. This implies that every projective plane of order $n$ with an abelian collineation group of order $n(n-1)$ is Desarguesian, proving a conjecture of Jungnickel and de Resmini. As a consequence, we obtain the classification of circular Costas maps and of Costas polynomials conjectured by Muratovic-Ribic, Pott, Thomson and Wang and by Torres and Rubio.

title: Discriminants and resultants of orthogonal polynomials
abstract: The concept of a linked pair of two sequences of polynomials, one of which is orthogonal, is introduced. Such a pair always has a resultant that factors. Two methods for producing such linked pairs are given: one for general orthogonal polynomials and the other for any polynomial in the Askey scheme. Generalized discriminants are introduced and evaluated, including a general product formula for each operator in the Askey scheme. A new notion of companion orthogonal polynomials is also introduced and used to evaluate the discriminants of orthogonal polynomials. These methods recover all known formulas for the generalized discriminants of classical polynomials and provide new ones.

title: Triples in matroid circuits
abstract: We prove that, if $X$ is a four-element independent set in a vertically $5$-connected representable matroid $M$, then either there is a circuit of $M$ that contains at least three elements of $X$, or there is a representation $A$ of $M$ such that each column of $A$ has at most two non-zero elements and each of the columns indexed by $X$ has exactly one non-zero element. We also prove a version of this result without the connectivity assumptions.

title: From Vision to Interaction: Evaluating Dynamic Social Intelligence of VLM Agents in ALIVE-World
abstract: As AI agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications and take on social roles, dynamic social intelligence, the ability to continuously perceive multimodal cues, infer latent cognitive states, intervene through embodied actions, and ultimately achieve social goals, has become essential. However, existing evaluations largely fragment social intelligence into text-based abstractions, static reasoning tasks, or embodied simulators that lack social dynamics. These approaches fail to capture the multimodal, continuous, and interpersonal complexity of authentic human interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce ALIVE-World, an embodied simulation environment supporting dynamic multimodal interactions encompassing egocentric vision, language, and non-verbal action. To provide socially grounded interactive feedback, we populate this environment with counterpart agents driven by a profile-conditioned, dual-system (intuitive-affective and logical-cognitive) architecture. Building upon this platform, we propose ALIVE-Bench to transform the assessment of social intelligence into a trackable quantitative framework. By deeply leveraging underlying environmental states and agents' internal variables, ALIVE-Bench systematically evaluates Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents across four critical dimensions: perception, understanding, influence, and outcome. Extensive evaluations reveal that dynamic social intelligence is fundamentally multi-dimensional and scenario-dependent. We identify a critical bottleneck between upstream perception and downstream social intervention, exposing VLM vulnerabilities in fine-grained proxemic awareness, adaptive intervention, and multi-party coordination. By uncovering these limitations and the diverse interaction strategies they produce, this benchmark provides actionable insights for the future behavioral alignment of multimodal agents.

title: List colouring of circular-arc graphs
abstract: A circular-arc graph takes a set of nonempty closed arcs on a circle as its vertex set, and two vertices are adjacent when their corresponding arcs intersect on the circle. We show the chromatic number of any circular-arc graph equals its list chromatic number. Our methodology is an application of Schauz's coefficient formula within the Alon-Tarsi and Combinatorial Nullstellensatz framework.

title: LEDGER: Auditable Agent Memory Under Change
abstract: Agent memory systems are mostly evaluated on fixed histories, and only their final answers are scored. In real use, facts change, sources differ in reliability, and users ask the agent to forget things. We present LEDGER, a memory layer in which a language model proposes facts and explicit rules decide which value is current, which source to trust, and what to delete. Each fact keeps its source and the period in which it held. LEDGER+EP adds a search over raw conversation turns for questions the ledger does not cover, and scrubs these turns on deletion. We compare both against no memory, full-history replay, retrieval over raw transcripts, and Mem0, with the same answering model and prompt, on a synthetic multi-session coding-agent workload and a 210-question subset of LongMemEval, and we score both the evidence each memory sends to the model and the answer. On the coding workload, LEDGER+EP in fallback mode answers 94.3% of questions correctly on five development seeds and 91.1% on five held-out seeds, against 82.1% and 83.3% for full replay, the strongest baseline. When a deletion request only describes the fact, no deleted value reached our systems' evidence in any evaluated probe. On LongMemEval, LEDGER+EP in augment mode has the same observed accuracy as full replay (74.8%) with 1% of its context.
