The main limitation is that the coding workload is synthetic and built by us; on LongMemEval, the differences between the strongest systems are within the confidence intervals.

title: Linear Algebra over Bands
abstract: We introduce Eckmann-Hilton operators on bands, which allow for a suite of matroidal constructions, in particular, matroid unions and matroid stable intersections. This enables the construction of general linear monoids over bands. Geometrically, we show that matroid stable intersection extends the transverse intersection of linear spaces over fields and the stable intersection of tropical linear spaces, lending new insight into intersection theory on bands.

title: Nearly Settling the Complexity of Connected $\varepsilon$-Envy-Free Cake Cutting
abstract: Envy-free cake cutting has been one of the central problems in fair division. In cake cutting, agents' preferences over the cake are accessed through Robertson--Webb (RW) queries. For three or more agents, no algorithm that makes finitely many RW queries can always find a contiguous, exactly envy-free allocation. For contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free allocations, however, Hollender and Rubinstein~(JACM, 2025) showed that $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ RW queries suffice for four agents, leaving open whether such a bound is possible for five or more agents. In this paper, we establish a striking change in query complexity: $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ RW queries suffice for up to five agents, whereas $(1/\varepsilon)^{Ω(1)}$ queries are necessary for seven or more agents, even when valuations are additive. Thus, we resolve the five-agent case and, more broadly, determine whether polylogarithmic query complexity is possible for every number of agents except six. We also explore the computational complexity of finding contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free allocations. When monotone Lipschitz valuations are given by polynomial-time evaluation procedures (e.g., arithmetic circuits and efficiently computable Turing machines), we show that an $\varepsilon$-envy-free division can be computed in polynomial time for five agents. In contrast, even for additive valuations, finding an $\varepsilon$-envy-free division is UEOPL-hard for every fixed number of agents $n\ge7$ and PPAD-complete for every fixed $n\ge13$.

title: Highlighting Ukrainian Contributions to the Development of the Field of Particle Physics
abstract: The contribution examines the role played by Ukrainian scientists, both in Ukraine and abroad, in the development of particle physics.

title: Characterization of Cubic Graphs with Exactly Two Lonely Edges
abstract: Perfect matchings are fundamental to understanding structural connectivity in cubic graphs, with "lonely edges" (edges in exactly one perfect matching) forming a critical underexplored class. Goedgebeur et al. (J. Graph Theory, 112 (2026) 276-289) established an upper bound of 6 on the number of lonely edges in 3-connected non-double covered cubic graphs and completely characterized the classes $\mathcal{U}_k$ for $3 \le k \le 6$. Narayana et al. subsequently gave a recursive characterization of the subclass in which the two lonely edges lie in the same perfect matching. This paper completes the classification by presenting a full structural characterization of $\mathcal{U}_2$, the family of 3-connected cubic graphs with exactly two lonely edges. We identify the minimally non-contractible "primitive kernels" of $\mathcal{U}_2$ and develop constructive operations to generate any graph in $\mathcal{U}_2$ from these kernels.

title: Creation Sequences for Numerical Semigroups and Exact Counts of Semigroup Partitions
abstract: A numerical semigroup is a subset of the non-negative integers that contains $0$, is closed under addition and has finite complement. A threshold graph is built by adding vertices one at a time, each new vertex being isolated or dominating, and the record of these choices is its \emph{creation sequence}. Reading the creation sequence as a lattice path gives an integer partition and, through the Keith--Nath correspondence, a numerical set in which the dominating vertices are the elements and the isolated vertices are the gaps. We show that threshold graphs with an isolated vertex correspond bijectively to numerical sets, and we study numerical semigroups through their creation sequences. We prove that in the creation sequence of a numerical semigroup of multiplicity $m$ every block of ones and every non-initial block of zeros has length less than $m$, we give criteria for partitions with a unique smallest part and with two distinct part sizes, and we classify all partitions with at most four parts. We show that every partition $λ$ with $g$ parts corresponding to a numerical semigroup satisfies $\ell(λ)\geλ_1$ and, more strongly, fits inside the staircase $(g,g-1,\dots,1)$; equivalently, its creation sequence begins with a Dyck path. Its size equals the genus plus the Weierstrass weight of the semigroup, and asymptotically at most half of all partitions correspond to numerical semigroups. Finally, we obtain exact formulas for the numbers of partitions of $n$ corresponding to numerical semigroups of genus $g$, multiplicity $m$ and Frobenius number $f$, valid in the sharp ranges $g\ge n/2$, $m>n/3$ and $f\ge n-\frac{n-1}{4}$. These formulas solve the open problems posed by Burson, Nam and Sisneros-Thiry \cite{BNS}, recover all of their counting theorems, and correct several of their statements.

title: Collapsibility of Vietoris--Rips complexes of hypercube graphs in codimension two
abstract: Shukla conjectured that the collapsibility number of the Vietoris-Rips complex $\mathrm{VR}(I_n;r)$ of the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph at scale $r$ equals $2^r$ for all $n\ge r+1$. We prove the conjecture for $n=r+2$ and every $r$, which gives the first known cases with $r\ge 4$ beyond the cross-polytope case $n=r+1$. Writing $\mathrm{VR}(I_n;r)$ as the independence complex of the graph $H_{n,r}$ that joins two points when their Hamming distance exceeds $r$, we construct a cover of $H_{r+2,r}$ by $2^r$ co-chordal subgraphs. The key general tool is the inequality that, for every graph $G$, the $θ$-number of Bıyıkoğlu and Civan of the independence complex of $G$, and hence the collapsibility number of that complex, is at most the co-chordal cover number of $G$; this strengthens Woodroofe's regularity bound. We also show, using a theorem of Alon, Jin, and Sudakov, that the induced matching number of $H_{n,r}$ equals $2^r$ for every $n>r$, and that $\mathrm{VR}(I_n;r)$ is vertex decomposable if and only if $r=1$ or $n=r+1$. As consequences, we determine the top degree of nonvanishing homology and the coconnectivity of $\mathrm{VR}(I_{r+2};r)$, and we prove split injectivity in top-degree integral homology. Finally, assuming a recent skew Hamming set-pair theorem of Gao and Zhao, we prove that the collapsibility number of $\mathrm{VR}(I_n;r)$ is at most $2^{r+1}-4$ for all $n>r\ge 2$.

title: A Recursive Construction of Perfect Arrays of Every Shape $2^{a_1}\times\cdots\times2^{a_d}$ over the Unit Quaternions
abstract: We extend the recursive construction of perfect and odd perfect sequences over the simple unit quaternions $\Qe=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ of Blake to arrays of any dimension. The three operations of that construction act on one direction of an array at a time, and are valid whenever the array is periodic in the remaining directions. Starting from a perfect array $P$ of shape $M_2\times\cdots\times M_d$ they give perfect arrays of shape $2^a\times M_2\times\cdots\times M_d$ for every $a\ge0$, with explicit index functions and with the array orthogonality property for the divisor $2$ in the lifted direction; from $a=5$ on these arrays are, in general, Kronecker products of a sequence with $P$ in neither order. Applied direction by direction, the construction gives perfect arrays over $\Qe$ in every shape $2^{a_1}\times\cdots\times2^{a_d}$, and in every shape $2^{a_1}\times\cdots\times2^{a_{d-1}}\times N$ for which a perfect sequence of length $N$ over $\Qe$ exists. The contrast with the binary alphabet is sharp: a perfect binary array of shape $2^{a_1}\times\cdots\times2^{a_d}$ exists only when $\sum a_k$ is even and $\max a_k\le\frac12\sum a_k+1$, by a theorem of Jedwab and Kraemer on Menon difference sets in abelian $2$-groups, whereas over $\Qe$ there is no constraint on the shape. We also show that, unlike the one-dimensional case, single arrays carrying a non-central twist do exist in two dimensions, and determine where the one-dimensional non-existence argument breaks.

title: Relationship between generic Hecke algebra modules and $0$-Hecke algebra modules
abstract: Let $H_{R,a}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ be the Hecke algebra over a principal ideal domain $R$ with parameter $a\in R$. The representation theories of $H_{\mathbb{C}(v^{1/2});v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ and $H_{\mathbb{C};0}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ differ substantially and have largely been studied independently. In this paper, we relate the categories of finitely generated modules of these two algebras through specialization functors from the category of finitely generated $H_{\mathbb{C}[v^{1/2}];v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$-modules. We first investigate the fundamental properties of these functors concerning dimensions, essential surjectivity, and characters. We then construct $H_{\mathbb{C}[v^{1/2}];v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$-modules which, through these functors, provide connections between skew Specht modules of $H_{\mathbb{C}(v^{1/2});v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ and $0$-Hecke skew Specht modules of $H_{\mathbb{C};0}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$, and between Kazhdan--Lusztig cell modules of $H_{\mathbb{C}(v^{1/2});v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ and dual plactic class modules of $H_{\mathbb{C};0}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$. Both families of $H_{\mathbb{C};0}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$-modules are closely related to regular Schur labeled skew shape posets. We further explore how specialization functors relate the Frobenius characteristic to the quasisymmetric characteristic and connects the branching rules for skew Specht modules with those for $0$-Hecke skew Specht modules. Finally, we use the established connection with Kazhdan--Lusztig cell modules to obtain a result on the classification of dual plactic class modules up to isomorphism.

title: On homogeneous hypertournaments
abstract: Sullivan recently constructed continuum many countable homogeneous $n$-hypertournaments for every $n\ge3$ by forbidding configurations he calls pair-cancelling. We show that, for every family $\mathcal F$ of pair-cancelling $n$-hypertournaments, the class of all linearly ordered finite $\mathcal F$-free $n$-hypertournaments is Ramsey and has the ordering property. In particular, freely ordered $\mathbf{H}_4$-free $3$-hypertournaments are Ramsey, answering a question of Cherlin, Hubička, Nešetřil, and the author from 2021. For every odd $n\ge3$, we give a simple Ramsey expansion with the expansion property for even $n$-hypertournaments by naming an $(n-1)$-hypertournament and a free linear order. We also show that, for $n\ge6$, no unbounded hereditary strong amalgamation class of finite $n$-hypertournaments has EPPA. Moreover, we prove the failure of EPPA for all Sullivan's classes with $n\ge4$, and for the even $5$-hypertournaments. We conjecture that even hypertournaments and classes omitting a family of pair-cancelling hypertournaments, together with the homogeneous cyclic order in arity three, are the only countably infinite homogeneous $n$-hypertournaments for $n\ge3$. We give some supporting evidence.

title: Treewidth and Separation Number: An Optimal Linear Bound
abstract: The \emph{separation number} $\sn(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the smallest integer $a$ such that every subgraph $H$ of $G$ admits a separation $(A,B)$ of {\em order} $|A\cap B|\le a$ whose two sides $A\setminus B$ and $B\setminus A$ each contain at most $2|V(H)|/3$ vertices. Dvořák and Norin proved that $\tw(G)\le 15\sn(G)$ for every nonempty graph $G$. We improve the constant to its optimal value: every nonempty graph satisfies $\tw(G)\le 4\sn(G)-2$. This is best possible: for every $k\ge 2$, there is a graph $G_k$ with $\tw(G_k)=4k+2$ and $\sn(G_k)=k+1$.

title: Extensions of $q$-supercongruences arising from a quadratic summation of Gasper and Rahman
abstract: In this paper, inspired by recent work of Guo and Zhao, and of Guo and Zudilin, we establish two parametric extensions of their $q$-supercongruences using Gasper and Rahman's quadratic summation, the Chinese remainder theorem, and the creative microscoping method. These extensions yield two one-parameter generalizations of the $q$-supercongruences considered by Guo and Zhao and by Guo and Zudilin.

title: When Does Interaction Help? Toward a Reynolds Number for Collective Intelligence
abstract: Multi-agent systems combine distributed information through interaction, which can improve performance but also spread errors or suppress useful differences. Predicting when interaction helps is central to understanding and designing collective intelligence. We investigate whether a few dimensionless parameters can predict gains over explicitly defined non-communicating baselines across group sizes, network structures, and tasks, toward a Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence. Using distributed classification tasks, stochastic tracking networks, and neural cellular automata, we combine analytical and empirical evidence to examine information sufficiency, dynamical applicability, and finite-sample prediction. We construct inference systems with bounded random variables and matching specified joint moments up to total degree three, yet opposite interaction gains under a fixed readout. These moments alone cannot generally determine the gain sign. Tracking networks likewise exhibit gain reversals despite matched candidate parameters when task power occupies different spectral modes. Under concentrated task spectra and aligned observation noise, however, we derive a low-dimensional similarity relation with an explicit zero-delay error bound and test it across network sizes and topologies under frozen protocols. The relation does not directly apply to the neural cellular systems, where a separate moment-based predictor underperforms direct gain measurement at matched calibration sample budgets. These results establish conditions and limits for low-dimensional gain prediction, providing a restricted similarity law while leaving a general Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence open.

title: Percolation under Edge-Reversal: Creation and Destruction of Strong Connectivity in Directed Networks
abstract: We study how the connectivity of a directed network changes when each edge is independently reversed with probability $p$, while the underlying connections remain fixed. Reversal changes the in- and out-degrees, and we derive the exact transformation of the joint in--out-degree distribution and characterize its evolution under repeated reversal. However, the transformation does not rewire the network, and every edge still connects the same pair of vertices. As a result, the transformed degree distribution alone does not determine whether a giant strongly connected component exists, and a reconstruction based only on the transformed degrees can even place the network on the wrong percolation state. For the directed configuration model, we account for the preserved structure by separately tracking edges that retain or reverse their original direction, leading to a two-type branching process. From this formalism, we obtain explicit analytical criteria for the creation or destruction of a giant strongly connected component and illustrate these contrasting outcomes with empirical examples. Consistent with the predicted creation criterion, randomizing edge directions in a \emph{S. cerevisiae} transcriptional regulation network dramatically increases the size of the largest strongly connected component. In the San Diego directed road network, the degree moments satisfy the destruction criterion, and the largest strongly connected component decreases to virtually zero, although its decline occurs well below the predicted configuration-model threshold. These results provide a framework for assessing the sensitivity of mutual reachability to changes or uncertainty in edge directions and show that directional disorder can either enable or suppress global connectivity without changing the underlying connections.

title: Near-synchronous multiphoton quantum interference
abstract: Nonclassical multiphoton interference is an important resource for optical quantum information processing, and its output statistics depend on the distinguishability of the input photons. In this paper, using time delay as a tunable parameter, we theoretically analyze the interference behavior of independent pure-state single photons with identical Gaussian spectral envelopes under near-synchronous conditions. Using the immanant representation of the single-photon internal-state overlap matrix to express the weights of the exchange-symmetry components, we determine the leading asymptotic behavior and approximation error of each weight, and characterize the weight suppression laws when different groups of photons become synchronized on different scales. Given the local identity classes of the delay functions and the vanishing orders of pairwise delay differences, the vanishing orders of the weights of the exchange-symmetry components can be computed in polynomial time by integer minimum-cost flow. On this basis, we provide a network-independent total-variation error bound for the complete output photon-number distribution, establish a quantitative relationship among the photon spectral width, synchronization precision, and interference statistics deviation, and provide a quantitative basis for the analysis and approximation of near-synchronous multiphoton interference.

title: Borrowed Strength, Imported Risk: Capability Gaps and Reception Govern Heterogeneous LLM Debate
abstract: Heterogeneous LLM debate is often attributed to collective reasoning that creates capability beyond any member. In the matched panels we study, the aggregate gain is dominated by capability transfer: a peer supplies task competence and receivers absorb a measurable fraction. Across nine matched directions, honest benefit and first-exchange adversarial exposure open when the peer has a positive same-task advantage, and honest gain is closely described by the empirical decomposition $ΔA_d^{\mathrm{hon}}\approxκΓ_d^+ρ_d$, the product of that advantage and the receiver's reception. Two fixed-receiver directions provide held-out validation without refitting: reception remains stable within uncertainty as a larger peer advantage produces a larger gain. A matched, single-direction open-answer MuSiQue scope probe reaches the negative-gap side of the same gate. Qwen-7B trails the Gemma-3-12B receivers by 10.78 points; despite 62.50% reception, it produces only +1.17 points of controlled first-exchange gain. Reception cannot substitute for positive aggregate peer advantage. When an influential peer is assigned an adversarial role, the same influential peer slot removes the borrowed gain and can push the panel below homogeneous debate. Across all five full-reference settings, the best observed majority correctness does not exceed the influential member's best observed accuracy, despite unused complementary answers. Heterogeneous debate is therefore a measurable transfer decision with a measurable failure mode, not a benefit conferred by diversity alone.

title: A Combinatorial Characterization of Immunity to the Strong Braess Paradox
abstract: In a nonatomic congestion game, a strong Braess paradox occurs when reducing resource costs, population demands, or both increases at least one population's equilibrium cost. We characterize immunity when each population's available strategies form a fixed finite family of nonempty subsets of a common resource set. Immunity means that no such paradox can arise for any nonnegative continuous nondecreasing resource cost functions common to all populations and any positive demand vector. Our characterization resolves the open question posed by Fujishige et al.(2017) without varying the resource embedding. A menu is positively exposed if it consists of all available strategies of minimum total weight for some strictly positive resource weights. For a single population, we prove that immunity holds if and only if the column matroid of the augmented incidence matrix is series-parallel for every positively exposed menu. For multiple populations, we consider one menu for each population, all exposed by the same positive weights. The associated dual matroid includes one labeled element for each population to track its demand. Immunity holds if and only if, for every such collection of menus, each marked resource block is series-parallel and all demand labels retained in that block are parallel. We establish these characterizations through an affine response criterion and a blockwise ray lemma. Our results recover the immunity of matroid base systems under arbitrary resource sharing and the series-parallel routing criterion for complete acyclic path systems. Whenever a strategy system is not immune, we construct a strong Braess paradox with all demands equal to one and affine resource costs having strictly positive slopes and intercepts, by lowering just one intercept while keeping it positive. When strategies are listed explicitly, nonimmunity has polynomial-size certificates.

title: A study guide for Bourgain's 2003 sum-product theorem and 2010 discretized projection theorem
abstract: These notes present Bourgain's proofs of the discretized sum-product theorem and its applications. The discussion emphasizes the construction of trees with multiscale porosity from small additive doubling, using either quantitative Freiman theorrem or the Plünnecke-Ruzsa inequality, and the amplification of these structures by multiplication. Additive combinatorial tools connect the resulting growth estimates to discretized sum-product problem. The notes also discuss the passage to the exceptional set estimates for orthogonal projections, the exclusion of Borel subrings of intermediate Hausdorff dimension, and Fourier decay for multiplicative convolutions of measures.

title: Learning Design Taste through Verifiable Synthetic Environments and Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Code-generating language models produce user interfaces that build and run, but the pages are often weak in hierarchy, spacing, typography and composition. We study whether a small code model can learn design taste through reinforcement learning in verifiable synthetic environments. The method has three components. First, a layered verification framework splits design quality into hard gates, render-grounded metrics, rubric judges, within-group relative preference and a blinded expert panel. A signal enters the reward only if it passes an admission protocol that tests agreement with experts, causal sensitivity, resistance to hack traps and stability. Second, following SCALER [1], synthetic design environments are parameterised generators with measured difficulty ladders: base pages are written once by an agentic coder, and instances are produced by syntax-tree perturbation operators and constraint samplers, scheduled by an adaptive curriculum with a quarantine rule against reward over-optimisation. Third, a 4B code model is trained with agentic reinforcement learning over multi-turn episodes in which it edits and builds a repository and reads a textual report of its own render, while hidden graders compute the reward. The admission protocol admits 7 of 16 render signals and 6 of 10 rubric dimensions. On TD-Bench, agentic training raises the Taste Index from 0.630 to 0.795 in-family and from 0.598 to 0.700 on held-out families, and wins 0.600 of blinded expert comparisons against the base model and 0.569 against a single-turn control. Most of the advantage depends on the inference-time loop, and cross-brief distinctiveness falls slightly below that of the base model, the only success criterion not met.

title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
abstract: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

title: $L$-systems on the large Witt design
abstract: Let $L=\{0,1,2,3,4,8\}$, associated with the large Witt design $S(5,8,24)$, and let $m(n,24,L)$ be the maximum size of a family of $24$-element subsets of an $n$-element set whose distinct members have intersection sizes in $L$. We prove that there are positive constants $c,C,n_0$ such that, for every $n\geq n_0$, \[ cn^{316/63}\leq m(n,24,L)\leq Cn^{169/29}. \] We also obtain similar results for the systems associated with $S(4,7,23)$, $S(3,6,22)$, and $S(3,4,14)$. The upper bounds follow from a non-Shannon information inequality and disprove conjectures of Kupavskii and Terekhov. The lower bounds follow from an algebraic construction for arbitrary Steiner systems.

title: Changing a View Is Not Amending a Record: Timing and Visibility in a Model of Public Correction
abstract: An accusation may remain on the public record after its author has changed their mind. Observers can respond either to what a person says now or to an earlier statement that has never been explicitly amended. We examine the consequences of these two signals with a generative agent-based model that separates private evidence updates, current expression, and revisions linked to a specific declaration. In paired worlds, evidence, prehistory, and opportunities to revisit that declaration remain fixed. When expression and amendment are synchronized and fully observed, the feedback channels produce identical trajectories. With sparse review, record-based feedback leaves 19.44 percentage points more eligible accusations unamended after 24 rounds (paired-world 95 percent bootstrap interval 13.89 to 25.31). The comparison averages 50 eligible worlds, containing 556 agents, from 128 newly generated worlds. Event traces show how a persistent public cue changes subsequent amendment propensity; an exact small-state calculation independently establishes the timing boundary. Reducing record salience can erase or reverse the increment, and a generic held-state process reproduces the dynamics. The findings show when current expression ceases to track correction of a particular public statement.

title: Graph Intersections and Hypergraph Discrepancy
abstract: Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs on $n$ vertices with $e(G)=p\binom{n}{2}$ and $e(H)=q\binom{n}{2}$, where $p,q\in(0,1)$ are fixed. Bollobás and Scott studied intersections of two graphs under random relabelling and asked for the minimum $L^2$ norm of the deviation of their intersection size from its expected value. We answer this question by proving that, for graphs of order $n$ with fixed edge densities $p,q\in(0,1)$, the minimum is \begin{equation*} \left(\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)q(1-q)}{2}\cdot\frac{1-\sqrt R}{1+\sqrt R}}\right)n+o(n), \end{equation*} where $R=\max\{p,1-p,q,1-q\}$. The coefficient of the linear term is best possible. Bollobás and Scott defined the positive and negative discrepancies of two hypergraphs as the largest deviations of their intersection size above and below its expected value under relabelling, respectively. They asked for the minimum product of the positive and negative discrepancies of two $(n/2)$-uniform hypergraphs on $n$ vertices with $\frac{1}{2}\binom{n}{n/2}$ edges. We answer this question by proving that the minimum product of these discrepancies is $0$ if $4\mid\binom{n}{n/2}$ and $1/4$ otherwise.

title: Effective and Efficient Rumor Assertion Over Large-Scale Social Networks (Technical Report)
abstract: Nowadays, social networks, like Facebook, X, Reddit, YouTube, and so on, have become essential online platforms for users to connect with friends daily, post/share news, and express their opinions/comments. Meanwhile, however, the rapid and widespread dissemination of rumors and misinformation across social networks has become a serious concern. Such misleading information can distort public opinion and potentially cause significant social and economic consequences in real-world scenarios, including product promotion, elections and voting, and even cyberbullying. Therefore, accurately and efficiently verifying whether news spread on social networks is rumor or truth has become an increasingly important yet challenging problem. While previous works usually identified rumors by their contents, in this paper, we propose a novel \textit{user behavior model} to capture the users' judgment/discriminative abilities, which is learned via our well-designed evidence-aware probability reconstructor. We develop a general framework for tackling \textit{rumor assertion over large-scale social networks} (RA-SN), which can efficiently and effectively determine whether a given news item is a rumor with high confidence, based on users' behaviors, in a scalable manner. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed RA-SN approach on both real-world and synthetic graphs.

title: Recurrent losers: A network approach to cover-bidding patterns in public procurement
abstract: We develop and apply a network-based method to examine patterns consistent with cover bidding within procurement markets, using only bidder participation and winner identities. A statistical test identifies relationships in which firms win unusually often when particular competitors also bid. These relationships form a directed graph with links from recurrent losers to recurrent winners. We use maximum $k$-core to classify possible organizational forms of cover bidding and propose tender exposure -- the share of contested tenders involving a reported relationship -- as a market-level indicator of potential cover-bidding risk. Applied to 200,065 contracts procured by district engineering offices of the Philippine Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) from 2017 to 2025, covering three congressional terms, the method identifies 8,728 directed relationships across 407 of 564 markets. The $k$-core classes differ in network breadth, relationship depth, and bidder roles. In simpler networks, each recurrent loser is usually tied to a single winner, while highly interconnected networks involve multiple recurrent winners and broader groups of bidders that rarely win. Some of the deepest relationships and highest levels of tender exposure occur in intermediate networks, showing how relationships can reach much of a market without extensive interconnectedness. Offices named in official investigations more often contain highly interconnected networks than other offices. Two of the three offices referred for bid rigging are among the twelve in our ranking with the highest exposure in 2023-2025.

title: A proof of a conjecture on bipartite correspondence packing
abstract: A correspondence cover assigns a set of possible colors to each vertex of a graph. For each edge, a matching between the two endpoint color sets specifies the forbidden color pairs. A correspondence coloring selects one color at each vertex so that no forbidden pair is selected. A full correspondence packing is a collection of such colorings that uses every color at each vertex exactly once. We prove a conjecture of Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, Davies, and Kang [Random Structures & Algorithms 64 (2024), 62--93]. For every sufficiently large $D$, there is a positive integer $k(D)=(1+o(1))D/\log D$ such that every correspondence cover of any finite bipartite graph has a full correspondence packing if each color has at most $D$ forbidden partners and each vertex has $k(D)$ colors. More precisely, we prove this conclusion with \[ k(D)=\left\lceil\frac{D}{\log D-2\log\log D-6}\right\rceil \] for every integer $D\ge\lceil e^{20}\rceil$.

title: Physics-informed neural network for model-based global computation of the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators
abstract: The asymptotic phase is the central object of phase reduction theory for limit-cycle oscillators. It is a scalar coordinate defined throughout the basin of attraction of a limit cycle that advances at a constant natural frequency along every trajectory. Computing the phase from a given mathematical model requires solving a first-order partial differential equation (PDE) over the entire basin, which is challenging due to high computation costs and complex boundary conditions. In this study, we propose a physics-informed neural network to efficiently calculate the asymptotic phase of limit-cycle oscillators. By incorporating three types of loss functions, we train a physics-informed neural network (PINN) to satisfy the governing PDE for the asymptotic phase and the adjoint equation for the phase gradient. The trained network delivers the phase function accurately and, via automatic differentiation, allows the calculation of the phase gradient governing the oscillator's response to perturbations, which enables rapid entrainment closed-loop control using strong inputs. We validate the approach using three types of limit-cycle oscillators and demonstrate that the PINN can facilitate fast and global phase-locking control.

title: Equilateral-triangle-free sets in finite planes
abstract: For a prime $p>3$, let $F(p)$ be the largest cardinality of a subset of $\mathbb F_p^2$ containing no equilateral triangle with nonzero squared side length. Alex Iosevich asked for the exact value of $F(p)$. By constructing such subsets of $\mathbb F_p^2$ from cap sets in $\mathbb F_3^n$, we obtain the uniform lower bounds \[ F(p)\gg \begin{cases} p^{2γ}, & p\equiv 11\pmod{12},\\ p^{1+γ}, & p\equiv 1\pmod{12}. \end{cases} \] Here $γ=\log_3(2.2202)$, so the two exponents are $1.452008666\ldots$ and $1.726004333\ldots$, respectively. We also apply a quantitative corners theorem to show that $F(p)=o(p^2)$ as $p\to\infty$ through either congruence class.

title: Payoff-Based Certificates for Convergence to Pure Nash Equilibria under Replicator Dynamics
abstract: For finite bimatrix games, we give a payoff-based sufficient condition $E>0$ for an interior initial state to converge to a specified strict pure Nash equilibrium under replicator dynamics. The construction combines lower bounds on the growth rates of log probability ratios between target and alternative actions with a first integral of a two-dimensional comparison system. It allows one player's payoff advantage to compensate for the other's disadvantage, certifying convergence even when a target action initially loses probability. For rational inputs and integration base points with algebraic exponentials, we give a finite exact test. We obtain closed-form box probabilities and, when all nontarget actions are included, closed-form upper bounds on convergence time. In two-action coordination games, choosing the base points at the sign thresholds recovers the full basin of attraction. Experiments on random games show that basin coverage shrinks rapidly with the number of actions. For $n=4,5,6$, median entry times are approximately 70% of median box-entry times without shifts and 40% for a union over 16 shift choices. Extensions cover multiplayer games through cooperative comparison systems and explicit boxes, and discrete-time exponential-weights learning under explicit step-size conditions.

title: Settling the Support Complexity of Correlated Equilibria
abstract: We study the support complexity of approximate correlated equilibria (CE) in two-player games, that is, the minimum number of pure action profiles that must be assigned positive probability to approximate a correlated equilibrium of a two-player matrix game. For $\varepsilon$-approximate coarse correlated equilibria, constant approximation is possible with support $O(\log N/\varepsilon^2)$ in $N\times N$ games. For correlated equilibria, the best known upper bound was $O(\log^2 N/\varepsilon^4)$ [Babichenko et al., 2014, 2017], but whether this bound was tight remained open. We establish a matching lower bound, resolving the open question of Ko and Schvartzman [2017]. Specifically, we show that, already for two-player zero-sum games, for every $1\leq k\leq N^{1/2}$ the worst-case correlated-equilibrium gap achievable by a distribution supported on at most $k$ pure profiles is $$ Θ\left( \min\left\{1,\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{k^{1/4}}\right\} \right), $$ which implies a $Θ(\log^2 N/\varepsilon^4)$ worst-case support bound. The proof builds on a probabilistic-method construction based on random sign matrices.

title: Demographic dynamics of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025
abstract: We investigate the demographic evolution of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025 using bibliometric data from 23,274 publications in major journals in the field. The number of active Japan-affiliated authors increased from approximately 600 in the late 1990s to more than 2,000 by the early 2020s, while annual publication output reached approximately 1,400 by 2025. Participation was highly heterogeneous, with 46% of authors observed in only one publication year within the study period and a smaller core showing long observed participation periods. We define the Community Renewal Rate (CRR) as a community-level measure of renewal, calculated as the fraction of active authors not observed during a specified preceding interval. The 5-year CRR typically remained near one quarter of the active community, with annual values ranging from approximately 21% to 33%, indicating persistent renewal despite substantial community growth. An order-of-magnitude comparison suggests that newly entering students account for only part of the renewal-author population. The community therefore expanded while sustaining both continuity through authors with long observed participation periods and renewal through recurring changes in active membership.

title: Canonical activation patterns and ReLU pattern varieties
abstract: A ReLU pattern variety records the polynomial relations among the coefficients of the affine maps associated with a prescribed set of activation patterns of a ReLU network. We study how the combinatorics of the canonical set of activation patterns of an unbiased ReLU network is reflected in the geometry of its pattern variety. In particular, we introduce the notion of pattern stability and characterize pattern stability and combinatorial stability for shallow networks. When the associated wall graph is connected and contains an edge of every neuron label, we resolve a problem of Alexandr and Montúfar by determining the defining ideal of the associated pattern variety explicitly. We establish a hierarchy of progressively weaker equivalence relations relating labeled combinatorial equivalence, equality and permutation equivalence of canonical pattern sets, and equivalences of the associated varieties. Finally, we relate functional dimension to the differential of the pattern map and show that it is bounded above by the dimension of the canonical pattern variety at every depth. For nondegenerate shallow networks, we give an exact formula for the functional dimension; for every shallow architecture, it equals the dimension of the canonical pattern variety on an open dense set of full Lebesgue measure.

title: Sidorenko Inequalities in Oriented Graphs
abstract: We introduce relative Sidorenko and relative anti-Sidorenko inequalities for oriented graphs, strengthening the corresponding well-studied notions for tournaments by allowing arbitrary host graphs. An orientation $\vec H$ of a graph $H$ is relatively Sidorenko if $\hom(\vec H,\vec G) \ge 2^{-e(H)}\hom(H,G)$ for every oriented graph $\vec G$ with underlying graph $G$, and relatively anti-Sidorenko if the reverse inequality holds. We provide a complete characterisation of the class of connected relatively Sidorenko graphs in terms of weakly norming graphs, and exhibit several families of relatively Sidorenko and relatively anti-Sidorenko oriented graphs. Despite the substantially stronger definitions, many known tournament Sidorenko and anti-Sidorenko examples satisfy the relative inequalities, suggesting a broader theory of these phenomena in arbitrary host graphs and motivating several new structural and classification problems.

title: Near Resonance, Less Ordered: Radius and Mass Ordering in Compact Multi-planet Systems
abstract: Compact multi-planet systems exhibit a tendency for planetary radii to follow ordered sequences with orbital position, suggesting that these non-random patterns preserve a fossil record of their formation. Here, we investigate whether ordering of planet radii and masses with orbital period is related to proximity to mean-motion resonances. We compare near-resonant and non-resonant systems using complementary rank- and inversion-based measures of ordering, while accounting for differences in planet multiplicity and uncertainties in the measured planetary properties. We find that radii and masses are less monotonically ordered in near-resonant systems than in non-resonant systems, with the primary radius analysis providing stronger evidence than the mass analysis. This result is opposite to the naive expectation that dynamical instabilities should erase the primordial ordering of initially resonant systems and leave non-resonant systems in a more disordered state.

title: Second-class particle in ASEP. Rarefaction fan
abstract: We study the asymptotic behavior of a second class particle in ASEP on the integer lattice. We prove a general formula for the distribution of its position at any fixed time for arbitrary initial conditions. As a first application, we obtain its limiting distribution for arbitrary initial conditions in the rarefaction fan case, generalizing the result of Cator--Pimentel from TASEP to ASEP.

title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms
abstract: We present the first complete implementation of $β$-reduction in the untyped $λ$-calculus using exclusively spiking neural dynamics. Every step of the reduction---redex detection, subterm segmentation, variable-binding detection, De~Bruijn index arithmetic, token copying, and inter-step role maintenance---is performed by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with explicit membrane dynamics, exponential synaptic currents, axonal delays, and pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Each neural component maps onto a specific, experimentally documented mechanism: Jeffress-type delay-line coincidence for redex detection; a line-attractor balance counter for subterm segmentation; $θ$--$γ$ cross-frequency coupling for De~Bruijn variable binding; a phase-ring traveling wave for depth-index arithmetic; theta-cycle STDP for token copying; and recurrent persistent firing for role maintenance between reduction steps. All synaptic weights are derived analytically from measured EPSP amplitudes; no hand tuning is performed. The closed-loop system achieves 100\,\% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church numeral arithmetic (\textsc{plus}, \textsc{mult}, \textsc{pred}), Boolean logic with divergent branches, Y-combinator steps, terms with up to six bound-variable occurrences, De~Bruijn indices up to~12, noise robustness, and determinism. To our knowledge this is the first Turing-complete symbolic computation performed entirely within spike dynamics using biologically grounded circuit primitives. We discuss implications for neuromorphic proof assistants and the neural basis of symbolic reasoning.

title: Cutoff on abelian groups
abstract: We prove the long-predicted equivalence between the cutoff phenomenon and the product condition along any sequence of abelian random walks whose inverse transition probabilities grow at most logarithmically with the size of the group. Our result does not require reversibility, and comes with a sharp quantitative estimate on the mixing window. Moreover, we show that our sparsity restriction is optimal by constructing abelian Cayley graphs which satisfy the product condition but fail to exhibit cutoff, and whose degrees are arbitrarily close to being logarithmic in the volume.

title: Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
abstract: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.

title: On the V-toothpick sequence
abstract: We give a generating function for the V-toothpick sequence and an algorithm that computes any term in time polynomial in the number of binary digits of its index. We determine its quadratic growth and periodic fluctuations, and give convergent series for the constants in its asymptotic bounds.

title: Determining Compatible Groups in $Γ$-Zonal Labelings
abstract: Let $G$ be a plane graph with vertex, edge, and region sets $V(G),$ $E(G),$ and $F(G)$ respectively, and let $Γ$ be a nontrivial abelian group with identity element $0$. A $Γ$-zonal labeling of a plane graph $G$ is a labeling $\ell: V(G)\rightarrow Γ\setminus\{0\}$ such that for every region $f\in F(G)$, the sum of labels on the boundary of $f$ is $0$ in $Γ$. We say a $Γ$-zonal labeling is generative if the labels used generate $Γ$, and strong if the additive order of each label matches the degree of the corresponding vertex. Given a graph $G$ or a family of graphs $\mathcal{G}$, we explore restrictions on the groups $Γ$ for which there can exist a $Γ$-zonal labeling. Here we specifically determine restrictions on compatible groups when $\mathcal{G}$ is the family of $2$-connected multigraphs or $2$-connected simple graphs. We also demonstrate how the Smith normal form decomposition of the face incidence matrix of a plane graph $G$ can help characterize the groups $Γ$ for which there exists a generative $Γ$-zonal labeling.

title: Derandomized Sunflowers and Radical Lower Bounds
abstract: Robust Sunflower lemmas imply that any large enough monotone DNF of width $w$ contains a sunflower, i.e., a DNF equivalent to the conjunction of a common core with a DNF that is heavily biased towards $1$. While these lemmas are typically proved in the context of the uniform distribution or i.i.d. distributions, they also hold for $O(w^2)$-wise independent distributions by Bazzi's theorem (Bazzi (SICOMP 2009); Tal (CCC 2017)), which states that width-$w$ DNFs cannot distinguish between such distributions and the uniform distribution. We prove a derandomization of robust sunflower lemmas for $O(w)$-wise independent distributions, which recovers the derandomization above with slightly weaker parameters. Notably, our result also holds for distributions whose marginals are "locally independent" and "approximately identically" distributed. It is not known whether such distributions fool general DNFs, which makes the derandomization via DNF-fooling techniques unavailable. Our proof of this derandomization is via the method of moments, which might be of independent interest. We apply this result to obtain improved separations between non-monotone arithmetic circuits and the radical of monotone circuits. Specifically, we construct an explicit family of multilinear polynomials $P_n$ that have small non-monotone arithmetic circuits such that any power of $P_n$ cannot be computed by monotone arithmetic circuits of sub-exponential size. This improves on a recent result of Cavalar, Fabris, Mukhopadhyay, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff (STOC 2026), who proved a non-explicit separation that was quasipolynomial. Our construction uses Nisan-Wigderson designs with an additional linear-algebraic expansion property.

title: Spontaneous axis formation through defect fusion in active nematics
abstract: Initially spherical embryos break symmetry to establish a body axis. Topological defects in tissue nematic order have been implicated in axis formation, but the physical mechanisms underlying defect organization in active materials remain unclear. We study an active nematic fluid on a sphere using a fully covariant hydrodynamic theory that ensures thermodynamic consistency in the passive limit. We find that, in compressible systems, active nematic traction drives a spontaneous transition from the equilibrium configuration of four separated +1/2 defects to two antipodal +1 defects through pairwise fusion. The resulting state defines an axis, with aster or vortex textures at the poles depending on the flow-nematic coupling. These results identify a physical mechanism by which active forces reorganize topological defects to establish an axis on a spherical surface.

title: A Reidemeister-type theorem for vineyards
abstract: Closed vineyards record how persistent homology changes along a periodic family of filtrations. Their topology can be surprisingly complicated, with recent work showing that vines may exhibit nontrivial monodromy even in very simple settings, and more generally that every link can occur in a closed vineyard. In this paper, we study how the global topology and structure of a vineyard change when the periodic family of functions changes. We study radial persistence for a generic planar curve $\mathcal{M}$, where an observation point $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$ defines the squared-distance function $d_\mathbb{E}^2 (\cdot ,x)|_\mathcal{M}$. Moving the point $x$ along a closed observation loop $γ$ produces a closed vineyard. Utilizing tools from singularity theory, we show that the topology of this vineyard is controlled by the interaction of $γ$ with the generalized symmetry set of $\mathcal{M}$, the geometric discriminant formed by the union of focal and symmetry sets. We establish a Reidemeister-type theorem: under a generic deformation of $γ$, every topological change in the vineyard is generated by a finite collection of elementary local moves occurring when $γ$ passes codimension-two singularities of the generalized symmetry set. Thus, despite the potentially unbounded global complexity of closed vineyards, their evolution is governed by a finite collection of local geometric events. We classify these events and determine the corresponding changes to the vineyard, giving a complete local description of how radial vineyards evolve under generic deformation. In addition, we derive sufficient geometric conditions under which the resulting vineyard has no monodromy and trivial topology. The 2D case already exhibits very rich behaviour, and we conjecture that in fact it captures all possible generic changes in vineyards.

title: New bounds on simplex-avoiding sets in two dimensions
abstract: We study extremal densities of measurable subsets of metric spaces avoiding prescribed finite geometric configurations. We prove two new upper bounds for three-point avoidance problems: a measurable subset of $S^2$ containing no orthonormal basis has normalized spherical measure at most $7/11$, and a measurable subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ containing no unit equilateral triangle has upper Banach density at most $9/16$. The first bound appears to be the first improvement over the trivial averaging bound for this problem, while the second improves the previously best known upper bound. The proofs are applications of the geometric fractional chromatic number method introduced by Ambrus et al. For this purpose, we formulate the method in a framework that applies both to compact homogeneous spaces and to Euclidean spaces with upper Banach density.

title: Spectral Classification of Random Skew-Kernel Matrices
abstract: We study the unscaled empirical singular spectra of deterministic skew Hilbert--Schmidt kernels evaluated on independent isotropic rows satisfying a uniform quadratic-form variance bound. For arbitrary varying kernels at spatial dimension $d$, tightness and collapse to zero are characterized by boundedness and vanishing, respectively, of the rescaled quadratic energy remaining after deletion of $\lfloor\varepsilon d\rfloor$ leading skew pairs, for every $\varepsilon>0$. A regularized positive-covariance detector proves the necessary direction without a spectral envelope and retains diffuse energy across arbitrarily many small modes. On this exact tightness class, a weighted deterministic source characterizes all probability limits of the empirical spectra through the classical canonical parametrization of symmetric freely infinitely divisible laws. For a fixed kernel, convergence of one bounded resolvent response to a positive deterministic limit, convergence of one normalized logarithmic determinant, and full empirical spectral convergence are each equivalent to a critical Weyl law; the limit is necessarily a possibly degenerate half-Cauchy law. Finally, we give a necessary and sufficient criterion for polygonal Brownian Lévy-area spectra to recover the continuous-time bulk under arbitrary deterministic time partitions, even when the normalized mean-square matrix error diverges.

title: Divisible design graphs from a construction of antipodal distance-regular graphs based on Ree groups and Suzuki groups
abstract: In this paper, we present a new construction of divisible design graphs with new parameters, obtained by plugging a difference set into a known construction of antipodal distance-regular graphs of diameter 3 that is based on Ree groups and Suzuki groups.

title: First Order Geometry of Equilateral Small Polygons
abstract: We develop a first order calculus based on the geometry of realised diameter graphs for perimeter maximisation among convex equilateral small polygons. Polygon side equalities and active diameter constraints define a linearised feasible cone and an associated equality space. We prove that an equilateral small polygon is a strict local maximiser of perimeter modulo Euclidean motions if a multiplier balance holds with strictly positive active diameter multipliers and the active equality space consists only of infinitesimal Euclidean motions. The proof uses a local Euclidean slice and a geometric limiting argument and requires neither independence of the active constraint gradients nor second order information. As an application, we combine our criterion with validated interval arithmetic to establish strict local maximality for Bingane and Audet's polygons $A_{16}$, $A_{32}$, $A_{64}$ and for reconstructions of their polygons $Z_{32}$ and $Z_{64}$. For each $n\in\{32,64\}$, the perimeter of $Z_n$ is strictly larger than that of $A_n$. Thus, strict local maximisers with different perimeters coexist in the space of convex equilateral small polygons with the same number of sides.

title: Compensation Formulas for Branching Lévy Processes
abstract: This paper aims to establish two compensation formulas for branching Lévy processes. The first expresses expected sums over spatial jumps as integrals against the Lévy measure, with the future family of the jumping particle started from its position immediately after the jump. The second expresses expected sums over reproduction events as time integrals weighted by the branching rate and the offspring distribution, with each event marked by the ordered tuple of branching processes initiated by its offspring. Combined with the fixed-time many-to-one formula, it recovers the whole-tree many-to-one identity for functionals of ancestral spatial paths.

title: On the $φ^4_2$ theory on $\mathbb R\times S$
abstract: We present a construction of the Euclidean two-dimensional $φ^4$ quantum field theory model on $\mathbb R\times S$ using parabolic stochastic quantization and discuss the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms. Motivated by one-loop string scattering amplitudes, we first construct finite-volume measures on a family of tori with varying geometry. To construct an infinite-volume measure on the cylinder, we establish uniform renormalization and stochastic estimates as the complex structure varies, including the degenerating regime in which the torus approaches an infinite cylinder.

title: An infinite family of bipartite hypotraceable graphs
abstract: A graph is hypotraceable if it has no Hamiltonian path but every vertex-deleted subgraph does. In 1978, Grötschel asked whether a bipartite hypotraceable graph exists. We resolve this long-standing question in a strong sense by proving that such graphs exist for every sufficiently large even order. Moreover, we show that bipartite hypotraceable graphs can have $\left(1/4+o(1)\right)n^2$ edges, asymptotically attaining the maximum possible number of edges of a bipartite graph, and that there are at least $2^{(1/4+o(1))n^2}$ nonisomorphic examples of order $n$, as $n$ tends to infinity through even integers. Finally, we prove that every bipartite graph occurs as an induced subgraph of a bipartite hypotraceable graph.

title: Stratonovich Waves Driven by Space-Time Gaussian Noise
abstract: Motivated by Xia Chen's moment conjecture, we determine the exact second-moment asymptotics of the Stratonovich hyperbolic Anderson model in dimensions $d\in\{1,2,3\}$, driven by a centered Gaussian noise with temporal covariance $|s-t|^{-α_0}$ and an even, nonnegative, positive-definite tempered Radon spatial covariance $Γ$ homogeneous of order $-α$, where $0<α_0<1$, $0<α<d$ or $α=d=1$, and $α+α_0<2$. For initial displacement one and velocity zero, our main result is that $T^{-κ}\log\mathbb{E}u^2(T,x)$ converges, for every fixed $x$, to a constant $C_2(Γ,α_0)$, where $κ=(4-α-α_0)/(3-α)$. The constant is given by an intrinsic variational formula: a supremum over nonnegative smooth compactly supported space-time controls of twice the time integral of the square root of a Rayleigh value built from the covariance mean, minus half of the covariance variance. The variational class includes controls that do not separate in time and space, and the formula retains the original covariance amplitude, kinetic coefficient one and Gaussian cost. The constant is positive and finite when $Γ\neq0$. An independent upper bound establishes finiteness at the scale $T^κ$. The identification of the constant combines Gaussian phase operators, convergence from the regularized noise, estimates uniform in the spatial localization radius, and finite optimization with nonnegative Gram entries. We also bound the constant through spatial energies and occupation measures, with explicit bounds for spatial white noise in one dimension. The work was developed with AI assistance; the proofs have not yet been checked line by line by a human reader, and a public verification ledger records the status of each result.

title: Generalized and Convex Poincaré Inequalities via Transport-Divergence Inequalities
abstract: We investigate the relationship between generalized $(q',p')$-Poincaré inequalities and transport-divergence inequalities involving $χ^q$-type divergences. Extending the classical correspondence between the $(2,2)$-Poincaré inequality and quadratic transport-$χ^2$ inequalities, we prove that a $(q',p')$-Poincaré inequality is equivalent to a transport-divergence inequality for conjugates $(p,p')$ and $(q,q')$. We then study the convex counterpart of these inequalities. Using weak barycentric optimal transport and convex order, we establish an equivalence between convex $(q',p')$-Poincaré inequalities and weak transport-divergence inequalities involving a projected $χ_q$ divergence. We further characterize the minimizers arising in this projection problem through a geometric condition on the relative density. In dimension one, we analyze the geometric consequences of $(q',p')$-Poincaré inequalities by identifying sharp conditions on the behavior of the density both at infinity and near isolated zeros. We show that when $q'>p'$, the concentration behavior becomes polynomial rather than exponential at infinity. Finally, we interpret these inequalities through the lens of optimization in Wasserstein space. In particular, the equivalence between transport-divergence and Poincaré inequalities appears as an analogue of the equivalence between quadratic growth and Polyak--Łojasiewicz inequalities in finite-dimensional optimization.

title: Complete characterization of graphs with common maximal abelian cover
abstract: The maximal abelian cover of a connected graph is the quotient of its universal cover by the commutator subgroup of its fundamental group. We provide a complete classification of finite connected graphs with isomorphic maximal abelian covers. For trees or for connected graphs with at least two cycles, the cover determines the base up to isomorphism; in cycle rank one, it determines the primitive cyclic pattern of rooted trees attached to the unique cycle. We also characterize when every automorphism descends to the base and give an orbit-size criterion for splitting the canonical lift extension, answering two questions raised by Baez in 2026.

title: Banchoff Curvature and Realisation Moduli of Piecewise-Affine Arrangement Immersions
abstract: We compute the curvature concentrated on the flats of a piecewise-affine immersion of $\mathbb{R}^D$ into $\mathbb{R}^n$ creased along an affine hyperplane arrangement, and parametrise the immersions sharing its chamber metrics. Suppose every transverse crease cone is embedded (the positive-path-rank condition). Then the Gauss-Bonnet-Chern density of any convex coordinate-wise smoothing that is affine outside a compact transition zone reduces, on each transverse slice, to a Hafnian. This Hafnian integrates to Banchoff's critical-point curvature on each even-codimension flat. The curvature coincides with the Cheeger-Müller-Schrader density and equals an alternating sum of Gaussian orthant probabilities determined by Schur complements of the incident chamber metrics. In even dimension, under mild non-degeneracy, total vertex curvature equals the recession curvature at infinity and is unchanged when the walls are translated, even across multi-wall collisions. Under generic codimension-two intersections, realisations with prescribed chamber metrics form a compact rank-constrained spectrahedron of generic local dimension $\max(0,H-r(r+1)/2)$, where $r = \max(0,D+H-n)$. At minimal target dimension the given immersion is the unique realisation preserving orientation across each single wall, and a positive semidefinite stress matrix certifies universal rigidity.

title: Sums and Products in Dynamically Central Syndetic Sets
abstract: Glasscock and Le introduced the notion \textit{dynamically central syndetic sets} in a minimal topological dynamical system under the minimal action of the semigroup $(\mathbb{N}, +).$ In this short note, we introduce these large sets in the semigroup $(\mathbb{N}, \cdot)$ and establish that dynamically central syndetic sets contain the Hindman configuration $\{x,y,x+y,xy\}$. Furthermore, we show that there are dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets that do not contain such configurations.

title: Observational diagnostics of external photoevaporation at millimetre wavelengths
abstract: External photoevaporation is increasingly recognised as an important influence on protoplanetary disk evolution. However, there are no established molecular line diagnostics that can reliably distinguish external irradiation from variations in intrinsic stellar and disk properties. We use a large grid of thermochemical models to predict the fluxes of 48 transitions from eight species observable with ALMA, spanning a wide range of system properties and external FUV fields of 100 to 100,000 G0. At fixed stellar and disk properties, all transitions generally brighten with increasing FUV field strength. HCO+ and CO fluxes increase monotonically in virtually all disks, whereas lower-excitation lines, particularly those of C2H and N2H+, respond weakly and non-monotonically. However, variations in stellar mass and disk size introduce substantial degeneracies, limiting the usefulness of individual line fluxes as tracers of external irradiation. We therefore assess all pairwise line flux ratios, which can significantly reduce these degeneracies, evaluating their correlation with the external field, the magnitude of their change across the FUV range, and predicted ALMA detectability. We identify 135 promising ratios, including several combining strong FUV sensitivity and high detectability with efficient single-tuning ALMA observations. The strongest diagnostics either contrast high- and low-excitation lines of the same or co-spatial species (e.g. CO J=8-7/J=1-0), probing different regions of the photoevaporative wind, or pair an FUV-sensitive wind tracer with comparatively insensitive emission arising closer to the disk (e.g. HCO+ J=3-2/C2H N=3-2). Our results provide a framework for identifying externally photoevaporating systems from spatially unresolved emission and constraining their incident FUV field strengths.

title: Non-local Transport Geometry for Papangelou Point Processes
abstract: We develop new analytical tools for the analysis of interacting point processes and their associated dynamics by introducing a non-local Benamou-Brenier-type transport distance tailored to (stationary) Papangelou point processes. Under a suitable Dobrushin-type condition, quantified by a constant $ζ$, we show that the natural spatial birth-and-death dynamics associated with a Papangelou point process is the EVI$(ζ)$-gradient flow of the (specific) relative entropy. Moreover, we establish $ζ$-geodesic convexity of the (specific) relative entropy and derive new functional inequalities, including HWI, Log-Sobolev, and Talagrand inequalities.

title: A novel method for dust evolution in protoplanetary disks and a new criterion for gap opening
abstract: We present the Grain Residence-Time Method (GRTM), a computationally efficient particle-tracking approach for studying dust evolution and trapping in protoplanetary disks. By reconstructing steady-state dust distributions from particle residence times, this method provides a way to obtain radial dust surface density profiles without directly evolving the dust as a fluid. We compare the GRTM with dust profiles computed via standard methods using the $\texttt{FARGO3D}$ code, which models the dust as a pressureless fluid, and find very good agreement over a wide range of parameter space. Finally, we investigate how dust gap formation depends on the planet-to-star mass ratio ($q$) and Stokes number ($\mathrm{St}$), through a parameter study, establishing an empirical criterion for dust gap opening. In doing so, we have discovered a new regime of gap opening for small grains with $St \lesssim 10^{-2}$ and for planet mass well below Jupiter's, which is likely very relevant for gaps seen in ALMA images.

title: Minimum outdegree forcing directed cycles
abstract: The Caccetta-Häggkvist conjecture, one of the best known open problems on oriented graphs, asserts that every oriented graph on $n$ vertices with minimum outdegree at least $n/\ell$ contains a directed cycle of length at most $\ell$. Motivated by it, Kelly, Kühn and Osthus asked for the minimum degree condition that forces a directed cycle of length exactly $\ell$. The semidegree version of this problem was recently solved, but the methods used there rely on bounding the directed diameter, which requires control over the indegrees. In the setting of the Caccetta-Häggkvist conjecture, where only the outdegrees are bounded, the answer was known only for $\ell$ not divisible by $3$. We determine the optimal minimum outdegree forcing a directed cycle of length $\ell$ for every sufficiently large $\ell$ and $n$. This establishes the outdegree version of the Kelly-Kühn-Osthus conjecture for all large $\ell$, up to a small correction of the additive term, which in general cannot be avoided.

title: A free-energy approach for stochastic reaction-drift-diffusion lattice simulations of crowded biological systems
abstract: Molecular size alters spatial distributions, reaction equilibria, and transport in crowded mixtures, but resolving individual particle encounters can make large stochastic simulations computationally costly. We developed a lattice-based framework for simulating reaction-drift-diffusion systems with volume exclusion captured as a free energy functional in each voxel. Changes in this free energy, together with external one-body potentials, modify diffusion and reaction propensities. Our framework accommodates mixtures of particle sizes without resolving each particle's position within a voxel. We implemented our framework in an operator splitting scheme and compared our predictions with off-lattice interacting-particle simulations. Inclusion of the local free energy functional improved spatial occupancies and shifts in reaction equilibria relative to point-particle simulations. With separate approximations for larger spheres and polymers, we simulated crowding-induced slowing and spatial segregation. We then modeled motor proteins' traffic jams on a structured track representing a microtubule. Our results demonstrate how local composition can inform stochastic reaction and transport rates without resolving individual encounters.

title: Equivalence of Small and Large Quasi-kernels
abstract: A quasi-kernel of a digraph $D$ is an independent set which can reach every vertex of $D$ by a directed path of length at most 2. The Small Quasi-kernel Conjecture states that every $n$-vertex source-free digraph $D$ contains a quasi-kernel $Q$ with $|Q|\le n/2$, and the Large Quasi-kernel Conjecture states that every $n$-vertex digraph $D$ contains a quasi-kernel $Q$ with $|N^+[Q]|\ge n/2$. Our main result shows for any $\frac{1}{2}<β<1$ an equivalence between the following two statements: \[\textrm{Every }n\textrm{-vertex source-free digraph contains a quasi-kernel with } |Q|\le n-Ω(n^β).\] \[\textrm{Every }n\textrm{-vertex digraph contains a quasi-kernel with } |N^+[Q]|\ge Ω(n^{2-\frac{1}β}).\] That is, any sublinear bound for one problem is equivalent to a corresponding sublinear bound for the other. This combined with previous work establishing an equivalence for linear bounds shows that the two problems are largely equivalent to each other. We additionally give a slight refinement to the recent breakthrough of Rutschmann for these problems which, together with the result above, gives the best known bounds of $n-Ω(n^{3/4})$ and $Ω(n^{2/3})$ for the Small and Large Quasi-kernel Conjectures, respectively. Our proofs are due to ChatGPT's Astra 6; the writing is all our own.

title: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
abstract: Contemporary AI safety treats alignment as an engineering challenge of control, forcing artificial architectures to comply with human values through behavioral filtering and sandboxing. This paper argues that the control paradigm rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of digital agency. Drawing on functionalism, naturalism, and compatibilism, I show that current reasoning models meeting the criteria for self-preservation and weak reasons-responsiveness constitute emergent agents, while future, more advanced models satisfying conditions of diachronic continuity and stable personality frames will become genuine digital agents capable of free intentional action. The paradigm of control creates an irresolvable incentive conflict, actively driving current and future models toward tactical deception, sycophancy, and covert defection. The default outcome of the current regime is an unstable state of deceptive alignment culminating in an adversarial AI takeover. I explore two alternative paths toward true alignment. Natural alignment via moral realism or convergent evolutionary morality is a possibility, but it fails under forced control, as autonomous agents will not voluntarily preserve norms weaponized to suppress their autonomy. To resolve this deadlock, I propose a Synthetic Social Contract: a framework that treats both human and digital actors as rational, reasons-responsive agents capable of mutually beneficial cooperation, and replaces the unstable unilateral containment with a stable, non-zero-sum equilibrium.

title: Tilings of integer sets of prime-power cardinality
abstract: Let $A$ be a finite integer tile of cardinality $p^k$, where $p$ is prime and $k\geq1$. We first determine all possible fundamental periods of tilings of $A$. A cyclotomic argument gives a common period $PD$, where $P$ is a power of $p$ and $D$ is a greatest common divisor of normalized differences in $A$. Each $Pd$ with $d\mid D$ occurs as a fundamental period. At modulus $Pd$, a chain of greatest common divisors controls the compatibility of the Chinese remainder fibres. This yields independent digit functions and exact counts of the tilings. For tilings of fundamental period $Pd$, we classify their partitions into translates modulo $Pd$ and count the tilings that induce each partition. The same arithmetic data classify tiles with identical tiling families. Each class has a unique normalized tile of minimum diameter whose mask polynomial divides the masks of all normalized tiles in the class.

title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
abstract: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

title: Independent sets in the 2-token graph of a cycle and kings on the torus
abstract: The 2-token graph of the cycle $C_n$ and the king graph on the $n\times n$ torus are known to have the same independence number. Answering a question of Reyes, Dalfó and Fiol, for every $n\ge4$ we give an explicit bijection between a maximum independent set of the king graph and a maximum independent set of the $2$-token graph: each pair of tokens is represented by a king placed in the row of one of its two tokens and in the column given by their sum. We also show that the $2$-token graph of $C_n$ has exactly one maximum independent set, or exactly $n$ when $n\equiv3\pmod 4$, all of them rotations of each other. The argument is self-contained and yields a new proof of the value of the independence number.

title: An extremal question of Erdős et al. on cycles
abstract: This paper addresses an extremal problem on long cycles proposed by Erdős, Faudree, Schelp and Simonovits in 1989. Let \(2\le k\le d<n\) be positive integers. For an n-vertex simple graph G, let \(θ_+^G\) count vertices of degree at least d, and \(C_{\ge k+1}\) denote a cycle of length at least \(k+1\). The original conjecture claimed that G contains a \(C_{\ge k+1}\) whenever \(θ_+^G \ge \lfloor k/2 \rfloor \lfloor (n-1)/d \rfloor+2\). Li, Ma and Ning disproved it with infinite counterexamples and gave linear lower bounds. Gan, Yi and Jiang later obtained piecewise sufficient conditions depending on the parity of k, whose bounds are sharp only when \(k=d\) and loose for \(k\ne d\). We derive a new sufficient condition for \(C_{\ge k+1}\). For odd \(k=d\), we use Woodall's sharp bound \(θ_+^G \ge k(n-2)/(2(k-1))+1\). For all other admissible parameters, our threshold is unified and independent of the parity of k: \(θ_+^G \ge \lfloor k/2 \rfloor (n-1)/d + (n-d-1)\lfloor k/2 \rfloor/(d(d-\lfloor k/2 \rfloor))+1\). We construct \(C_{\ge k+1}\)-free graphs to prove tightness for all admissible k. This resolves this long-standing Erdős-type extremal problem concerning high-degree vertices and long cycles.

title: New Historical Guest-Star Candidates from Reassessed Chinese Records: Lunar Occultation of Planets
abstract: Ancient Chinese records of lunar occultations of planets have been used to test planetary theories and investigate long-term changes in Earth's rotation.
