However, certain records contain identification errors whose origins remain poorly understood; we propose that some of these errors may arise from misidentifying guest stars, such as novae or supernovae, as planets. We analyzed 67 errata on lunar occultations of planets from Liu Ci-Yuan's (2015) monograph using modern ephemerides and the open-source Python package \texttt{occultsky}, publicly available on GitHub. Using recorded dates and dynastic capital coordinates, we constructed observing windows anchored at solar noon and extending by $\pm 1$ day. Each window covered the preceding and recorded nights because the date may be off by one day. For each of the 67 records, we cataloged the apparent right ascension and declination $(α, δ)$ at the midpoint of the Moon's visibility window on each candidate night. The band swept by the lunar disk confines a possible transient to a narrow region a few degrees across; these midpoint coordinates serve as proxies for the implied guest-star positions. The catalog supplies candidate positions rather than identifications, enabling remnant and compact-object searches to test the guest-star hypothesis directly. If associations are established, these records could become dated guest-star candidates, and their dates could anchor remnant ages.

title: Heap-type permutation generation with a prescribed final arrangement
abstract: Heap's algorithm generates all permutations of an array of n items, obtaining each one from its predecessor by a single swap. We determine the net permutation applied to the array by every complete recursive call: a transposition when the number of items is odd and at least three, and a cycle through all items when it is even. We show that the output of each call is a concatenation of right cosets of the symmetric group on one item fewer, and we prove a general formula: the order in which the items are parked at the last position may be chosen freely, every such order corresponds to exactly one valid schedule, and it determines the net permutation of the call. Two variants follow. In the cyclic variant a complete sweep over an even number of items rotates the array by one position. In the extremal variant, for even n, a sweep started from the identity ends in the lexicographically largest arrangement that any single-swap enumeration can leave; by a parity argument this is the reversal exactly when n is congruent to 2 modulo 4. The construction of the extremal variant is proved correct when n is divisible by 4 and verified by computer for all even n up to 10000.

title: Edge behavior of the KPZ fixed point under upper-tail conditioning
abstract: We consider the KPZ fixed point $\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{KPZ}}(x,t)$ with the narrow-wedge initial profile, conditioned on $\{\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{KPZ}}(0,1)\ge L\}$ as $L\to\infty$. Our main result describes its fluctuations near the boundary of the region affected by the conditioning. More precisely, in the spatial window $x=t\sqrt L+O(1)$, the centered field converges in finite-dimensional distributions to the KPZ fixed point with a half-Brownian initial profile. The convergence holds jointly at arbitrary positive times, including times before and after the conditioning time. The proof is based on an asymptotic correspondence between conditional narrow-wedge multipoint formulas and those for the half-Brownian KPZ fixed point.

title: Sharp lower bounds for weighted bisections of graphs with bounded maximum degree
abstract: A bisection of a graph is a partition of its vertex set into two parts the sizes of which differ by at most one. We prove that every finite simple graph of maximum degree at most an odd positive integer $k$, with arbitrary nonnegative real edge weights, has a bisection of weight at least $(k+1)/(2k)$ times its total edge weight. The corresponding bound $(k+2)/(2(k+1))$ for even $k$ follows immediately. Both coefficients are best possible. Somewhat surprisingly, these are exactly the sharp coefficients known for maximum weighted cuts, despite the additional balance requirement.

title: Maximum number of cells in a matroid subdivision of hypersimplex
abstract: David Speyer proved that the maximum number of cells in a regular matroid subdivision of the hypersimplex $Δ(m,t)$ is $\binom{t-2}{m-1}$ , using the language of tropical geometry and properties of the Tutte polynomial of a matroid \cite[Theorem 6.1]{Speyer}. In this paper, we prove this result in general, i.e. for arbitrary matroid subdivisions including the non-regular ones. We perform a different combinatorial way using our results in \cite{HHH} and independent of tropical language.

title: Sharp Gaussian Brunn-Minkowski inequalities
abstract: We prove Gaussian Brunn-Minkowski inequalities for multiple sets. These are of the type: $$\prod_{i=1}^I γ_{Σ_i}(K_i)^{\tilde λ_i} \le C_{\text{sharp}}γ_Γ\Big(\sum_{i=1}^I λ_i K_i\Big),$$ with convex sets $K_i \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, whose barycenter $b_{K_i,Σ_i}$ with respect to the Gaussian measure $γ_{Σ_i}$ is zero, where $λ_i, \tilde λ_i \in (0;1)$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^I λ_i=\sum_{i=1}^I \tilde λ_i=1.$ In addition, we provide natural conditions on the matrices $Γ, Σ_1,\cdots,Σ_I \in \mathrm{Sym}_{>0}(n)$, which are given through a pointwise inequality involving the Karcher mean. Furthermore, we study equality cases of the corresponding functional forms in such situations. We also investigate the role of centering in the (B)-property by giving a counterexample for convex bodies with zero Lebesgue barycenters in dimensions at least three and thereby answering negatively a question of Faifman-Polterovich in \cite{Faifman_Polt}. Finally, a new slicing approach is introduced, which allows us to pass from centered convex sets to sets with arbitrary barycenters such that their weighted sum is convex. Based on this idea, we show a new Gaussian Brunn-Minkowski inequality $$e^{|\sum_{i=1}^I λ_i b_{K_i,I_n}|^2/2n} γ_n \Big(\sum_{i=1}^I λ_i K_i \Big)^{1/n} \ge \sum_{i=1}^I λ_i e^{|b_{K_i,I_n}|^2/2n} γ_n(K_i)^{1/n},$$ and consider a further application in the direction of the Gaussian correlation inequality, together with the rigidity for both inequalities.

title: Positivity of Signed Odd-Multiplicity Partitions
abstract: We establish coefficientwise nonnegativity for the signed partition $q$-series \[ A_k(q)= \sum_{1\le j_1<\cdots<j_k} \prod_{i=1}^k\frac{q^{j_i}}{1+q^{2j_i}} =\sum_{n\ge0}a_k(n)q^n, \qquad k\ge0, \] with $A_0(q)=1$. The coefficient $a_k(n)$ counts, with signs, partitions of $n$ having exactly $k$ distinct part sizes, each occurring with odd multiplicity. A partition with multiplicities $2t_1+1,\ldots,2t_k+1$ is assigned the sign $(-1)^{t_1+\cdots+t_k}$. We prove that $a_k(n)\ge0$ for all $k,n\ge0$, thereby resolving a conjecture on signed odd-multiplicity partitions. Our proof combines a positive theta--MacMahon factorization for the generating functions restricted to odd part sizes with a dyadic product decomposition that extends positivity to arbitrary part sizes. Moreover, we establish strict positivity $a_k(n)>0$ for every $k\ge2$ and $n\ge\binom{k+1}{2}$.

title: The minimum degree of minimally k-extendable graphs for some k
abstract: A graph on at least 2k+2 vertices is k-extendable if every matching of size k extends to a perfect matching, and it is minimally k-extendable if it is k-extendable but deleting any edge is not. Plummer proved that every k-extendable graph is (k+1)-connected. So its minimum degree is at least k+1. Lou and Yu conjectured that a minimally k-extendable graph on at most 4k vertices has minimum degree in {k+1,2k,2k+1}; the case k=1 and the claw-free case of k=2 have been settled previously. We determine the minimum degree of minimally k-extendable graphs for k=2 and k=3, thereby settling the Lou--Yu conjecture for these two values. For k=2 the minimum degree is in {3,4,5}. For k=3 it is in {4,7} at orders 8 and 10, and in {4,6,7} at order 12. The proofs pass to the complement graph and combine Tutte's perfect matching theorem with a classification of four-vertex and six-vertex obstructions. All predicted values are realized by explicit constructions.

title: Exact and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Multivariate Diffusions under High-Frequency Sampling
abstract: We establish the asymptotic theory of the exact maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for discretely observed multivariate ergodic diffusions under high-frequency, long-span sampling, solving an open problem posed by \citet{YCW2019} and \citet{Li2013}. The drift may grow linearly, and the volatility is bounded away from zero and either bounded or proportional to $1+|x|$. When the sampling interval decays polynomially, the exact MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient, with rates $\sqrt{nΔ_n}$ for drift and $\sqrt n$ for diffusion parameters. Under an additional condition on ergodic averages, and when the time span $nΔ_n$ also grows polynomially, its moments converge as well. The proof never analyzes the exact likelihood directly: it shows that a closed-form density expansion of sufficiently high order is uniformly accurate in relative terms at every observed transition, so that the two log-likelihoods differ by $o_P(1)$ uniformly in the parameter. The same argument yields accuracy conditions under which an approximate likelihood is asymptotically equivalent to the exact one; in particular, the approximate MLE of Yang, Chen and Wan converges to the true parameter. For the delta-expansion estimator of fixed order $K\ge1$, we derive the leading bias explicitly. It shows that $nΔ_n^{K+1}\to0$ cannot be weakened when the bias constant is nonzero, and that the bias falls on the drift parameters for even $K$ and on the diffusion parameters for odd $K$. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the predicted biases.

title: Golomb rulers with real marks: the real and integer optima agree up to ten marks
abstract: A Golomb ruler is a set of integer marks whose pairwise differences are distinct. We let the marks be real numbers and ask that every difference be at least 1 and that any two differences be at least 1 apart. Every integer Golomb ruler satisfies these conditions, so the least length $G_R(n)$ of such a real ruler with $n$ marks is at most the optimal Golomb length $G_Z(n)$. Fixing the order of all differences splits the real problem into finitely many polyhedral chambers. A branch-and-bound over these chambers, with an exact rational certificate at every leaf, proves $G_R(n) = G_Z(n)$ for $n \le 10$. Each proof takes under a minute and is verified by an independent checker that uses only exact arithmetic. An exhaustive exact enumeration of all chamber vertices confirms the result for $n \le 7$, and shows that there the shortest real rulers are exactly the optimal integer rulers and their mirror images. For every $n$ we show $n(\sqrt{n}-1)^2 \le G_R(n) \le G_Z(n)$, so that $G_R(n) \sim G_Z(n) \sim n^2$. Non-integral chamber vertices first appear at $n = 7$: there are 84, all half-integral. Already there, 80 of them are shortest points of their chambers, 40 of them the only one, although the global optimum is integral; a twelve-mark example of the same kind comes from Singer's construction. On the other hand, every Singer ruler with at most 104 marks, cut at the largest gap, is the only shortest point of its own chamber; we conjecture this for all prime powers.

title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.

title: Stochastic Representation-Inspired Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Fluid Flows
abstract: The effectiveness of neural networks in solving partial differential equations depends not only on their approximation capability but also on the suitability of their representations for the underlying solutions. Motivated by stochastic integral representations of incompressible fluid flows and the associated Biot--Savart kernel, we propose a Biot--Savart-informed (i.e. physics-informed) neural network (BS-PINN) for the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations. By extracting a rational profile from a regularized Biot--Savart kernel, we construct a smooth activation function with fixed and learnable kernel scales. Both variants retain the conventional velocity--pressure formulation and physics-informed training framework, allowing the influence of the activation function to be examined independently. We evaluate the method on five benchmarks, including Kovasznay flow, cylinder wake, three-dimensional Beltrami flow, Taylor--Green vortex, and double shear layer. Across 21 benchmark--architecture comparisons, both variants consistently reduce the combined velocity error relative to the conventional $\tanh$-based PINN, achieving mean relative error reductions of 31.7\% and 33.2\%, respectively. Improvements are also observed in reported pressure and vorticity errors. Notably, the double-shear-layer experiments demonstrate improved resolution of localized shear structures and, for BS-PINN-F, qualitatively clearer vortex-roll-up patterns in the long-time simulation. These findings highlight the potential of incorporating analytical flow structures into neural-network representations for incompressible flow simulations.

title: The Cooperstein conjecture and additive alternating $d$-codes
abstract: Let $\bigwedge^2 V$ be the second exterior power of a vector space $V$ over a finite field. The Cooperstein conjecture asserts a dimension bound for flats external to varieties consisting of points of bounded rank in $\mathrm{PG}(\bigwedge^2 V)$. This geometric problem can be translated into a question about linear spaces of alternating matrices whose nonzero elements have rank at least a prescribed value. For matrices of odd order, the sharp cardinality bound was already established by Delsarte and Goethals (1975). In this paper, we prove the Cooperstein conjecture for matrices of even order and, more generally, we prove its additive analogue by determining, for all admissible parameters, the maximum size of an additive subgroup of alternating matrices in which every nonzero matrix has at least the prescribed rank. Our proof uses Pfaffian equations to characterize alternating matrices of rank below the prescribed minimum. We study the minimal graded free resolutions of the corresponding Pfaffian rings. The Cohen--Macaulay property and the $a$-invariant of each Pfaffian ring determine the largest shift in its resolution. We use trace functions on evaluation quotients to construct polynomial indicators for the matrices of small rank in an additive subgroup. The largest shift controls their degrees, yielding the upper bound by a counting argument. Finally, we give explicit trace constructions attaining the bound.

title: Dependence properties between marginals of discrete-time maximum processes
abstract: Consider a discrete time sequence $(X_n,n\in\mathbb{N})$ and the corresponding process $(M_n,n\in\mathbb{N})$ which, at any time $n\in\mathbb{N}$, takes the maximum value reached by the process $(X_n,n\in\mathbb{N})$ up to that time. Clearly, there exists a dependence between the values assumed by the process $(M_n,n\in\mathbb{N})$ at two distinct points in time. This paper formally describes such a dependence in terms of the copula of the two random values. Various scenarios with respect to the sequence $(X_n,n\in\mathbb{N})$ are considered, e.g., without assuming independence in its components and/or identical distribution. Such explicit expressions of the copula are then used to provide results that describe how the dependence between the maxima reached by the sequence $(X_n,n\in\mathbb{N})$ in different times varies when both the time interval between them and/or their positions in the sequence are increased. In this context, asymptotic results are also provided.

title: Planet Formation in a Warped Disc: Gravitational Instability and Misaligned Infall
abstract: We perform three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations to investigate the impact of misaligned infall on a gravitationally unstable protoplanetary disc. The interaction between the disc and the infalling gas does not occur uniformly across all radii. As infall impacts the outer disc first, the outer disc experiences stronger torques than the inner disc, resulting in a warped disc where the angular momentum vector of the disc varies with radius. The surrounding infalling gas reprocesses stellar irradiation and re-emits it back towards the disc, resulting in a warmer disc. The higher temperatures cause the disc to become more gravitationally stable resulting in weaker spiral arms. However, over time, infall also continuously increases the disc mass, gradually altering the local conditions and strengthening gravitational instabilities despite the azimuthally averaged Toomre $Q$ indicating that the disc is stable against gravitational instability. Eventually, one of the spiral arms fragments, forming a giant planet by gravitational instability in a disc warped by misaligned infall. Hence, the impact of infall on gravitational instability in general will vary depending on the infall and disc properties due to the balance between the stabilising and destabilising effects. We also find that infall alters the expected signatures of gravitationally unstable discs by introducing asymmetries in scattered-light, continuum, and molecular line emission.

title: Critical heavy traffic and diffusion limits for shortest-of-d dynamic routing
abstract: We study shortest-of-$d$ routing, with fixed $d\ge2$, in $N$ parallel queues with independent finite-state Markov service environments switching at rate $κ_N$. At the critical load $ρ_N=1-1/N$, the empirical measure of the centered queue lengths, under stationarity, converges in distribution to a random probability measure determined by its mean. We identify the mean's density and the conditional independence of fixed finite collections of centered queues in the limit. On time scales of order $N$, the centered empirical mean converges to a diffusion with explicit drift and constant diffusion coefficient. These limits hold when $κ_N/N\to\infty$, along subsequences with convergent lattice phase. The diffusion limit extends to centered initial empirical measures tight in the first Wasserstein topology, with means converging in law. A short initial layer prepares the limiting family while preserving the limiting mean. Empirical approximation holds in time-integrated Wasserstein distance.

title: Nonreciprocal Hopfield nets for angiogenesis
abstract: During sprouting angiogenesis, endothelial cells dynamically reorganize among three relevant phenotypes (glycolytic, stalk and tip) to form new blood vessels, with cells transitioning from one phenotype to another. These cell-state transitions may involve intrinsic nonequilibrium dynamics that go beyond relaxation of the conventional Waddington landscape. We investigate this possibility using a nonreciprocal Hopfield network inferred from single-cell RNA sequencing and RNA velocity data for 1896 endothelial cells on a panel of 1873 genes. We encode the three experimentally identified phenotypes as correlated memory patterns and introduce an asymmetric mixing matrix describing their effective interactions. A dynamical mean- field reduction yields a three-dimensional system for the overlaps with these phenotypic memories, whose parameters are fitted to RNA-velocity-derived trajectories. The nonreciprocal model outperforms its reciprocal counterpart on held-out testing data. Remarkably, its long-time dynamics exhibit either stationary attractors or sustained cycles connecting phenotypic states, depending on the inference timescale. These results suggest that angiogenic cell fate decisions may involve directed, non-relaxational dynamics that cannot be captured by a conventional energy landscape. This approach may also provide a useful framework for investigating how perturbations constrain cellular differentiation.

title: On (Pathwidth, Clique)-boundedness
abstract: We prove that every $(\pw,ω)$-bounded class of graphs has bounded tree-independence number, answering a question of Bešter Štorgel, Dallard, Lozin, Milanič, and Zamaraev. We deduce this from a bound on the tree-independence number of graphs with neither $\B_ρ$ nor $K_{σ,σ}$ as an induced minor, where $\B_ρ$ is the complete binary tree of height $ρ$ and the bound depends only on $ρ$ and $σ$. We then obtain an asymptotically sharp bound on the path-independence number of $n$-vertex graphs in any $(\pw,ω)$-bounded class. The lower-bound examples also give counterexamples to a conjecture of Hickingbotham and Joret. We further prove that, for every forest $F$ and every $\ell\in\N$, there is a constant $k=k(F,\ell)\in\N$ such that every graph $G$ with no induced theta or $\ell$-long prism and no induced subgraph isomorphic to $F$ satisfies tree-independence number at most $k$. This proves a strengthened form of a conjecture of Chudnovsky, Hajebi, and Trotignon. Finally, for every integer $s\ge2$, we characterize the forests $F$ for which excluding $F$ as an induced minor and $K_{s,s}$ as an induced subgraph bounds tree-independence number. This extends the characterization of Bonnet, Duhamel, and Hickingbotham, who considered bounded pathwidth with $K_{s,s}$ excluded as a subgraph.

title: Asymptotic enumeration of histories and limit laws in two random graph evolution models
abstract: We study growth models for random graphs where the growth is established by vertex or edge creations and where there is no dependence between vertices and edges. Creations are logged by time stamps such that the history of the resulting graph can be reconstructed. We investigate two prototypical models, an undirected and a directed one, called undirected independent growth model (UIG-model) and directed independent growth model (DIG-model). The generating functions for the number of histories have radius of convergence equal to zero. In the UIG-model, we express the asymptotic number of histories as a sum that is amenable to the discrete Laplace method. We derive the asymptotic number of histories, study the number of vertices of a random history, and prove a central limit theorem. In the DIG-model we use a rescaled Borel transform to get an entire function. Then we show that this function is Hayman admissible, which enables us to derive the asymptotic number of histories in this model. The counting sequence is closely related to the framework of generalized Legendre-Stirling numbers. To determine the number of vertices in a random history, we prove that the bivariate generating function is e-admissible and infer that again a normal limit law holds. Finally, we discuss a correspondence to set partitions with even block sizes and present an algorithm based on Boltzmann samplers that generates such graphs uniformly at random.

title: Flip Combinatorial Invariance for flipclasses with small residues
abstract: We establish (Normal) Flip Combinatorial Invariance for flipclasses with no residues longer than 8. Actually, we show more generally that all flipclasses of finite type with no residues longer than 8 have only one increasing path. For flipclasses of Weyl type, these are precisely the flipclasses having only one increasing path. This marks a refinement of the classical Combinatorial Invariance of Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials.

title: A sharp minimum degree condition for Hamiltonicity in line graphs of 3-hypergraphs
abstract: Let $G$ be the line graph of a $3$-hypergraph, and let $n$ be its order. We prove that if $G$ is $3$-connected, $n\ge4936$, and $δ(G)\ge(n+5)/10$, then $G$ is Hamiltonian if and only if it does not belong to an explicitly described family of exceptional graphs. This extends the sharp minimum degree bound of Lai, Shao, and Zhan for $3$-connected claw-free graphs beyond the claw-free setting, since line graphs of $3$-hypergraphs may contain induced claws. The coefficient $1/10$ cannot be decreased, and the constant $5$ in the numerator cannot be replaced by $4$.

title: On representation-theoretic and homological properties of distance algebras of finite graphs
abstract: Distance algebras were introduced by Asao and Ivanov to realize magnitude homology and cohomology as bigraded Tor and Ext groups. We study the representation-theoretic and homological properties of the distance algebra $Σ_G$ of a finite connected graph $G$. We characterize the graphs for which $Σ_G$ is representation-finite, multiserial, biserial, or self-injective by an explicit graph-theoretic classification. We also compute the finitistic, self-injective, and dominant dimensions for several natural families of graphs. For a finite modular lattice $L$, we consider the distance algebra $Σ_L$ associated to the Hasse graph of $L$, and show that $Σ_L$ is Auslander--Gorenstein precisely when $L$ is a finite direct product of chains. We also present a family of minimal Auslander--Gorenstein distance algebras, namely, those associated to punctured hypercubes, whose finitistic (equivalently, self-injective; equivalently, dominant) dimension can be arbitrarily large.

title: Unveiling the mutual inclination distribution in astrometric surveys
abstract: Mutual inclination in three (or more) body systems (triple stars, circumbinary planets, multi-planetary systems, etc.) is a tracer of their formation and evolution. Gaia Data Release 4 will provide for the first time a catalog of orbital solutions for three-body systems. Because astrometry is only sensitive to the motion in the plane of the sky, there is a degeneracy in the orbital solutions leading to two possible solutions for the mutual inclination in three-body systems. We propose a hierarchical Bayesian framework to circumvent this degeneracy and unveil the mutual inclination distribution in the population. We tested our methods on simulated datasets, and showed that it reliably recovered the injected mutual inclination distributions in various cases. The method is thus promising for the statistical analysis of Gaia DR4 three-body systems.

title: The shape of individual differences in judgment: shared axes, personal weights, and when their spread crosses the consensus
abstract: People differ in how they judge faces, artworks, photographs and jokes. Previous work measured the size of these differences; we ask what shape they take. We wrote three candidate shapes as nested generative models (same-sign reweighting of shared dimensions, a linear transform that allows reversal, and stimulus-specific offsets) and compared how well they predict people unseen in training, using ten public datasets (about 20,000 raters). The models recovered a person's judgment space from 10-20 judgments and predicted judgments of unseen stimuli. For faces, reweighting was sufficient, and weights opposing the population were not statistically detected. For artworks, weights spread continuously along the shared abstract-figurative direction, and 28 percent of raters fell on the opposite side from the population. This tail was much smaller when a different rater sample judged the same artworks. Individual differences thus differ in shape as well as size, and the shape depends on domain and raters.

title: SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding, yet remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Recent studies explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. However, these approaches either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme, regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. Through systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion, we find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels (e.g., distance estimation vs. route planning) require geometric representations of different granularities, revealing that fixed fusion cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations. SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics, and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate, and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. Furthermore, we introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse. Gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. Experiments demonstrate that SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhaosb-star/SpatialMind.

title: Small-ball asymptotics of Gaussian matrix products: Open Fermi shells and the Grassmannian
abstract: Let $P=A_N\cdots A_1$ be a product of independent standard real or complex Gaussian matrices of arbitrary fixed sizes. For complex entries we determine the exact leading terms, of the form $κ\,\varepsilon^C(\log1/\varepsilon)^q$, of the operator-norm and Frobenius small-ball probabilities of $P$, together with the corresponding asymptotics of the Laplace transform of $\|P^2\|_{F}$. The exponent $C$ is the known diversity order, while the logarithmic power follows a filling rule: when fermions are placed on ladders of states determined by the sizes and the last occupied level has degeneracy $μ$ and contains $h$ particles, $q=h(μ-h)$. The determinant of this last shell expands in Plücker coordinates graded by the Schubert cells of the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}(h,μ)$, with leading coefficients proportional to normalized degrees of Schubert varieties. For real entries we prove that the Frobenius small-ball probability has an exact positive leading term of order $\varepsilon^{C/2}(\log1/\varepsilon)^q$ and that the operator-norm probability has the same order, which gives a proof of the known real log canonical threshold and its multiplicity that needs no explicit resolution of singularities. We evaluate the real leading coefficient in closed form for every shell with at most one logarithm, a class that contains all products of two factors, and we conjecture its general form, which agrees with the classical constant of vector chains. Applications include the outage probability of cascaded multi-antenna channels at high signal-to-noise ratio and the Bayesian evidence of deep linear networks.

title: Earth-strength magnetic-field axis modulates non-spatial probabilistic decision-making in humans
abstract: Magnetoreception has been primarily studied in orientation and navigation, but whether Earth-strength magnetic fields influence non-spatial decisions remains unclear. Evidence for human magnetic responses is limited, and the transduction mechanism is unknown. Using a Go stone selection paradigm in which near-zero geomagnetic field and Larmor-frequency conditions previously showed lower black stone rates, we tested whether non-spatial choice depends on magnetic-field geometry. Fasted men played in pairs under ten static two-seat configurations varied component-wise at near-constant north-seat intensity. The north-seat black stone rate was lower under the two configurations with horizontal fields transverse to the geomagnetic field than under the other eight, which did not differ detectably. The difference emerged promptly, without evidence of outcome-driven learning or configuration-dependent associations with the partner's preceding actions, and process analyses linked it to the joint parity-choice outcome without isolating either step. A Larmor-frequency difference observed over the ambient field was not detected over horizontal-only or vertical-only backgrounds, suggesting a potential magnetoresponsive axis, although the background difference was statistically unresolved. Frequency, light-spectrum, and posture analyses support a radical-pair mechanism as a leading working hypothesis. These findings associate the geomagnetic field axis with human non-spatial choice, providing a paradigm linking magnetic sensing to decision processes.

title: On the volume growth assumption in the Eulerian definition of RCD spaces
abstract: We prove that every infinitesimally Hilbertian metric measure space whose reference measure is a Radon measure, and which satisfies the Sobolev-to-Lipschitz property and the weak Bochner inequality with a lower Ricci bound, has Gaussian volume growth; in particular, balls have finite measure. Hence, in the Eulerian definition of $\mathsf{RCD}(K,\infty)$ spaces, both the volume growth assumption and the finiteness of the measure of balls are redundant. The proof combines the self-improvement of the Bakry--Émery gradient estimate, obtained without using the conservation of mass of the heat flow, with a dimension-free Harnack inequality derived from the Sobolev-to-Lipschitz property.

title: Minimum degree thresholds for even cycle residues
abstract: Dean's conjecture asserts that, for every integer $m\ge3$, every graph of minimum degree at least $m$ has a cycle whose length is divisible by $m$. This degree bound is best possible for odd $m$. For every integer $k\ge2$, we prove that every graph of minimum degree at least $2k-1$ has a cycle whose length is congruent to $r$ modulo $2k$ for every even $r\not\equiv2\pmod{2k}$. Consequently, $2k-1$ is the sharp minimum degree threshold for a cycle whose length is divisible by $2k$. For bipartite graphs, we prove that minimum degree at least $k$ guarantees the same residue classes for every $k\ge4$, and we characterize their end-blocks when no cycle has length congruent to $2$ modulo $2k$. The bipartite degree bound is also sharp, and the exclusion of residue $2$ is necessary even for connected graphs of arbitrarily large order.

title: The Zaks--Perles--Wills volume conjecture I: three-dimensional lattice polytopes
abstract: We prove the three-dimensional Zaks--Perles--Wills volume bound for lattice polytopes with $k\ge3$ interior lattice points: the Euclidean volume of such a lattice polytope is at most $6(k+1)$, with equality if and only if the polytope is affinely unimodularly equivalent to $\operatorname{conv}(0,2e_1,3e_2,6(k+1)e_3)$. The inequality is strict when the minimum lattice width is at least three. Together with the known cases $k=1,2$, this completely resolves the three-dimensional Zaks--Perles--Wills volume conjecture.

title: Stability of Homochiral Peptides in Capillary Environments: Implications for the Origin of Biological Homochirality
abstract: The homochiral proteins in living organisms are rather stable, but they tend to lose their secondary conformations and homochiral order over time. This instability is found in all living organisms, from bacteria to humans. The aging of living organisms, with the destruction of their vital homochiral order, raises the questions about the emergence of homochirality and how the homochiral order in the building molecules was ensured in prebiotic times before life evolved. Based on thermodynamic arguments, we propose that the homochiral order was achieved by a ``Frank-synthesis'' of homochiral peptides from racemic amino acids and in a capillary environment in the vents in the Earth's crust, perhaps at crystalline chiral surfaces, and that the peptides are stable over long times in such an environment. The $hypothesis$ can be confirmed by experimental analysis of the stability of the secondary structures in proteins as a function of water activity and in a capillary environment.

title: Uniform spatial Schauder estimates for backward stochastic partial differential equations with random coefficients
abstract: We prove spatial Schauder estimates for super-parabolic backward stochastic partial differential equations. All coefficients can be random and depend on time and space, and the estimates are uniform in probability and time. The key ingredient is a weighted conditional energy norm adapted to the parabolic scale of each frequency block. Together with heat-kernel bounds and coefficient freezing, it controls the gradient-martingale coupling without assuming a bounded martingale integrand. As an application, we establish Schauder solvability for semilinear stochastic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equations.

title: Approximating Itô Processes in Adapted Wasserstein Distance with Finite Support Laws
abstract: Motivated by finite-scenario surrogates in stopping and control problems, we study the approximation of Itô diffusion laws by laws supported on $M$ paths in an adapted Wasserstein distance, which we term adapted functional quantization. Under the strict adapted Wasserstein distance, no finite-support approximation can achieve vanishing error, while even under its relaxed counterpart, naive empirical measures still fail to converge. To resolve this, we develop a recursive conditional sampling algorithm and derive constructive upper bounds on the adapted quantization error. In one dimension, this yields the Brownian rate $(\log M)^{-1/2}$ for every diffusion with continuous coefficients of linear growth and pathwise uniqueness. In several dimensions, a quantitative Osgood stability condition with exponent $β$ yields the rate $(\log M)^{-η_p}$, where $η_p=\min\{1/2,β/(β+4p-2)\}$. Without the Osgood condition, we construct a two-dimensional diffusion with smooth bounded coefficients whose adapted quantization error decays more slowly than $(\log M)^{-γ}$ for any $γ>0$.

title: ST-FateFlow: Continuous Gene-Spatial Reconstruction with Differentiation-Potential Learning from Time-Resolved Spatial Transcriptomics
abstract: Time-resolved spatial transcriptomics provides a powerful view of dynamic biological processes by measuring cellular states together with their spatial organization across time. However, destructive profiling and experimental cost restrict observations to a few discrete time points collected from independent samples, with no known cell pairing across time. This makes it difficult to reconstruct gene expression and tissue organization at unobserved stages and to characterize differentiation-associated dynamics. Here, we introduce ST-FateFlow, a flow-matching framework for continuous gene-spatial dynamics and differentiation-potential learning. ST-FateFlow jointly learns gene-expression and spatial-coordinate velocity fields, enabling interpolation of missing time points and continuous modeling of transcriptional evolution and tissue remodeling. In parallel, it independently learns a time-conditioned differentiation potential, whose values organize cell states along inferred differentiation progressions and support the analysis of differentiation-associated transcriptional changes. Across multiple time-resolved spatial transcriptomics datasets, ST-FateFlow effectively captures coordinated gene-expression and spatial dynamics. Case studies further show that the learned potential landscapes are consistent with known developmental and regenerative trajectories and help identify candidate genes associated with differentiation progression.

title: Between proper and strong edge-colorings of graphs with maximum degree at most four
abstract: A $(1^j,2^k)$-packing edge-coloring of a graph $G$ is a partition of its edge set $E(G)$ into $j$ matchings and $k$ induced matchings. It can be viewed as intermediate colorings between proper and strong edge-coloring. The study of this topic on subcubic graphs has drawn considerable attention recently, with many conjectures and open problems proposed and resolved. However, very few results are known for graphs with maximum degree four or more. Henderson, Kennedy, and Santana showed that every graph with degree at most four has a $(1,2^{19})$-packing edge-coloring and a $(1^2,2^{17})$-packing edge-coloring. In this paper, we improve the results of Henderson, Kennedy, and Santana by showing every graph with degree at most four has a $(1,2^{17})$-packing edge-coloring. As a corollary of our result, every graph with degree at most four has a $(1^2,2^{16})$-packing edge-coloring.

title: Discovery of new antiviral agents through artificial intelligence: in vitro and in vivo results
abstract: In this research, we employed a deep reinforcement learning (RL)-based molecule design platform to generate a diverse set of compounds targeting the neuraminidase (NA) of influenza A and B viruses. A total of 60291 compounds were generated, of which 86.5% displayed superior physicochemical properties compared to oseltamivir. After narrowing down the selection through computational filters, nine compounds with non-sialic acid-like structures were selected for in vitro experiments. We identified two compounds, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 that effectively inhibited the NAs of both influenza A and B viruses (IAV and IBV), including H275Y mutant strains at low micromolar concentrations. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed a similar pattern of interaction with amino acid residues as oseltamivir. In cell-based assays, DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 inhibited IAV and IBV in a dose-dependent manner with EC50 values ranging from 0.29 uM to 2.31 uM. Furthermore, animal experiments showed that both DS-22-inf-009 and DS-22-inf-021 exerted antiviral activity in mice, conferring 65% and 85% protection from IAV (H1N1 pdm09), and 65% and 100% protection from IBV (Yamagata lineage), respectively. Thus, these findings demonstrate the potential of RL to generate compounds with promising antiviral properties.

title: 3D and 2D Radiation Non-ideal MHD modeling of the decay of FUor outbursts
abstract: FU Orionis (FUor) outbursts are high-accretion events in protoplanetary disks thought to be driven by the magnetorotational instability (MRI). Although these outbursts span a wide range of observed durations and can thermally process and potentially transport disk material, the physical processes governing their decay remain poorly understood. We present a three-dimensional radiative non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation of the decay of an MRI-driven FUor outburst, complemented by a suite of two-dimensional models that explore its dependence on disk properties. During the decay, rings and gaps form naturally within the inner disk. Magnetic flux preferentially concentrates in the gaps, while the rings remain comparatively weakly magnetized. We show that MRI-active rings act as ``magnetic dams,'' confining magnetic flux within adjacent gaps. As the rings cool below the MRI activation temperature, non-ideal MHD effects decouple the gas from the magnetic field, allowing the trapped flux to diffuse outward. This outward diffusion can sometimes transiently reactivate MRI in neighboring rings, producing localized reheating events that we term ``Reactivation.'' By comparing otherwise identical two- and three-dimensional simulations, we find that MRI heating is systematically less efficient in two dimensions, leading to outburst durations shorter by a factor of $\sim3$--4. Our model suite further shows that the decay timescale depends primarily on the disk surface density and distance from the central star, with only a weak dependence on the magnetic field strength. We further derive an empirical relation linking the outburst duration to these quantities.

title: More lower bounds for Hales--Jewett and van der Waerden numbers
abstract: We give explicit colourings improving the comparison lower bounds assembled here for several Hales--Jewett and van der Waerden numbers. The main algebraic tool generalises Rabung's power-residue colouring from arithmetic progressions to arbitrary sets. If every translate of a t-element set S in F_p meets at least two classes of the r-th power character, and the integer weights have both parities, then a period-2p one-weight colouring of [t]^p has no monochromatic combinatorial line. The 19 displayed algebraic certificates comprise 18 improvements and one closed-form reproduction; they include HJ(4,3)>=164, HJ(5,4)>=7418, and HJ(5,6)>=34034. The underlying period-p construction also proves kappa_ow(t,r)>=p-1 for the one-weight bracket ceiling, in particular kappa_ow(5,4)>=7416 and kappa_ow(5,6)>=34032. Warm breakout-weighted tabu search on the type simplex gives HJ(3,4)>=51. Whole-colouring local search gives W(8,3)>522, W(11,3)>1193, and W(17,3)>3620. All accepted certificates are available separately and are checked by direct enumeration; unresolved searches are reported as UNKNOWN, not UNSAT.

title: On Threshold Probabilities for the Stability of the Independence Number of a Random Subgraph
abstract: For an arbitrary sequence of graphs $G_n$, we consider a random spanning subgraph $G_{n,p}$ in which each edge of the graph $G_n$ survives independently of the others with probability $p$. We obtain a general upper bound for the independence number $α(G_{n,p})$, from which, for an arbitrary probability $p=p(n)$, we derive sufficient conditions for asymptotic stability, i.e., for the equality $α(G_{n,p})=(1+o(1))α(G_n)$ asymptotically almost surely, as well as upper bounds for the independence number of the random subgraph, including unconditional ones; for $p=1/2$ they recover A. M. Raigorodskii's results of 2017 and 2026. Under additional conditions on the structure of the independent sets of the graph $G_n$, we find, up to a constant factor, the threshold probabilities for both asymptotic and exact stability (the equality $α(G_{n,p})=α(G_n)$). Special cases include results on the graphs $G(n,r,<s)$ for growing $r$ and $s$, including Kneser graphs for growing $r$; we also give examples of complete multipartite graphs, graphs on the blocks of Steiner systems, and $q$-analogues of Kneser graphs.

title: On Contractibility of Geometric Joins
abstract: The geometric join of a family of sets in $\mathbb R^d$ is the union of the convex hulls of all colorful sets. For every $d \geq 4$, we construct $\lceil\frac{(d-1)^2}{2}\rceil$ sets in $\mathbb R^d$ whose geometric join is not contractible, disproving the conjecture of Bárány, Holmsen, and Karasev that the geometric join of at least $d+1$ sets is contractible.

title: A Brownian web invariance principle: Localized disturbance flows and Hastings-Levitov(0)
abstract: We establish a Brownian web invariance principle for localized disturbance flows, providing a criterion that strengthens the weak-flow convergence of [Norris--Turner 2015, Ann. Probab. 43, 935--970] to path-Hausdorff convergence of their full trajectory collections. We apply this approach to the radial, stationary, and cylindrical versions of the Hastings--Levitov$(0)$ aggregation model, proving path-Hausdorff convergence of the full harmonic measure path collections to the (Cylindrical) Brownian web, together with joint convergence of the full gap--finger collections to geometric embeddings of the corresponding double Brownian webs. This extends the radial HL$(0)$ small-particle limits of [Norris--Turner 2012, Commun. Math. Phys. 316, 809--841] for the harmonic measure flow and finite gap--finger collections. In the radial and cylindrical HL$(0)$, we also show that the rescaled one-arm domination time converges to a multiple of the global coalescence time of coalescing Brownian motion on $\mathbb T$, with convergence of expectations. The main new ingredient is a three-point survival estimate, proved via a multiscale stopping-time decomposition.

title: Exomoons and Exorings with the Habitable Worlds Observatory. III. Icy Moons and Rings Often Outshine Their Planets
abstract: If we could observe the Solar System's giant planets with the upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), the dominant sources of reflected near-infrared light would not always be the planets themselves. In fact, the brightest sources are split roughly evenly between the giants and their icy companions: at the locations of the giant planets, the dominant point sources would be Jupiter, Saturn's rings, Uranus, and Triton (Neptune's icy moon). Motivated by these Solar System cases in which rings or moons outshine their host planets, we investigate the detectability of analogous exomoons and exorings with HWO. We compute the expected signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) for moons and rings with the same albedos as their Solar System counterparts over a range of sizes, system distances, and star to planet+moon or star to planet+ring separations. We find that reflected light from Triton-analog exomoons and Saturn-analog exorings is detectable with HWO over a broad parameter space. In the nearest systems, icy Titan-sized moons are detectable at star-moon separations of ~2 AU and icy Earth-sized moons out to ~6 AU. Moreover, Saturn-like exorings are likely to be the brightest point sources in many extrasolar systems, capable of greatly outshining any planets, while remaining potentially detectable at system distances out to 100 pc. These results highlight the need for further work to develop methods for identifying and disentangling exoring and exomoon signatures from exoplanet signals in HWO observations, where these sources will be blended and spatially unresolved.

title: Continuous improved Hölder and reverse Hölder inequalities for Gaussian random vectors
abstract: We establish continuous versions of the improved Hölder and reverse Hölder inequalities for correlated Gaussian random vectors, where a finite covariance matrix is replaced by a covariance operator acting on a Hilbert space of parameter fields. Under operator comparisons between the covariance and the exponent multiplier, we prove both inequalities and characterize equality in terms of a compatible probability density on the underlying Gaussian space. We further describe this density as a product of independent factors on common eigenspaces and a Gaussian factor whose mean and covariance satisfy explicit algebraic conditions. In the reverse setting, positive and negative exponents may coexist. The continuous product is defined by ordered truncation, allowing zeros in the positive-exponent factors. The equality proof combines an exact Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup comparison, a spectral gap away from the kernel of the governing operator difference, and characteristic-function deconvolution. We also treat exponential quadratic functions without requiring a uniform positive-definiteness margin on the precision matrices.

title: A Butterfly-Inspired Agent Learns to Climb with Self-Generated Wingbeats
abstract: Butterfly free climbing involves dynamic coupling between wing motion and unsteady aerodynamic forces that drive the animal's ascent. Four-wing coordination determines how these forces combine to support weight and direct propulsion. How aerodynamic feedback shapes such coordination remains difficult to establish when wing kinematics are prescribed in experiments and simulations. Here, we construct a virtual flight environment with rapid aerodynamic feedback and train a butterfly-inspired agent using the soft actor-critic algorithm. Without a wingbeat generator, the agent spontaneously develops non-sinusoidal wingbeats and achieves reward-directed climbing. The climbing angle varies primarily with wingbeat frequency and mean angle of attack, and force-balance analysis links these adaptations to gravity projections along and normal to the flight direction. The aerodynamic forces are faithfully recovered only when the agent-generated wing motions are reconstructed with higher-order harmonics, rather than the commonly used first harmonic. Independent and combined modulation of frequency and mean angle of attack further reveals their nonlinear coupling in regulating climbing direction. These findings reveal how coordinated propulsion strategies emerge under physical constraints and provide a theoretical framework for studying strategy formation through interactions between organisms and their fluid environment.

title: Three Circles in a Unit Disk: Three Solutions to an Extremal Problem
abstract: We place two disks inside the unit disk so that they touch each other and the unit circle. We then insert a disk of the largest possible radius, requiring it to touch both original disks. We show that the smallest possible sum of the three areas is $11π/18$, and find all equality cases. We give three solutions, using Descartes' circle theorem, inversion, and contact-point coordinates. The main difficulty is checking that the third disk is largest among all disks that fit, not only among disks touching the first two.

title: Real-Rootedness and Log-Concavity of Zigzag Eulerian Polynomials
abstract: We prove that the zigzag Eulerian polynomials have only real, negative, simple zeros, and hence strictly log-concave coefficients, settling the first two parts of a conjecture of Petersen and Zhuang. Real-rootedness in combinatorics is usually proved inside a single algebraic framework, such as interlacing or stability. Our proof rests on a different premise: different parts of a zero set become visible in different representations of the same polynomial, and classical tools suffice once each part is viewed in the right one. The bridge between representations is a local rule. Forgetting the order in which a bounded-jump path visits positions leaves only a nearest-neighbor condition on sorted gaps, which makes an encoding via a transfer matrix much simpler to see. From there the argument passes to complex analysis. The sizes of the matrix's eigenmodes locate the zeros at the two ends of the negative axis, through Rouché's theorem. In a logarithmic coordinate the generating function becomes a combination of derivatives of the hyperbolic secant, akin to the classical derivative polynomials, and the arguments of its nearest poles produce a sine that fixes the signs between consecutive central zeros. The zeros are thus read off from the poles of an associated kernel. More broadly, the proof suggests that combinatorial polynomials defined by local constraints carry analytic structure, in their spectra and in the poles of their kernels, that is complementary to the usual algebraic methods and that classical complex analysis can exploit directly.

title: Directed triangles in oriented graphs without a directed cycle of length $3t$
abstract: For integers $k,\ell\ge 3$, let $\operatorname{ex}(n,\Cdir_k,\Cdir_\ell)$ denote the maximum number of directed cycles of length $k$ in an $n$-vertex oriented graph containing no directed cycles of length $\ell$. Grzesik, Jaworska, Kielak, Kuc and Ślusarczyk~\cite{GJ} systematically studied the generalized Turán problem for directed cycles and conjectured that, for every fixed integer $t\ge 2$, $\operatorname{ex}(n,\Cdir_3,\Cdir_{3t})=\frac{t-1}{4}n^2+o(n^2)$. They proved this asymptotic formula for $t=2$. In this paper, we prove it for every fixed integer $t\ge 3$, thereby confirming the conjecture.

title: An Omnidirectional WECT: Closed-Form Computation of the Directionally Integrated Weighted Euler Characteristic Transform
abstract: The weighted Euler characteristic transform (WECT) and related directional descriptors have become popular, efficiently computable tools for shape analysis across a variety of domains. In practice, however, they are approximated over a finite set of filtration directions, and thus the vectorized descriptor depends on this choice of directions and the rotational orientation of the data. In this manuscript, we formally introduce the directionally integrated weighted Euler characteristic transform (DIWECT), which averages the WECT over all directions $s \in \mathbb{S}^n$ for a weighted simplicial complex immersed in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. A framework for computing the DIWECT exactly, without sampling directions, is outlined: for each simplex, we partition $\mathbb{S}^n$ into the sets of directions in which a given vertex enters the filtration last, and then the DIWECT at height $t$ reduces to measuring intersections of these regions with a set of directions in which the simplex has entered the filtration by height~$t$. We provide implementations for complexes immersed in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$, in which case the problem reduces to computing arc lengths and spherical areas. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the DIWECT, while resulting in more compact vectorizations, also successfully encodes shape information and discards noise from data orientation. On a barley seed classification task, it outperforms the WECT in every pose except a hand-curated frame, whose advantage disappears under a two-degree rotation error. Compared with averaging the WECT over sampled directions, the DIWECT is often faster at matched accuracy. In one instance, this is upwards of a $50 \times$ speedup on a one-million-cell image with an error of $10^{-3}$.

title: Toroidal Obstructions with No K_5 Minor
abstract: Finding the complete set of forbidden minors for the torus remains an open problem. We determine the complete list of toroidal minor obstructions with no $K_5$ minor and prove that there are exactly $74$, each with between $10$ and $14$ vertices. Combined with the known classification of toroidal obstructions with no $K_{3,3}$ minor, this determines every toroidal obstruction that excludes one of the forbidden minors for planarity. The proof uses three-vertex cuts to show that, apart from $K_{3,7}$, every three-connected obstruction in this class has two distinct independent triples, each the common neighborhood of at least two degree-three vertices. The classification proceeds by considering the possible intersections of these triples and reduces each case by planarity tests and enumeration of the possible graph forms. From the $74$ minor obstructions we also obtain a complete list of $381$ topological obstructions for the torus with no $K_5$ minor.

title: Enumerating orbits of finite classical groups on their Lie algebras
abstract: We enumerate the orbits of a finite classical group in the adjoint action on its Lie algebra, giving exact generating functions and very good upper bounds. We treat the general linear, unitary, symplectic and orthogonal groups, in both odd and even characteristic. In even characteristic, we get very nice formulas for the number of orbits on nilpotent classes both in the finite and algebraically closed case. We discuss the connection with commuting varieties.

title: Why do continual physical learners need sleep?
abstract: Sleep is widespread across the animal kingdom, including in organisms without a centralized nervous system. Does learning create a need for sleep, even without biology? To explore this question, we study a disordered spring network trained to perform a sequence of mechanical allosteric tasks through local changes in bond stiffness. We find that continual learning progressively reduces the network's ability to acquire new tasks as individual bonds become increasingly specialized. We identify an exact algebraic relationship between the polarization of bond dominance and the network's remaining learning capacity, providing a quantitative measure of this loss of adaptability. We then demonstrate that random internal perturbations allow individual bonds to estimate their mechanical dominance and locally adjust their stiffnesses to restore learning capacity. However, the forces associated with active learning bias these local measurements and interfere with restoration. Separating learning and repair into wake-like and sleep-like phases removes this interference and improves continual-learning performance. Our results suggest that the need for offline restorative phases can emerge from the mechanics of physical learning, even in systems without biological components.

title: Fixed-Point Results and Disequilibrium for Negators of Hyperbolic-Valued Probability Distributions
abstract: Hyperbolic-valued probability distributions provide a probabilistic setting in which mass, order, and uncertainty take values in the positive cone of the hyperbolic algebra. We study the fixed-point structure of hyperbolic probability negators and the behavior of hyperbolic-valued disequilibrium along their iterates. Starting from a hyperbolic-valued metric on each mass stratum, we define the associated disequilibrium as the separation between a distribution and the uniform distribution determined by its hyperbolic mass. We consider the disequilibria induced by the hyperbolic Euclidean, \(\ell_1\), and Jensen--Shannon metrics. Their hyperbolic Schur-convexity is established and sharp lower and upper bounds are obtained. We also characterize the possible fixed-point sets of hyperbolic negators through an order-theoretic condition and derive criteria ensuring uniqueness of the associated uniform distribution. The behavior of disequilibrium along the iterates of hyperbolic negators is then analyzed through two complementary mechanisms. Domination by Yager's negator yields exact decay factors for the Euclidean and \(\ell_1\) disequilibria and a uniform decay factor for the Jensen--Shannon disequilibrium. Independently, Lipschitz conditions for generated negators lead to positive linear comparison maps whose spectral radii control the asymptotic decay of disequilibrium. These results provide structural and quantitative conditions ensuring that hyperbolic-valued disequilibrium converges to zero under repeated probability negation.

title: Positivity in symmetric webs and block permanents
abstract: We use symmetric webs to prove Marcus's block-permanent inequality for up to four blocks of every size, for five blocks of size at least three, and for any fixed number of blocks above an explicit logarithmic bound on the block size. The proof idea is easy: Bending strands in the Schur relation turns the comparison into a calculation with squared norms.

title: A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory
abstract: Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.

title: A Linear-Size Well-Separated Pair Decomposition for Unit Disk Graphs
abstract: Given a metric space $(X, d)$ a $c$-well separated pair decomposition (WSPD) is a collection of `dumbbell' pairs of subsets $(A, B)$, $A, B\subseteq X$, where the distance between the two sets is at least $c$ times the diameter of each set and every pair of points in $X$ is covered by one such pair. It is known that for a weighted unit disk graph metric of $n$ points, there is a WSPD of size $O(n\log n)$. But it is open whether this bound can be improved to $O(n)$. In this note, we answer this question affirmatively and provide an algorithm that yields a linear-size WSPD for unit disk graphs.

title: Cubic graphs with circumference ratio 21/22 and cyclic connectivity 5
abstract: We construct a cyclically $5$-connected cubic graph of order $22m$ and circumference $21m$ for every $m\geq 3$. Consequently, the shortness coefficient of the class of cyclically $5$-connected cubic graphs is at most $21/22$, improving the previously known upper bound of $24/25$. We also demonstrate how I-reductions, which delete an edge and suppress its two end-vertices, can be used to prove cyclic connectivity.

title: FunSearch and Structured SAT Search for Weak Schur Partitions
abstract: The weak Schur problem asks how large an interval of consecutive integers can be partitioned into a fixed number of classes with no class containing a monochromatic solution to $a+b=c$ with $a\neq b$. We investigate whether FunSearch, an evolutionary program-search method guided by a large language model, can discover effective construction strategies for this classical combinatorial problem. In our adaptation, FunSearch evolves a priority function used by a fixed greedy solver, while a separate validity check enforces the weakly sum-free condition. This approach matches the known exact values for two, three, and four classes and reaches $WS(5)\geq195$. We then explore a complementary SAT-based approach. Guided by structural information from a 207-element construction communicated by Fred Rowley (Rowley, 2026), our SAT search produces and verifies a distinct valid five-class partition of $\{1,\ldots,207\}$. Thus the strongest construction obtained in this project reaches $WS(5)\geq207$, eleven integers beyond the best published lower bound of 196. The contrast between the two approaches also exposes a limitation of our FunSearch formulation: its greedy solver makes local, irreversible decisions, whereas SAT can enforce global structure across the whole partition.

title: An improved bound on the strong chromatic index via local flag algebras
abstract: A strong edge coloring is an edge coloring where two edges receive different colors if they are incident or joined by a third edge. For a graph $G$, the strong chromatic index of $G$, denoted by $χ'_s(G)$, is the minimum number of colors needed for a strong edge coloring of $G$. In this paper, using a local flag algebra method, we prove that for every graph $G$ of sufficiently large maximum degree $Δ$, $χ'_s(G)\le 1.642Δ^2$, improving the previous best bound $1.73Δ^2$ due to Davey, Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos, Kang, and Volec.

title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

title: Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching
abstract: Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.

title: Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI
abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.

title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

title: One size does not fit all: session-specific effects of deep brain stimulation on hand-motor kinematics in Parkinson's disease
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) effectively treats motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is unclear whether it changes fine hand movements in the same way for every patient. We analyzed 35 sessions of 19 patients with PD from a multi-center cohort performing the CopyDraw task, a drawing task designed to overcome the subjectivity and limited granularity of clinical assessments. Besides standard kinematics (mean velocity, acceleration, jerk, and drawing accuracy), we derived higher distributional moments and non-linear complexity measures, for 38 features in total. DBS effects were quantified with linear mixed models at the group level and with residualized regression and a random-effects meta-analysis per session. The DBS state was decoded per session with regularized linear discriminant analysis to compare feature sets as behavioral labels for deriving physiomarkers for adaptive DBS (aDBS). DBS modulated all 38 features at the group level, most strongly velocity-related features. However, for every feature, the between-subject variability of the DBS effect exceeded the group-level effect. Only one feature, the detrended fluctuation analysis of the distance to the template, showed a significant mean effect across sessions, and it is not a standard kinematic feature. In six sessions without any significant modulation of standard features, complexity measures were modulated instead. For decoding, standard features alone were the best choice in ten of 35 sessions, but combining all 38 features yielded the highest average area under the ROC curve (0.700 vs. 0.677), with the largest gains in sessions that were hard to decode from standard features. DBS effects on hand-motor behavior are individual. Deriving neural markers for aDBS from behavior therefore requires session-specific analyses with individualized features beyond standard kinematics and group-level effects.

title: Data-driven simulation of the brain's response to stimulation: a system identification approach for closed-loop neuromodulation, piloted in adaptive deep brain stimulation
abstract: Closed-loop neuromodulation uses a physiomarker to control stimulation. Developing such controllers requires exploring a large space of strategies and parameters, which is often not feasible with the human-in-the-loop. Simulation environments offer an alternative. Adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS) for Parkinson's disease is a stereotypical application: while physiomarker identification progresses rapidly, clinically available control is limited to threshold and proportional strategies. We propose to identify dynamical models of the brain with and without deep brain stimulation (DBS) using the sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) framework. Identified ex post from existing recordings, such models are a middle ground between abstract bottom-up models and the realistic but difficult-to-access human-in-the-loop. Forecasting neural activity from real initial conditions, the models create a simulation environment for "what if" analyses of DBS changes. In a proof-of-concept with EEG data from a single subject, we train and evaluate threshold, proportional, proportional-integral-derivative (PID), and proximal policy optimization (PPO) control, aiming to have the simulated data classified as DBS ON at minimal energy. SINDy models fitted on spatially filtered EEG maintained DBS condition-specific characteristics. All aDBS controllers delivered DBS more efficiently than continuous DBS (cDBS), with up to 20.2% energy reduction. Proportional control yielded a small but significant gain over threshold control. PID and PPO achieved a comparable reward advantage over cDBS, with PPO stimulating more conservatively and PID saving the most energy.
