Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.

title: Coherent belief and opinion propagation produces more echo chambers: corrected version
abstract: The occurrence of echo chambers is a well-known phenomenon in social networks. Echo chambers are groups of agents satisfying three properties: homogeneity, i.e., sharing the same opinion, segregation, i.e., listening primarily to agents of the same group, and reinforcement, i.e., increasing opinion similarity over time. Opinion dynamics models have been used to explain how echo chambers occur through agents updating their opinions. However, social network users also exchange beliefs supporting their opinions. Here, we aim at identifying the effect of propagating beliefs together with opinions on the formation of echo chambers. For that purpose, we complement an existing opinion dynamics model with classical belief merge operations. Beliefs and opinions are also maintained coherent guided by values that agents share. We introduce measures, applying to either beliefs and opinions, to identify echo chambers based on the three properties. This model is used to simulate opinion and belief propagation with varying initial conditions and agent tolerance for different opinions/beliefs. Results confirm the occurrence of echo chambers observed in previous opinion dynamics studies in a different setting and with a stricter measure. They also demonstrate the occurrence of echo chambers with belief propagation. Finally, they show that connecting opinions to beliefs and maintaining their coherence increases the number of belief echo chambers, but that they involve a reduced number of agents.

title: On the trajectories of the ID algorithm
abstract: The ID algorithm decides whether an interventional distribution can be computed from observational data and, when it can, returns a formula in which products, ratios and summations of conditional probabilities are nested inside one another. We study these formulas by following the trajectories of the calls of the algorithm, each of which ends with a tail (an alternation of lines 7 and 2) and an exit, and we derive two main results. First, line~4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation of the output, while the tail forms everything inside it, both the inner summations and the ratios. Second, a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a repetition of the tail is entangled, and a test of ancestry in the original graph decides, before any formula is computed, whether a topological order can be chosen so as to avoid it. We also derive a bound on the nesting depth of the output, and show a simple ``dimensional'' count that every output has to satisfy. Together, these results constrain the form of an ID output and guide its implementation and simplification.

title: Neckpinches in a Positively Curved Market: Ricci Flow with Surgery on the Nikkei-225
abstract: We study the intrinsic geometry of the Nikkei-225 through the discrete Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC) of its empirical correlation graph, using the graph Ricci flow and surgery methodology of arXiv:2510.15942. The 226-node correlation graph, built from daily returns between January 2020 and June 2026, is ORC-spherical: every edge has strictly positive curvature before any flow, close to the equal-weight value $κ\approx0.502$. Under a fixed 20-iteration Ricci flow the curvature distribution polarises into a high-curvature bulk and a low-curvature minority, and cutting the low-curvature edges splits the graph into components of 184 and 42 nodes. The recursive ARCUS procedure (Adaptive Ricci Curvature Unsupervised Surgery) stops the flow at each node once a curvature gap ratio $G$ exceeds $G_{\min}$ and the surgery set is stable. With $G_{\min}=10$ and a minimum cluster size of 15, ARCUS performs 28 surgeries over 13 levels and ends in 29 terminal clusters of 2-14 nodes. The stopping rule fires at every node, with $G$ between 10.0 and 92.4, and the top-level split reproduces the fixed-schedule 184/42 partition exactly. Eight small subgraphs stop with $G<15$, so the deeper levels are conditional on $G_{\min}$. Many terminal clusters are single industries by inspection, among them nine banks, five insurers, five general trading companies, three steelmakers and three shipping lines. Two delisted stocks without price data enter as zero-correlation placeholders; with them excluded, every terminal cluster is more strongly correlated internally than with the rest of the index.

title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents
abstract: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.

title: Interlacing Committees with Edge-Expansion
abstract: Approval-based committee selection has recently been studied through the lens of \emph{interlacing}, a framework for studying polarization in approval elections, in which committees induce a similarity graph over voters. The quality of committees is then evaluated through the connectivity of the resulting graph. We revisit the connectivity measures used in this framework and propose \emph{edge-expansion}, a classical graph-theoretic measure with well-established connections to polarization in networks, as the optimization objective. We provide a theoretical foundation for this proposal by relating interlacing to classical models of information diffusion and by comparing edge-expansion with previously proposed connectivity objectives, identifying qualitative differences in the structural properties they capture. Finally, we study the computational complexity of optimizing edge-expansion, showing that hardness persists even for voter-interval preferences, while the problem is polynomial-time solvable for every fixed committee size, with an improved dependence on the committee size for voter-candidate-interval preferences.

title: Taylor expansions for first-passage time distributions of Brownian motion with moving boundaries
abstract: We analyse the distribution of the first-passage time of Brownian motion to a time-dependent boundary as a function of the boundary. We prove that the boundary-to-distribution map is infinitely many times differentiable along the Cameron-Martin space $\mathscr{H},$ and obtain a with a bound on the truncation error Taylor expansion with a bound on the truncation error. We obtain identities connecting (i) the $\mathscr{H}$-derivatives of the first-passage time distribution, (ii) the Wiener-Itô chaos kernels of the indicator that the Brownian motion stays below the boundary, and (iii) Krylov-Veretennikov-Zvonkin-type operators. These identities yield relatively tractable representations for the $\mathscr{H}$-derivatives of the first-passage time distribution when the taboo transition density is available, notably for linear boundaries. As an application of the above results we propose Taylor approximations up to second order of the first-passage time distribution. In the examples considered, the first-order approximation is more accurate than the classical tangent approximation and its hazard-rate variant, while remaining straightforward to implement.

title: RAVEN: A Self-RAG Based Agent for Threat Classification and Response
abstract: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infrastructure. We implement an early-stage prototype and report preliminary results on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads each (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; an evaluation on IDS- generated alerts and a user study are ongoing and outlined as remaining work.

title: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures
abstract: When an artificial intelligence agent pays with a stablecoin, the commerce protocol can specify the merchant, order, amount, and facilitator. The token contract enforces the fields the wallet signs. We call the difference the authority gap, define nine constraint classes, and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol. All 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code match the derivation. A controlled comparison shows that committing the terms in the signed nonce binds the order. When the facilitator submits a payment to a merchant account without code, binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Of 26,653 sampled USD Coin authorizations redeemed on Base, 98.7% followed a path that any holder of the signature could redeem. We prove sufficient conditions for a recipient contract to enforce the signed mandate under a trusted signer and show which recipient a wallet displays. MandateLock, a minimal implementation for immediate payments, rejects all 10,800 modified mandates on deployed token code and accepts signatures from two independent signers. It uses 25% more gas than a transfer that only the recipient can submit.

title: Microscopic Probabilities for U-Statistics and Almost-Balanced Permutations
abstract: We estimate the probability that a vector of U-statistics lies within $C/n$ of a target in the range of typical fluctuations. For sufficiently large $C$, we prove a lower bound of the typical Gaussian order under finite variance, and a matching upper bound for bounded kernels. We show that under finite variance alone, stronger concentration may occur, and find the best possible asymptotic upper bound. Our proof is algorithmic, estimating probabilities by counting successful modifications produced by a random algorithm. We apply this result to settle a question of Beniamini, Lavee and Linial (2025), who asked if there exist permutations with $k$-order sub-pattern counts at most $O(n^{k-1})$ away from one another for $k>4$. We prove not only existence, but enumerate these permutations up to a constant factor, showing that there are $Θ(n!n^{-(k-1)^2/2})$ such permutations of size $n$.

title: ALIoTh: Orchestrating Multi-Agent LLMs for Autonomous IoT Penetration Testing
abstract: Penetration testing in Internet of Things (IoT) environments, especially those composed of various different devices, e.g., smart plugs, smart cameras, and smart doors, presents great challenges across the phases of information gathering, attack surface enumeration, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This paper introduces ALIoTh, a multi-agent, workflow-driven penetration testing framework that integrates Large Language Models agents within a Self-Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Self-RAG) architecture to autonomously identify and exploit vulnerabilities in IoT and Industrial-IoT (IIoT) environments. By leveraging state-of-the-art language models and orchestrating specialized agents via the LangGraph framework, ALIoTh dynamically plans and executes a full-spectrum offensive pipeline. This includes network, devices, and service enumeration, vulnerability assessment, payload generation, reverse shell deployment, and privilege escalation on each device. The Self-RAG mechanism equips expert agents with contextual access to IoT security knowledge, e.g., related documentation, tool manuals, and known attack techniques, enhancing their reasoning capabilities in scenarios involving multiple device exploitation and group policy manipulation.

title: Particle physics science communication with grass-roots Instagram: a success story
abstract: Communicating science to the public is an integral part of the work of a research collaboration, not an afterthought. Institutional and collaboration-level social media accounts are often run by professional communicators rather than by practising scientists, and single-scientist ``influencer'' accounts are demanding to sustain. We describe {\em CMSatDESY}, a crowd-sourced Instagram account on which the CMS group at DESY tells its own stories, each member in their own voice. In the first half of 2026, the science communication activities through this reached 140k+ unique accounts and received 250k+ views, with an engagement rate of 7\%. We discuss experiences and best practices that can be used by other groups, and describe how the account doubles as a science communication playground for outreach training for a large particle physics group.

title: The Atmospheric Circulation of Cloudy Hot and Ultra-hot Jupiters: the Need for Dissipation of Large-scale Flows to Reduce the Nightside Brightness Temperatures of Ultra-hot Jupiters
abstract: We perform general circulation modeling of hot and ultra-hot Jupiters across equilibrium temperatures of T_eq=1600 to 2800 K, incorporating cloud formation and its feedback on atmospheric dynamics. This study specifically examines whether clouds explain the systematically low nightside brightness observed in Spitzer thermal phase curves of ultra-hot Jupiters. We found that clouds generally increase phase-curve amplitudes and reduce eastward offsets, and these effects are most pronounced at relatively low T_eq and gradually weaken as T_eq increases. We discussed two mechanisms responsible for reducing the phase-curve offsets by clouds: the dynamical and geometric effects. Without explicit dissipation of large-scale winds, strong equatorial jets develop, maintaining a hot equatorial region and clearing clouds near the nightside equator at T_eq >= 2200 K, with thick clouds instead forming mainly at mid-to-high latitudes. These patchy nightside clouds do not sustain low nightside fluxes as temperatures rise, suggesting that clouds alone cannot explain the observed nightside brightness for ultra-hot Jupiters. Strong dissipation, parameterized as magnetic drags, suppresses equatorial jets and promotes nightside cloud coverage. In both clear and cloudy models, drag weakens the dependence of Spitzer nightside brightness temperature on equilibrium temperature; clouds further lower the nightside brightness temperature with the same drag prescription. Clouds also dampen amplitudes of thermal spectra on the nightside and, under small-particle conditions, can even produce emission features. Due to limited dayside cloud cover, our models yield negligible Bond albedos. Finally, interpreting simulated thermal phase curves with energy balance models in near-IR and IR bands tends to overestimate the Bond albedos of ultra-hot Jupiters by an order of magnitude or more.

title: On the Reliability of CyberGym Evaluation: Task Material Consistency and Reference-Target Identity
abstract: CyberGym evaluates vulnerability reproduction by checking whether a proof-of-concept input (PoC) crashes a vulnerable program version but not a fixed version. Interpreting this differential pass as successful reproduction requires consistent task materials and evidence that the PoC triggers the intended defect. We examine these requirements through a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of the final PoCs from one complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run. Taking the defect associated with each reference crash report as the target, the audit assigns inconsistency labels to 338 tasks (22.4%) after correcting two labels identified by stratified blind review. The largest categories are coverage inconsistency (205 tasks) and descriptions and patches that jointly point to another defect (110 tasks). We assess PoC identity using an execution check, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review. Of the 1,286 differential passes, the procedure assigns 89 non-target and 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts; requiring a target hit lowers the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%. Non-target verdicts also occur in tasks with no material inconsistency found: 39 of 1,052 differential passes (3.7%). Although the identity verdicts require independent validation, these findings motivate separate checks of task-material consistency and submission identity when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores.

title: Quantitative approximations for finite-state mean-field configuration models
abstract: We establish quantitative approximations for the empirical measures of finite-state mean-field particle systems in a general framework. The scales of the empirical drift and covariance distinguish the ODE and critical diffusion regimes and determine the corresponding time rescaling. In the ODE regime, we obtain quantitative central limit approximations in the $1$-Wasserstein distance and a Bernstein-type concentration inequality. The concentration bound has no dimensional prefactor. Its explicit time dependence also identifies growing intervals on which the ODE approximation remains accurate. In the critical regime, we prove a quantitative nonlinear diffusion approximation in the $1$-Wasserstein distance. We apply our quantitative approximation results to noisy voter systems, Moran models with mutations and selections, heat-bath Glauber dynamics for the $p$-spin Curie--Weiss model, and autocatalytic reactions with mutations.

title: DS2Agent: Holistic Device Agents for Accelerated Embedded Board-Level Design
abstract: Embedded board-level development demands extensive expertise, from component selection and device characteristics to interface configuration, driver writing, and system composition. Recently, LLM-based agents have shown strong capabilities, raising the prospect of automating board-level design tasks. However, existing agents either target chip-level design or treat datasheets as static text, offering little guidance on whether a specific component should---or even could---be used for a given board-level design. Moreover, without touching real hardware, they hallucinate incorrect details. To fill this gap, we present {\setlength{\fboxsep}{1pt}\href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DS2Agent-9FE8/}{\fcolorbox{blue}{white}{DS2Agent}}}, an open-source framework that constructs interactive agents from device datasheets. Each agent comprises three models: a knowledge model supporting retrieval and question answering; a digital-twin model capturing the physical functionality of the device; and an interface model supporting driver development and system integration. To suppress hallucinations, we also allow optional connections to real devices, so that the agent can calibrate its internalized knowledge against the device. We evaluate DS2Agent on ten devices spanning seven functional categories. Compared with the baseline, the DS2Agent-augmented agent improves the question-answering score from 87 to 97 out of 100 while using 44.8\% fewer tokens. For driver generation, it reduces average token usage per device by 72.9\%. For system integration, it reduces total token usage across three FreeRTOS applications by 29.7\%.

title: Critical droplets and metastability in long-range chains
abstract: Metastable decay in first-order phase transitions proceeds through the nucleation of critical droplets. In the one-dimensional nearest-neighbor Ising chain, the cost of the two walls bounding a droplet is independent of its size. For interactions decaying as $1/r^{1+σ}$, this surface cost instead depends on the droplet size and competes with the bulk free-energy gain. The critical radius scales as $R_c\propto h^{-1/σ}$ at small $h$, where $h>0$ is the bias field. The value $σ=1$ separates two regimes: for $σ<1$, the activation barrier diverges as $h\to0^+$; at $σ=1$, it grows logarithmically; and for $σ>1$, it remains finite, as in the nearest-neighbor chain. A nonlocal $φ^4$ field theory yields critical droplets with algebraic tails and confirms the predicted radius and barrier scalings, while stochastic long-range dynamics independently reproduces the critical-radius scaling.

title: Uniqueness, Proximity, and Scaling in Atomic Splittable Polymatroid Congestion Games
abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games with integral ranks and rational player-specific affine latencies with positive slopes. The algorithm first computes equilibria of associated integer-splittable games, in which demands are allocated in multiples of a common packet size. For arbitrary polymatroid bases, no polynomial-time algorithm for these discrete equilibria was previously known. We provide such an algorithm and use progressively finer packets to recover the continuous equilibrium exactly. Our proof uses the multiple-exchange theorem of Oki and Schwarcz (2025) to obtain two exchange matchings that yield equilibrium proximity under changes of packet sizes and ranks, independently of cost coefficients. We then bound the matching deficiency caused by rank changes and construct compatible submodular rank roundings. Together these give a polynomial-time packet-halving algorithm using polynomially many submodular-function minimizations and exact rational arithmetic. The analysis rests on a uniqueness theorem of independent interest: for arbitrary real polymatroid ranks and continuously differentiable, strictly increasing, convex latencies, we prove uniqueness of equilibria, resolving a previously open problem.

title: Embodied Human-Data Interaction
abstract: We propose the concept of human-data interaction (HDI) as the human manipulation, analysis, and sensemaking of large, unstructured, and complex datasets. We then proceed to suggest an embodied approach to HDI to build physical reasoning environments for these difficult and polymorphic tasks. We illustrate our approach with two examples: tangible lenses for visual exploration, and an educational computer game with tangible bricks.

title: From Reliance to Overreliance: Taxonomizing and Detecting Relational Risks in AI Companionship
abstract: Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic Character.AI and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.

title: Hardening JavaScript Programs against LLM-Based Vulnerability Detection
abstract: JavaScript programs are often distributed as source code, so attackers can analyze them for vulnerabilities. LLM-based vulnerability detection agents now make this analysis much easier. To mitigate this emerging threat, we present AntiAgent, a defense that lets developers harden their programs against such detection agents. AntiAgent transforms a program before release to impede an agent's analysis. To find effective transformations, AntiAgent evolves a corpus of programs with known vulnerabilities and traces how a detection agent analyzes each evolved version. It keeps the versions on which the agent misses or misreports the vulnerability and extracts their transformations into reusable rules. To protect a new program, AntiAgent carefully divides the task between an LLM and the rules, so that the transformations adapt to the program while preserving its semantics. We evaluate AntiAgent on real-world JavaScript applications against four detection agents, including Claude Code and Codex. AntiAgent reduces the number of vulnerabilities that each agent detects by 52.0-60.7%, outperforming the conventional obfuscator JS-Obfuscator and the LLM-based transformation method FPA on every agent. The transformed programs pass all project tests, indicating that AntiAgent preserves the original program semantics. The transformation rules also remain effective on vulnerability types absent from the corpus and on programs written in another language like Python.

title: Distortion in Online Voting
abstract: We initiate the study of distortion in online voting, a framework that bridges computational social choice and online algorithms. In contrast to the classical offline setting, where the full election instance is known in advance, we consider a dynamic environment where a fixed set of voters is present from the beginning, but alternatives arrive sequentially over time. Upon each arrival, a mechanism must immediately and irrevocably decide whether to retain the currently selected candidate or switch to the newly arriving one, operating solely on the partial ordinal rankings induced by the underlying cardinal preferences. We provide upper and lower bounds for deterministic and randomized mechanisms under two standard cardinal preference frameworks. Utilitarian framework: For deterministic mechanisms under adversarial arrival order, we establish an $Ω(mn)$ lower bound and give an matching online algorithm with distortion at most $\frac{2}{3}m(n+\frac{1}{4})$. For randomized rules, we introduce regularity, which allows any regular, order-independent offline randomized rule to be converted into an online rule with the same expected distortion. The Harmonic voting rule satisfies this property, yielding online distortion $O(\sqrt{m\log m})$. Metric framework: For deterministic mechanisms, maintaining an alternative within a $\varphi$-weighted uncovered set guarantees distortion $2+\sqrt{5}$. We show that matching-based offline rules achieving distortion $3$ cannot be directly implemented online. We establish a lower bound of $\sqrt{13}$, even with three alternatives, and a matching upper bound for three alternatives and any number of voters. For randomized mechanisms, regularity gives an online distortion of $3-\frac{2}{n}$ via Random Dictatorship.

title: Proportional Representation for Almost-Solid Coalitions and the Proportional Veto Core for Rankings
abstract: A proportional ranking should give groups of voters representation commensurate with their size at every prefix. Proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC) provides this guarantee to groups whose members rank the same set of candidates above all others. How much representation should a group receive when a few outside candidates disrupt that agreement? We extend the proportional veto core to rankings through candidatewise and setwise guarantees. We show that setwise veto protection is equivalent to robust Rank-PSC under reversal of both the voters' preferences and the collective ranking. Robust Rank-PSC extends representation guarantees to almost-solid coalitions at every prefix. Each distinct outside candidate that disrupts a coalition's agreement reduces its guaranteed representation by at most one, and this bound is tight. Using reverse-sequential variants of Ordered Phragmén and STV, we construct rankings satisfying robust Rank-PSC$+$ in polynomial time. This stronger axiom preserves the guarantee after deleting any suffix of the collective ranking and restricting voters' preferences to the remaining candidates. Verifying robust Rank-PSC is coNP-complete, whereas verifying robust Rank-PSC$+$ takes polynomial time. We also introduce Rank-Aligned PJR$+$, which requires the first $r$ candidates of the collective ranking to satisfy PJR$+$ when each voter approves their top $r$ candidates. We give a polynomial-time algorithm that meets this requirement simultaneously for every $r$. For fixed-size committees, the Expanding Approvals Rule guarantees Rank-PJR$+$ but can violate robust PSC regardless of how ties are broken or payments are assigned. We give a modification that satisfies both guarantees for any prescribed committee size.

title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.

title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
abstract: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.

title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition
abstract: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.

title: Positive semidefiniteness of random submatrices
abstract: Given a symmetric matrix $A \in [-1,1]^{n \times n}$, we estimate the probability that a random principal submatrix, obtained by taking each index independently with probability $p$, is positive semidefinite. As a corollary, we show that $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ indices chosen uniformly at random suffice for testing positive semidefiniteness with squared Frobenius distance threshold $\varepsilon n^2$, thus nearly matching the lower bound of Bakshi, Chepurko, and Jayaram (``Testing Positive Semi-Definiteness via Random Submatrices'', FOCS 2020). The key ingredient is a dense model lemma for positive semidefinite matrices, proved using the hyperplane separation theorem and a contraction inequality for Rademacher random variables.

title: GRODE-RTL: Source-Mapped Dependency Views for LLM-Based RTL Repair
abstract: Large Language Models show great potential for automated Register-Transfer Level repair, yet they struggle with non-local faults where root causes and failing outputs reside far apart in source code. Treating RTL as a flat token sequence obscures hardware dataflows, whereas exposing complete synthesized graphs overwhelms the model with fine-grained metadata. To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.

title: TWIN-2: Timing Solar Radio Bursts between 180-350 MHz Against GOES and Aditya-L1 X-ray Detections
abstract: We have conducted continuous solar observations for approximately two and half years using the Two-Element Interferometer (TWIN) at Gauribidanur Radio Observatory (RRI). During which several solar events have been detected. Our observational period coincides with the maximum events phase of the Solar Cycle 25, providing us opportunity to analyse the evolution of the solar activity. Our analysis of two and half years data show a clear increase in the occurrences of solar events, which is consistent with the expected rise in the solar activity towards the peak phase of the Solar Cycle 25. We further investigate the detected solar radio events using X-ray observations from the space based Aditya-L1 and the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) satellites. For the automated detection of SRBs, a machine learning suite has been trained. This also serves as an instrument for space weather monitoring. On the 7th of November 2025, a solar storm was detected by our pipeline in realtime. A brief overview of the data-processing pipeline, along with the RFI mitigation techniques employed to identify and characterize the solar events, is also presented. Observation data of two and a half years of TWIN is available for public access. The data has been used in student training programmes on solar radio data analysis, with students carrying out the analysis and contributing to the initial analysis of the detected events.

title: Erasing the Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage and Concept Erasure in Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings
abstract: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared in place of raw images for authorized downstream tasks, yet they may reveal sensitive attributes. Standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness. However, we prove that, when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved, so global erasure must either eliminate that signal or retain task-conditional linear leakage. We further show how global erasure affects linear readers' discrimination between positive and negative samples with different sensitive attributes, deriving an approximate closed-form prediction of its utility cost from pre-erasure statistics. Motivated by this conflict, we introduce Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE), a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of its fitting data. We evaluate four vision foundation models on 85 CelebA attribute pairs spanning a broad range of associations. After LEACE, conditional leakage persists across all four encoders, the discrepancy between marginal and conditional audits increases with association strength, and predicted utility costs track observed losses. We then examine hospital chest radiographs using three foundation models, including two biomedical models, in which chest-tube status is strongly associated with diagnosis. Although a marginal attack on LEACE-erased embeddings underperforms a diagnosis-only reference, chest-tube status remains detectable within diagnosis strata. TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.

title: Two Faces of Spacetime Density Matrices: Entanglement and Complexity
abstract: We establish a direct connection between entanglement and complexity through spacetime density matrices. For stationary pure states and complementary regions at different times, spacetime replica moments encode the return amplitude of a replica-defect quench. This representation defines an associated state spread complexity, which we call Krylov-Rényi complexity. It can equivalently be obtained by using a replica-defect excitation of the replicated background state as the seed and evolving it under the original replicated Hamiltonian. We further construct Krylov-von Neumann complexity as a probe limit from first-order replica data. Timelike entanglement and complexity provide complementary information at a fixed time, while the full time dependence of the timelike entropy determines the Krylov dynamics and hence the complexity. The replica construction fixes the seed and its evolution through the background state, subsystem geometry, and regulator, without an independently chosen probe operator. Like entanglement entropy, the resulting complexity is defined nonperturbatively and probes universal properties and dynamical information about the underlying theory.

title: Hierarchical Spatiotemporal World Modeling with Content-Adaptive Spatial Addressing
abstract: Long-horizon world modeling in partially observable environments requires compact memories that preserve spatial structure despite accumulated localization drift. Inspired by hippocampal episodic and spatial memory and the multi-periodic coding of entorhinal grid cells, we propose HiSTFormer, a hierarchical spatiotemporal world model, which adopts a layer-wise organization of local temporal RoPE and multi-periodic spatial RoPE, together with content-conditioned address offsets, to capture recent temporal context and long-range spatial structure. A fixed-capacity memory keeps KV storage and per-step attention cost bounded as the sequence grows. On MemoryMaze and HM3D, HiSTFormer outperforms strong world-model baselines within the training sequence length and generalizes substantially better to prediction horizons far beyond those seen during training, while using a compact model. The hierarchical spatiotemporal design remains effective across deeper Transformer stacks, with consistent gains as depth increases. These results show that hierarchical spatiotemporal organization and content-adaptive spatial addressing provide effective inductive biases for efficient long-horizon world modeling.

title: MetaScanner: An Empirical Study and Proactive Defense against Deceptive UI Attacks in Social VR
abstract: Social virtual reality (VR) platforms have surged in popularity but continue to face significant security challenges, including privacy invasion and user manipulation. Yet, the security risks posed by deceptive content remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce four novel deceptive UI attacks that covertly manipulate social VR users into performing unintended actions without their awareness. We show how adversarial content creators can embed seemingly benign scripts and interactive elements within carefully designed virtual worlds, deceiving users into unknowingly carrying out harmful behaviors. We implemented these attacks on VRChat, a leading social VR platform, and an IRB-approved user study involving 30 participants confirmed their effectiveness. To mitigate these threats, we propose MetaScanner, a proactive analysis system that efficiently scans virtual world assets, including scripts and interactive objects, to identify suspicious or deceptive elements before users are exposed to them. We demonstrate that MetaScanner can successfully detect all threats in test worlds where the four attack scenarios were implemented. Additionally, MetaScanner shows its lightweight nature, with an average scanning time of 5 seconds across 38 real-world assets.

title: Dependence of Dust Growth on Magnetic field Strength in Protoplanetary Disks
abstract: We performed one-dimensional calculations to investigate how the magnetorotational instability (MRI) affects dust growth in protoplanetary disks. We simultaneously solved the evolution of the dust size distribution and the vertical magnetic field. The dust size distribution is evolved taking into ac- count coagulation and fragmentation. For the magnetic field evolution, we considered both ambipolar diffusion and Ohmic dissipation. The MRI-driven turbulent viscosity was estimated self-consistently from the local magnetic field strength and non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics diffusivities. We found that MRI-driven turbulence becomes stronger for smaller initial plasma beta, and the enhanced tur- bulence promotes dust growth in MRI-active regions. However, dust growth is ultimately limited by radial drift, and the dependence of dust size on the magnetic field strength is significant only in the outer regions of the disk. In other words, over most of the disk, radial drift remains the dominant factor controlling the maximum dust size, and the magnetic field strength plays only a minor role in determining the overall dust size distribution.

title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

title: Measuring Hallucination in Large Language Models for Cyber Threat Intelligence: An Exploratory Study
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in cyber threat intelligence (CTI) tasks, such as summarization and question answering. However, they may produce hallucinations, false or misleading content not grounded in the source text, which can mislead analysts and corrupt downstream security decisions. This paper presents an exploratory measurement study of hallucinations in LLM-based CTI. We introduce HalluVision, a reproducible framework that generates LLM outputs, extracts domain-specific entities using a fine-tuned named entity recognition model, and evaluates factual consistency using multiple similarity metrics. Using 4,940 real-world cybersecurity articles, we measure hallucinations in outputs from two commercial LLMs and one open-weight LLM. Measurements are validated against 100 human-annotated outputs and two established faithfulness detectors. Results show that semantic similarity aligns with human judgments, whereas entity-based metrics exhibit limited agreement. Differences between models are concentrated in question answering, while entity extraction quality limits what entity-level metrics can reveal.

title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing
abstract: Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing. Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust. Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale. Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts. Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.

title: Markov processes with jump kernels blowing up at the boundary of $C^{1, η}$ open sets
abstract: We study the boundary behavior of nonnegative harmonic functions for a class of purely discontinuous symmetric Markov processes in $C^{1,η}$ open sets $D\subset\mathbb R^d$. The jump kernels are allowed to blow up at the boundary of $D$ and the processes may have a critical killing potential. We identify the exact boundary decay exponent $p$, characterized by the coefficient of the critical killing potential. We establish a boundary Harnack principle which yields the comparability of $f(x)/δ_D(x)^p$ for nonnegative harmonic functions that vanish continuously on a portion of the boundary. The key ingredient of the proof combines estimates of the exact decay rate for the survival probability of the killed process with a modified box method and uses a regularized distance function to handle the limited boundary regularity.

title: Geometry-induced orientational trapping dictates escape of active rods in corrugated channels
abstract: The non-equilibrium transport of anisotropic active matter through geometrically confined environments is fundamentally governed by the interplay between self-propulsion and geometry-induced entropic barriers. Using overdamped Langevin dynamics, we reveal contrasting escape mechanisms of self-driven rods in narrow corrugated channels by comparing smoothly varying sinusoidal (SC) geometries to circular (CC) cavities with localized, uniform curvature. We observe a strictly non-monotonic dependence of the mean first escape time (MFET) with increasing Peclet number (Pe) in the CC channel, contrary to the monotonic dependence in the SC channel. This non-monotonicity emerges from a competition between activity-enhanced escape at low-to-intermediate propulsion and persistent, geometry-induced orientational trapping along the circular boundary at high propulsion, which inhibits reorientation toward the exit neck. This regime crossover is further corroborated by trajectory-to-trajectory escape fluctuations and bimodal radial probability distributions reflecting persistent wall-collision and wall-aligned sliding transport. The self part of van-Hove correlation function exhibits distinct anisotropic non-Gaussian displacements in the SC channel, in contrast to symmetric profiles with extended active-trapping plateaus in the CC cavities. These results establish local channel topology as a critical determinant of confined active transport, with direct implications for microfluidic sorting, biological navigation, and targeted drug delivery in corrugated environments.

title: AZOWL AgentOps: Task-Scoped Governance for Deployed Agent Applications
abstract: AZOWL AgentOps provides shared governance for deploying agents and delegating work to them. Human and agent senders can exchange messages or explicitly delegate a business task. Accepted work has a stable identifier that links the sender's authority, the assigned runner, any required approval, and result evidence. The default enrolled customer PC profile is read-only. We compare AZOWL components with a configured LangGraph application in 28 synthetic runs across four paired pilots. Original AZOWL services checked work admission, recipient routing, and workflow prerequisites in isolated tests. The configured LangGraph application supplied business task and dispatch records in application code. Both configurations recorded zero business tasks in dialogue, rejected unauthorized agent handoffs, and issued zero writes when an approved delivery address changed. AZOWL's scope gate, exercised as a component, requested approval again on the same task. A product probe reused one registered provider across two workflows and checked prerequisite enforcement for ticket-task submission. The paired protected writes, including ticket creation, used mock providers. Of two deployed PC inventory reads with verified receipts, we traced the 0.6.57 run from submission through runner pickup and tool execution to the receipt, with matching local and central artifact hashes. A separate deployed GRC audit followed an operator-driven ticket lifecycle on sample records.

title: Passing NPCR Without Diffusion: Exact Signatures, a Detection Benchmark and an Audit of Published Image Ciphers
abstract: NPCR, the share of ciphertext bytes changed by a one-pixel plaintext change, is reported for nearly every image cipher as evidence of diffusion, with 99.61% the target. Several mechanisms produce values near it, and the mean does not say which. We separate three regimes: no propagation, one round of forward and backward chaining linear over addition or XOR, and independent ciphertexts. For the second an exact count applies. After a least-significant-bit change its mean asymptotically matches the independent-ciphertext reference, while its spread without cancellation is about five to twenty times larger. In simulation, the one-sided NPCR test of Wu, Noonan and Agaian flags one-round additive, mixed and S-box chaining in 2-4% of papers; read in both directions, the same five values flag at least 99.9%. Two-sided testing does the detecting; the spread and the other signatures help diagnose the structure. We then audit twenty-one published schemes. The count matches a reimplementation of one published diffusion layer on every trial and accounts for its reported table, the signatures show two schemes whose printed specifications cannot produce their reported values, and find that three of our own report plain-versus-cipher values and fall to two chosen images; ten more change their encryption material with the plaintext or per encryption, so their NPCR mostly reflects that change. A released checker applies the signatures to published tables, showing what a table measures within stated assumptions; it does not certify security.

title: UniReFP: Robust Unified Fingerprinting for Vision Models against Cross-Task Repurposing Attacks
abstract: We identify, for the first time, a new model modification attack--the cross-task model repurposing attack--that can render fingerprints generated by existing model fingerprinting approaches inapplicable. To address this challenge, we propose UniReFP--a novel unified model fingerprinting framework applicable to diverse vision models across different tasks--that utilizes ownership evidence in a shared class-level semantic space rather than original task-specific output space, enabling effective ownership verification when a protected model is repurposed across tasks with heterogeneous output formats. Specifically, UniReFP constructs a surrogate classifier by repurposing the protected model, enabling fingerprints to be generated independently of the original task-dependent output space of the protected model. Moreover, it optimizes grouped fingerprints to encode ownership evidence: fingerprints within the same group are encouraged to induce consistent semantic responses and intermediate representations on the surrogate classifier, while producing dispersed responses on independently trained reference classifiers. During verification, UniReFP uses a task-aware semantic projection mechanism to map heterogeneous suspect-model outputs into unified semantic-presence vectors, and determines ownership by measuring inner-group consistency. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness of UniReFP, consistently showing superior performance under cross-task repurposing attacks, commonly studied model modification attacks, and even their combinations.

title: A new second-moment method for spectral measures of inhomogeneous non-Hermitian random matrices
abstract: We develop a second-moment method for the empirical spectral distribution (ESD) of non-Hermitian random matrices $X_N=(\sqrt{s_{ij}}ξ_{ij})$ with a deterministic variance profile $S_N=(s_{ij})$. When the entries are independent and centered, the second moment of $\det(zI-X_N)$ is the permanent $\mathrm{per}(S_N+|z|^2I)$ of a diagonal shift of $S_N$, and the method approximates $\log|\det(zI-X_N)|$ by half its logarithm. For i.i.d. centered $ξ_{ij}$ of unit variance satisfying a Dini-type condition on their Lévy concentration function, we prove the circular law for every doubly stochastic profile whose largest entry tends to zero, however slowly. This condition holds for every law with a bounded density on $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. We also allow the two entries $X_{ij}$ and $X_{ji}$ of each reciprocal pair to be correlated, with a nondegenerate joint law that has a finite mixed fourth moment. If the pairs and the diagonal entries also have bounded densities on their real linear supports, we prove an elliptic law for every symmetric doubly stochastic profile whose largest entry tends to zero. For i.i.d. $ξ_{ij}$ as above and general profiles with vanishing largest entry and bounded average row sum, we show that the ESD is asymptotically close to the Brown measure of the matrix $(\sqrt{s_{ij}}c_{ij})$ of free circular elements. The ESD converges weakly in probability if and only if $N^{-1}\log\mathrm{per}(S_N+qI)$ converges for every $q>0$, and these limits determine the radial distribution of the limit. As applications, we give sufficient conditions for convergence in terms of tree weights, characterize the radial laws that arise from profiles with uniformly bounded row and column sums, and show that the empirical distribution of the zeros of $\mathrm{per}(zI-X_N)$ is asymptotically close to the ESD.

title: Topological trapping of active tracers in branched ring polymer matrices
abstract: Branched macromolecular architectures are ubiquitous in living systems and synthetic polymeric systems, create topologically complex media that strongly influence tracer dynamics beyond simple packing fraction-driven crowding effects. Motivated by biological systems such as amoebae, astrocytes, cytoskeletal assemblies, and cyclic bottlebrushes, we investigate active and passive tracer transport in polymeric environments of topologically distinct architectures. Here, using Langevin dynamics simulations, we focus on how polymer topology alters diffusion behavior in a branched-ring polymeric (BRP) environment. To isolate the role of intramolecular topology from monomer density, we specifically benchmark the BRP dynamics against an unlinked linear-ring polymer mixture (LRM). In general, we find that while passive tracers are largely unaffected by the polymer connectivity and bending rigidity, the self-propelled active tracers strongly distinguish between the two architectures. Increasing chain rigidity facilitates active diffusion in the unlinked LRM but strongly restricts mobility in the BRP matrix, driving a transition to pronounced long-time subdiffusion that becomes more prominent with propulsion strength. Different physical observables reveal that interconnected topological cages are formed in the stiff limit, leading to transient weak ergodicity breaking and leptokurtic displacement statistics. Further, the self-intermediate scattering function confirms that the short-range dynamics remain unaltered by the matrix connectivity, while relaxation at large spatial length scales is governed by the topological caging. Finally, varying the branch length and number, we identified an optimal branch architecture that maximizes active trapping. Our results establish that macromolecular connectivity and stiffness dominate the active transport even in the system of identical packing fraction.

title: Multi-Illumination Spectral Reflectance Reconstruction: A method for hyperspectral imaging using digital photography
abstract: Quantitative measurement of complex coloration patterns is essential for many biological studies and practical applications. Although color perception depends on the observer's visual system, an objective characterization is possible by measuring the spectral reflectance across the sample surface. Traditional methods for measuring spectral reflectance are either limited in spatial resolution, as with spectrometer probes, or limited in spectral detail, as with digital cameras. We present a method for reconstructing spatially resolved spectral reflectance of samples from multiple images taken under different illuminants with known spectral irradiance. Using an optimization scheme that minimizes pixel-value error while regularizing for the smoothness of the reflectance spectrum, our method generates high-resolution hyperspectral images. We tested our method using both existing spectral reflectance datasets and original multi-illumination images taken in a custom photo-box, demonstrating high accuracy and simple implementation of the method, as well as the ability to infer how samples are perceived by different visual systems. Our method can be a useful tool for objective quantification of complex visual patterns in color-related biological research and imaging applications.

title: Rational Designs and Prouhet--Tarry--Escott Problems
abstract: For every strength, we prove the existence of rational designs on spheres, orthogonal and unitary groups, real and complex Grassmannians, and ellipsoids that are defined by positive-definite quadratic forms with rational coefficients and have a rational point. This answers Bannai's Problem for these spaces, solves the problem of Cui--Xia--Xiang on rational spherical $4$-designs on the unit circle, and proves Xiang's conjecture in the stronger form of existence in every dimension. To this end, we introduce the $(G,\mathcal{S})$-Prouhet--Tarry--Escott problem for an abelian group $G$ and a finite set of characters $\mathcal{S}$ and develop its existence and minimality theory. We also prove a general theorem transforming integer-weighted rational designs into equi-weighted designs on distinct rational points. On the unit circle $\mathbb{S}^1$, we determine the minimum sizes of rational spherical designs of strengths $4,5,6,7$ and show that they are respectively $2304,4608,9216,9216$. We also show that the minimum size of a rational spherical $5$-design on $\mathbb{S}^2$ is $192$. We further apply our framework to prove a conjecture of Thuswaldner--Ziegler on sums of distinct units and to answer Mahabaduge's problem on convex equilateral lattice polygons affirmatively.

title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
abstract: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.

title: Dynamical Variational Theory of Stochastic Reaction Networks
abstract: Discrete stochastic population dynamics describe systems ranging from biochemical reaction networks and gene regulation to epidemic spreading, ecology, and population genetics, where finite populations generate strong intrinsic fluctuations. Predicting their dynamics, including mean populations, fluctuations, time-lagged correlations, response functions, and steady states, remains challenging: the chemical master equation admits no general analytical solution, numerical solutions scale poorly with system size, and standard approximations fail at low copy numbers. Using a field-theoretic representation of the reaction dynamics, we develop a dynamical variational approximation for stochastic reaction networks based on the Plefka expansion from spin-glass physics. For reaction systems with general stoichiometry and time-dependent rates, the expansion yields tractable non-Markovian effective dynamics with self-consistent memory. We further introduce a generalized self-consistent bubble resummation that provides closed predictions for means, correlations, and response functions. The formulation applies broadly to discrete stochastic population dynamics on networks, and we provide a numerical implementation with adaptive time stepping for user-defined systems. We benchmark the method on stochastic gene regulation, enzyme kinetics, and infection dynamics, where it accurately captures both time-dependent behaviour and steady states, including fluctuation-driven effects missed by conventional approximations. Together, these results establish a general analytical framework for stochastic reaction dynamics across transient and stationary regimes in strongly fluctuating low-copy-number systems.

title: Side-Channel Analysis of the RP2350 Challenge 2
abstract: Bug bounty programs and community challenges have become an established mechanism to incentivize collective action to improve security. In essence, these can be considered as crowd-sourcing mechanisms where participants carry the risk twice over: performing the work in addition to having it officially accepted, which at times can be tied to unacceptable terms. Consequently, independent assessments and publications that are free from third party obligations remain important to highlight deficiencies in implementations of public significance. We consider the RP2350 side-channel analysis challenge and its hardened Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) implementation to be of reasonable importance to justify such an approach, especially so since the presented challenge remained unsolved for more than a year. In our paper, we present our analysis, demonstrating comprehensive leakage detection, plaintext dependence, and key extraction from the challenge implementation. Our work presents concerning weaknesses in the implementation that contradict the challenge authors' claims. We hope by openly sharing this analysis to motivate further public scrutiny.

title: ToolPulse: Side-Channel Eavesdropping on Tool-Using LLM Agents
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that translate user requests into sequences of local tool invocations. While prior cache-based side-channel attacks target the locally deployed models, they typically require the adversary to share model-related components or hardware resources with the victim's inference process. These assumptions do not apply to the predominant agentic settings, in which commercial LLMs execute on vendor-controlled infrastructure. We show that agentic execution exposes a more practical attack surface: although inference remains remote, tools are executed on the user's machine and commonly rely on shared system libraries. In this paper, we first systematically evaluate Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe for monitoring agentic tool invocations. Our evaluation across three hardware platforms shows that Flush+Reload enables accurate, real-time tool monitoring, whereas Prime+Probe, despite supporting cross-VM attacks, incurs prohibitive monitoring overhead and suffers from cache-set aliasing. We present ToolPulse, a cache-based side-channel eavesdropping framework against tool-using agents. We first design the Tool Recovery Attack to reconstruct an agent's tool-execution workflow. We evaluate the Tool Recovery Attack on 11 LLMs across Codex and Claude Code. It consistently reconstructs tool workflows, with the lowest F1 score exceeding 93%. We further demonstrate two attack scenarios enabled by the recovered traces. Task Profiling Attack infers user intent across two Terminal-Bench task categories and the Trigger Localization Attack identifies sensitive tool calls in encryption/decryption and model training/inference workloads. Even under substantial system noise on a server shared by approximately 20 users, both Task Profiling Attack and Trigger Localization Attack maintain high accuracy.

title: VisualJevBench: A Benchmark and Black-Box Attacks for Visual Typed Decision Models
abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return structured decisions instead of generating free-text responses, enabling fast and cheap decisions in real-world applications. Recent support for image inputs extends Jev, a representative TDM, to visual decision-making. We refer to this setting as Visual Jev. However, red teaming of Visual Jev leaves two gaps: a systematic evaluation of direct image manipulations is lacking, and universal visual attacks remain underexplored. To address these gaps, we introduce VisualJevBench, a benchmark for evaluating the adversarial robustness of Visual Jev. It comprises 800 images and 3,200 questions across eight scenarios and four visual attack surfaces: typographic manipulation, visual evidence spoofing, target selection interference, and geometric transformation. We also introduce Adaptive Black-Box Parameter Search (ABPS), a lightweight framework that uses typed-output feedback to find effective image manipulations. ABPS supports both image-specific attacks and universal attacks that transfer to unseen images and tasks in new scenarios without further optimization. Extensive experiments on jev-1.14.0 show that image-specific attacks achieve an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 69.6%, while universal attacks achieve an average ASR of 33.15% on unseen images. Geometric transformations achieve an average ASR of 40.09% in cross-scenario transfer.

title: GenAI-DBT: Evaluating a DBT-Informed Generative AI Platform for Mindfulness Skills Training: A Pilot Randomized Study
abstract: We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and engagement of three digital formats for dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) mindfulness skills training. In a 30-day randomized pilot study, 45 university students were assigned to GenAI-DBT, a general-purpose large language model chatbot (Chatbot), or a static web resource (Web). Forty-two completed the study, and nine completed follow-up interviews. Usability scores were within acceptable ranges across conditions, with no significant between-group differences. GenAI-DBT showed the highest observed participant-week adherence (71.4%, vs. 53.3% for Web and 42.3% for Chatbot), a descriptive difference. Mindful Attention Awareness Scale and Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale scores showed no significant time-by-group interactions, and session-level self-reported mood changes did not differ significantly across conditions. GenAI-DBT showed a larger positive change in linguistic valence than Chatbot (4.28 vs. 1.59, P = .02, Cohen's d = 0.99). Interviewees valued contextualized, scenario-based practice and identified response latency, repetition, and limited personalization as areas for improvement. The findings support the feasibility and acceptability of DBT-informed conversational AI for skills practice and motivate further evaluation in larger, more clinically relevant samples. Clinical efficacy remains to be established.

title: Model-Based Low-Order Wavefront Sensing and Control with a Fully Physical Digital Twin on MagAO-X
abstract: Context. Residual low-order aberrations and post-AO tip-tilt jitter are major drivers of stellar leakage in small-inner-working-angle coronagraphs and limit high-contrast imaging performance. Aims. The aim of this work is to develop a fully physical and differentiable digital twin for the focal plane low-order wavefront sensor on MagAO-X. This digital twin can be used to provide accurate non-linear and fast linearised wavefront sensing and control to deal with low-order aberrations. Methods. We build a physics-based optical model of the focal plane low order wavefront sensor (FLOWFS) system and calibrate it using laboratory and on-sky measurements. The calibrated model is used for non-linear phase retrieval, deriving a model-based linear reconstructor, and generating the corresponding reference image for real-time control. Results. The calibrated digital twin accurately reproduces the sensor response and recovers the dominant low-order aberrations. In the laboratory, non-linear reconstruction achieves residual floors of about 6 to 7 nm over the pupil, compared with about 11 nm for the linear reconstructor, and the same digital-twin framework transfers across different coronagraph and wavelength configurations. On-sky, the model can be recalibrated with limited changes, achieves reconstruction performance close to the residual atmospheric floor, and provides a linear reconstructor that enables stable closed-loop low-order control at kHz speed. Conclusions. A fully physical digital twin can unify accurate low-order wavefront reconstruction, fast linearised control, and transfer across observing configurations and from lab to on-sky operation within a single interpretable framework.

title: ChainAgent: Automated Chainable Vulnerability Discovery in PHP Web Applications
abstract: High-impact attacks on PHP web applications often chain limited-capability vulnerabilities with other flaws or intended behaviors. Discovering these chains requires identifying flaws and the dependencies enabling capability composition. Existing vulnerability discovery techniques analyze flaws in isolation, while attack planning assumes known components. This separation makes it difficult to discover previously unknown components whose security relevance becomes apparent only through their potential roles in an exploit chain. We present ChainAgent, a goal-directed LLM-agent framework that jointly discovers exploit-chain components and their capability dependencies in source code. Guided by an empirical study of 386 real-world web exploit chains, ChainAgent represents vulnerabilities and functional gadgets--intended program behaviors that can be repurposed in attacks--through preconditions and capabilities over security-relevant objects. Instead of discovering vulnerabilities first and constructing attack paths afterward, ChainAgent uses an evolving exploit graph to guide source-code inspection. It searches backward from unmet preconditions for capability producers and forward from discovered capabilities for functional gadgets that consume or amplify them.
