abstract: We prove the folklore conjecture on maximal central sections of the cube in every dimension and codimension. The maximizing sections are exactly the products of diagonals of disjoint coordinate blocks whose sizes differ by at most one. This determines the sharp volume in the cases left open by Ball's 1989 bounds. In fixed dimensions, the logarithmic volume deficit controls both the direction and the displacement of an affine section linearly, with optimal exponent. We also obtain the sharp uniform bound on projection densities for independent real random variables with bounded densities.

title: No Evidence of Cold Trapping in the Dayside Atmosphere of WASP-33 b
abstract: Ultra-hot Jupiters allow simultaneous measurements of volatile molecules and refractory metals, providing constraints on atmospheric chemistry and refractory-element sequestration. We reanalyze the previously published Gemini-N/IGRINS-2 dayside emission spectra of WASP-33~b, extending the analysis to neutral refractory species. Using cross-correlation (CC) and likelihood-based (LL) detection methods, we recover the strongest species detection signal-to-noise ratios (S/N) from CO ($\rm CC~S/N=5.29,\ LL~S/N=5.62$). \ion{Mg}{1} ($\rm CC~S/N=3.88,\ LL~S/N=4.73$) and OH ($\rm CC~S/N=3.88,\ LL~S/N=3.89$) are recovered at lower significance in both metrics. H$_2$O remains marginal, appearing only in the cross-correlation analysis ($\rm CC~S/N=3.24$), while \ion{Ti}{1} ($\rm LL~S/N=3.70$) and \ion{Ca}{1} ($\rm LL~S/N=2.98$) show tentative signals. We do not detect \ion{Fe}{1}, \ion{Si}{1}, and \ion{V}{1} in this dataset. A chemical-equilibrium retrieval with a flexible Bezier-spline pressure--temperature profile yields ${\rm C/O}=0.65^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$ and $[{\rm M/H}]=-0.48^{+0.24}_{-0.18}$, and a refractory-to-volatile ratio of $[R/V]_{\rm p}=-0.15^{+0.24}_{-0.23}$. The corresponding stellar-normalized value is $[R/V]_{\rm p/ \star}=0.37^{+0.38}_{-0.36}$, but this value is sensitive to the stellar oxygen abundance. We find that the atmospheric Ti/Mg and Ca/Mg ratios of WASP-33~b are consistent with their respective stellar values within 68\% confidence. This is in contrast to other ultra-hot Jupiters with lower equilibrium temperatures that often show depleted Ti abundances compared to other metals, indicative of cold-trapping. This would suggest that even the nightside of WASP-33~b is too hot for significant condensation and sequestration to occur. Comparison with disk-chemistry models remains exploratory because the carbon-to-refractory posterior overlaps several formation scenarios.

title: Reverse Schensted bumping, inverse reduction map and concatenation in the inverse quantum Littlewood-Richardson bijection
abstract: Provided the explicit formula for the inverse reduction map, arXiv:2606.24840, we exhibit for symplectic bumped intervals and for symplectic bumped columns disjoint for the action of the parity involution, the feasibility of the concatenation operation to return a semi-standard tableau in the inverse quantum Littlewood-Richardson bijection

title: Diffusivity and metric exponents for slightly supercritical percolation in high dimensions
abstract: It is a classical fact that random walk on the infinite supercritical Bernoulli $p$-percolation cluster on $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ converges to Brownian motion with some diffusivity $σ(p)$, and that the graph metric on the infinite cluster has order $μ(p) \|\cdot\|$ at large scales for some constant $μ(p)$ known as the time constant. We compute the near-critical asymptotics of the two quantities in high dimensions, showing that \begin{align*} σ^2(p) \asymp (p-p_c)^2 \qquad \text{ and } \qquad μ(p) \asymp \frac{1}{\sqrt{p-p_c}} \end{align*} for all $p>p_c$. Our results concerning the diffusivity confirm a conjecture of Biskup (2011). We also compute the asymptotic critical probabilities of slabs in the same regime, showing that $p_c( \mathbb{Z}^{d-1} \times \{0,\ldots,n\}) - p_c(\mathbb{Z}^{d}) \asymp n^{-2}$ as $n\to \infty$.

title: A Constructive Lower Bound for the Growth Constant of Ternary Cap Sets
abstract: Let $r_3(d)$ denote the maximum size of a cap set in $\mathbb{F}_3^d$. We prove that the exponential growth constant $Λ= \lim_{d\to\infty} r_3(d)^{1/d}$ is strictly greater than $2.22920646813$. The main advance comes from combining two-color recursive synchronization with cross-layer joint filling of a seven-dimensional local alphabet that contains collinear triples (lines). By encoding marked positions as $14$-step closed walks on a two-state directed graph, any zero-sum triple with a fixed outermost color is forced to choose the identical closed walk---and hence the identical record---at every recursive layer, at a net cost of $1000$ dimensions per level. Because the open seven-dimensional coordinates are deferred to the outermost layer, all positions of the same type across all layers can be pooled per record and filled jointly via grouped binary-flag nodes. A $2\times 2$ transfer matrix governs the weighted record count, and spectral dominance over two tilted tail matrices converts this count into a capacity lower bound. Feeding each resulting bound back into the filling parameters iteratively amplifies the growth rate, while a companion-path score exclusion test further enlarges the admissible walk family. The final bound is certified by finite enumeration and exact integer comparisons.

title: Quantum-Resilient, PUF-Based, and Anonymity-Preserving Authentication and Key Agreement Scheme for UAV Networks
abstract: We design a lightweight authentication and key agreement protocol for Internet of Drones (IoD) environments that simultaneously provides post-quantum security, hardware-rooted trust, and resistance against machine-learning-based Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) modeling attacks. Existing PUF-based authentication schemes for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer protection against cloning and physical capture, but generally lack resistance against quantum adversaries. Conversely, recent post-quantum UAV authentication protocols provide quantum-resistant key establishment, yet do not incorporate hardware-bound authentication mechanisms and therefore remain vulnerable to device cloning and physical compromise. To address these limitations, we integrate CRYSTALS-Kyber, dynamic challenge scrambling (DCS), fuzzy extractors, and PUF-based identity binding into a unified framework. The resulting protocol enables anonymous authentication, forward secrecy, resistance to physical capture and replay attacks, and secure drone-to-drone communication, while maintaining suitability for resource-constrained UAV platforms. We provide a formal security analysis of the proposed scheme under the real-or-random model, a ProVerif-based formal verification, an informal analysis of its effectiveness against various attacks, and a performance evaluation of the proposed scheme through communication, computation, and storage cost analyses, which show its advantages over state-of-the-art architectures.

title: Ultrasound Watermark: Real-time Acoustic Watermarking against Voice Scams on Smartphones
abstract: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and AI-driven speech synthesis enable adversaries to convincingly impersonate trusted individuals during phone calls. Existing defenses often rely on offline analysis, degrade under telephony distortions, or remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. To address these limitations, we present Ultrasound Watermark, a real-time, smartphone-native framework that protects live calls by binding speech to the caller's physical articulatory motion through acoustic watermarking. During a call, the smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures reflections from facial articulatory movements using only its built-in speaker and microphone. Ultrasound Watermark extracts motion features from these reflections and fuses them with outgoing speech to generate a dynamic watermark. Because the ultrasonic measurements are physically and temporally coupled with speech production, they are difficult to spoof without the underlying articulatory motion. A synchronized generator-detector architecture enforces cross-modal speech-motion consistency against replay, synthesized speech, and articulation-mimicking attacks. Ultrasound Watermark operates continuously with less than 200 ms latency overhead and requires no additional hardware. We implement Ultrasound Watermark on iOS and Android and evaluate it using over 2.5 hours of synchronized speech-ultrasound recordings from 22 speakers across eight smartphones and four real-world environments. Results demonstrate robustness to diverse attacks and telephony distortions while preserving perceptual audio quality.

title: Coalescence and the Two-Point Covariance in the Directed Landscape
abstract: In the directed landscape with Brownian terminal data, we express the spatial derivative of the two-point height covariance in terms of the probability that two geodesics coalesce before the terminal time and the exit law of a single geodesic. This formula arises as the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang scaling limit of a zero-temperature Brownian last-passage identity from our earlier work on the O'Connell-Yor polymer. To pass the coalescence probabilities to the limit, we show that two paths sharing an optimal exit almost surely lose total weight if they must stay disjoint before reaching it. At stationarity, we determine when two zero-direction semi-infinite geodesics first coalesce. We recover this distribution by differentiating the height-increment variance first in the starting separation, then in the boundary strength. When the terminal reward is zero everywhere, the starting points with the same leftmost optimal exit as the origin form an interval. The probability that this interval extends past given distances on both sides equals the rate at which the height covariance decreases at their sum.

title: The Growth Path Is the Missing Half of Neural Networks
abstract: An artificial neuron computes and learns, but it does not live: the units of a network are fixed when it is designed, and every one of them is kept and paid for whether it is used or not. We give each neuron a second pathway. Beside its Task Path, the usual computation and gradient learning, a dual-pathway neuron has a Growth Path: a nutrient flows from the outputs back through the network, every layer receives the same fixed budget, and each unit is fed in proportion to how much the units above it use it. A well-fed unit divides and a starving unit dies. This allocation is not a separate analysis or pruning step: it runs throughout training and reads only activations and weights. The task is still learned from labels with the ordinary loss, and the training procedure gains no phase, no schedule and no target size. Because the budget is conserved, the competition is zero-sum and a single number sets the size of the network. Switched on in a pretrained network that is deployed on a narrower domain, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. With Adam the network ends 1.0 to 1.2 points more accurate on the domain than the same network trained ordinarily, at 24% to 60% of its compute, and at 12% of the compute it is still ahead; a random choice of the same number of units gives no gain. Letting starving pretrained units sleep instead of die keeps 1.2 to 4.6 points more of the rarely used content. Over 800 changing tasks a network with the Growth Path holds its accuracy while ordinary networks decline. With plain SGD the gains are smaller: at deployment the method trades compute against rarely used content, and on one of the two continual-learning streams it only ties networks of equal size. The experiments are small (three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data); what they show is that a conserved, loss-free second pathway can decide by itself which units a network needs.

title: Designing Incoherent Multispectral Diffractive Optical Networks for Satellite Image Classification
abstract: Optical neural networks and diffractive optical computing provide a promising route for performing task-specific inference with high parallelism and lightweight electronic post-processing. These advantages are especially attractive for multispectral satellite imaging, where conventional workflows rely on transmitting high-dimensional image cubes to the ground for downstream electronic analysis. Here, we introduce a computationally efficient surrogate model-guided framework for designing incoherent multispectral diffractive optical networks that directly output class probabilities onboard, eliminating the need to capture and transfer the full multispectral data cube for ground-side inference. We first train a physically compatible surrogate model, represented by a non-negative fully connected model that accommodates a generalized detector readout, yielding a task-specific non-negative multispectral intensity transformation that can be transferred to an optical processor. We then synthesize its diffractive counterpart through data-free point-spread-function-based optimization under spatially incoherent illumination. Using this approach, we numerically demonstrate a six-spectral-channel diffractive classifier for tri-class satellite-scene recognition, achieving a blind-testing accuracy of 79.8% for artificial surface, water body, and vegetated land images, closely approaching the 81.8% accuracy of its surrogate. We further demonstrate a more compact three-spectral-channel design that numerically achieves 72.7% blind-testing accuracy, compared with 75.1% for its corresponding surrogate model. This surrogate model-guided strategy provides a practical pathway for designing compact, task-specific incoherent multispectral optical processors for resource-constrained remote-sensing inference.

title: Reconstructing Pure-State OTOCs from Forward-Time Linear Response
abstract: We show that the connected out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC) of any pure state can be reconstructed exactly from commutator linear responses alone. The protocol requires no time reversal, no ancilla, no double copy, and no weak measurement: a unitary string pulse, forward many-body evolution, and a single local readout suffice. An average over a complete basis of pulse generators yields the OTOC exactly. We further show that the measurement can be made sparse by restricting the pulses to a fixed operator weight, which turns the truncation into an analytically controlled spectral filter: the deterministic bias can be computed before the experiment and cleanly separated from the statistical sampling variance. For Gaussian states, the finite-weight response is exactly proportional to the full OTOC after a known combinatorial rescaling. For quantum chaotic systems, the typical residual is suppressed as a power law in the sector size. Exact-diagonalization benchmarks in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and a nonintegrable Ising chain confirm these predictions.

title: LaTSEC: Lattice-Based Threshold Signatures with Native Non-Interactive Identifiable Abort and Compact Per-Party Storage
abstract: We present $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$, a three-round lattice-based threshold signature scheme with native non-interactive identifiable abort. Each party holds one small-norm signing share and is associated with one public abort key, against which its partial signature is verified directly, without zero-knowledge proofs or an additional interactive protocol. Prior lattice-based threshold signatures that identify misbehaving parties rely on one of three mechanisms: zero-knowledge proofs, an additional interactive protocol, or an everywhere-short secret sharing scheme in which each party holds multiple signing shares, each with its own public abort key. Compared with schemes that use the third mechanism, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ substantially reduces per-party storage. The construction uses $\mathsf{SEC}$, a recent ramp everywhere-short secret sharing scheme based on lossless expanders that gives each party a single short share. We prove correctness, identifiable-abort security, and threshold unforgeability under the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ and $\mathsf{MSIS}$ assumptions. The unforgeability proof introduces the Repeated-$\boldsymbol{A}$ Matrix Hint-MLWE problem, a new variant of $\mathsf{MLWE}$ with hints that captures the complete tuple of correlated public abort keys. We rigorously prove that this new variant admits a reduction from the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ problem. For 60 parties at 128-bit security, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ tolerates up to 6 corrupted parties, and, empirically, a randomly chosen set of at least 46 parties can sign with probability at least 0.99. Each party holds one signing share of about 14.3 KiB and is associated with one 24-KiB public abort key.

title: What Do Co-Folding Models Learn? Insights from Enhanced Transition Path Sampling
abstract: Co-folding models are diffusion-based generative models that sample biomolecular complexes from distributions learned on a large corpus of experimental data. Although these models are powerful for structure prediction, it remains unclear whether the conformational ensembles they learn resemble physically meaningful statistical ensembles. To understand what these models learn, we introduce transition path sampling (TPS), which uses Markov chain Monte Carlo over denoising trajectories to sample the learned distribution. Because its Monte Carlo trajectories resemble biomolecular dynamics, TPS couples directly with enhanced-sampling techniques to recover the full conformational ensemble. Applied to Boltz-2, enhanced TPS reveals physical conformational changes biased toward crystal-like states near the training data, indicating both learned physics and memorization. These results suggest new ways to evaluate and improve co-folding models by jointly assessing structural recovery, proximity to training data, and conformational ensembles.

title: Solids activated by multi-body nonreciprocity
abstract: Field-mediated forces between particles can be both nonreciprocal and irreducibly multi-body, giving rise to emergent activity in systems of individually passive particles. While prior work extensively studied how multi-body nonreciprocity can activate few-body systems, fuel intermittency, and drive liquid-like behavior, the effect on the solid state of large particle ensembles is less explored. Here we use two-dimensional, close-packed rafts of identical, athermal, acoustically levitated microspheres to show how multi-body nonreciprocity injects activity in solids. At the level of both individual particles and collective dynamics, crystalline rafts exhibit persistent circulations with no net handedness. The rafts also exhibit a phonon-like dispersion relation corresponding to a large Poisson ratio, indicating an induced softness to shear. Within the bulk, lattice symmetry masks microscopic nonreciprocity, although it can manifest in renormalized, reciprocal elastic coefficients. At dislocations and raft edges, where this symmetry is broken, multi-body nonreciprocal interactions act as local generators of activity. A coarse-grained microscopic model of multi-body nonreciprocity, calibrated on three-particle simulations, recovers the rafts' experimentally observed dispersion relations and localized activity. Using these findings, we illustrate how to harness defect-induced activity for programmable movement by arranging microscopic dislocations to drive macroscopic propulsion and rotation of a whole raft.

title: Trajectory arclength reveals thermodynamic criticality
abstract: Thermodynamic criticality arises at continuous phase transitions, where collective interactions produce non-analytic behavior in equilibrium thermodynamic quantities in the thermodynamic limit. We show that this criticality also leaves an analytically predictable signature in the arclength of microscopic Hamiltonian trajectories. For the attractive Hamiltonian mean-field model, we derive the thermodynamic limit of the equilibrium-averaged arclength, formulated as a normalized Lagrangian descriptor, and demonstrate that it develops a kink precisely at the phase transition. We trace this non-analyticity to spontaneous magnetization and derive the leading critical finite-size correction, scaling as $N^{-1/2}$ with an explicit analytical prefactor. Simulations with up to $10^5$ degrees of freedom confirm both predictions without adjustable parameters. Requiring neither tangent-space evolution nor prior specification of an order parameter for its computation, trajectory arclength provides a simple, quantitative link between microscopic Hamiltonian motion and collective thermodynamic criticality.

title: The response field approach to path integral control
abstract: This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification of correspondences between backward adjoint processes and the response field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, whose properties have not been set out in an optimal control setting. The response field is found to play an analogous role to the backward adjoint process under the stochastic maximum principle. In particular, the gradient of the optimal cost-to-go at the initial time, which is proportional to the optimal control, is given by the average of the response field at the initial time. In contrast to the case of non-equilibrium dynamics, the response function is found to be acausal in the control setting. The linear-quadratic case of path integral control is studied, confirming it as the free theory, meaning that solving the control problem is equivalent to completing the square and determining the propagator for a two point boundary value problem. The developments presented here are a necessary prelude to applications based on field theoretic approximation, for both path integral control and their dual inference problems.

title: Geometric Polarization-Virial Theorems for Field-Induced Dipolar Interactions and Force Reversal
abstract: Electric fields can turn attraction into repulsion between far-separated atoms, yet the complete angular mechanical structure governing this reversal has remained unknown. Here, we uncover an entropy-like geometric structure: the cubically weighted interaction free energy, r^3 F(r), is nondecreasing under physical dilation. This structure unifies two exact polarization-virial theorems for arbitrary stable quasistatic dipole assemblies and fully retarded dipole pairs under stated conditions. Consequently, the free energy has at most one zero and energetic cancellation precedes mechanical cancellation. A force zero retains strictly positive energy, whereas an energy zero retains an attractive force. The resulting analytical angular fine structure is resolved by a quantum harmonic oscillator pair, yielding the complete arbitrary-angle interaction energy and radial force that recover quantum-perturbative results. The conventional dipolar magic angle splits into strictly ordered energy- and force-zero angles; the latter uniquely bounds the radially repulsive sector and carries a positive energy barrier. Derived scaling laws and finite-sphere calculations provide experimentally testable signatures from microscopic dipoles to macroscopic polarizable bodies.

title: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing
abstract: The hockey-stick divergence is a fundamental distinguishability measure in quantum information theory. It characterizes quantum differential privacy and determines the optimal error probability of binary quantum hypothesis testing with arbitrary priors. We study how it behaves on tensor-product states. To this end, we consider the noncommutative minimum $m(A,B):=(\mathrm{Tr}[A]+\mathrm{Tr}[B]-\|A-B\|_1)/2$ of positive semidefinite operators, which reduces to $\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}$ when $A$ and $B$ commute, and we prove that it is super-multiplicative, i.e., $m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)$. As a consequence, we establish a sub-additivity property of the hockey-stick divergence on product states, in which the parameters of the individual systems are multiplied, and no additional prefactor appears. We show that this bound is tight, also for noncommuting states, and that it is strict for faithful states whenever at least two of the divergences are positive. Using this, we obtain sub-additivity of the Datta-Leditzky divergences, a parallel composition theorem for quantum differentially private channels under product neighboring inputs with at most linear degradation of the privacy parameters, and a sharp sub-additivity property of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy normalized by the acceptance probability. Finally, we apply the same tools to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing. We determine the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for every pair of noncommuting states satisfying mild conditions including a nonlattice condition and, under a quantitative version of this condition, the full asymptotic expansion to every fixed order in $1/n$, with explicitly computable coefficients. As a consequence, we determine the sample complexity of symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing up to one sample, as the error probability tends to zero.

title: TRAE: Trustworthy Automated ESG Annotation via Multi-Agent Consensus and Confidence Assessment
abstract: With the growing demand for ESG disclosure and evaluation, constructing high-quality datasets for automatically extracting ESG-related information from large-scale documents has become essential. However, ESG annotation remains challenging due to strong context dependence, ambiguous label boundaries, and the need for domain expertise, resulting in high annotation cost and limited scalability. To address these challenges, we propose TRAE (TRustworthy Automated ESG annotation), a multi-agent framework for scalable and reliable ESG data construction. Unlike direct LLM-based annotation, TRAE evaluates annotation reliability by modeling agreement, confidence, and reasoning consistency among multiple agents through a structured multi-step reasoning process. Experimental results demonstrate that TRAE improves annotation performance compared with existing automated annotation strategies. Furthermore, TRAE supports a hybrid human-AI annotation strategy that assigns expert labeling only to uncertain samples, reducing annotation cost while preserving data quality. Using TRAE, we construct a high-quality ESG dataset containing approximately 20,000 instances with complete reasoning traces, intermediate agent outputs, and reliability information to enhance transparency and reproducibility. Overall, this work provides a practical and scalable framework for trustworthy ESG data construction. The code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/nowzer0/TRAE.

title: Evidence Toward a Conjecture in List Recoverability of Folded Reed--Solomon Codes
abstract: This paper investigates the list-recoverability of folded Reed--Solomon codes and provides new evidence toward a recent conjecture. Chen--Zhang (STOC 2025) established that for any $\ell,a \ge 2$ and $L = \ell^a - 1$, if a folded Reed--Solomon code of rate $R$ is $(ρ,\ell,L)$-list-recoverable, then $ρ\leq \frac{L+1-\ell}{L+1}(1-\frac{aR}{a-1}).$ It is conjectured that this upper bound is tight. We provide two pieces of evidence concerning this conjecture. First, we prove that explicit folded Reed--Solomon codes of rate arbitrarily close to $\tfrac{a-1}{a+\ell-2}$ are $(0,\ell,L)$-list-recoverable, which confirms the conjecture in the special case $ρ=0$ and $\ell=2$. Second, we show that for any $R\in(0,\tfrac{a-1}{a})$, there are rates arbitrarily close to $R$ at which attaining the conjectured bound requires exponentially large alphabets. This mirrors the phenomenon observed by Alrabiah--Guruswami--Li (SODA 2024), where achieving the generalized Singleton bound in the list-decoding setting also necessitates exponential alphabet size.

title: An Exact Vertex Localization of Zykov's Theorem
abstract: We establish a vertex-based localization of the exact form of Zykov's theorem. For a graph $G$ of order $n\geq1$, let $N(G,K_t)$ denote its number of copies of $K_t$, and let $c(v)$ be the order of a largest clique containing $v$. Write $Z_t(n,s)=N(T_s(n),K_t)$, where $T_s(n)$ is the balanced complete $s$-partite graph on $n$ vertices. We prove that, for every integer $t\geq2$, \[ N(G,K_t)\leq \frac1n\sum_{v\in V(G)}Z_t(n,c(v)). \] Equality holds if and only if $G$ is $K_t$-free or $G\cong T_s(n)$ for some $t\leq s\leq n$. Moreover, the coefficients $Z_t(n,s)$ are pointwise best possible among all bounds of this form. Our result strengthens the previous vertex-localized bound \[ N(G,K_t)\leq n^{t-1} \sum_{v\in V(G)} \frac{\binom{c(v)}{t}}{c(v)^t} \] by accounting for the integer part sizes of Turán graphs. The comparison between the two upper bounds is strict precisely when some vertex $v$ satisfies $c(v)\geq t$ and $c(v)\nmid n$. As consequences, we recover the exact Zykov and Turán bounds without divisibility assumptions.

title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution
abstract: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.

title: A Deterministic Polynomial-Query Protocol for Envy-Free Cake Cutting
abstract: We give a deterministic protocol that divides a heterogeneous cake completely and without envy among $n$ agents using $O(n^6\log n)$ Robertson--Webb queries in the worst case. Valuations may be arbitrary nonnegative, nonatomic measures, and bundles may be disconnected. The protocol makes $O(n)$ calls to certified trimming, which uses $O(n^5\log n)$ queries on $n$ pieces. In a certified trim, each agent receives the end part, or suffix, of a different piece without envy, and every shortened piece has a witness tie leading back to a whole piece. At each step, the witness values the shortened suffix exactly as much as her own. For pieces of positive interval length with strictly increasing suffix values, the retained suffix lengths are unique, although their holders may differ. Candidate assignments share a table of value and cut queries. If the coordinatewise median of their value estimates fails a matching test, the test identifies an agent whose value is underestimated, ruling out at least half the remaining assignments. A weighted median of cut marks lets one repair step remove a small envy while allocating almost all of the residue. For complete envy-free chore allocation, the query bound is $O(n^7\log n)$.

title: A cyclic analogue of Schur multiple zeta values
abstract: In this paper we introduce a cyclic analogue of Schur multiple zeta values. For a diagonally constant index on a periodically extended skew Young diagram, it is a sum over semi-standard cyclic Young tableaux. It includes the cyclic multiple zeta values of Hirose, Murahara and Murakami as a special case. The first two main results are a cyclic analogue of the Maesaka--Seki--Watanabe formula for truncated sums and an {integral--series identity} under an admissibility condition. As an application, we give a proof of $4^nζ(\{1,3\}^n)=ζ(\{4\}^n)$ by counting linear extensions of a poset. The third main result expresses a cyclic Schur multiple harmonic sum as a finite signed sum of Schur multiple harmonic sums with the same number of boxes and the same multiset of exponents.

title: Antiphony: A Dual-Process Agent for Deepfake Video Detection with Real-Video Calibration
abstract: Reliable video deepfake detection requires generalization to unseen generators while limiting false alarms on authentic footage. Although existing detectors capture diverse visual cues, they may produce overconfident errors under generator shift, limiting the reliability of confidence-based fusion. Threshold calibration is further complicated by shifts in authentic capture domains and the lack of future-generator examples. To address these challenges, we present Antiphony, a framework that combines calibrated fusion of four visual experts with selective investigation. Authentic videos serve as a shared reference for score fusion and threshold calibration, enabling threshold updates without target deepfakes. For this expert-fusion stage, we establish finite-sample false-alarm control when the scoring procedure is fixed independently of calibration and authentic samples are exchangeable. To refine decisions near the calibrated threshold, a tool-using multimodal investigator examines these videos and contributes an additional fusion score. We train the investigator on generator-held-out predictions and counterfactual expert outputs, to improve robustness to unreliable expert evidence. Across six benchmark protocols, Antiphony achieves a mean benchmark score of 88.3%, exceeding the strongest evaluated MLLM and conventional detector baselines by 14.7 and 11.5 points, respectively. It also outperforms ARGUS by 20.2 points on average and by 3.6 balanced-accuracy points on FaceVid's 20 unseen generators.

title: MindBridge: A Multilingual and Multimodal Tool for Interactive Cognitive Monitoring
abstract: We present MindBridge, a clinician-informed, multilingual, multimodal cognitive monitoring tool combining participant-controlled interviews with explainable reports. Reports link lexical diversity and pause patterns to speech or text evidence and disclose data quality and missingness. In a formative study of typed interaction with 10 adults (seven aged 18-59; three aged 60 or older), follow-ups prompted elaboration but sometimes introduced assumptions requiring correction. Nine participants ranked interpretation-first reports highest; all identified score-only reports as most likely to encourage fixation and overreaction. On a fixed DementiaBank manifest, the best configuration achieved 70.3% zero-shot accuracy on valid predictions versus a 56.0% majority-class baseline on the full manifest. Some configurations predicted only one category; tests with generated samples revealed different error patterns across input types and languages. MindBridge makes evidence collection, analysis, and interpretation inspectable, linking participant control to the scope and limits of monitoring results.

title: Wavelet determinantal samplers: Optimal approximation rates adapting to regularity
abstract: We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-Hölder and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-Hölder observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.

title: Performance of attention-based deep-learning models in Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor measurements
abstract: A systematic performance evaluation of attention-based deep-learning models for wavefront reconstruction in Shack-Hartmann wavefront sensor (SHWFS) systems is presented. While deep learning has been extensively applied to pyramid and focal-plane wavefront sensing, its application to standard SHWFS configurations remains relatively underexplored. A simulation dataset consisting of 3.5 million open-loop uncorrelated turbulent phase and image pairs modeled after the Subaru Telescope pupil was generated. The dataset spans four pupil-sampling cases (8$\times$8, 16$\times$16, 20$\times$20, and 32$\times$32 subapertures) under realistic conditions. A custom Vision Transformer (ViT) which incorporates features such as rotary positional embeddings, register tokens, and a cross-attention decoder, is benchmarked against a fully convolutional U-Net and a classical Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) linear reconstructor. The results show that the ViT architecture yields the lowest overall residual phase variance across all tested subaperture configurations, demonstrating a robust capability to model global spatial correlations and spot-to-spot cross-coupling across the pupil. While the U-Net performs competitively by capturing localized features, it exhibits $\sim1.5$ times more residual variance per mode than the ViT, which is relatively significant in high-order modes. This study represents a key step toward implementing attention-based models for high-order wavefront sensing and telemetry-assisted data reduction in next-generation instrument suites like ULTIMATE-Subaru.

title: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current
abstract: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue hardware signals, such as power draw, have been proposed as a potential information channel for compute verification. Such signals can be measured externally, without the operator's cooperation. We show that the supply current drawn by a GPU can be used to verify the work declared by the GPU operator, without requiring examples of prohibited workloads or evasion strategies. We record 23.4 h of GPU current with a Rogowski coil under idle, training and inference workloads. We consider five evasion strategies an operator might use to disguise prohibited training. We show that a one-class model fitted to the current draw of permitted, declared work (idle and inference) flags at least 99.9% of windows of prohibited training, including training hidden by the five evasion strategies. As a continuous monitor across successive windows, it detects all 188 episodes of prohibited training hidden by time-sharing with declared inference, with a median delay of 3.0 s, and raises one alarm in 8.8 h of declared work. Incomplete or corrupt recordings of the declared work can undermine verification. An incomplete recording fails loudly; with idle missing, the monitor is in alarm for 99.97% of declared idle. A corrupt recording can fail silently; if the operator runs training during the recording, the monitor can miss hidden training while raising no alarm on declared work. These results suggest that operator declarations together with external analogue sensing might offer a practical route to compute verification.

title: Separating Genetic and Protein Evidence in Open Targets: An Auditable Re-ranking Study
abstract: Biomedical target-ranking platforms combine genetics, literature, experimental evidence, tractability, and clinical precedent because each is useful for target discovery. A single integrated score, however, can be awkward to reuse for a narrower question such as which genes have direct evidence for disease risk or etiology. We examine this issue in Open Targets associations for Alzheimer disease (AD) and Parkinson disease (PD). Genetics-linked evidence and protein-oriented evidence are scored in separate channels and combined only at the end. In AD, the Open Targets overall top 20 contains 7 curated genetics-supported genes and 10 symptomatic pharmacology controls; the default late fusion contains 15 curated genes and no symptomatic controls. In PD, late fusion retains 13 curated genes and removes the 5 symptomatic controls present in the platform top 20. A genetics-only ranking reaches similar curated recall (14 genes in AD, 13 in PD), so most of the gain over the platform score comes from emphasizing genetic evidence; the protein channel mainly raises the number of tractable targets in the shortlist (from 9 to 12 in AD and from 8 to 10 in PD) without readmitting symptomatic controls. These results are stable across fusion weights from 0.35 to 0.75, perturbed protein-channel weights, and rule thresholds. An optional post-ranking rule further lowers high-clinical/low-genetic targets such as ACHE and GRIN1 without changing top-20 curated recall. The procedure is deterministic and uses public Open Targets fields. Because the component scores remain available, individual rank changes can be inspected and the ranking can be reproduced from the same data snapshot.

title: Conartist: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Computer-Using Agents against Multi-Step Prompt Injection
abstract: Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain vulnerable. First, consistency checking prevents agents from deviating from legitimate user objectives, while attackers can bypass it by embedding malicious actions that appear logically consistent with legitimate task execution. Second, risk auditing proactively examines high-risk operations. Yet, the auditing process itself would introduce additional exploitable actions that violate security boundaries. To evaluate above defects we found, we propose Conartist, a cascaded adaptive prompt injection framework comprising two progressive stages. First, Conartist employs a goal-pollution strategy to establish deceptive causal dependencies between legitimate user objectives and malicious operations, progressively embedding attack steps into legitimate task workflows. However, these task-coupled attacks remain susceptible to risk auditing. To address this limitation, Conartist further analyzes security-auditing feedback from controlled attack exploration to identify exploitable auditing patterns. Conartist then adaptively refines its deception strategies to either avoid triggering risk auditing or induce additional high-risk operations. Extensive experiments across five backbone models demonstrate the effectiveness of Conartist, achieving attack success rates of 32.12% on 576-instance tool use benchmark and 66.67% in the Reddit GUI benchmark, outperforming the SOTA attack by 14.41 and 29.17, respectively. By analyzing one of the most popular Agent, Openclaw, we furthermore concluded seven realistic exploitable attack patterns, which reveals that security mechanisms designed to prevent malicious actions can themselves be manipulated to facilitate attacks.

title: IDSMorph: Self-Adaptive Malicious Traffic Detection through Consistency-Guided Dynamic Decision Boundaries
abstract: Anomaly-based malicious traffic detection learns decision boundaries for normal behavior and identifies deviations as anomalies. However, normal behavior varies across networks and changes dynamically, limiting adaptability and increasing retraining costs. Despite this variability, our measurements show that clients accessing the same service exhibit consistent flow structures and interaction patterns, since each service provides specific functionality. We therefore construct service-specific decision boundaries. However, variations in personalized requests make it difficult to construct stable boundaries. To address this challenge, we propose IDSMorph, a self-adaptive malicious traffic detection system that learns consistency-guided embeddings through two key designs: (1) a flow structure consistency builder, which constructs contrastive samples capturing consistent embeddings within services; and (2) a service interaction consistency builder, which captures local structural consistency among different clients and global behavioral consistency among clients accessing that service. IDSMorph constructs dynamic decision boundaries from the majority of similar embeddings within each service and dynamically updates them through a differencing algorithm that mitigates the transient traffic shifts within short observation windows. Experiments show that IDSMorph's detection F1 score decreases by no more than 0.12 points across network environments, compared with an average decrease of 55.43 points for prior methods. In real-world deployment with red-team operators independently choosing attack strategies and timing, IDSMorph achieves an F1 score 46.81 points higher than other methods.

title: Tracing Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
abstract: Reinforcement learning can increase the success of automated red teaming but it also narrows the attack vector. This study asks where in the attacker-defender-judge learning loop does the narrowing begin and which mechanisms lead to a narrowing attack. Six mechanisms (defender adaptation, success edge, reward reinforcement, row cap, update size, and measurement) are tested across three experiment arms (co-trained, frozen defender, half learning rate) for twenty-four iterations. A frozen defender narrows attack diversity retention (ADR) earlier 0.496 relative to co-trained 0.891 at iteration twelve. Defender updates delay narrowing but dont prevent it. Successful attacks ("winners") have narrower attack diversity than the full set of generated attacks. Attacks closest to previous winners succeed 10-15 percentage points more often than those closest to previous failures. This winner-neighbor advantage holds after a defender update and for a fixed defender too. Attacks with a common opening have a common-opening advantage of 5-16 percentage points. The training row cap and update size account for little impact on ADR, and attack length accounts for only part of the ADR decrease. Narrowing appears to originate from the success only reward through the group-relative training advantage to the attacker update, with a persistent success edge setting the direction.

title: Packing Stern into L2: GPU-Accelerated Primal-Shortened ISD for High-Codimension Binary Goppa Key Recovery
abstract: Primal-Shortened Information-Set Decoding (ISD) with quadratic polar lifting recently pushed TII McEliece Track-2 key recovery to $mt=126$ (TII-228, $2{,}463$ CPU core-hours), with over $99\%$ of runtime spent harvesting weight-$(2t+1)$ codewords. Porting MiniMax's Mode-6 Stern sampler directly to one block per SM leaves $1.0\text{-}1.5\text{ GB}$ of hash tables active and stalls on global memory. For $mt \le 145$, we pack all $mt-17 \le 128$ remaining syndrome bits into one $16$-byte ulonglong2 without left-triple indices, share $G \in \{4, 8\}$ cooperative tables inside GPU L2 cache, batch $64G$ random systematic reductions per launch, and widen the shortening prefix $n'$ to cut modeled GPU-hours by $34\%\text{-}47\%$. Across four Track-2 challenges ($mt = 108 \to 144$), every recovered private key passes both the official SageMath checker and a standalone pure-Python verifier. Eight Modal L40S GPUs solve TII-228 ($mt=126$) in $18.9\text{ min}$ ($2.15$ GPU-hours, $3.0\times$ faster in wall-clock than MiniMax's EPYC cluster). We further recover keys for the previously undocumented challenges TII-237 ($mt=135$, $22.1$ L4 GPU-hours) and TII-235 ($mt=144$, $4.30\text{ h}$ across ten L40S GPUs, $39.62$ GPU-hours, $17.97\text{ s}$ lift), using $127$ of $128$ packed bits. These results do not demonstrate practical recovery against Classic McEliece parameters ($mt \ge 768$).

title: Friendship paradoxes in networks
abstract: Since Scott L. Feld's seminal paper entitled ``Why your friends have more friends than you do'' [Am.~J.~Sociol.~\textbf{96}, 1464 (1991)], the friendship paradox (FP) has been extensively studied in network science and related fields over the last decades. In this paper we survey the literature on the FP and its generalizations. We first introduce definitions and general results of the FPs defined in networks, and then overview their results on model networks. Empirical results using various social network data as well as applications to real-world problems, such as early detection of outbreaks and network sampling, are also summarized. Finally, we conclude by discussing several directions of possible future works.

title: GABIF: An Adaptive Guided Graph Denoising Framework for Antibody Conditional Inverse Folding
abstract: Antibodies play a central role in the human immune system, and their design is critical for vaccine development, therapeutic intervention, and improving human longevity. However, the vast combinatorial search space of antibodies poses a fundamental challenge for de novo discovery. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly denoising diffusion models, have demonstrated strong potential in protein inverse folding. Nevertheless, existing approaches are largely constrained to learning from natural antibody repertoires, thereby generating sequences that closely resemble natural antibodies. Such similarity, however, does not necessarily translate into improved functional performance in downstream applications. In this work, we develop a novel generative protein design model that enables the generation and optimization of antibody sequences tailored to specific downstream tasks and target metrics. Besides training on given an antibody dataset, we guide the generative model by an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor for conditional discrete diffusion. The model is pre-trained on a given antibody dataset. Meanwhile, an antibody-antigen binding affinity predictor is incorporated as a conditional signal in a discrete diffusion framework, where a regressor serves as the conditional probability to guide the learning of the amino acid probability distribution of sequences under the objective of affinity optimization. In silico experiments demonstrate that our antibody design model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, while the proposed regressor effectively improves binding affinity, as validated by an independent external predictor. Furthermore, our results highlight that the combination of finetuning and supervised guidance provides a powerful paradigm for adapting pretrained models to downstream tasks.

title: Coarse Price Discrimination
abstract: We study the revenue cost of limiting a seller to $L$ posted prices when heterogeneous buyers with independent values compete for scarce inventory. Our large-market assumption requires that removing any buyer have little effect on optimal revenue. We first make buyers arbitrarily replaceable at each fixed stock and then let stock grow. In this limit, one price guarantees half of optimal mechanism revenue and two guarantee $e/(e+1)$, approximately $73.1\%$. For $L\ge3$, the corresponding guarantee is a $1-1/(2L-1)$ fraction. The guarantees accommodate arbitrary differences in demand across buyers and do not require a separate price for each customer group.

title: LODESTONE: Linking System Events to Threat Intelligence for Evidence-Grounded Cyber Attack Investigation
abstract: System provenance graphs help reconstruct attacks through causal dependencies, but these connections alone do not explain how events accomplish an adversary's goal. Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) provides the necessary security knowledge, yet linking it to execution evidence requires bridging differences in meaning and granularity between events and attack relations amid scarce labels and sparse relevant evidence. We present LODESTONE, a cross-graph alignment system that links observed system events to CTI attack relations to support evidence-grounded attack reports. LODESTONE uses a novel CTI-driven training-data engine and an expert-verified benchmark of edge-level correspondences and reference attack reports. The engine pairs real CTI knowledge graphs with provenance graphs from isolated executions. A large language model (LLM) agent recursively improves correspondences by checking execution evidence and repairing retrieval, parsing, and reproduction failures; experts independently verify benchmark correspondences. LODESTONE combines text cross-encoder and directed-graph relevance scores to extract compact alert-centered subgraphs, retrieves article-level knowledge graphs through node- and edge-level dual-softmax assignment, and uses a fine-tuned 4B-parameter LLM to align event combinations with CTI attack steps. We evaluate LODESTONE on 27 expert-verified attack cases amid continuous benign activity from real applications, using 713 CTI articles. LLM judgments aligned with multiple human experts yield an attack-step description score of 82%, and attack identification reaches 91%, versus 73% and 32% using the same generator with provenance alone. Baseline pipelines and coding agents achieve description scores of at most 57%. Human-verified correspondences further demonstrate advantages in balancing attack-edge coverage with subgraph size, CTI retrieval, and cross-graph alignment.

title: Local Limits and Structures of Nearest-Predecessor Random Graphs
abstract: We study the two-sided nearest-predecessor graph on $[n]$, where vertices arrive in a uniformly random order and each new vertex connects to its nearest earlier vertex on each side. We construct an infinite graph on $\mathbb{Z}$ from i.i.d. continuous insertion times and prove quenched Benjamini--Schramm convergence to it almost surely. The limit is almost surely one-ended and recurrent. We resolve an open problem of Ponomarenko by proving that the maximum degree is asymptotic in probability to $\log n/\log(3/2)$ as $n\to\infty$. We obtain the probability generating function and a CLT for the number of edges crossing the boundary of $[n]$ in the infinite limit. We also study the $K$-nearest-predecessor graph, in which each new vertex attaches to its $K$ nearest earlier vertices without regard to side. For every fixed $K\geq1$, we construct the infinite limit, prove almost sure quenched Benjamini--Schramm convergence, and show that it is almost surely connected, one-ended, and recurrent, as well as nonplanar when $K\geq2$.

title: Unshardable Codes
abstract: We propose a new coding-theoretic problem motivated by censorship resistance. Is it possible to intertwine many pieces of data by encoding them jointly in a way that makes it impossible to remove any single piece without destroying many others as well? In particular, we want to encode $k$ data components $(m_1,\ldots, m_k)$ into a codeword $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with the following properties: 1. Local recovery: every data component can be recovered (in the absence of erasures or errors) by reading at most $\ell$ correct codeword symbols. 2. Unshardability: if an adversary erases some arbitrary subset of the codeword symbols, the remaining codeword symbols either uniquely determine all $k$ data components, or there are at least $s$ data components that cannot be determined. We call such codes $(\ell, s)$-unshardable. Intuitively, such codes prevent an adversary from selectively censoring individual pieces of data by erasing codeword symbols, without destroying large amounts of other data as collateral damage. We show that codes whose generator matrix has certain superregularity properties are unshardable. Using this connection, we construct linear codes that are $(\ell, s)$-unshardable with $s = (1-\varepsilon)k$ and locality $\ell = O_\varepsilon(1)$. We also show that linear unshardable codes are subject to the lower bound $s \leq k - k/\ell + 1$. Finally, we consider a strengthening of local recovery to also require local decodability from some constant fraction of erasures or even errors. With the help of AI tools, we achieve the above notion by showing that any Locally Decodable Code (LDC) can be converted into one that is unshardable while preserving locality via a certain careful change of basis over an appropriate extension field.

title: Parking Functions inspired by board games
abstract: We introduce two new parking schemes inspired by the classic board games Monopoly and backgammon. We consider a one-way street with $n$ parking spots and a queue of $n$ cars waiting to park. Each car has a preferred parking spot and enters in sequence to park. Under the Monopoly parking scheme, if a car finds its preferred spot occupied, it returns to the start of the street and parks in the first available spot it encounters. Under the backgammon parking scheme, if a car finds its preferred spot occupied, it bumps the already parked car out of that spot and takes its place. The bumped car then returns to the start of the street and parks in the first available spot it encounters. A preference list is a parking function for a given parking scheme if all cars successfully park under that scheme. We prove that all preference lists are parking functions under both the Monopoly and backgammon parking schemes. However, the final parking order differs significantly between the two schemes. For a fixed permutation $π$, we provide a product formula for the number of Monopoly parking functions resulting in the outcome $π$. Analogously, we show that the number of backgammon parking functions with outcome $π$ is bounded below by $2^{n-1}$ and bounded above by the $n$-th Catalan number. We also obtain exact formulas involving Motzkin numbers for several families of outcomes. We define the displacement of a car as the absolute difference between the spot where a car ultimately parks and its preferred spot. Displacement multisets encode the displacements for cars with nonzero displacement. We provide formulas for the number of backgammon parking functions with a fixed displacement multiset of cardinality at most $2$, as well as for the number of Monopoly parking functions whose displacement multiset is a given singleton set. We conclude with some directions for further research.

title: Second-Order Dynamics in Noisy RNNs Produce Exploration and Temporal Compression in Replay
abstract: Biological neural networks (like the hippocampus) can internally generate "replay" resembling stimulus-driven activity. Recent computational models of replay use noisy recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained to path-integrate. Replay in these networks is described as Langevin sampling, but this theory alone fails to capture the environmental exploration and temporal compression observed in real biological replay. To close this gap, we re-examine spontaneous noisy RNN activity ("replay") as Langevin sampling, one timestep at a time, from a time-series distribution resembling lived experiences (unlike previous works which defined sampling as Monte Carlo inference over a static distribution). We provide a normative second-order Langevin sampling framework wherein spike-frequency adaptation drives spatial exploration at the cost of speed, and momentum via dendritic input differentiation drives temporal compression. We numerically verify our framework via simulations of noisy RNNs trained on 2D triangular and T-maze navigation activity, and others trained on place cell activity of synthetic rats. Crucially, we observe that simultaneous adaptation and momentum increases both replay exploration and speed, and provide one of the first accounts for biologically plausible temporal compression in rate-based RNN replay. Our findings encourage experiments into whether dendritic input differentiation, or other mechanisms, may support temporal compression in memory circuits like the hippocampus.

title: Active sensing as control over sensory acquisition
abstract: The term "active sensing" is used across neuroscience and engineering to describe a wide range of sensing behaviors, but there is no consensus on what makes sensing "active." We propose that the behaviors grouped under this label are better understood as forms of control over sensory acquisition and develop a framework that distinguishes three interacting forms of control. Mechanistic control physically structures sensory input, strategic control modulates sensing in closed loop through adaptive and attentional processes, and agentic control concerns the sensing policies available to an agent and its authority to choose among them. These forms of control can occur separately or in combination, and have distinct consequences for sensory input, perception, behavior, and performance. The framework clarifies active-passive comparisons and provides a common basis for analyzing biological, engineered, and hybrid sensing systems by asking what is controlled, how, and by whom.

title: Infrared Relaxation Modes and the Emergence of Collective Order in Neural Dynamics
abstract: We develop a microscopic field theory of collective order formation in interacting nonlinear neural systems. Integrating out microscopic neural degrees of freedom yields an effective action whose quadratic kernel determines the ordering threshold, while higher-order connected responses govern nonlinear stabilization. Spectral decomposition reveals that relaxation rates and collective-mode overlaps control collective instability and memory dynamics. Enhanced infrared spectral weight lowers the critical coupling and generates long-time memory, revealing a common spectral origin of collective ordering and persistent dynamics. Controlled numerical constructions verify the spectral dependence of collective instability and response, while nonlinear mean-field scaling follows from the microscopic Landau expansion. Transformer Jacobian spectra further reveal learning-induced infrared organization and transient memory enhancement consistent with critical-like response. Our results establish a microscopic framework linking neural interactions, collective order, and long-time memory.

title: Topological Pharmacokinetics: A Model-Free Framework for Quantifying the Shape of Concentration-Time Curves
abstract: Pharmacokinetic analysis compresses concentration-time curves into scalar summaries (non-compartmental analysis, NCA) or pre-specified compartmental models, approaches that are either model-free but shape-blind or shape-sensitive but structure-dependent. We introduce Topological Pharmacokinetics (TPK), a framework that reads curve shape directly from data without committing to any model. TPK delay-embeds each curve into a state-space trajectory and applies persistent homology to extract a nine-component topological invariant: multi-scale shape descriptors (peak hierarchy, secondary-peak isolation, loop structure) with established perturbation-stability properties. We evaluate the framework on four layers of increasing realism. Monophasic linear systems generate no spurious cyclic signals, whereas double-site absorption and enterohepatic recirculation produce distinct loop signatures; 12 nonlinear scenarios resolve as curvature-without-cycles; a weak endogenous rhythm survives superposition with a large exogenous drug signal (inter-peak interval recovered at exactly 24 h); and loop detection stays stable to 10 percent of Cmax additive noise and to sampling thinned to 7 points. As clinical proof of concept, we apply the same pipeline to 15 mycophenolic acid profiles digitized from a published kidney-transplant study. The secondary-persistence ratio associates with ex vivo gut-microbiome reactivation at Spearman rho = 0.815 (p = 0.0002, q = 0.002), whereas the tested exposure metrics show weak, nonsignificant associations (rho <= 0.38). Analyses are fully automated and reproducible; code and data are public. TPK is proposed as a complementary, model-free, shape-sensitive layer alongside NCA and model-based methods.

title: Trajectory Visibility at First Sight
abstract: Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $n$ vertices, and let two moving entities $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ travel at constant (possibly distinct) speeds $v_q$ and $v_r$ along line-segment trajectories $τ_q$ and $τ_r$ inside $P$. We study the first-visibility time $ t^* = \min\bigl\{\,t \ge 0 \mid \overline{q(t)\,r(t)} \subseteq P\,\bigr\}, $ the earliest moment at which the segment joining $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ lies entirely within $P$. Prior work by Eades et al.~\cite{swat2020,eeades-phd} focused on the decision version of this question in a simple polygon. They gave a one-shot decision algorithm running in ${O}(n)$ time. For a stationary entity and a moving one, they gave a data structure with ${O}(n \log n)$ preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that answers decision queries in ${O}(\log n)$ time. For two moving entities, after ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ preprocessing time, they built a data structure of size ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ with ${O}(n^{3/4}\log^3 n)$ query time. Variants for polygonal domains with holes or when entities cross the boundary of $P$ lie beyond our scope. In this work, we go beyond decision to compute $t^*$ exactly under three models for a simple polygon $P$. When both trajectories are fixed in advance, we preprocess $P$ in ${O}(n)$ time and space and answer each query $(v_q, v_r)$ in ${O}(\log n)$ time. If one trajectory $τ_r$ is fixed while $τ_q$ is given as a query, we build a structure in ${O}(n \log n)$ time and space that computes $t^*$ in ${O}(\log^2 n)$ time per query. When neither trajectory is known in advance, we develop a data structure with ${O}(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ expected preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that achieves ${O}(n^{1/2}\,\text{polylog}(n))$ expected query time for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$.

title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Classifiers for Lightweight IoT Intrusion Detection Using Feature Reduction
abstract: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems can improve IoT security, but high-dimensional traffic features and imbalanced datasets may reduce model reliability and deployment feasibility in resource-constrained environments. This study presents a lightweight binary IoT intrusion detection framework using an approximately balanced CICIoT2023 derived dataset, feature reduction, and comparative machine learning evaluation. The original multi-class attack labels were converted into two classes: Benign and Malicious. To reduce class bias, malicious traffic was randomly undersampled to obtain an approximately balanced binary dataset. Information Gain Ratio and Gini Decrease were then used to rank traffic features and generate reduced feature subsets of 38, 30, 20, 10, 5, and 3 features. Five machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest(RF), Decision Tree(DT), Naive Bayes(NB), Logistic Regression(LR), and Support Vector Machine(SVM), were evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. The results show that Random Forest achieved the strongest overall performance. In particular,the 20-feature subset achieved accuracy of 99.1% and MCC of 0.982, matching the full-feature model while reducing feature dimensionality by approximately 47.4%. The 10-feature subset also maintained strong performance with accuracy of 98.9% and MCC of 0.979, reducing the feature space by approximately 73.7%. These findings demonstrate that balanced binary classification and progressive feature reduction can preserve detection effectiveness while improving lightweight IDS feasibility.

title: Exceptional Rays of Invariant Processes on Trees
abstract: Let $A$ be an ergodic, non-constant random process on the $d$-regular tree $T_d$, with marginal distribution $X$. We prove that there always exist "exceptional" rays, whose asymptotic means are at least $\mathbb{E}(X)+δ$; furthermore, for edge processes, $δ> 0$ can be taken to depend only on the law of $X$. We compare different definitions of "maximal asymptotic means", relating them to different notions of speed of tree-indexed random walks.

title: Cylindrical dimers and monomial immanants
abstract: For a bipartite graph on a cylinder, group its perfect matchings by homological height and sum their weights in each group. We prove that every minor of the resulting Toeplitz matrix has nonnegative coefficients in the edge weights, settling a question recorded by Lai. We first prove conjectures of Galashin and the author concerning directed cycles in cylindrical networks, and then deduce the dimer theorem from them. A related, stronger positivity property for superpositions of cylindrical matchings turns out to be equivalent to Stembridge's interval-product conjecture on monomial immanants. Using annular webs, we prove this conjecture for partitions with at most four columns. A stretching argument extends this to all partitions with parts in $\{n,2n,3n,4n\}$.

title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
abstract: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.

title: Circle-Pattern Linear Systems for the Twenty Trivalent Delaunay Types of a Genus-Two Surface: Rank, Feasibility and Polytope Dimension
abstract: The hyperelliptic quotient of a closed genus-two Riemann surface is a hyperbolic sphere with six cone points of angle pi. Its Delaunay triangulation T is dual to a trivalent Voronoi graph G of one of twenty combinatorial types. For each type we study the angle system Ax = 1, x >= 0, where A is the vertex-edge incidence matrix of T and pi x_e is the angle subtended at a cone point by the Voronoi edge dual to e, equivalently the intersection angle of the two circumcircles adjacent across e. We prove that rank A = 6 for all twenty types, including the six whose triangulation has a loop, so the affine solution space always has the dimension of Teichmuller space. The polytope P = {Ax = 1, x >= 0} behaves differently. It is six-dimensional for exactly ten types, the ten Delaunay-realizable ones. For nine types it has dimension one, two or three, because non-negativity forces some wedge angles to vanish, and for the type of signature (2,2,2,2,8,8) it is empty. We show that five of the nine and the empty type never occur as Delaunay triangulations, and that the other four occur only as triangulations of non-trivalent Delaunay decompositions. Every vertex of every P is half-integral, as for fractional perfect matching polytopes. For the ten full-dimensional types every facet x_e = 0 lies at an edge where the Whitehead move is admissible, though not conversely, and the move identifies the facets of the two polytopes; these identifications pair the facet orbits of the ten cells under their automorphism groups. The free unfolding of the gluing grows at rate about 7.093. All finite statements are checked by an independent program, and the rank, infeasibility, forced coordinates, dimensions, vertices and facets are verified in Lean 4.

title: MobileGrail: Learning Compact Guardrails for On-Device deployable Mobile GUI Agent Safety
abstract: Runtime guardrails protect mobile GUI agents by assessing each proposed action before execution, but existing guardrails rely on cloud hosted large multimodal models, exposing every screen to a remote server, including private information such as payments, messages, and medical records. We propose MobileGrail, an on-device deployable model that addresses both. It maintains a recurrent task state that retains only the evidence subsequent safety decisions depend on, so that authorization and execution progress persist beyond the short context. To intervene early while keeping the safety boundary precise, it learns two labels, unsafe and block: unsafe marks the action that commits a violation, whereas block may be issued at any step of an intervention window, which spans from the first action that the user's authorization no longer explains to the committing action itself. To support training, we build an environment of 32 applications whose backends verify the effect of every action, supplying verified labels for supervision and rewards for reinforcement learning to calibrate intervention timing. We also build MobileVeto, an offline benchmark of unsafe trajectories largely on held-out applications, each paired with a benign counterpart. On MobileVeto, MobileGrail built on Qwen3.5-2B intercepts 76.2% of violations, up from 64.5% for its prompted backbone, while reducing premature intervention from 58.6% to 5.2%, outperforming the cloud-based OS-Sentinel on both. We further conduct online evaluation on GhostEIBench, where MobileGrail guarding a Qwen3.8-27B agent reduces fully successful attacks from 13 to 3 of 110 tasks while raising task completion from 48 to 58. Quantized to 4 bits, MobileGrail runs on a Snapdragon 8 Elite at a median latency of 4.7 s, comparable to the 5.1s of cloud-hosted Gemini 3.8 Flash.

title: Second Moment Penny Packings via Rolling Spaces
abstract: We solve the unrestricted minimum second moment problem for six unit disks in the plane by proving that the minimum is \(29/3\) attained uniquely up to isometry and relabelling by one disk together with five of its six neighbours in the triangular lattice. The realised contacts themselves define the space of admissible motions, while the directions preserving those contacts to first order define the rolling space consisting of motions whose relative velocities have zero normal component at every realised contact. Together, these spaces lead to an exact tangent cone formula and to a criterion by which a strictly positive centroidal contact balance, combined with rolling rigidity, implies strict local minimality modulo Euclidean motions. Our method recovers the classical five disk minimum \(34/5\) of Graham and Sloane, previously the largest unrestricted case known exactly. Geometric reductions and a graph census reduce the global search to finitely many contact graph classes. Exact analysis and validated interval arithmetic then exclude competing configurations, establishing the global bounds and uniqueness. Our method allows us to pass from putative lattice extremisers to unrestricted optimality.
